Concept seemed strong and the art work was amazing it reminded me so much of the old Final Fantasty Tactics box art. This is gonna be abit on the bias side, so I appologize I've had a string of back luck when it comes to the asian mmo market and the NA markets seem really lack luster, in particular every mmo from NCsoft.
However, HOWEVER...
I felt like a lot was missing or poorly mis used. The class system felt very similar to Aion, you start off with your basic warrior, priest, range dps, caster concept and from there you branch out. The lay out they had was very confusing and hard to read and you weren't even sure which direction you wanted to go because of things like "the swords man class is a tank class, but we don't use a tradition tank system, but monsters still need to be taunted" so which is it? we tanking or not?
Basically trying figure out your build path is fairly obscure and it now being a free to play game if you make mistakes, I haven't really seen any options to reset, so I would imagine that would cost you money in the long run.
UI - clean but tedious almost borderline awful. The only time I really feel like arrow keys and z  / x keys should be used for any kinda combat system is in those browser games. I've been playing games since the early 90s and I really have no idea where this system came from. At least I haven't used my arrow keys for movement since, like, the Orgeon Trail days.
Or Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego?
I do however like they have the option to change your movement options around but at the very least the common consensus is that WASD is your defautl movment system, I found it particularly fustrating when I tried to use their mouse binds options that I kept getting a warning saying it works better for priest classes -- well it should work for every class.
I also found it troubling that the 2 key and numpad 2 kept getting confused by the interface when trying to make my keybinds. So when I attempted to make my own binds alt+2 it would turn out as alt+NUM2 which could pose problems in the future as it also affected a few other binds.
Macroing hasn't been a much better experience.
UI is rather laggy, trying to unequip or change out items has some kinda weird delay, the fact you can't delete characters without taking off all their items seems odd too since its all newbie / starter default gear anyway.
Force "team name" was rather confusing and irritating - Team Name Change Cost 150 TP. So running around with double names is kinda goofy.
There is more to add but it would just take forever. So here is the TL:DR
PROS
-Custom Classes
-Good Graphics
-Plays well with Controllers (sorta...)
CONS
-Bad Default KB/M Controls
-Bugs & Glitches
-Pay Only Customization
-Pay Only Respecs
-Bad Crafting System
-Can't Buyback Items from Shops
-Very bad skill upgrade system
-Obvious Cash Grabbing
-Gold Spammers & Bots (you really can't get away from these but I put it in here anyway)
-Game Gives Misinformation
-Too many Gold Sinks

I do not understand why there are so many negative reviews on this game. I must admit that currently I played only a few hours, but so far the overall feeling is positive.
The game´s graphic engine is demanding, yes. Especially in a crowded city you can feel lags, but hey, show me one MMORPG where is not happening from time to time. But the graphic is really nice, no area is just a clone of another one. Every area has it´s special atmosphere and monsters.
The quests are fair, playing alone or in a group does not matter, the loot is distributed equally if set up correctly, and quest items drop from monsters at a good rate. So far I did not had the feeling of grinding quests where you have only a chance of a few percent to get the needed items. Actually they drop on 80-100% I would assume. Respawn timers are really fair for the normal mobs, and okay for bigger ones.
The character development options are manifold: The character can be shaped via skill points, attribute points, item modifications etc. The usual stuff, but quite comprehensive. Crafting of items is in, as well as improving equipment via a small anvil that is consumable. Quite a nice idea!
One can find different ways to have fun: Play main storyline, make daily and repeating quests. level achievements, just discovering new areas. For nearly every path you take there is a reward that gets recorded.
One feature I want to expose here: getting in and out of fights with the team: Most of the quests "just happen" inside the normal public area, but the boss gets only visible to the questing party, and the questing party disappears from the public for the time it takes to fight the boss. Its is really seamless, no instance, no loading screen, just feels very smooth. Well done!
I did not look at the guild system and PvP so far.
If you are unsure about the game, give it a try. It might suffer still from the overall performance and the usual gold spammers, but it´s a free game forehand, and it´s worth spending some hours.

As a huge fan of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, I had very high expectations for this game.
Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs is a disturbing and distressing entry into the Amnesia universe. The story focuses on Mandus, a wealthy industrialist from the late 19th century who wakes up with, well, Amnesia. His intention is to find his children who are no where to be found.
The atmosphere in Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs (AMFP) is always spooky and unsettling. There is never a moment where you don't apprehend something scary happening. I suppose this could be argued to be a disadvantage. The environments are both visually good looking and interesting and always kept me staring at things.
I personally believe that AMFP does not live up to Amnesia: The Dark Descent(TDD). Although AMFP kept me on my toes for most of the game, I feel that there are some integral things missing. Those which made TDD a truly brilliant horror game.
First of all, the monsters. Probably the most important element in a horror game, the monsters are the beings which make you fear every door opening and puzzle completion. The monsters in AMFP were not terribly frightening as those in TDD. There is something about human form monsters being scarier than animal form monsters, in the sense that I suppose we can relate to human form monsters, rather than animal form. By human form I mean stand up straight on two legs, like the monsters in TDD. The monsters in TDD are horrific because of their disfigured bodies, especially The Grunt. As for the telsa pig...well... I found it to be a bit silly.
"You can look, but you can't touch" - If you know what this is, then you know what is coming next... Interaction. An important concept from TDD. But, it was completely removed in AMFP, apart from a few essential things required to progress through the story. This was... dissapointing. I loved the aspect in TDD. Picking up books and looking at them made the game even more immersive. The fact that this is not present in AMFP seems a bit...lazy. Yes I said it. The Chinese Room were very aware that this was an important concept in TDD and yet failed to implement it properly in AMFP.
Another important point that may seem trivial to some, is the absence of "Danger close monster music". The monster music in TDD was brilliantly composed. The truly chilling and terrifying music, that played when a monster was near, rang in my mind after playing TDD. I think that it would have been an excellent addition to AMFP if this was implemented. Although, when a monster is near in AMFP, the absence of music is still fairly scary. Also...the flickering lamp concept. Just seems like it ruins the point of a horror game, being warned that something scary is approaching.
OK, rant over.
Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a fantastic game, don't get me wrong. It just seems like it could be better. It is a very disturbing game that focuses on a distrurbing and strong story.
If you enjoyed Amnesia: The Dark Descent, then you may be a little disappointed by AMFP, but none the less, you will enjoy this game for what there is. So try to avoid comparing if to TDD because the truth is that it is not as good, but it is still enjoyable.

In terms of creativity this is a very successful sequel and a loving continuation of the Just Cause series. This game is totally gorgeous, fun and loaded with cool content. It’s just such a shame though, that there are some serious problems with the performance. The outstanding quality of the design work, makes it shocking, that it could have been released in such a poorly optimised state. As so much love and consideration seem to have gone into making it something special. However, it appears to be yet another example, of the economic side of things pushing the release date forward. Resulting in an incredible game with mediocre performance at best. The pricing and distribution of the DLC content also represents some shady business practises. Although again, from a design stand-point, this additional content is fantastic stuff.
Following some tweaks which included making some changes in Windows 10. I managed to get it running, just well enough, to be able to enjoy myself. However I am still experiencing crashes, stuttering and poor framerate. I’m running it on a GTX 980, an AMD FX 8350 and 8 Gigs of RAM. Apparently it’s the RAM that’s the main problem, as there is a warning every time I start up the game, stating that my system memory is low. Typically however, my 8 Gigs of system RAM, is totally fine for gaming in 2016. Especially since I spent over 700 Euro to get a GTX 980 with 4 Gigs of VRAM.
Basically, Just Cause 3 runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥and you’ll need a powerful rig to get it running even moderately well. I have read online that if you have 16 Gigs or more of system RAM, it helps a lot but that is not normal. I get how people are angry about the performance problems but this game still deserves a lot of praise. I’m going to recommend it because it is an example of how amazing videogames can be in 2016. Even though, the corporate money making side of the industry, seem to be determined to ruin things with short term thinking. If you have a decent PC, you can probably still get it running well enough to appreciate how incredible it is.
Edit: I got some feedback in the comments and it seems like some people might also get 'okay' performance, on low to medium end PC'S, with low settings. This seems to be a bit random though, so maybe you should do some research before you buy.
I said in the comments below, that 'okay' performance for me would be something like 45-60 FPS with occasional crashes and stuttering. This shouldn't really be acceptable with my GTX 980 but I still think the game is worth playing.
Anyway, just know that you are gonna be compromising on performance, one way or another. It also seems to be a bit more of a gamble when you are using a lower end rig.

I'm not sure what I expected from this interactive. (And I did only one playthrough to preserve the narrative.)
I did peruse the reviews before playing, though frankly they did little to affect my opinion or experience.
There is very little to spoil in this from my own perspective.
That and a few of the top reviews are downright unhelpful, proclaming the grandiose nature of this "art."
The atmosphere does make the interactive I must admit, as while I'm not one to "remember the days" where the XP AOL messaging was commonplace, I felt it strongly from the setup.
As for the interactive itself, I see the frustrations some people are having, what they really want from the interactions you get between yourself the player and Emily.
However, I cannot agree with them for the sake of wanting them, but because the dialog options in my opinion were rather lackluster, some being practically or literally the same as other options.
BUT, I did realise it is because there is an overarching narrative in the background that is immutable to the choices you make, outside perhaps the outcome (Only one playthrough).
Really this is a simulation of classic schoolhood relationships more interested in your "yes's and no's" than what you really want to say or think.
I personally didn't care about this "Emily" or any other character mentioned, but I did see the power of a barrier between two people, the point when you realise that things are so bad, all you can do is say goodbye.

I just finished my frist playthrough and I will say this, I will be playing a second round. The game, visually is beautiful, music and voices are also beautiful. The story, though a little confusing at first, worked its way into something amazing and had me smiling towards the end. You can feel real emotions coming from these characters even though one is only a voice and the other as completely lost hers.
The combat is different from other games, while it can be hectic at times and the AI (especially during higher levels) can get a bit silly. Now that I've played through once, I plan to play through using limiters just to see how much harder the game play will be (I ran for a bit with 3 and found it a bit more challenging, but I'm curious as to how much further I can travel down that road.) Being able to mix up your skills means you can find different attacks that work on different enemies. The same move might not be as effective against another target, but this also means that swapping your skills around keeps the combat interesting and gets rid of that "grinding" feel. I also like the ability to add "passives" to your main attacks with other attacks. Usue your regular "ping" attack and add in "switch" and suddenly your damaged enemy is on your side. Swap it around and use your normal attacks but also add in Flood() and you're suddenly doing way more damage. Mixing them up and finding combos is actually quite fun.
I got this game from a friend as a gift while it was on sale (14.99), but don't shy away from the 19.99 price tag. Despite only having a little over 4 hours of game play in it so far, Transistor is well worth 20$. (The music is also well worth the 9.99 tag.)

When you speak I hear silence, Every word a defiance.
You are Red, famous singer of Cloudbank--persecuted for reasons unknown, you barely manage to escape with the Transistor; your friend, weapon, savior. But you did not get away unscathed, you've lost your voice to this dystopian TRON-like city.
Transistor is a unique piece of interactive art filled with an extraordinary protagonist in an superlative universe. I couldn't help but be enchanted by the score and immersed in the game. Backed with a stellar art direction in detailing vivid environments and cityscapes. Take a break from the story and retreat to your private beach getaway filled with minigames and music of your choice. You even get your very own beach ball! The minigames will help players of any range of skill learn core mechanics and execution without feeling frustrated nor overwhelmed.
Most of the combat is in a strategic turn-planning mode instructing Red where to move, what skills to combo. While, accounting for the planning cost of each ability you use and the cooldown timer where you are back in real-time. The gameplay mechanics are fantastic, simple - easy to learn, but hard to master with plenty of skills at your disposal and a per mutational number of customizations to suit the situation and your gameplay style. Use the skills on their own or augment other abilities with those traits. What do you need for this situation? Penetrating, Splitting, Chain-reactive, Concealing? Check.  I personally love using Help+Spark to get two dog minions and Jaunt+Breach for setup with dashing damage. There are incentives for you to experiment, namely, the character lore.
The cast is fleshed out and alive. Red and the unknown voice of the Transistor are the core characters in the game and develop into something truly mesmerizing. Let's not exclude the villains, each antagonist has their own personality and goal that can be sympathized/empathized with.
In conclusion, Transistor is among one of my favorites. It combines all I can ask for: excellent art, score, narration, gameplay, character, etc. Words alone cannot describe how I feel about Transistor. Indeed a marvelous unparalleled title this year. Oh we all, we all become…

The menus in Codemasters's F1 2017 are very simple and well looking. You can easily find what you are looking for and never get lost. It does not take up too much space of the screen and they like adding pictures to the main menu which makes it look even better.
As in previous games, there is no mouse support which could make one or the other hardcore pc gamers raise their pulse rate.
I really like the way that Codemasters went with the graphics. The previous title, F1 2016, had too much color and brightness. F1 2017 looks much cooler and welcome compared to its predecessor. In the options menu you can change many settings to fine tune your visual experience and performance. The Benchmark tool is one of the best that the games of the current time have to offer and it lets you test your performance with the settings you have selected on any track as well as condition you like.
There are a few flaws in the game connected to the graphics. Even with motion blur set to 0%, the surrounding textures start to blur when the car is in motion. This can make the game look fuzzy and irritating while driving. There are also many reports of missing textures (textures are completely black) and colored lines appearing on the screen.
The audio of the game has not changed too much from its predecessor. The engine sounds are the same with a little louder whistle from the turbo. Contact and crash sounds are also mostly the same. In the options menu, you can change the volume of the different sounds, such as master sound, voice, car etc. . You can also switch to push to talk or deactivate voice chat from others in multiplayer lobbies completely. Your ingame engineer, Jeff, can also be changed to speak only when there are critical situations.
There are also issues with audio in the game as well. After patch 1.6, many players report missing audio or audio stutter. Unfortunately, in order to turn off the commentators at the beginning and end of a session, the player must turn down the voice volume, which also turns down the individuals talking to you in the paddock area.
Setting up the controls in the menu has become more detailed and user friendly compared to the previous title. The player can now use presets for his wheel or change them to make his/her own mapping which he/she can save. There are also wheel specific settings that the player can change, like the throttle saturation or wheel dead zone.
The handling of the cars is the best that Codemasters has ever programmed. The the cars have a lot of mechanical and aerodynamical grip meaning that the car has very good traction exiting and very good grip through high speed corners. It just feels like you can do everything with the car. The force feedback on the wheels has been increased and the player can now feel every single bump on the road.
Many players report the force feedback disabling completely all of a sudden in multiplayer races. Decreasing the enviromental effects can make up a few tenths of a second.
The modern cars models have been recreated very accurately from the first grand prix.
The liveries are not correct though. FIA have made a rule to make the drivers more visible by increasing the driver number and short name on the cars. The goal was to personalize the cars more to their drivers. F1 2017 players are still waiting for an update from Codemasters to make the liveries accurate to the current ones in real life. Due to the PEGI 3 rating of the game, Codemasters are not allowed to include alcoholic sponsors, which are on the cars in real life as well.
Codemasters brought back the classic cars mode that was last seen in F1 2013. The player can do custom events and challenges using one of the 12 available classic cars from the past 30 years. The handling and the looks of the cars are breathtaking and the same goes for the sounds. The player can also use them in multiplayer.
Due to the different programming of the engines and gearboxes, they cannot be set to the same performance in multiplayer lobbies.
Codemasters use the event mode to challenge the F1 players. They also use it as a qualifying method for the new esports event that was announced. The events are changed from week to week.
Codemasters have again taken the career mode to a higher level of realism, expanding on the fundaments of its predecessor, by adding more practice programms such as fuel saving and race strategy as well as adding the ability to change parts of the engine and the entire gearbox should they wear to much. Like in the real sport, the player will receive grid penalties should he/she resort to a fifth unit of an engine part or change a gearbox. The player can reduce the wear by either following the instructions in the parts descriptions or upgrading the duration department of the Research&Development Tree, which is a massive upgrade to the previous, simple and overpowerd upgrade system of the last title. It is devided into 4 departments, which are durability, powertrain, aerodynamics and chassis. Each of the departments have their own branches of minor and major upgrades that increase the performance of the upgraded department. The process is much slower and more expensive than in the previous game, making the comletion of practice programms vital for the car development. In total the R&D tree covers 115 unlockable upgrades. The safety car (SC) and virtual safety car (VSC) have been improved. Players will not be able to exploit the VSC without being penalized by pushing over the delta limit right before it ends.
The replay mode has not changed.
The multiplayer of the game has not changed a lot from the previous title. The only additions are 2 spectator slots in lobbies, short layouts of a few tracks and a ranking system, which saves the players stats and increases his/her level by gaining points through races.
From launch onwards, the multiplayer was very unstable. Players were disqualified at the end of races and collsions did not work. Cars that retire stop on the side of the roads and never disappear, causing a constant yellow flag situation in that sector. Blue flags are not shown and corner cutting is very easy to get away with as the system somehow does not recognize the player going 10 feet left or right from where they are supposed to be. The spectator cameras have not been improved at all from its predecessor and there are still no live standings with gaps. The multiplayer still has no report option to report players who crash others out on purpose, ruining the experience for others.
F1 2017, in terms of the single player aspect, it is by far the best that Codemasters have ever created. The rules and regulations as well as practice programs and upgrades are very realistic, accurate, balanced and a lot of fun. The cars feel amazing to drive the classic cars make you feel like Michael Schumacher in his glory days. The multiplayer however is a literal mess. The bugs and glitches as well as trolls ruin the experience. There have been no major improvements except 2 spectator slots, which do not have the tools to make good live streams for esports and league events. Through already many patches and a little luck, some multiplayer sessions work well and as they are supposed to, but most times they unfortunately do not, making leagues not possible at this point.
The multiplayer has been ignored this year too. It is a mess and league cannot run properly like in F1 2013. Leagues are as much of a reason for Codemasters success as the Career mode, making it as important.
Unfortunately Codemasters does not seem to care too much.
I still recommend the game though.
My rating: 8/10 (the career mode saved it from a 5/10)

I wasn't expecting much, never played a "clicker" game before... but from the moment I started I haven't closed the game, and got 100% achievements easily.

Genre: Casual
Plantera is a cute take on the clicker genre, a genre which is already gone beyond over populated with most of them being free to play. What does Plantera do to set itself apart from its competition, let’s find out
Plantera starts out by giving you an empty garden with the purpose of making it bloom. You click onto flying butterflies and bash moles to get the initial coins needed to plant your first carrot plants. From here, you have a little blue helper who helps out by pulling them out and picking them up. As a general clicker game, from there you start unlocking different trees, bushes, farm animals and special items by collecting coins.
I was surprised at the speed at which these items unlock. Since it’s a paid game and not a free to play title, there is less grinding here than say games like Adventure Capitalist or Clicker Heroes. There are various critters who annoy who throughout the game like magpies who steal fruits fallen down from trees, dogs who scares away your animals and stuff like that. You can counter them by placing various special items like scarecrows and pets of your own to scare away these critters.
You unlock more helpers when you expand your garden which slowly eliminates the need to click. This pace also makes feel you a little useless later on as you see the coins being gathered up faster than they drop. There are huge price spikes on more expensive trees, bushes, animals etc as you place a few.
Unlocking more garden area also helps in increasing the limit of the amount of things you can place in your garden. In middle of the game, you will see loot hero and ladybugs coming in sometimes who give lots of coins when clicked on. In latter game, your only job seems to be limited to look out for these as clicking doesn’t seem as helpful as it would in other games of the genre.
In a normal clicker game, the time you spent away from the game also made you money for the time you were gone. While this is implemented here, it is applied in a different way. There is a limited time for which your workers will work after you’ve closed the game which can be upgraded slowly.
You can also double the coins you receive every time with one of these special upgrades. Being a clicker game, there is a certain level of grind which slowly settles in with the huge price spikes. But, the time taken to unlock everything is surprisingly quite low. What disappointed me was the lack of options of the plants themselves, with 4 of each type running out of steam far early.
Plantera is a cute game. From your little helpers to the critters that invade, it is an eye popping game with colours raining down. Plantera keeps its cutesy touch down to the facial expressions. When a magpie steals your fruit, it looks so happy that you just want to let it take the fruit. When you come back to the game after sometime and all your helpers and pets are asleep, they look so peaceful that you do not want to wake them up.
In the start of the game, it is just a empty palette, but as you progress through the game, there is so much going on the screen that it’s hard to keep track of what’s going on. The butterflies which give you coins have a golden glow on outside which helps them distinguish them from normal butterflies and so on.
All the plants, trees and bushes have less variety but are distinguishable from each other, especially the cherry tree which when planted throughout the garden, gives a sense of bloom like no other. Overall, Plantera is a very cute and relaxing game to look at.
Plantera has a very soothing soundtrack loop. This keeps you in the game as you watch the animals go about their duties and listen to the music. It really mends in with the graphical design of the game and helps create a very good environment.
Rest of the sounds are fairly generic with coin drops, dog barks and magpies chirping pretty fairly done. Later on in the game though, these sounds overwhelm you as you hear your pets scaring away the critters, coins getting picked up and so on. This almost drowns out the background score which is nothing short of stellar.
If you like clicker games, you will like plantera. It runs well on even the oldest of PC’s and there are no obvious bugs present. It is marred by the usual grindy tropes of the genre but it handles it surprisingly well and does an excellent job of keeping you hooked. It does not overstay its welcome and gives away everything it has to offer in a short period of time. Its graphical cuteness combined with the very good soundtrack makes it easy on eyes and ears. If you are tired of clicker games, Plantera might not change your mind much, but on 3$, it is worth a try

Like many who bought the brilliant Amnesia: The Dark Descent, I was hesitant to listen to the negative reviews of this "sequel" and instead opted to focus more on the positive ones and give Machine For Pigs a chance.  Boy, was that a mistake and a waste of $20.
So much of what made the first game great is gone.  No longer is there an inventory system incorporating smart, fun puzzle-solving.  Gone is the sanity system, and with it much of the tension that comes with encountering foes.  And last but certainly not least, gone is the ability to explore and fully interact with the environment.  99% of the objects you encounter can't be interacted with, i.e. you can't open most cabinets, go off the beaten path, scour for interesting items that enhance the story, none of that.  I don't know where certain reviewers are coming from when they talk about how great the atmosphere is in this game.  When you're surrounded by the exact same objects as the first Amnesia game, yet you can't touch them or explore for some reason, it pulls you straight out of the game world.  Side note: I have a very powerful system which can run Amnesia: The Dark Descent at full settings at 60fps... it would seem that The Chinese Room didn't do a very job of making this a stable game on top of it all because this game runs like garbage.  It's hard to be consumed by the atmosphere of the game when you can barely do anything and it's glitching all the time.
But on to the story.  Simply put, it's crap.  It focuses so heavily on the "pig" metaphor that after a while, you'll grow tired of hearing the word.  The voice acting is weak and the dialogue and scattered notes are pretentious.  The Dark Descent had such style and such a rich story.  This game seems to me like an uninspired cash-in.
Listen to all the other reviews.  Stick to The Dark Descent and if you've beat that, get your hands on Outlast.  Both of those games will be staying on my hard drive whereas this one will be getting uninstalled and probably never revisited once I've finished it and feel like I got my money's worth.

Just Cause 3 is ridiculously delightful, and delightfully ridiculous. This is evident from the very beginning, which starts you off standing on top of an airplane using a rocket launcher to take out SAM sites. It only becomes more ridiculous from there.
Just Cause 3 thinks that running around is far too slow, and thus gives you a grappling hook, a parachute, and a wingsuit. The grappling hook lets you move around the battlefield in an ultra-fast version of the Vanquish slide. That same grappling hook combined with a parachute will launch you into the air. Get high enough, or jump off a great height, and switch to the wingsuit to fly across the islands. Keep using the grappling hook while flying to build up speed and you can navigate the island at speed without ever touching the ground.
But that's not all the grappling hook can do. Grapple an enemy, and launch yourself at them to deliver a flying kick. Grapple two items - like an explosive barrel and an enemy jeep, or an enemy and the ceiling - and use the tether to pull one into the other. You can also grapple onto vehicles to ride on top, or below, or hijack them.
The ridiculousnous continues as you fly into a town or base, run around causing chaos and mayhem, kill countless enemies while destroying their tanks and helicopters, liberate the area, and then be on your way.
The ridiculousnous extends beyond the combat. One of my favorite moments - as I was driving a prized car back to the garage to unlock it - was when my GPS malfunctioned and sent me driving off a cliff and into the ocean. I was okay, but my prized car was now at the bottom of the sea. But wait! Maybe if I... Yes! I was able to tether the mangled remains up out of the water, flip the car up onto the dock by the garage, and use the tether to drag the wreckage - sparks and debris flying off of it - to the garage. It was enough to make a copy, and unlock it. Success!
But my favorite moment was when my young son climbed into my lap and we flew over the island until we found an orange car (his favorite color), and then just drove around the island. No combat, no missions, just following the road wherever it takes us and soaking in the beauty. The driving is slick arcade style, drifting through tight turns, and AI cars are usually smart enough to slow down or get out of your way. In a game of chaos and destruction, we found peaceful relaxation in just driving around the beautiful island and watching the hills and ocean roll by.
[Update]
One significant negative, however, is the default always-online server connection. It's used to provide times for your friends, so you can see how you did in comparison and encourage competition. That part is fine. What's not is that the server seems unstable. The first week, I never encountered a single server issue. This week, though, the server seems to be down every day. You can play offline, but every time you pause the game or open the map / drop / mod menu it tries to reconnect, which results in waiting and watching a wheel spin for 20 second. It greatly interupts the flow of the game when you open the map for a sec, but have to spend 20 seconds doing nothing while the game tries to re-connect to a server that's down.
I had to block JustCause3.exe in the Windows Firewall to avoid the constant reconnections while they got their server issues sorted out. It let me play the game without interruptions, but it meant that any Feats I accomplished while off-line didn't count once I went back online.
In addition, there are a couple mods I recommend you get, one practically essential and one optional but fun.
First, pretty essential, is the No Intro mod, to remove the 30 second unskippable intro. The intro is cool the first time you see it, but the length and inability to skip it is inexcusable. Download the mod here:
Second, optional, is the double range grappling hook. I find it makes it more fun without breaking the game. Just be sure to only install the double range one, as the infinite does break some aspects. Download the mod here:

After years and years of disappointment, Codemasters have finally published a title that does F1 justice.  I have been a fan of F1 since the 2012 season, and started playing the Codemasters games since 2013. Year after year the games kept getting worse. F1 2016 was a breath of fresh air, but still not the title that I was looking for. The career mode was heavily hyped, but the car development was just a gimmick.
When F1 2017 came out this year, I was skeptical. I did not pre-order it, breaking the 4 year chain of pre-ordering f1 games. After seeing a couple of positive reviews, I paid the premium price and so far I have not regretted it one bit. The cars are much more exciting to drive than they have been on previous games, and the career mode progression finally feels realistic. For me, its the small details that make this game better than all the previous f1 games. F1 2016 had a great  feel on track, but the menus and controls were a mess. This year, it feels like Codies have actually put in some effort into every aspect.
-
Career mode finally feels progressive and realistic. The practice programs have expanded, giving them more relevance. You really need the resource points for car development this year. The R n D feels great this year. The resource tree gives you the ability to upgrade certain elements of your car that might be lacking in performance. Unlike 2016, each car you drive will have different needs. A McLaren Honda will need a lot of work on the engine, while a Williams will need a lot of chassis work done. The classic car events are a nice deviation from your standard career mode, although putting them right after a race can make them tedious, especially after you just finished an 100% race at Monaco.
-
The handling model keeps getting better and better every year. The cars this year are much faster, making them much more fun to drive. The AI has been tweaked this year, and is much more aggressive. They are still quite dumb, but it is an upgrade over 2017. Codies have also implemented manual clutch on pitstops as well as the pit limiter for entering the pits. It really doesnt change much at all, but I like it.
-
Glad they are back. Really enjoyed them in F1 2013, really enjoying them now. Nice to have a more modern selection of "classics"
-
Finally, Codies has given us a more unpredictable weather system. There is no longer a clear crossover point in between dry and wet. This year you will actually need to think about when to come in to change compounds, and you might get it wrong.
-
The menu is cleaner, it is somewhat easier to map controls, Loading screens have some pictures now, not just a boring white screen, AI now has a difficulty slider (THANK GOD)
-
While the aggressiveness of the AI makes them more racey, they still can be quite stupid at times. The AI really likes to park it on the racing line in qualifying, which is really annoying when you are on a fast lap.
-
While we have classic cars, we don't have the historic driver names.
-
Could have been a bit more polished, quite a few glitches and bugs. I got boosted up 10 places while on the formation lap for no reason.
-
Still neglected
-
This has been a big problem since 2015. Before, you could mod the games. Custom helmets, liveries and championships used to add a huge amount of replayability. Every year, Codemasters have made it harder and harder to mod the game files. This is a huge disappointment.
-
Although Codies have seriously improved the game's small detalis compared to last year, there are still some aspects that are lacking. In career, your driver name and number still does not appear on the racing suit. If it is possible to put your number on the car, it can't be that hard to put it on the suit. Same goes with the names on the shark fins. I also wish that codies would improve the crash physics even more. They had advertised a new physics model for crashes, but it is extremely underwhelming and feels identical to 2016.

When the game is working it's a good game. But i already had several game crashes where the screen freezes and the sound hangs.

The gameplay is sadly the weakest part of this game. WTF, WHY DID YOU DESIGN IT LIKE THAT. I know I missed a bloody note, and i cant get it without restarting the entire game. ♥♥♥♥ you.

Well The Chinese Room did an excellent job creating a creepy atmosphere.  I was pretty much at the edge of my seat throughtout the entirety of my exploration of the compound you're trapped in.  The problem for me was that since the game was branded as an Amnesia title I had assumed it would follow some of the more traditional elements of The Dark Descent.  It didn't do anything that I was expecting.  I was never "afraid for my life" and I never felt lost and in despair...which were the pretty big parts of The Dark Descent that I took away.  In Machine for Pigs I felt like I was on rails the whole time and I couldn't make very many bad decisions in the game.
But the story was very compelling.  There were only a few puzzles in the game and those weren't challenging or difficult on any level, but the story is what really had me hooked.  There was something sinister going on at this particular compound and the point of the game was to figure out WTF and where TF you were going/have been.  The greater portion of the game is spent trying to come to an understanding of your situation and surroundings.  And that, preciely, is what makes this an Amnesia title.
Despite that, there was still something missing.  All the other reviews can probably capture the exact element that's missing better than I could, but what was glaring for me was the absent terror.  There were other creatures in this game but they bordered on cute rather than terrifying.  The psychological stress was farily absent, too.  The story progressed coherently but it never disturbed me in a way that The Dark Descent did.  The subjects being what they were in Machine for Pigs didn't really make anything all that more terrible to think about either.
Surprisingly, the ending was quite satisfying even though it was very anti-climatic.  It was a fitting ending as opposed to The Dark Descent's which didn't really fit in with the story that game had told.
Because it's branded an Amnesia title it will -- and has to -- be compared with The Dark Descent.  Side by side, there is a clear disappointment.  Machine for Pigs doesn't deliver as an Amensia title.  But take the Amnesia branding away and the game stands farily well on its own as I wouldn't have gone into it without expecting an experience like what I found with the first in the series.  I'm going to recommend this title, but only if you can play it without any sort of expectations of what you found in The Dark Descent.

Just Cause 3 is ridiculously delightful, and delightfully ridiculous. This is evident from the very beginning, which starts you off standing on top of an airplane using a rocket launcher to take out SAM sites. It only becomes more ridiculous from there.
Just Cause 3 thinks that running around is far too slow, and thus gives you a grappling hook, a parachute, and a wingsuit. The grappling hook lets you move around the battlefield in an ultra-fast version of the Vanquish slide. That same grappling hook combined with a parachute will launch you into the air. Get high enough, or jump off a great height, and switch to the wingsuit to fly across the islands. Keep using the grappling hook while flying to build up speed and you can navigate the island at speed without ever touching the ground.
But that's not all the grappling hook can do. Grapple an enemy, and launch yourself at them to deliver a flying kick. Grapple two items - like an explosive barrel and an enemy jeep, or an enemy and the ceiling - and use the tether to pull one into the other. You can also grapple onto vehicles to ride on top, or below, or hijack them.
The ridiculousnous continues as you fly into a town or base, run around causing chaos and mayhem, kill countless enemies while destroying their tanks and helicopters, liberate the area, and then be on your way.
The ridiculousnous extends beyond the combat. One of my favorite moments - as I was driving a prized car back to the garage to unlock it - was when my GPS malfunctioned and sent me driving off a cliff and into the ocean. I was okay, but my prized car was now at the bottom of the sea. But wait! Maybe if I... Yes! I was able to tether the mangled remains up out of the water, flip the car up onto the dock by the garage, and use the tether to drag the wreckage - sparks and debris flying off of it - to the garage. It was enough to make a copy, and unlock it. Success!
But my favorite moment was when my young son climbed into my lap and we flew over the island until we found an orange car (his favorite color), and then just drove around the island. No combat, no missions, just following the road wherever it takes us and soaking in the beauty. The driving is slick arcade style, drifting through tight turns, and AI cars are usually smart enough to slow down or get out of your way. In a game of chaos and destruction, we found peaceful relaxation in just driving around the beautiful island and watching the hills and ocean roll by.
[Update]
One significant negative, however, is the default always-online server connection. It's used to provide times for your friends, so you can see how you did in comparison and encourage competition. That part is fine. What's not is that the server seems unstable. The first week, I never encountered a single server issue. This week, though, the server seems to be down every day. You can play offline, but every time you pause the game or open the map / drop / mod menu it tries to reconnect, which results in waiting and watching a wheel spin for 20 second. It greatly interupts the flow of the game when you open the map for a sec, but have to spend 20 seconds doing nothing while the game tries to re-connect to a server that's down.
I had to block JustCause3.exe in the Windows Firewall to avoid the constant reconnections while they got their server issues sorted out. It let me play the game without interruptions, but it meant that any Feats I accomplished while off-line didn't count once I went back online.
In addition, there are a couple mods I recommend you get, one practically essential and one optional but fun.
First, pretty essential, is the No Intro mod, to remove the 30 second unskippable intro. The intro is cool the first time you see it, but the length and inability to skip it is inexcusable. Download the mod here:
Second, optional, is the double range grappling hook. I find it makes it more fun without breaking the game. Just be sure to only install the double range one, as the infinite does break some aspects. Download the mod here:

No, I haven't played the game very much at all, but you don't have to in order to see everything thats wrong with it. Why?:
When you start the game, you get lost really fast because it lacks any true tutorial guidance. Once you go to liberate your first outpost, it will tell you to go there...... Thats it. I went there and took the police station, but noticed the outpost was still red... There were no way points any where else, so I spent like 15 minutes just screwing around till I ended up figuring it out, turns out there is a check list of things you have to do to take the outpost that can be viewed by the map.
Ok, so I go to do them, but since I don't understand anything about the objectives, I wasted like 5 minutes looking for that dang flag pole! ... There isn't one! You have to complete everything else first, then it will tell you to go to the flag and actually place a marker on it for once... So I finally take it, and the only thing that is explained ok enough is the vehicles garage/rebel drop system.
I go to do the last "tutorial" base, I go through the check list but get stumped on the turbines... This is the worst part! I spent like 10 minutes of just exploring the base and gunning down enemies ... I am thinking either I missed some dialogue or I am just being a dumb a-s... Nope! I Googled where the turbines were, turns out, there is litterally this entire system of buttons and timing to open the doors to destroy them! How am I suposed to just know that!?
I finally take my first territory.... and I am still disoriented! I understand how to take territory, which was a huge hassle, but what the hell else is there!? I am sure it "might" have explained it through missions, but after that I was pretty much free to do whatever... It didn't tell me where to go to learn about the rest of the game, and there wasn't any ingame guides to tell me about all the systems and their true purpose.
It's so bad, the game even fails to explain simple controls. I like to use a gamepad for a game like this, and when I winch 2 things together, it just says something like "Press ( B ) to detach". It didn't work though, my guy would just melee... it was kind of frustrating since it wasn't even in the controller map. Turns out, you have to do something like hold LT first... They cared SO little they weren't bothered to say "Press LT + ( B ) to detach". Holy hell! ... It's just... so, terrible!
The game lacks a propper introduction, which is essential to a game like this. I played 2 hours and I still have no idea what I am actually suposed to do and how to really play the game.
I have to admit, the game does have really good physics, its extremely fun to collapse watch towers into explosives and watch the domino effect unfold! I also really enjoy blowing down bridges.... That's where it kind of stops though, you can't really level buildings or anything, which would have been cool, but I can let that pass because what they had was satisfying.
Unfortunately, when it comes to assential things like vehicles, the physics just becomes annoying. Driving in that game is basically impossible, if you thought Watch_Dogs 2 was bad, Watch_Dogs 2 is like Forza compared to JC3! Its like they started to develop driving but decided to wrap it up after the first beta so they could pump out other shotty vehicle controls, I guess they figured the player wouldn't use vehicles all too much... Which is BS because vehicles are actually very essential to the game.... You learn that really quickly.
I didn't really make the physics, but I theorize it has something to do with the fact that vehicle driving physics try to combat the physics engine, rather then use the physics engine to it's advantage. When it come to steering the car doesn't naturally go forward like a normal car, it forces itself to go only the direction of the steering, relying on the steering to straiten itself out overtime. It should just push against the steering and only use it as a guide, not a forced direction, that way you can have better drifts and smoothly guide the vehicle. I am no expert, or programmer, but to me, that seems logical.
The physics are fun, but the vehicle driving is just flat unacceptable by any standards.

Fast paced, stylish and satisfying first person shooter. Like a movie of Quentin Tarantino's as a game.
The game begins as the main character enters a saloon and sits down with a few people to tell them a story about his adventures, as the game itself is the story being told. The main character keeps narrating the story throughout the game, and the people sitting with him talk as well, so in a way you are following two stories at the same time. What makes it really interesting, is that the interraction between the story-teller and the listeners sometimes affect your surroundings and the events in the game, keeping it interesting and full of surprises. So story-wise, the game is excellent.
The visual style of the game is very stylish, comic-like and gritty. There's a lot of blood, just like you'd expect. The music, the sound effects and the voice acting are all excellent and complement that certain wild west feel.
The controls are smooth and responsive, and shooting enemies is satisfying. There are three weapon classes for you to select depending on your preferred playstyle. The game has some well implemented quicktime events.
I completed the game on Hard difficulty setting, and I think it was sometimes hard to follow the narrative in a tight spot as you try to survive, but I don't think it should be passed as a critique. There were also a couple of moments that, in my opinion, required more trial and error than good reflexes and timing. I encountered a few minor bugs in the game, but nothing that would affect the gameplay experience. The game is a bit short, but one hell of a ride.
If you get it for about 10 euros (or dollars) or even less, it's definitely worth it.
As a bonus note: It's almost like playing a modern version of Sunset Riders.

I just finished my frist playthrough and I will say this, I will be playing a second round. The game, visually is beautiful, music and voices are also beautiful. The story, though a little confusing at first, worked its way into something amazing and had me smiling towards the end. You can feel real emotions coming from these characters even though one is only a voice and the other as completely lost hers.
The combat is different from other games, while it can be hectic at times and the AI (especially during higher levels) can get a bit silly. Now that I've played through once, I plan to play through using limiters just to see how much harder the game play will be (I ran for a bit with 3 and found it a bit more challenging, but I'm curious as to how much further I can travel down that road.) Being able to mix up your skills means you can find different attacks that work on different enemies. The same move might not be as effective against another target, but this also means that swapping your skills around keeps the combat interesting and gets rid of that "grinding" feel. I also like the ability to add "passives" to your main attacks with other attacks. Usue your regular "ping" attack and add in "switch" and suddenly your damaged enemy is on your side. Swap it around and use your normal attacks but also add in Flood() and you're suddenly doing way more damage. Mixing them up and finding combos is actually quite fun.
I got this game from a friend as a gift while it was on sale (14.99), but don't shy away from the 19.99 price tag. Despite only having a little over 4 hours of game play in it so far, Transistor is well worth 20$. (The music is also well worth the 9.99 tag.)

Supergiant brings back the fantastic story, unique narattion element, and great music from their debut game "Bastion" and adds amazing gameplay mechanics.
Everyone of the games 16 abilities (called functions) can be used directly, passively, or to modify another function. Unless my math is way off, that gives something like 576 function combinations. Not that every combination is optimal or useful, but provides plenty of combat variety. And there is a mechanic, where instead of dying, you lose one of your active functions (you die and lose progress when you lose all 4 active) and have to play for awile with out it. Some people may find this frustrating, but I feel its a great way to force the player to try out some new function combinations.

When you speak I hear silence, Every word a defiance.
You are Red, famous singer of Cloudbank--persecuted for reasons unknown, you barely manage to escape with the Transistor; your friend, weapon, savior. But you did not get away unscathed, you've lost your voice to this dystopian TRON-like city.
Transistor is a unique piece of interactive art filled with an extraordinary protagonist in an superlative universe. I couldn't help but be enchanted by the score and immersed in the game. Backed with a stellar art direction in detailing vivid environments and cityscapes. Take a break from the story and retreat to your private beach getaway filled with minigames and music of your choice. You even get your very own beach ball! The minigames will help players of any range of skill learn core mechanics and execution without feeling frustrated nor overwhelmed.
Most of the combat is in a strategic turn-planning mode instructing Red where to move, what skills to combo. While, accounting for the planning cost of each ability you use and the cooldown timer where you are back in real-time. The gameplay mechanics are fantastic, simple - easy to learn, but hard to master with plenty of skills at your disposal and a per mutational number of customizations to suit the situation and your gameplay style. Use the skills on their own or augment other abilities with those traits. What do you need for this situation? Penetrating, Splitting, Chain-reactive, Concealing? Check.  I personally love using Help+Spark to get two dog minions and Jaunt+Breach for setup with dashing damage. There are incentives for you to experiment, namely, the character lore.
The cast is fleshed out and alive. Red and the unknown voice of the Transistor are the core characters in the game and develop into something truly mesmerizing. Let's not exclude the villains, each antagonist has their own personality and goal that can be sympathized/empathized with.
In conclusion, Transistor is among one of my favorites. It combines all I can ask for: excellent art, score, narration, gameplay, character, etc. Words alone cannot describe how I feel about Transistor. Indeed a marvelous unparalleled title this year. Oh we all, we all become…

Dark Souls II was my first foray into the Souls series, and as such I'm willing to forgive some of its minor weaknesses that the most ardent fans of the series decry as damnable failings.
So what works in the game? First of all, the level design is mostly spot-on. While not as open as the first Dark Souls, it's a nice blend of the focused, linear progression of Demon's Souls and the interconnected labyrinth of the former. Some levels do dead-end instead of looping back into another area, but for me, that provided a satisfying sense of completion that the first Dark Souls seemed a bit too hesitant to give.
Secondly, there's a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of variety in the game, be it in the environmental design, weapon types, armor sets, enemies, bosses, or factions. Some argue that the enemy and boss designs are too frequently "dudes in armor," but I don't think that really matters too much since the majority of them are still artistically distinct and have nuanced movesets that set them apart from each other.
Finally, there's that awesome sense of progression that the Souls games are so good at fostering in their players. Whether you're picking up a shiny new weapon, defeating a boss that's stumped you for hours, or completing an area that initially intimidated you with its atmosphere and tough-looking enemies, you're always overcoming something.
Despite my adament endorsement of the game, though, I'll be the first to admit it has its flaws. Although you can respec your character with a rare item, some stats still should have been explained a bit better so that new players don't invest in, say, ADP without knowing that its true benefit is increasing the number of invincibility frames in dodge animations. Soft caps and hard caps (numeric values of diminishing returns within individual stats) should have also been made note of in the leveling menu up front instead of being something that players have to look up.
Additionally, there are hitbox issues, but only with a handful of enemies that seem to prefer obnoxious grapple moves, and there are also some random non-telegraphed backswing attacks from certain enemies that result in cheap deaths. Finally, the bonfire (checkpoint) placement in the game is sometimes too helter-skelter. Do we really need two bonfires in an area as small as Black Gulch? Couldn't From have simply implemented a shortcut to bypass the annoying poison statues once players have circumnavigated them the first time? Mechanically, the bonfires work, but their prevalence sometimes seems lazy, and it diminishes the game's cardinal rule: always play cautiously, and never let your guard down.
So, Dark Souls II is not a perfect game; that's a given. But it's a damn good one that any dungeon crawling/ARPG fan should check out.

Dark Souls 2 is probably my favorite game ever. When I firist bought it a while back I didn't really get into it. I started watching some speedrunners like Lobos Jr and Elajjaz and I felt quite motivated to speedrun this game myself. First off, I of course had to beat the game. Started with just a simple strength build and I beat the game in about 5 days (I beat the game so quick because I watched a lot of videos and learned the game really without playing it myself). I tried ng+ (new game plus) but, I struggled with it because I wasn't very good at the game yet. So, I beat it about another 4 times with different types of classes. I did another strength build, tried a dexterity build but, wasn't a fan, did a scorcery build and fell in love. Once I really started to understand the game and the enimies I tried "speedrunning" it for my first time. I beat it in about 10 hours which obviously, isn't good at all, I really felt like I knew the game now. I made myself familar with some other things like mechanics and strats. I still havn't beaten my own personal record yet but, I can tell you, one day I will really put time into speedrunning. Anyways enought about me and more about the game. This game is no doubt easier than dark souls 1. If you've stayed away from DS2 videos up untill now, congrats but, the game doesn't really tell you where to go and it can be VERY confusing. I love all the differnt types of classes in this game. I feel it's easier to be a cleric or a scorcer because the game introduces you to a lot of people on the way that sell some spells and miracles whereas in DS1 you had to really look in every nook and cranny to find NPC's that sold you spells. Scorcery in DS2 is so much better than DS1 (in my  opinion). Since my very first scorcery character I havn't had a character that isn't miracle or spell based. So, to pretty much wrap up my "little" review, I would HIGHLY recommend this game. If you've never played it, it will be such a new experience from other souls games. I love DS2 so much that just a week ago, I bought a PS4 and DS2:SOTFS and I can't stop playing it. In about a month I've beaten the game about 7 times. I will love this game forever and I would pay double or even triple the price for this game for the experience you'll have.

A lot of people seem to hate on this game for being shorter and with less game mechanics than the first Amnesia.
Honestly, I thought of it as trimming the excess fat off Amnesia: The Dark Decent.
This takes place in just about the year 1900.
They have electricity, therefore electric lamps, electric lights, no need for candles to be spread around with tinderboxes for you to manage or oil to ration.
Gone are the moments of, "Let's go down this hallway! Oh wait! The ceiling collapsed/Goo appeared over the door/The door is just broken or barricaded... again... Time to puzzle our way through an hour of jumpscares."
They also removed the incredibly annoying sanity mechanic that, let's face it, only got in our way for the first half of the game. Then we just kept running around in the dark because we saw better anyway.
There are substantially less jump scares than TDD. But the horror comes from other sources. This game is almost like an exploration horror game. But it's great. I loved it. There's a lot of small things that really give this game some great touches.
Grab your best pair of headphones and get immersed. And please read the journals and try to peice everything together. This ain't no Pewdiepie video.

I'm very ambivalent about this game. The reason Amnesia The Dark Descent was so successful is that it was so isolated and lacking in contact with anyone except the antagonist, Alexander. The game was small on scale in the sense it was one mans quest for revenge, against one man.
The problem with A Machine for Pigs is that it hasn't learnt from these two elements. There are so many characters other than Oswald himself. His children are always talking and luring him on, as is the mysterious man. The scale of the game fights with the atmosphere it is trying so desperately to create. The juxtaposition between vast isolated patches with sections where you literally see people running less than a few meters from you is quite jarring, pulling you out from the cloistered approach that Penumbra and ATTD managed so well.
To pull a quote from Penumbra: Overture;
"Once again, I felt like I did when I was in school, surrounded by a closing ring of older kids, knowing anyone that might help me - friends, parents, teachers - were too scared, or too far away."
This is what is wrong with the game. The people he's referring to, are not too far away. They are all too real, too physical, for the game to be even remotely threatening as a horror game.

Short version: I would say that this is not a bad game, but I can't because of the way it pales in comparison to its predecessor, and I won't because of how many times the bloody thing crashed on me.
I'd love to review this without having to revoke the nostalgia of the first game, but the fact remains that this is a sequel, and as such, I expect a progression from the elements in the first game. Sadly, Machine for Pigs opts to remove many elements that made The Dark Descent fun instead of improving upon them. For example, the sanity meter added uniqueness to the first game and made the prospect of even encountering a monster into a terrifying prospect. Now, however, you can just stroll right past the monsters or stare at them from safety without ever feeling threatened. And even if a monster catches you, all you need to do to restore health is wait in a corner for a little while as you automatically heal (like in a modern FPS).  The lack of an inventory also means puzzles are much simpler, almost as if they intentionally dumbed it down for me.
The game has its merits, however. I enjoyed the story (though somewhat predictable) and the fantastic writing (though somewhat chatty), and the build-up of tension before the first monster is truly unnerving. However, the tension was easily broken by a pop-up telling me my game had crashed, a problem that persisted (and then reappearred at another point in the game) even as I took the settings down to embarassingly low qualities. My computer can play much bigger games at great quality with no hassle, so I don't understand why this six-hour, single-mode game was causing so much of a problem. It was the frustration I experienced resolving this issue that finally convinced me that my anticpation for a sequel worthy of the Amnesia name had been a mistake.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game from beginning to end!
If you enjoyed Dear Esther then you will likely enjoy Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. This is a first person interactive novel/film experience. There are no guns or weapons or inventory system and, honestly, this "experience" doesn't need such features ("experience" seems a better description than "game").  The developers have thought outside the box and created a brilliant work of entertainment that doesn't need to conform to the norms.  You'll have a thoroughly enjoyable (and sometimes disturbing) adventure.
This really shouldn't be thought of as "Amnesia 2".  You should probably look elsewhere if you want an Amnesia sequel.  This is more like a "mod" of Amnesia to create a different type of product.
The graphics, sound and environment are immersive. Set your gamma low and turn your sound up and get ready to be swept away in the adventure.  It's not super scary but it's certainly enough to bring a smile and chuckle after a fright scene.
The gore and blood is relatively tame but (personally) I wouldn't recommend this one for children or people of a sensitive disposition (although "scariness" is a subjective thing).
A very worthy successor to Dear Esther.  The Chinese Room have done it again.  A royal shame that their next game "Everybody's Gone to the Rapture" will be exclusively Sony PS4.

What all this amounts to is a total lack of tension. Give the original a go instead for some proper thrills.

TheHunter, Why I enjoy this game.
1- For everybody who appreciates realism, I belive this one is as close as it gets.
2- A very mature community (usually older people who have the patientce to hunt, yes less than in real life but still this game  requires patience to bring home those beautiful animal trophies).
3- The game is constantly updated and it keeps a very strong data base tracking every animal you hunted/spotted, every shot fired with each weapon so you can see how you are doing comparing to others not to mention that daily there are competitions with trophies and prizes.

I would like to say a few words about why this game is unjustifiably "trashed" on steam.
1- Notice, that absolutly 99.9% of all negative reviews are by people who barely played and just seem not to understand the bussiness model, no single negative comment is actually made about the game it self.
2- The bussiness model of this game is different and it requires understanding.
Bussiness model:
1- As a "Free to Play" what you get is a limited experience of being able to visit all the maps  but to hunt only 2  species (Mule Deer, Cottontail Rabbit). Clearly this will not last you for hundreds of hours but you must consider this as a 5-10 hours of "demo" that will show you wether you would like the game or not.
2- TheHunter is constantly being updated (Its the same game from 2009) so the bussiness model here is a subscription bussiness model. In reallity depending on the time you commit to 3-12 monthes you can pay as little as 3$ for a month (35$ per year).
3- The items/ gear that is sold in thehunter is also sold for real money, you must consider this as DLCs (steam languge).
4- Even if you absolutly want to a lot of new content yearly it shouldnt cost you more than 50$ per year.
In case you are intrested in trying:
1- Just download the game.
2- Tune up graphics in settings to max (relative to your rig ofc.)
3- Start and finish the tutorial.
4- Start / Join a hunt in "Logger's Point" and go on tracking and hunting "Mule Deers" and "Cottontail Rabbits"
5- After a few hours you will see if the game is for you ;)

Note this is not a free 2 play game and the free 2 play content is limited in scope to the point where it is just a demo.
This game is a game that takes time and some investment to enjoy, first off I suggest buying a membership after trying the game, this will allow you to hunt all game. I have a Trailrunner (1 year) membership, this gives you a few guns some calls and a membership, also the membership gives you 3 replenishing boxes of ammo after every hunt, so you hunt use it all quit start a new hunt and it will be available again. I also bought every call, and some set up bundles, but that was after around 40 hours in the game. The graphics are great and immerse you into these beautiful reserves. The tracking and spotting of animals is excellent. Animals have a nice variety in size and antlers. There also rare coloration differences and for some deer non typical antlers. There are dogs for waterfowl and they are a nice premium item. There is also bow hunting which involves stalking and getting up close to your prey, an intense and fun experience.
Ok enough rambling, basically this game, is more like an iracing you need to narrow what you want to hunt or do or be prepared to spend more than what an average game costs. More on hunting on a budget, pick a style not species say bow hunting, competition hunting, waterfowl, big game etc. Then buy some the items that help you hunt in that style, for bow hunting maybe some camo and an upgraded bow, competition, the calls can be key, waterfowl a blind and decoys, big game calls and a nice rifle. So it can be played on a budget but to be the best at hunting everything can get expensive, now the setups mentioned above can be had for around $20 - $30 a piece and this is on the high end.
This is not a free to play game but a hardcore hunting simulation, but if you find what you want to hunt through watching videos or trying to hunt them you can immerse yourself even on a budget.

No, I haven't played the game very much at all, but you don't have to in order to see everything thats wrong with it. Why?:
When you start the game, you get lost really fast because it lacks any true tutorial guidance. Once you go to liberate your first outpost, it will tell you to go there...... Thats it. I went there and took the police station, but noticed the outpost was still red... There were no way points any where else, so I spent like 15 minutes just screwing around till I ended up figuring it out, turns out there is a check list of things you have to do to take the outpost that can be viewed by the map.
Ok, so I go to do them, but since I don't understand anything about the objectives, I wasted like 5 minutes looking for that dang flag pole! ... There isn't one! You have to complete everything else first, then it will tell you to go to the flag and actually place a marker on it for once... So I finally take it, and the only thing that is explained ok enough is the vehicles garage/rebel drop system.
I go to do the last "tutorial" base, I go through the check list but get stumped on the turbines... This is the worst part! I spent like 10 minutes of just exploring the base and gunning down enemies ... I am thinking either I missed some dialogue or I am just being a dumb a-s... Nope! I Googled where the turbines were, turns out, there is litterally this entire system of buttons and timing to open the doors to destroy them! How am I suposed to just know that!?
I finally take my first territory.... and I am still disoriented! I understand how to take territory, which was a huge hassle, but what the hell else is there!? I am sure it "might" have explained it through missions, but after that I was pretty much free to do whatever... It didn't tell me where to go to learn about the rest of the game, and there wasn't any ingame guides to tell me about all the systems and their true purpose.
It's so bad, the game even fails to explain simple controls. I like to use a gamepad for a game like this, and when I winch 2 things together, it just says something like "Press ( B ) to detach". It didn't work though, my guy would just melee... it was kind of frustrating since it wasn't even in the controller map. Turns out, you have to do something like hold LT first... They cared SO little they weren't bothered to say "Press LT + ( B ) to detach". Holy hell! ... It's just... so, terrible!
The game lacks a propper introduction, which is essential to a game like this. I played 2 hours and I still have no idea what I am actually suposed to do and how to really play the game.
I have to admit, the game does have really good physics, its extremely fun to collapse watch towers into explosives and watch the domino effect unfold! I also really enjoy blowing down bridges.... That's where it kind of stops though, you can't really level buildings or anything, which would have been cool, but I can let that pass because what they had was satisfying.
Unfortunately, when it comes to assential things like vehicles, the physics just becomes annoying. Driving in that game is basically impossible, if you thought Watch_Dogs 2 was bad, Watch_Dogs 2 is like Forza compared to JC3! Its like they started to develop driving but decided to wrap it up after the first beta so they could pump out other shotty vehicle controls, I guess they figured the player wouldn't use vehicles all too much... Which is BS because vehicles are actually very essential to the game.... You learn that really quickly.
I didn't really make the physics, but I theorize it has something to do with the fact that vehicle driving physics try to combat the physics engine, rather then use the physics engine to it's advantage. When it come to steering the car doesn't naturally go forward like a normal car, it forces itself to go only the direction of the steering, relying on the steering to straiten itself out overtime. It should just push against the steering and only use it as a guide, not a forced direction, that way you can have better drifts and smoothly guide the vehicle. I am no expert, or programmer, but to me, that seems logical.
The physics are fun, but the vehicle driving is just flat unacceptable by any standards.

i bought this for the PS4 back when it was newer (late 2015?) and it chug-a-lugged real bad because you can't disable features on a console. 10FPS when more than 2 explosions were going at once! First PS4 game i ever had to refund.
Now, on PC, it's still a chugging, stupid mess, but good news! You can disable all the worthless, gimmicky cracked bells and tone-deaf whistles, and it'll run butter-smooth on even a mid-grade PC.
Seriously. put all water effects to Low, and turn off their "dynamic" field of view settings and edge blurring, and you could run the game with Ultra textures without ever once seeing the framerate dip.
That said. The game itself is still a creature in itself, right?
Someone said you're playing as spider-iron-man and really that's about right. You're nigh-bulletproof and the only truly lethal tactic in the game is to strap yourself with bombs, or wingdive headfirst into a guy with a minigun and wait 10 seconds.
Surprisingly, the game's a lot less mobile and twitchy than JC2 was. it's more focused on gunplay and maneuverability in form of vehicles and gimmicks beyond the grappling hook and parachute.
They definitely improved on some aspects; the hot/cold game of finding collectibles is still there but much less intensely annoying than it was in JC2, and in settlements, though you now have to do everything to "complete" them (instead of hitting them for 80% and bolting like in 2), you get a visual checklist, so you know what to look for to cross everything off. What's good about that system, as well, is that they issue challenges for outposts. Like "hit the switches and blow up all the hidden turbines before the time runs out" and if you die even after finishing it, you have to redo it. The idea is, each outpost, while you can hit-and-die a few things (misc bomb tanks, billboards, whatever), there's core things you must strike and succeed at fleeing with to win. It's much more focused on a holistic terrorist experience than 2's "do whatever really" approach.
The gunplay's more smooth with bullets being slot-universal and equipment drops being friendlier than in 2 as well. enemies are spongier so you can enjoy riddling them with shots, too, though shooting the enemies once or twice in the back still does it.
We don't talk about the story. But it's funny how everybody supposedly personally was saved by Rico in various insane ways, like this is some ridiculous B movie starring stallone.
The challenges are fun, too, surprisingly. In JC2 I dreaded doing any racing or parachuting or whatever else, because they took forever and had no incentive at all, but in this one, most challenges are short bursts that let you restart even if you succeed so you can aim for the top score.
Overall it's fun if you like checklists, that's for sure. Not as massive as JC2's "literally play forever because it's procedural" stunt, but it's still impressive enough, and the focus they put on specific areas helps make the gameplay more impressive and versatile than 2's touch-and-go approaches had.
Also I can actually run it at a respectable framerate, so that's cool, too.
