A short fall for the Rome: Total War Series.
R2TW (Rome II Total War/Total War Rome II) was not the worthy successor of all time great Total War game Rome Total War at its release date. It's a stripped RTW (Rome Total War) with upgraded graphics and effects.
Imagine comparing 2 cars, one from the 80s taht looks ugly today but have great performance, with a 2010 car that looks shiny and all but have half the performance.
That's what this game is, RTW getting more shiny but stripped of it features and the fun managing every little bits of the roman empire. Good Family Tree system=Gone, Senate system=gone, choosing 1 of 3 roman family having a gameplay difference=gone, sending troops without general=gone, builidng fort=gone, building watch tower=gone, placing govenor easily by putting a general on the city=gone, Guard mode = gone, Great pre-battle speech=gone, good music=gone, diplomats to open a diplomacy dialogue=gone (it seems they have a telephone in 14BC), battle mechanism that actually more realistic = gone, a detailed settlement information presented in graphical settings = gone, And a lot more features of Rome Total War gone.
However it does have far better graphics suited for it release time, better optimization (not really at release) but as of Emperor edition, it's far better than RTW in terms of optimization due to the limitation of RTW of using only 2GB of memory and 1 core, maxxing out RTW usually causes problem as all of the processing is loaded only to a single core. R2TW also have ship battles as RTW have not. I guess R2TW also have better more realistic proportion of weapons and gear, in RTW a gladius looks like a butter knife, a hoplite spear looks like pike that too long to hold. Mind though that units in R2TW are not 100% historically accurate, as that would be hard.
This game is recommended for those who are new to Total War world, the btter choice is Shogun 2 total war, if you can't get that or doesn't like the japanese samurai theme, and prefer a roman age world this is quite the choice. Which then later you should play RTW after getting to know the world of Total war. RTW feels more of a complex game.
For those who are from RTW, which seeking for a Rome Total War upgrade, you would be quite disappointed, this is semi-recommended, at times that you feel you want RTW with better graphics play R2TW for a while, it's an okay game, not that bad anymore, but you might feel something is missing when you plays this after playing RTW for so long.

Best of the Call of Juarez titles, this game combines a great FPS experience, gorgeous graphics, and an engaging--and often downright funny--tall-tale cowboy narrative. For  old codger gamers like me, it's the backyard imaginary-gunslinger days of our youth transported into a very playable and enjoyable experience. Your character, the bounty hunter Silas Greaves, is adequately customizable to suit your preferred method of play. (I opted to emphasize sharpshooter skills over the more close-range styles, but you can mix and match your skillset as you see fit.) On the hunt for the men who killed your brothers and left you for dead, you wander across the West, encountering all manner of history's greatest bandits and scofflaws.
I've played several uneven and often frustrating games in this genre, but this one was non-stop fun from beginning to end, including the "nuggets of truth" history bits on many of the Old West's most (in)famous figures. Almost nothing was lacking in this game. It might have been intreesting to add some greater variation in the kinds of firearms that were available and popular during Silas' lifetime (up to the dawn of the 20th century), but the limited weaponry did not by any means detract from the gameplay. This eminently fun, fun--and did I mention FUN--game gives me a right hankerin' fer more rootin' tootin' six-shootin' games like it, but sadly, the Western sub-genre is limited.

I love the world of Dark Souls. It's an interesting world with a lot to discover, and I enjoy exploring it. I love the premise of the game as well. I do not like the gameplay of Dark Souls.
Everyone praises the game for not holding your hand, and punishing you hard for making mistakes. However, no one ever seems to take the time to point out the glaring flaws in its gameplay. It's as if they designed the animations and controls, THEN designed the world without any forethought of how the player character would interact and react to environmental obstacles. You often find yourself akwardly stuck on a table, rock or torch, fall in bottomless voids, or awkwardly jump toward a ledge at the wrong angle. The game's environments are designed to include many tight corridors and narrow spaces, to make the inclusion of surprise enemies easier to pull off. This becomes awkward because they didn't seem to plan the combat around this. You awkwardly strike the wall and recoil when trying to fight enemies in front of you, causing your sword to degrade 10 times faster than it should for some reason.
I don't have a problem with having a difficult but fair game. Dark Souls is difficult, but it's far from fair. The actual gameplay needs some serious improving. This isn't to say I hate the game, I've spent hours in this game. It just needs some polishing for another sequel.
I would recommend it, but only if you're ready for a challenge and a few BS deaths along the way.

Do not bother with this game. It suffers from horrendously poor coding and lack of developers and employees who actually have a say in what happens to the game on the international release team.
Some issues include not being able to play many of the classes such as those which have cast bars or consume items to use skills because casting is slowed artificially by the poor network code. The skills will take 4-5 seconds longer to do anything even though their cast bars have been full, and in the case of item consumption requirements (most later classes and several early-mid classes), the skill wont cast until the server notices the item has been used (4-5 seconds longer again).
You can expect a 4-5 second delay when interacting with any objects/NPCs in the game as well by the way.
Oh, and some skills, such as Psychokino's Gravity Pole cause the game to crash, which means you won't be finding many parties as that class or others that are similarly broken (you think this is temporary? Go look up how long this gamebreaking issue has been allowed to exist).
Other classes have random incompatibilities with the mouse and keyboard (the two main play modes) control modes such as not being able to turn while using channeling skills in the mouse mode or auto-targetting objects like fireballs as an archer who can't hit them while in keyboard mode (so all your auto attacks fizzle).
Issues beyond coding include free to play players only being able to sell one item at a time on the auction house (at 30% cut), and ALL players (including paying members) having to wait 48 hours to retrieve any sale profits. Silver is otherwise untradable (directly), so players have already begun using materials as currency. Traded equipment and materials either lose potential or become untradable, and many items in the game are untradable to begin with (gems for example).
You have four character slots and there will NEVER be an option to change one of your job classes for any of the 7 ranks that exist for each (eventually will be 10+). If you go X1 - X2 - Y1 - Y2 - Z1 - Z2 - Z3, and any of X, Y, Z get nerfed or just didn't work out for you, you have to remake your character.
You cannot transfer between your own characters without a token (198 TP), and even if you pay for one you can only transfer ONE item at a time (you can expand to 2 for 200,000 silver). Your personal storage is limited to 50 and many items, such as gems, don't stack.
Your gems drop on death and they disappear RAPIDLY, so rapidly that the server lag can sometimes make it impossible to get back in time solely from load screen durations.
You get 5 FREE TP maximum, which can only be used for megaphones, soul crystals (revive on spot), and repair kits. You may as well buy the crystals to avoid gem loss, and you will have to turn off megaphone shout to avoid losing brain cells since everyone using it is begging or spamming nonsense (says a lot about the playerbase).
The main issue that got me was the lack of support when things go wrong, which they will. You will NOT receive useful responses or support on the forums or to your support tickets since there's barely anyone on the international ToS team that can help (they most likely can't even communicate with the developers).
Not convinced? This is a copy of support's reply to the second of two tickets (they skipped the first) some (long) while after their submission:
"Hello Savior,
Thank you for contacting us. Unfortunately lost items or gems due to being dropped when dying in the field are not retrievable if left in the field for a couple of minutes. We advise that you put your gems in your storage for safe keeping, or use a Soul Crystals when you dies in the field to able to retrieve the dropped items immediately.
If you have any other concerns, please do contact us again.
Regards,
Tree of Savior Support Team"
The support tickets were about dying while in load screens and dying while in cutscenes, not about how to keep hundreds of gems in my fifty slot personal storage. But don't worry Saviors, "use a Soul Crystals when you dies in the field" and all will be well.
Ignoring other issues, the game content itself is currently shallow. Tree of Savior would not suddenly become amazing if they addressed all of the problems above. It feels like the game should still be in Alpha, MAYBE early Beta.
Most of the game is typical grind and there is only so much to do at the moment besides that. Max party size is 5, and there really aren't that many dungeons (which you have a limited number of entries to per day anyway). Like Ragnarok Online there are several open world bosses you can TRY to farm for rare gear (which are not nearly as interesting as items in Ragnarok Online and are far fewer in number), and there are also non-instanced dungeons to mess around in. However, this content is not particularly exciting even from the get go, so I can't imagine surviving on this game without deeper content. What's worse, overcrowding makes it so multiple parties are competing for notable farm locations, and all you can do is channel hop (never really helps), leave, or engage in KS wars.
You need someone in your buddy group to make a Templar (Rank 7) if you want to MAKE a guild (they are the only class that can be a guild master; you can't transfer to a different class type). Alternatively you can join someone else's guild for access to guild content (Guild Tower, Guild Wars, Guild Events), but none of said guild or dungeon content even compares to essentially any other well known MMORPG.
If you are interested in PVPing in this game, only horrible imbalance awaits you (worse than Ragnarok Online). There are arena matches from 1v1 to 5v5 in addition to guild wars, but the honest truth is the combat oriented classes aren't even remotely balanced, and I'm not talking about classes being equal for dueling or what not, I am taking into account niches and group play. Hell the stat system itself is broken since damage gains from Strength and Intelligence are severely limited. Only classes in the Cleric branch can heal by the way, not including minor indirect sources of recovery (vampire and increased natural regeneration) limited to a couple classes.
They did try to make a spiritual successor to Ragnarok Online (RO), but the fact is RO still exists. Making a game that is almost the same and only somewhat improving the graphical quality (at the cost of horrible instability; this game does NOT run smoothly) is not really an upgrade. Tree of Savior also has less content than RO even though many aspects were blatantly copied, so having to wait for the game to catch up is not a pleasant thought either.
In 2-3 years could this game be something worth talking about? Yes. Will it? No. As stated, the team behind Tree of Savior, particularly the international release, is not currently capable of ever making that possible. My suggestion is to avoid the game in its current state so that it is not ruined for you forever in case miracle improvements are made down the road.

If I had to give Alien: Isolation a score from 1 to 10, I'd say it deserves a 7/10. This game perfectly captures the aesthetic of Alien/Aliens. As you progress from the starting ship through the bowels of the Sevastopol station, there is the certain analog motif about all the machinery and equipment that surrounds you, from computer workstations to other set pieces such as door switches. This is especially prevalent in the first film. To go into further detail regarding the aesthetic, the feeling of isolation and claustrophobia that the first film conveyed is effectively mimicked in Alien: Isolation. Hallways are dimly lit and tight with a nice ambient lighting affect, mixed with smoke and fog.
The game feels fairly well-optimized. I'm currently running the game through my GTX 1080 Ti at 4k with all settings at their maximum. I also edited the game's config file to allow for a greater resolution for shadow mapping (setting the value to 4096). I keep the game locked to 60fps with VSYNC, and I haven't seen a single frame drop. Before upgrading to the GTX 1080 Ti, I ran the game through my GTX 970 in 1080p with all settings maxed out, also enabling VSYNC. There were no frame drops then either. The graphics look great, and along with things like ambient lighting, the film-grain setting really helps with the film-like aesthetic I mentioned earlier.
Now I'd like to touch on some of the things I didn't like so much about Alien: Isolation. Though the environment certainly captures the aesthetic of the movies, I feel the game was so long that the environments began to feel recycled and repetitive (save a few key areas). In the later chapters of the game, I wanted to begin back-tracking to gather things like ID tags for achievements' sake. Some of these things take what feels like way too much traveling to get to, and to make matters worse, some areas cannot be traveled back to (such as the beginning of Sevastopol). You can go back through by selecting the particular mission the area is included in, so I guess it's not that big of a deal, but still.
Secondly, the Alien gets old after a while. Encountering the Alien is definitely an interesting challenge at first (as it should be - it's the key set piece of the game). However, over time, when you're just wanting to explore the station and look for things like ID tags, it's still there, always lurking. Always having to avoid it and deal with it just gets old after a while. I think this feeds into what I mentioned earlier about the game feeling too long. Along with its ever-presence, the Alien's AI seems to become increasingly buggy as you get closer to the end of the game. Sometimes it'll spring on top of you from a vent without any indication that it's nearby (no drool flowing from the overhead vent or hissing-sounds). There were several instances where the Alien was facing the other direction and I was moving very stealthily, and it still made a bee-line to me. I could repeat these frustrations regarding the Working Joes, as they demonstrate this type of behavior too.
Lastly, the ending is pure, hot, unadulterated crap. It made me question if it was worth playing the game for such a crappy ending. Though I would now answer "yes" to that question, I was still very let down by the ending. The game feels insanely rushed at the end. It's obvious that the team ran out of time/budget, and just had to ship it out the door, which is a shame.
In spite of the negatives, I think the game still offers a lot of redeeming content. The atmosphere and aesthetic is spot on, and the story is compelling (until the end). Despite its flaws, I enjoyed the game, and would recommend it to others with a score of 7.

This is the greatest fun with friends.
First impression:
I spawn on the beach. Not sure what to do, I start hitting trees and crabs with my stick. I eventually come across other players, running around naked. Confused, I attempted to romance a man, alone on the beach. He did not take kindly to my words, and began hitting me with a stick until I died.
Next time, my friend Mike and I spawned on the beach together. He looked like the giant, canadian lumberjack that he is. After explaining the game mechanics I knew to Mike, we ran into the woods together. It soon became dark, and we ran into a wolf. The wolf crippled my legs to the point I could no longer run, and Mike finished the wolf off. thirsty, hungry, and crippled, I directed Mike to try to find some berries. He found them, and immediately ate all but one of them before figuring out how to drop it. We kept walking, and eventually found a light in the dark forest. It turned out to be an abandoned shack, which we took refuge in for the night. But before the night was over, we heard footsteps from outside. Scared, we both stayed quiet and cautious. The man who was outside the building had a strong victorian accent, and asked us, "Do any of you have any wares which you are willing to trade?" We had nothing, but we were both virgins. I quickly offered to him our virginities, to which he responded, "I am not sure I want to deal with such cheap wares. Good luck to you both." and walked away into the night. I looked at my friend Mike, and said, "We survived the night."
Mike then had to eat dinner, and I had to wait for him in the shack. It was then that I was rushed out of the shack by a crazy wooden man with an axe. He proceeded to chase me down until I ran into two other beginner players, and I quickly told them to run for their lives. They did, and scattered. I looked behind me, and the crazy wood man went after one of them. I was scared, I didn't know where my friend was, I became disoriented in the struggle of running. My friend eventually came back from dinner, his character alive. We tried finding each other for the next half hour.
My friend Tug then began the game, and after around 10 minutes, I found him on the beach. He looked like MC Ride. We found two empty houses which were mostly empty except for a wooden armor set, which Tug took before I had the chance. Tug and I, after two attempts at raiding people, tried to set up a base, only to be raided and killed ourselves. All the while, Mike was struggling to find us.
After we respawned on the beach, Tug and I found Mike wandering around, and it was then, that a glorious moment had befallen us.
The Church of the Jig had been born.
We had found the great pleasures that come with pressing the "J" key. We jigged and we jigged, laughed and laughed the day away together. Then, a stranger, a knight in full armor, with a green crescent moon banner walked up to us on the beach. He began to jig with us as well. Then he left. When he came back, he took Tug away with a rope, and tried running from us. This man was in armor; I was naked. I knew I could catch up to him. I began beating the man with the stick that I so lovingly beheld for so long, for this righteous duty: To save a fellow Brother of the Jig.
We began to run away together, but he would have caught us; I knew this to be true. I quickly understood, that the racing aspect is only half, maybe even less, of the game. I learned how to manage my fuel usage. I learned not to destroy my tires with my weird Fast&Furious drifting style. I learned that I needed to switch parts at some point, otherwise my engine just stops mid race. I dont have much racing game experience, basically Need for Speed, Gran Turismo and a few other titles, but not one of these games made me enjoy racing as much as this game. Take one pit stop too many? Say goodbye to your points. Choose the wrong tyres? Well, lets see how you enjoy beeing 4 seconds slower than everyone else. Thought, you could use your old turbocharger? And if you take the time to learn and understand the basics, even as a non-Formula 1 fan, it is very enjoyable.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a masterpiece. A masterpiece of storytelling, a masterpiece of atmosphere, and a masterpiece of thematic depth and cohesion.
What it is not, though, is a masterpiece of game design, simply because it's not a "game." No mechanical skill or special mental acuity are required to succeed. There are no choices to be made that affect the story or its conclusion. This is very much a spiritual successor to Dear Esther (it was designed by the same studio), with only superficial similarities to Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
At its core, The Dark Descent was an old school adventure game, something which I actually didn't like about it. It was incredibly atmospheric, scary, and downright disturbing, but to me the puzzles served as a frequently annoying distraction from exploring the grim and compelling world laid before me.
A Machine for Pigs almost entirely forgoes these game elements and transitions completely to the interactive fiction genre. And what a work of interactive fiction it is. Dear Esther was an extraordinarily well-crafted and moving experience, but AMfP improves on it in every way. The writing is masterful, weaving together themes of guilt, original sin, the duality of man, religion, and socio-political philosophy. The visuals are superb and nearly flawless, although I did find myself frustrated by the lack of reflecting mirrors and more naturalistic fog effects. Minor complaints to be sure, but ever so slightly immersion-breaking nonetheless.
I must also shower composer Jessica Curry with the highest praise. Her work in Dear Esther was breathtaking and here again we find her practicing at the pinnacle of her art. Music is absolutely integral to the success of AMfP. Not only does Curry manage to underscore the emotional significance of each section perfectly, but every cue is also a brilliantly original composition in its own right. Search out Mors Praematura online to hear exactly what I'm talking about. At the risk of sounding overly effusive I'd have to say that this is soundtrack of the year (or decade!) material.
In closing, I think Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a spectacular creative achievement and deserves to be experienced by almost everyone. Yes, it is unusual and is most definitely not a game, nor is it anything like Amnesia: The Dark Descent. As long as you are aware of these facts going in and are able to re-calibrate your expectations early on I guarantee that you're in for a deep, thought-provoking and one of a kind experience.

There are three things Transistor does well, that I shall focus on because I feel that they are the game's strength: mechanical execution, its musical score, and emotional impact.
On the mechanics: this game gives a huge amount of choice in how you play and the style of your fighting. Every 'Function' (think skill or spell for the closest comparison) serves as both an active spell, enhancements for other Functions, or as a passive buff. With thirteen Functions in the game, that is a heck of a lot of choice and customisation. Do you want to pull all of your enemies together, and then blitz them with a powered up AoE? Go ahead. Would you rather turn invisible, and backstab your target for huge damage? Also an option; plan ahead and you maybe be able to do both at the same time. A logical downside to this would be that, once you found a preferred set up, you'd never stray from it, and play every encounter of the game as such. Yes, that would be a problem, if it wasn't that almost everything else in the game is designed to encourage experimentation and variety. Different enemies need different skills to best be destroyed, and every skill has an unlock-able file if used in the three different functions of...the Function.
The only real downside to this is, if you don't really care much for the lore, you won't bother to try all the three combinations (unless it scratches that completion-ist itch). It's more personal whether this is true or not: I was really interested in all the different files and the lore they provided, but I'd understand if they weren't every one's thing.
Overall, combat is satisfying and strategic, and a joy to play. At the very, very least it's definitely different, and not a type of combat style that is regularly seen, if ever, being a mix of real time combat and a sort of turn based combat.
The second strength of the game I won't touch too much on: the music is absolutely great, and I can't think of another word for it. When it has to be, it can be tense and foreboding. When it is needed, it can be calming and enchanting. When it really connects, it sends a shiver down your spine. The main appeal is the fantastic vocals, and the singers and producers deserve all the props they get. I can't really say much else (I'm usually tone deaf at the best of times), but this is the first game I've really been tempted to buy the full soundtrack, so take that how you will.
Finally, emotional impact: this is the combination of the great art/atheistic design, perfectly timed and used music, and the subtle and effective characterisation of our two leads: Red, a singer without a voice, and some one very dear to her, a man without a body. With very few words, they build Red's character, as someone who refuses to turn and run when offered the opportunity, but still one who feels the overwhelming despair that comes from losing a very important part of who they are. Similarly, the man's voice direction and lines are delivered expertly, and you do feel a very genuine love in those words. I remember a line or two that sort of made me stop, and really appreciate just how much chemistry these two have, and how very believable this rather unbelievably likeable duo are.
I'm personally a sucker for subtle characterisation, and this game delivered fantastically.
Overall, I'm so glad I played this game, for the game play, story and characters. I hope that Supergiant know that they have made a real gem of a game.

Okay, the story of how I was introduced to the game is how I started. I was playing Bastion one day, and my friend sends me a link saying: "SuperGiant is making a new game." After learning that fact, I clicked on the link instantly, and I saw the words "Transistor" on the screen. I was confused because I thought this would be a sequel to Bastion. I went along with it anyways. I saw a Lady, dressed in a performer's attire, walk at a slow pace and then, a sword, laying in the ground. She grabs the Sword and her clothes are changed to battle-appropriate gear, if you can call it that. She moves a lot faster now, and the sword says her name, "Red" I can't remember much of the dialogue, but I remember that she eventually had four battle skills. I them see her stop time, and I question what's going on. That's when I learned of what made me absolutely hyped for that game, other than SuperGiant, the "TURN()" function. I watch the entire video, and my hype level reaches 100% after seeing only ~30 minutes of Gameplay.
Okay, music. Beautiful, they bring back the voice of Zia to voice who we can only assume to be Red in some of the music. My favorite track is "Paper Boats", the credits theme. SuperGiant's music is at its best in Credits, hands down.
Visuals, amazing. A different style from Bastion, but again, SuperGiant doesn't only make it work, but makes it something to want the game for. And I am not a graphics ***** at all. While at rare times the buildings would block my sight of enemies, it didn't matter because in TURN() you can see through the buildings.
The Plot is... It's confusing, as with Bastion. The general gist is the Process (The equivalent of the Calamity) has taken over, and you want to end it. The game starts with you in front of a Man who has a Sword that is somewhat like a USB drive. (The USBuster Sword! No, it's the Transistor.) impaled into him. You pull it out and it talks to you. This isn't the sword talking, but the man who was impaled by the blade. Also in the sword is your voice. The sword was meant to kill you, but the man saved you. The Camerata is also apparently trying to stop the Process as well and wants the Transistor so they can do it, but you don't trust them. It's a weird story, but SuperGiant makes it work.
Finally, the Gameplay. As with Bastion, many consider this "a generic hack-and-slash game" and that is further from the truth than saying Bastion is! Throughout the game, you collect functions, your skills. You are allowed 4 with you at a time, and each takes up a certain amount of "data" on the Transistor, depending on how useful they are in battle. Not only is each Function different, but you use the data left to either equip remaining functions to passive slots or upgrade slots. You have a maximum of 32 Data, 4 Passive Slots, and 2 Upgrade slots for each of the four Function slots, allowing for an insane amount of customization, as each function is different depending on which slot they're in. There are also the equivalent of Bastion's idols, Limiters. Each one making the game harder, but you get more experience. There are 10, just the same amount as in Bastion. The perfect finale the this is the TURN() function. It does not go into any of the Function slots, but you have a bar at the top of your screen. That is the "TURN() Meter". When it is fully charged you can activate TURN(), stopping time and allowing you to plan for what to do. You setup your plan, each function taking up a certain amount of space on the meter. When you finish planning, you go out of TURN() and watch your plan play out as you are normal speed while everything else is slowed. (Like the Matrix!)
This game is worth more than its $20 price on the Steam Shop, I would hands-down pay $40 if I had to. Do everyone, yourself included a favor and buy this game. Also, I said earlier I originally wanted a sequel to Bastion, and this provides it, not as a direct sequel, but as a spiritual sequel. Also, its the same Voice Actor for the Narration (The Man in the Transistor) as in Bastion! Hurrah!
This game gets a clear 10/10, no doubt.
So you see my time, not too much right? Well let me tell you, these have been amazing hours. This game is a perfect example of why games are art. It's beautiful in every way.

Papers, Please is a game about the morality of beaurocracy. It's not necessarily fun; in fact, I think it's generally experienced as either mundanely boring or extremely stressful, but it's extraordinarily rewarding. You play as a border checkpoint inspector overseeing the entry of immigrants, returnees, and visitors into a fictionalized analogue of East Berlin under the Soviet Bloc, and the game follows your everyday life in your job over the course of one month. You have a family to feed and the political situation is worsening. On the first day, your job is easy: the checkpoint has just opened, so you only have to let citizens back into the country and keep everyone else out. The next day, the restrictions loosen and foreigners can be let in if they have the correct documentation. Soon terrorist attacks stop your days short and the security requirements tighten. From there, things get complicated.
There's basically two parts to this game: you have to figure out what you're "supposed to" do and what the correct protocol is, and then you have to decide whether or not you should do it. Rigidly following the system of often sexist, transphobic, racist, classist, or just generally heartless beaurocratic policy will leave you facing the human results of those actions, but be too kind and your family will starve or you might be sent to prison. There's 20 different endings reflecting the variety of ways in which your actions can influence the game world, a standard RPG feature these days, but perhaps uniquely all of the most powerful moments in the game come on the way to those endings and not in them. It's a hugely moving and interesting experience, and the utilitarian faux-Soviet aesthetic of the thing never breaks for a second. One of my favourite games of all time.

So a Long while ago I wrote up a review for this game. originally, it was a Thumbs Down. that being said, the game has grown on me after a while. maybe it's a little stockholm syndrome, I dunno.
But heres the thing. after playing through bloodborne, playing the life outta dark souls I then coming back to DS II, I feel it has its own charm. Bloodborne was the successor to Dark souls I wanted. and with that I feel quite satiated, the story doesn't feel convoluted and stupid, item descriptions actually felt connected to the world instead of just a bunch of pronouns with question marks. But, neither game has anywhere near as much spell variety or weapon variety as Dark souls II. It feels like this game was designed, with less focus on the story and interesting boss fights, and more on gameplay.
things like Shield Breaking forces players in pvp to be on the offensive instead of turtling into a corner, invasions would occur actively due to the fact that you never really lose the ability to engage in pvp in an area, regardless if a boss is dead or not.  small soaps, while mostly selfish, would give you the ability to co-op for short commitments.
to end this bubble of ranting, I just want to say that the game has flaws, big ones (bosses are extremely boring. you will never get a story experience like that of Bloodborne, Demon's Souls or Dark Souls I, world is a badly designed mess, lazy level design, soulvessels leading to shortened playtime, disgusting copy-pasta textures in areas that should have recieved the most work) But, if you do it for the PVP or the Co-Op you'll be in for a treat.

Goalposts.
If I could give this game a rating based solely on the atmosphere, it would be 10/10. The art team deserves the awards for this game, and them alone. However, I can disregard some of the bugs, and the setbacks if you are feeling more lenient, especially considering it is a new IP for Creative Assembly, and would love if they were to either create a sequel in some way, OR use the engine to create another similar game, with great atmosphere as well. Taking everything into account, I would give the game a 6/10. If I were to disregard the bugs, and if you take the setbacks as more content, it could be an 8/10.
Pros:
Great Atmosphere, sound, etc.
Cool crafting system
Interesting items (although some, like the flashbang, and revolver are pretty bland and unused)
Love the Idea for a smart AI
Cons:
Alien is not free-roaming. At some parts sure, but he is left out of areas, and forced into some parts. Its pretty dumb when you see him over by a window, and then walk through to find him right in front of you because reasons.
Goalposting. This game would be spectacular..if it was 15hrs shorter. Its understandable that most people appreciate the extra length for more content, but sadly for most this is not the case, and people argue that "ITS JUST CUZ UR NEW-GEN GAMUR B PATIENT GIT GUD". I love stealth games, and being patient and tactical, but anyone who believes sitting in a locker for 30minutes(Yes, you read that right) is flat out wrong (that also falls under the other note, where it feels he isn't unpredictable, and is very obviously sitting in front of the locker because you are there).
The difficulty settings suck. If they made hard mode harder, and normal mode competent, it would be miles better. Easy mode, the alien is a nullfactor, but the bright side is that you find out the Xenomorph is actaully Ray Charles, so theres that. Normal mode is like when you were younger and your mother told you to quiet down because she had work in the morning. You can still walk around and do whatever the ♥♥♥♥ you want, you just gotta keep it down a little. Hard mode is extremely easy at times, and then super tedious during others. I played mildly conservative and still by the end of the game had maxed out on items, and crafting materials. Which sucked because in the later half of the game they become less useful because half of them don't effect the Xenomorph, and the androids start wearing suits that make them immune to everything.
Ending Fkin blows!! Not everyone may agree with this, and to some it may fit. BUT going through all the setbacks, all the "OH this just so happened to convienently blow up right in front of your face-but not enough to kill you-so you need to do an alternative thing now"
just feels like a big slap in the face.
BUGS:
I would give this game a yes if not for the bugs. Here is a list of what I encountered:
-Flamethrower sound bug; You will hear a rattling jug sound for no reason as if you had the flamethrower equipped, but you don't.
-Floating gun bug; a random gun from your arsenal will be floating around in the air away from you, and can be seen behind walls.
-Alien got moves; I could kinda give it a plus to see the alien moonwalking across the room backwards, so if thats your sort of thing by all means, count this one as that.
-Alien is actually nightwalker; the alien will be walking past the desk you are hidden under, then suddenly teleport right in front of your face (im practically french kissing his second mouth) prowling down, and murder you.
-Xenomorph.exe has stopped working; The Xeno will detect you (you will hear the audible screech) but he will continue walking past as if he didn't..and then WAM he teleports in front of you-like the last bug-but this time he will just stare you down, making the nosie that he detected you and is after you.
-Bullet time; The game will randomly crash, but more importantly there are times when if you aim and fire a gun (happened to me multiple times with the shotgun) it will just crash immediately, for no reason at all.
-Finger Pistol; If you aim with a weapon, and then use your scroll wheel to hotswap to another one, you will no longer see the gun, and instead just see her hands aiming/holding them. That, or this was put in on purpose, and Ripley simply transcended the need for weapons, and uses her hands for guns now.
Fantastic game! Not good for your overall health, though.

While many may find this game unsatisfying, I think that it has a great atmosphere and story, even if it is difficult to follow.  I was also decently scared by it, but others may not be as scared as me.  I reccomend this as a game that you should take somewhat seriously, because the story is the most important element of it.  Some games are for some people, though, and not everyone (as shown by other reviews) will like this game.  That's the way The Chinese Room does it. Finally, this game is not very similar to Amnesia: The Dark Descent in the realm of survival horror.

Atmosphere.
For any kind of horror game the most important factor is its atmosphere. Without it, games such as Silent Hill, Resident Evil, and Dead Space wouldn’t have been so memorable or horrific and would have just been regular games with some creepy zombies and monsters. Fun yes, but not terrifying or enough to keep your blood pumping and your heart racing. But when it comes to atmosphere in Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs? This game has it.
From the dark and gloomy lighting to the various background noises, or lack thereof at times, I was on the edge of my seat throughout the entire game. Always expecting something to jump out at me, I traversed through the various rooms of the mansion, factory, sewers, tunnels, and other locations – all of which looks great thanks to the graphics that add little touches such as lighting effects, fog, and debris.
The story was much better than A Machine for Pigs’ predecessor Amnesia: The Dark Descent, likely due to the collaboration between Frictional Games and Dear Esther developer The Chinese Room. I found it to be more intriguing as I wandered through the game and learned more about the character and the tragic events that transpired. I started to learn more about what had happened to the children and the factory, among other things, as I progressed through a mixture of reading journals, flashbacks, and narrated scenes (where the voice acting was great). These revelations continued to enhance the dark, gloomy, and horrifying atmosphere.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger has an old-west whiskey soaked narrative that rises above its arcade style FPS shooting and absolutely steals the show.
My good buddy, fellow The F Plus podcast participant, and United Gaming Clans TF2 superstar Frank West was kind enough to buy a copy of this game for me in exchange for a review, and how could I say no to that face? (By the way: Visit thefpl.us for horrifying things read with enthusiasm. No, I don't care about ethics in gaming journalism.)
So when I booted up Call of Juarez: Gunslinger for the first time, I noticed two things:
1: Oh, hey, the protagonist is narrating his story as I am shooting the bad guys.
2: Hold up, wait a minute. Techland made this? Dead Island Techland?
Yep, the same guys who made Dead Island made this. And I'm pretty surprised with how it turned out, given that Techland is known lately for making ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (like Dead Island, Dead Island: Riptide, Escape Dead Island), and the sequel that nearly killed this franchise dead: Call of Juarez The Cartel. Despite The Cartel being a pile of garbage with a cowboy hat on the top, Call of Juarez lived to fight another day, and I'm so glad it did because it resulted in Gunslinger. (It's not without its share of dumb visual design decisions, such as the quick-time bullet event happening when you've shot a cowboy to death and another dude shoots a killing shot that passes through his body and only appears through the other side when it's too ♥♥♥♥ing late to decide when to dodge. Or that entire level where you're fighting underneath a railroad bridge, where the shadows and the daylight contrast into this visually horrid mess that made my eyes cross.)
All the FPS elements here are solid, but what makes the game really stand out is that Silas Greaves (the dude you're playing as) is telling the story of his blood-soaked career as a bounty hunter. The entire game is framed through Silas's recollection and storytelling as he's sitting there, getting loaded in a bar while skeptics and dime-store novel junkies hang on his every word and call his story out at points. For a moment, one of the people listening to his story says that the Pinkertons were fighting the same train robbers as he was, and the Pinkertons arrive to help Silas. But then, he says "I've been there, I fought all those goddamn train robbers all by myself with no goddamn Pinkertons", and like that, The Pinkertons vanish. He embellishes, and we are him, fighting through his embellishments, with every kill and room clearing adding to his story. He gets progressively drunker through the game, and with every drink, his story becomes more outlandish and less believeable, and up until the end, I kept trying to figure out whether his story was real or not. The developers kind of tip their hand at the end, which kind of ruined it for me, but it's not like that invalidated the previous five hours of game I had played through, so who cares?
Gunslinger is tons of fun, like being told a story by your grandfather, but IN VIDEO GAME FORM.

Transistor is the second game from Bastion developer Super Giant Games, and it is another exceptionally crafted artistic RPG.
In Transistor you play the role of Red, a beautiful and talented musician who has seemingly lost her voice.  The game begins with Red pulling a sword like device known as the Transistor out of the chest of a dead man.  Immediately the Transistor begins talking to Red as if it knows her.  The voice of the Transistor is how we learn what's going on in this abandoned ghost town of a city called Cloudbank.   Much like the narrator in Bastion comments on the situation of Caelondia, the Transistor will talk to Red about things happening in Cloudbank.  It seems Super Giant Games really has a thing for mysterious apocalyptic events that wipe out flourishing cities.
Not only is the Transistor your talking guide through the game it's also a very powerful tool and weapon.   In the beginning the Transistor only has two functions loaded into it, thus giving you two different attack options.  As you level up you'll unlock   more functions, function upgrade slots, and passive function slots.  The function customization and use is incredibly deep and fun to experiment with as you explore combinations to fit your play style.  It really makes the combat an enjoyable sandbox of trial by fire.
Every function in the game has 3 optional ways of using it in the Transistor.  The first use is an Active attack and used to directly afflict damage or other debuffs on the enemies.   The second use is an upgrade slot to an existing Active attack.  This will add extra abilities to your attacks.   The final use is a passive slot which will grant you various buffs or abilities that are always active.  With 16 different functions to unlock, and each having 3 ways to potentially use them, you can see the amount of customization gets exponential.  And even more in new game plus when it allows you to unlock another copy of an already used function.
Using the functions in the variety of ways will also reward the story loving fanatics.  Each function you discover is linked to one pronounced citizen of Cloudbank, and as you use the functions in combat you'll unlock background information regarding their history.  It's a fun way to learn more about the story and reward players for trying new combinations of function loadouts.
While the story of Transistor may seem eerily similar to Bastion the combat game play is quite different.  Arguably Transistor can be played in the same real time hack-n-slash style of Bastion, but in all likelihood you'll be using the strategic pause mode for most battles.  This mode feels like a turn based strategy game.   When combat is paused you are shown a progress bar of action points to spend.  Every movement, every function will use up action points until the bar is full.   This allows you to plan out your attack before committing to the plan.  Once you execute a plan you'll see all your attacks played out in real time.  You'll then need to fight in real time as you wait for the cool down timer on strategic mode.  It really is a good balance of real time and turn based combat.
The thing I loved most about Bastion was it's story, soundtrack and art direction, and once again with Transistor they delivered.   A hauntingly desolate city again brought to life by beautiful landscapes and enchanting music you'll be humming along the way with Red.
While it may be relatively short it has replay value in new game plus, just to try more function combos.  If you enjoyed Bastion then you'll find Transistor worthy of a play.

This is a Sci-Fi Tactical RPG set in the luxurious neighborhood of a city. The RPG part is the usual leveling and acquiring of various attacks and abilities. The tactical side has you planning your moves and attacks during your 'turn' and during 'their turn' you run away. An interesting aspect in this game is that any ability can be used as an active ability, A passive ability or as an enhancement to an active ability. Gives a lot of different combinations to play with and the game encourages you to try them all out. It's also the main reason I'm considering playing again immediately. Something I rarely do.
Story wise, You're Red, A super pop star, and something bad happens. Fortunately your over-sized all-purpose weapon talks to you and fills you in on what's going on. Well, The talking stick doesn't tell you everything. A lot of background is given through text and I found the setting it painted compelling. So much so that I wanted to explore and experience more of the city. I kind of interpreted that as a reflection of Reds' yearning for a part of her life that has been interrupted. I saw the fatalistic vibe as Reds' also.
Visually the city is pleasing, clean and precise. While the more personal moments are done in a nice watercolor style. The music, Except for one stand out song, seems mostly ambient. Though there are some excellent subtle things done to the music, I wished it wasn't so subtle. Something to save for the next game perhaps.
Overall, While the gameplay is excellent, The narrative seems more like an interesting experiment if not entirely successful. But I'll be there for SuperGiants next game sight unseen.

Transistor: Endgame(ish) Review
(TL:DR Quick 'n' Dirty Version: GOTY 2014 candidate, right here. Get it, get the soundtrack. Go. Now. )
This is the best game I've played all year. $29AUD is a steal for the game and music; I think an experience with such stunning visuals, a magical soundtrack, brilliantly innovative customisation and a heartbreakingly moving ending is worth at least twice that price. I couldn't wait to do it all over again.
Transistor is a gem of an isometric turn-based♥♥♥♥♥realtime hack'slash action RPG, set in a gorgeous cyberpunk "anime deco" environment. You're thrown right in; Red, a singer in Cloudbank, finds herself in possession of the Transistor, a giant swordlike object which has stolen her voice and entrapped the personality of a man whose chest she has to pull it out of. The enemy? The Process: robots controlled by the mysterious Camerata who are attempting to take over everything. Our heroine shoulders the weapon intended to kill her, and sets off to make things right...
The hand-drawn style so popular with Bastion (Supergiant's previous game, which I haven't played...yet) is used to great effect in this sumptuous, futuristic world that has a touch of anime blended with cyberpunk and art deco aesthetics. Apparently, early anime artists took their inspiration from Disney cartoons; you'll notice the adorable Red looks like Ariel from The Little Mermaid! Every so often, the game presents you with touching, humorous visual vignettes of Red and the Transistor taking a break from the action; they make quite a pair, and these brief cut-scenes allow you to appreciate the artwork a little more.
Red isn't quite your typical silent protagonist. Though unable to speak, the gorgeous girl in the golden gown can hum along to the soundtrack, which closely ties in with the game's events and enhances the narrative. Darren Korb's soundtrack includes "voiced" versions of the songs, sung by Ashley Barrett, as well as the hummed versions and instrumentals. It's a haunting, beautiful blend of traditional and electro sounds that complements the visuals perfectly and won't leave your head for a while - especially the damned Sandbox music!
The real strength of this game is the sheer number of combinations with which you can outfit the Transistor. Each "function" - powers unlocked at various points in the game - can be equipped actively, used as an upgrade to augment an active function, or passively. This mechanic isn't explicitly spelled out; instead, players get to discover what works for themselves. Wide use of functions also unlocks the back-stories of NPCs, so there's an incentive to switch things around. Access points scattered through Cloudbank allow regular and quick tweaking of the Transistor, so you're never stuck with any one loadout for long. I've never seen this fantastic mechanic in any other game, and I hope to see more of it.
So -  the gameplay, imagery and sound are all exceptional. What about the story?
It affected me more profoundly than the ending of Bioshock Infinite.
I can't believe I just typed that - but it's true.
Infinite just scored 9th in Good Game's Top 100 games of all time, as voted by Australian gamers. We all know the game was praised for its story, but a strong narrative can only exist if we care about the characters and feel invested in their relationship as it unfolds. Mass Effect 2 - which beat Mass Effect 3 (Thank goodness!) and ranked 11th, is another great example of this. Red's relationship with her sword seems destined to go down as one of gaming's greats thanks to brilliant characterisation and voice acting.
----------------------------------Spoilers for Transistor and Bioshock Infinite follow.
Just like with Booker and Elizabeth, I was fascinated by the dynamic between Red and the Transistor, whom we hear almost exclusively throughout the game. And just like it was obvious (I thought anyway) that Booker was Elizabeth's father, It's obvious from the get-go that the man inside the Transistor is Red's boyfriend, and his primary concern is keeping her safe. They hit the nail right on the head with the voice acting; there's a tenderness in the Transistor's voice that is really touching. Funny, supportive and more than a bit mansplainy, the Transistor speaks to Red exactly like my husband speaks over my shoulder when he's watching me play games! Trapping your other half in a giant sword might not be such a bad idea. It's all the more emotional given that Red can't reply; one gets the feeling through her silence, and the way she cradles the Transistor when she's not slinging it around, that she cares about this guy deeply. This is confirmed when she eventually sacrifices herself to be with him. I was unprepared for the impact the Romeo-and-Juliet style ending would have, and I wasn't expecting it even though I was warned... I actually had tears in my eyes as the end credits started. I'm not sure if they were tears of sadness (because the awesome game was finished!) or tears of happiness for the ending itself and what it meant for the two characters.
---------------------------------------------------------End spoilers.
If Transistor doesn't win Indie Game of the Year 2014, or even GOTY 2014 outright, there is no justice in this world. I really couldn't fault anything with this game and I'm looking forward to multiple playthroughs. And now - shouldn't you be starting your first one?

Many people say that F1 2017 is a reskin of the previous game but it really isn't.  The handling especially when using a controller feels more measured.  It's not snapping at me and you can get a good sense of when the tires are beginning to slip.  The increased mechanical grip and downforce is felt quite readily.  I have to also say I was glad to find that it supports the Xbox trigger impulse vibration which not many games do readily which also helps you guage how close to the limit you are. You feel like you can really attack in the corners now.  You cannot really compare this game to Project Cars, Forza or any other big named racing game.  F1 is quite niche and what is here, is done well in realtion to the sport.
Graphics wise is a bit of a mixed bag.  There has been an update to the track surfaces, the grass and gravel traps as well as the building especially in Baku however there are a few things that are distracting.  There is no option to run SMAA or MSAA now.  There is only temporal filtering which should make objects that are in motion look better - here it doesn't.  Combine that with the motion blur, it looks like a real smudgy affair at mid to high speeds.  I feel that there is also something off with the lighting which I am guessing due to the HDR compatability.  I don't run a HDR monitor (it's good a great contrast ratio though) to see whether the blown out highlights are due to this.   I feel that maybe reworking the anti aliasing for a sharper image is in need here.
The career feels more in depth and from the outset, there is more of a sense that you should invest wisely in upgrades (as the parts can fail in development now) and the immersion factor of interacting with the other characters feels much more lifelike compared to the previous games.  The computer AI feels a lot better as well.  I typically run the difficulty medium to highest and the AI does actually push you on higher levels.  They also tend to be more aggressive as numerous times I have been run off the road or battled with the leaders.  Yes there is an issue with the parts wear but I have to admit that I drive quite smoothly most of the time so don't have too many problems myself, but it is something that needs to be balanced as many have cried out for it.  The system itself is a great addition as it does make you think a little more strategically about how you are going to race.  Are you going to go flat out and risk a part (or three) failing or are you going to play it safe at the cost of research points and your place in the driver standings.
There are a lot of positives but it echos what I said about Dirt 4.  It is a great start and although F1 doesn't lack as noticably in terms of content (like Dirt), there are bugs, glitches and apparent oversights that a quick look on the community hub will show.  My faith in the devs is being tested but the game on the whole is/will be fantastic once those bugs are sorted!

Papers, Please is a game about the morality of beaurocracy. It's not necessarily fun; in fact, I think it's generally experienced as either mundanely boring or extremely stressful, but it's extraordinarily rewarding. You play as a border checkpoint inspector overseeing the entry of immigrants, returnees, and visitors into a fictionalized analogue of East Berlin under the Soviet Bloc, and the game follows your everyday life in your job over the course of one month. You have a family to feed and the political situation is worsening. On the first day, your job is easy: the checkpoint has just opened, so you only have to let citizens back into the country and keep everyone else out. The next day, the restrictions loosen and foreigners can be let in if they have the correct documentation. Soon terrorist attacks stop your days short and the security requirements tighten. From there, things get complicated.
There's basically two parts to this game: you have to figure out what you're "supposed to" do and what the correct protocol is, and then you have to decide whether or not you should do it. Rigidly following the system of often sexist, transphobic, racist, classist, or just generally heartless beaurocratic policy will leave you facing the human results of those actions, but be too kind and your family will starve or you might be sent to prison. There's 20 different endings reflecting the variety of ways in which your actions can influence the game world, a standard RPG feature these days, but perhaps uniquely all of the most powerful moments in the game come on the way to those endings and not in them. It's a hugely moving and interesting experience, and the utilitarian faux-Soviet aesthetic of the thing never breaks for a second. One of my favourite games of all time.

Multiplayer support and quick load times.
Cons....

To sum it up...

Factorio is a great game and I do recommend it, to a certain point. I've gotten to the point in my life where video games just don't feel the same anymoire, and it takes a really amazing game to get me addicted and playing for hours without getting bored. Factorio was that game. I played it through the night and didn't stop, something I haven't done for over a decade. There is always something to do, always something to keep up with and manage and, while it can be overwhelming at times (especially when your base starts being attacked by aliens A LOT), is always satisfying in the end. Also, the learning curve is very smooth in the beginning. Crafting is simple and the machines you use to build your base are easy to use in creative ways. HOWEVER, the farther you make it through the game, the steeper the learning curve gets. I look at all the new things I need to craft and I don't know how any of them work. Yes, I could look it up and learn every single thing to learn about this game, but to me, that overwhelming learning curves ruins the experience and turns me off to playing the game again.
TL;DR: The game is amazing. When you build a world, you most likely won't stop playing for at least the first six hours. After that point however, when your world becomes more advanced and you get closer and closer to end game, the learning curve steepens tremendously. Whether it's worth it to you is your choice, and I may come back to learn everything (that's how truly addicting this game is), but for right now, the curve is too much.

It took Frictional Games a couple of tries to perfect their take on survival horror. The original Penumbra (2007) was original and nicely atmospheric, but flawed due to its atrocious combat. I get that they were going for difficult mechanics to make the player favour flight over fight, but I felt that their efforts back fired and hurt the game over all. The sequel (2008) fixed what was wrong with the original, and made for an excellent experience, and its famous spiritual successor, the outstanding Amnesia: The Dark Descent (2010) finally got the devs the acclaim that they deserved.
It should be of no surprise then that when it was announced that the provocatively titled Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs was to be developed by The Chinese Room (famous for their intriguing interactive poem Dear Ester (2012), I was plenty excited.  Whilst the game they released certainly contained the excellent prose and visuals they introduced to us with their former game, I was disappointed to find A Machine for Pigs played out like a rather dull ghost train, rather than the panicky terror Frictional had accustomed me to. The entire experience was over in a few short hours, there was only two enemy encounters, and dying had no consequence other than to mysteriously erase my foe.
I’m not at all against games being presented as a linear art piece to simply immerse yourself in and ride out, but when I was expecting this title to be consistent with its predecessors, I was left entirely disappointed. I imagine that I would have enjoyed my time in the belly of the beast far more had the title not bore the Amnesia moniker. This situation reminds me of the film Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within (2001) earning a hostile reaction for not feeling like a Final Fantasy adaptation (no, calling a character Cid is not enough).

Amnesia A Machine for Pigs text review edit:
To conclude, Amnesia A Machine for Pigs is an unusual gaming experience  that races the pulse in a more psychological manner as opposed to direct in your face scares, and with its excellent use of audio is definitely a game to play with headphones on and the lights off.  Despite a lack of pace, the game does a fine job of drawing players in, but the only let down here is that perhaps the entire premise of the main character is a little cliche.
Whilst the execution is admirable, a lack of replay and overall length might deter some players and prevents the game from receiving top marks; it's also not a game that's going to universally appeal to all gamers. If you like a more subdued gaming experience, then this is worth checking out. If you're more hands on this might leave you a little unfulfilled. Whilst there's a very good game here at heart, the question remains, is it worth the price of entry. A horror without horror. Despite this terrible contradiction, A Machine for Pigs loses nothing by getting rid of its main feature. Even being much closer to an interactive novel rather than to a horror game, it's almost as tense as before - all thanks to the cunning narration and that great setting it uses.
Although it's a bit frustrating that the game has lost a great part of its interactivity, leaving all the credits to the plot. The player is here to pull some triggers and watch the story, not to be an actual part of it. Not a big deal, but still.
So, Amnesia's choice now is to become a story-driven thriller. If it seems to be fine with you, there's nothing else to complain about. In other cases, it would be better to take a closer look at Outlast.

A word that comes to mind is disappointment. After the success of The Dark Descent, I expected nothing but further improvement upon the Amnesia series. However, with Frictional games taking the backseat as the publisher this time and allowing The Chinese Room to take over, disaster struck. The Chinese Room have morphed this Survival Horror game into an interactive horror story. Unlike The Dark Descent, the few puzzles there are provide no challenge. The lantern is infinite this time around, however you do not truly need it anyways, as there are no real moments in the game where you are completely unable to see without it. There are no tinderboxes, as most of the game is lighted anyways. In fact, there is no inventory system whatsoever. The only real "gameplay" in this unworthy successor is walking around to find the next exit, and occasionally strafing to avoid a monster that this time around isn't very scary at all, since they are dehumanized and you soon start to feel sorry for them rather than afraid. Letting The Chinese Room take the wheel on this one was a huge mistake, as this is no longer a game, but a walkthrough with the occasional scary atmosphere.

I really liked Amnesia: "The Dark Descent" and I don't think "A Machine for Pigs" has quite the same atmosphere that I enjoyed with the Dark Descent. However, it is still a fun game none the less. I'm hoping the game will start to have a more creepy feel as I get further along in the game.

(First Impression) The background and ambient of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is more sinister than it's predecesor. It keeps me with more suspense. Though I admit the first appearance of my "pursuer" didn't impress me much. I stood a while in front of *it* in the darkness and then runed to safety. Don't get me wrong, this game will keep you in suspense and uncertanity. I will update when I reach the end game.

I don't get why people are hating on this game. I personally felt it ws beautifully crafted by the hands of a small group of clearly passionate individuals who wanted to offer a different, immersive, and story driven title with a backbone of suspense. No, you don't blow off the heads of zombies or exagerate your way through a maze of bullets and fire. This game isn't meant to be a typical, run of the mill shooter. In fact, the sole reason for a first person perspective is to offer a perspective from the protagnist. It really sucks you into a wonderfully dark world. I was on the edge of my seat throughout gameplay, never expecting what was going to scream at me from the corner or grind from above. The complexity of the machine you explore, followed by the well-written plot, crystal detailed graphics, and whimsical voice acting, makes this game a gem in todays market. I recommend it for anyone who wants an atmospheric and progressive story with a twist of horror and symbolism. This game will make you think and it will make your heart thump from time to time. Give it a whirl, it's really not all that expensive, and you will be supporting a wonderful team of people I feel should continue working on such quality content.
As for those of you who played the first one, along with me, your in for a treat. The team defintley wanted to offer a different taste in the Amnesia universe. Your going to love it.

Dark Souls 2 doesn't actually exist. This game only displays the title, but it isn't a sequel to Dark Souls.
A sequel, in my opinion, is supposed to be a game that improves and expands upon the original, while still retaining the original's basic feel. New mechanics may be introduced, but they have to be interesting and also fit into the game's world and design for them to work.
This game doesn't do any of that.
What it does, is put a bunch of Dark Souls and Demon's Souls references in a world that feels more like a (bad) attempt at recreating TESV: Skyrim, rather than being its own, original idea.
Honestly, the level design in this is pretty forgettable. The bosses have multiple similarities between them, to the point where you have a hard time distinguishing between them (giant guy with giant weapon, unformed disgusting blob, random decomposing monster, etc.), and are really easy to beat even solo, except of course for THOSE bosses where, just for the sake of making them hard, there are a bunch of enemies together with the boss, constantly running towards you, that you have to deal with in addition to the main enemy.
About the multiplayer. The PvP is bad, there's just no other way to describe it. Those far away hits that in Dark Souls only happen while playing against distant people with unstable internet connection? Here happened all the time, every single time. Those sudden teleportations, once every year in Dark Souls? Here it's been one out of three matches.
You have to wonder how the netcode got worse, three years later...
Now for the funny part.
The store page for Dark Souls warns you that it is strongly recommended to be played with a controller, yet it's perfectly playable even with mouse&keyboard, after rebinding some keys to your liking.
This game, which ironically doesn't warn you of anything, is exhausting to play with m&k, first because of the natural (intended?) unresponsiveness of the controls, but mainly due to massive input lag generated by the (completely useless) double-click setting. Even though that can be disabled in the in-game options, the setting doesn't actually save between playing sessions and needs to be reset everytime the game is launched. I'm not kidding.
At the end of the day, this is a pretty bad game. It destroyed what makes Dark Souls an interesting game, it didn't improve upon the things Dark Souls lacks.
I think the reason nobody plays this anymore is because only someone who is new to the series (and to the genre) would actually like this and keep playing after the first time. Or maybe it's because the Scholar of the First Sin remaster killed the playerbase by splitting the community... yeah, that might be it. Lol.

Plantera is an idle game, which means that the game will somewhat progress while you do nothing and even, up to a point, when it is closed.
Idle games have to walk a thin line between making the player feel useless (in which case the game is actually a screensaver) and having very little idle progress (in which case the game is not much of an idle game). Plantera works that thin line rather well, giving the player incentive to interact with its colorful garden, but also progressing on its own.
The point here is to grow plants and raise animals. You can reap the results yourself or let your blue workers do it for you. Critters (rabbits, foxes, wolves and birds) will try to snatch your stuff, though thankfully they never attack the animals, so they never take your progress back. You can either scare the critters away by clicking on them or invest in scarecrows and dogs.
If you've spent time on idle games like Cookie Clicker, Time Clickers and the like, you will probably like Plantera. Just beware that the game is on the short side.
If you've never played an idle game before, I would advise you to try some of the free ones to see if you like the concept before buying one, Plantera included.

TLDR:The game is quite fun. Large world, lots of quests, lots of stories.   However, it is getting a thumbs down because of clunky handling through steam (don't get it through steam!), frequent crashes and server problems, not something I would expect for a mature MMO.
The Review: Updated 7/30/2017
Guilds: The game allows a player to be in up to 5 guilds. I have hoined only one guild, and it functions as expected, complete with guild chat, guld bank, and guild store.  The only thing missing is a guild house, which apparently is not a thing.  No big loss there, as guild leaders home can act as a guild house, and guild housing always seemed pointless.
Player Count:  Lots of people seem to be playing in all zones.
Story Telling:  Story telling is pretty good, lots of voice acting, but it could use a larger cast of actors.
Solo Friendly:  Most quests are solo friendly, but faster with a group.  You get credit for mob kills/quest completion as long as you help.  Not sure what the limits are, there a few times when I arrived right at the end, got off a couple of shots and got no credit, but most of the time I get credit for a kill, even if it was a token effort.
PVP friendly:  This game has open world PVP in Cyrodill, and imperial city (and one other zone), as well as arenas.  Imperial city was pretty much empty when I went there.  Cyrodill, however was always busy.  There are several versions of Cyrodill available depending upon your level, so you can jump in at level 10.  You will die a lot, but then you will die a lot anyway... For me, the open world realm v realm (three realms) is quite entertaining, and a highlight of the game.  I'm not a fan of arena's so can't comment on it.
Level Friendly:  Game auto adjusts player and/or monster so you can have a fun experience in any zone at any level.  It does the same thing in PVP and dungeons.
Leveling System:  You have standard levels 1-50, after 50 you accumulate champion points which buy buffs and powers that affect all the characters in your account.  The champion system goes quite high, but gear stops leveling at 160.  For me, champion points up to 100 went ridiculously fast and didn't seem to slow down until I hit about 105.  The consequence of this is that getting 'good' gear has been pretty much a waste of time as it is outleveled so fast.  After 100 leveling is brisk, but not ridiculously so.  My advice is to save any XP scrolls you get (from game purchase) until you notice your champion point gains slowing down.
Crafting:  Crafting system is pretty complex.  Luckily there are mods (yes mods are legal) that can help keep things organized.  Don't expect to be on par with veteran players anytime soon, no matter how much effort you put into crafting, armor and weapons have 9 traits, each trait takes longer than the one before it, and making some top-end gear requires knowing all 9 traits.  It can take the better part of a (real life) year to research all traits.
In retrospect, I wish I had not purchsed through Steam.  Steam has to be running just to launch the game, and if you want to subscribe you have to do so through Steam (and they don't seem to handle that very well).  Instead of dealing with one company and one online system you have to deal with two.  Frankly Steam just gets in the way and makes things more cumbersome than necessary.

Dark Souls 2 doesn't actually exist. This game only displays the title, but it isn't a sequel to Dark Souls.
A sequel, in my opinion, is supposed to be a game that improves and expands upon the original, while still retaining the original's basic feel. New mechanics may be introduced, but they have to be interesting and also fit into the game's world and design for them to work.
This game doesn't do any of that.
What it does, is put a bunch of Dark Souls and Demon's Souls references in a world that feels more like a (bad) attempt at recreating TESV: Skyrim, rather than being its own, original idea.
Honestly, the level design in this is pretty forgettable. The bosses have multiple similarities between them, to the point where you have a hard time distinguishing between them (giant guy with giant weapon, unformed disgusting blob, random decomposing monster, etc.), and are really easy to beat even solo, except of course for THOSE bosses where, just for the sake of making them hard, there are a bunch of enemies together with the boss, constantly running towards you, that you have to deal with in addition to the main enemy.
About the multiplayer. The PvP is bad, there's just no other way to describe it. Those far away hits that in Dark Souls only happen while playing against distant people with unstable internet connection? Here happened all the time, every single time. Those sudden teleportations, once every year in Dark Souls? Here it's been one out of three matches.
You have to wonder how the netcode got worse, three years later...
Now for the funny part.
The store page for Dark Souls warns you that it is strongly recommended to be played with a controller, yet it's perfectly playable even with mouse&keyboard, after rebinding some keys to your liking.
This game, which ironically doesn't warn you of anything, is exhausting to play with m&k, first because of the natural (intended?) unresponsiveness of the controls, but mainly due to massive input lag generated by the (completely useless) double-click setting. Even though that can be disabled in the in-game options, the setting doesn't actually save between playing sessions and needs to be reset everytime the game is launched. I'm not kidding.
At the end of the day, this is a pretty bad game. It destroyed what makes Dark Souls an interesting game, it didn't improve upon the things Dark Souls lacks.
I think the reason nobody plays this anymore is because only someone who is new to the series (and to the genre) would actually like this and keep playing after the first time. Or maybe it's because the Scholar of the First Sin remaster killed the playerbase by splitting the community... yeah, that might be it. Lol.

I'm changing my review of this game, because in hindsight it's a little bitter of me to not reccomend a fun game just because I think the pvp in the first game was loads better. The pve is great. It's Dark Souls. Everyone loves Dark Souls. Unless you hate Dark Souls, in which case you probably REALLY hate Dark Souls. Why are you even here?
Anyway, like I said, I think they messed up the pvp, and actually even the co-op. Admittedly it's been a while since I played, and the might have changed stuff with the dlc, but I doubt the core mechanics have changed significantly.
-Soul memory. This was a mistake in my eyes. There's no point in running min-max builds for pvp at a certain level range, which I thought was half the fun of pvp in places like anor londo in DS1. You can still do it in this game, but since you're constantly gaining more souls from pvp, the enemies you fight will constantly be getting stronger even if you choose to limit your own level.
-In additon, this also messed up how I liked to play helper characters. In ds1, I liked to make a character and lock it in a specific level range to help carry people though harder bosses. You can do that in this game too, but since you'll be killing the boss over and over and getting souls, you will eventually be locked out of the usual level ranges that people need help at due to soul memory increasing.
-Poise doesn't do anything; Barehanded punches can and do stagger you in full havels. Using shields will get you killed because of the ability to do laughably easy shield breaks that not only stagger you but set you up for a crit riposte. Together it makes fatroller heavy builds completely worthless which ruined how I liked to play pvp. I really didn't like how the game forced you into one of a few viable light builds for pvp.
It's griping about one aspect of the game, I know. But the multiplayer is what gave ds1 longevity for me, and conversely what made me set this game down after I had gone through the story. Individual experiences may vary. Praise the sun.
