OK, I don't write a lot of reviews, but having come across this little gem, I thought I should. I got this game reduced, and it's one of the best £2.49 I've ever spent. I happen to pretty much agree with the PC Gamer review and rating, though I liked the story more than they did. It's quirky and the frequent 'hold on, rewind' moments were actually often amusing and didn't jar with the flow. Pro'd and cons?
Pro's
Cheap and good value for money, esp. at the price I got it.
Enough choice, outside of the linear route of each level, such as skills and weapons. The game is relatively short (21 hours to complete for me) so too many guns etc. would have been overkill.
Graphics while somewhat simple (and often re-used) are quite evocative of the era, so I actually liked them. Almost like playing through a comic book.
Dialogue was OK, and pretty well characterised.
Quick fire (aka bullet time) was pretty well executed, though I didn't find the need to use it too often.
Cons
Short! But you gets what you pays for...
Music got a bit annoying after a while. needs more variety.
Too often relied upon instant reactions. I prefer a game to allow me to choose to go in all guns blazing OR creep up on my opponents (Sniper Elite 2/3 for example). On the other hand, it's the wild west so maybe there's a limit to how much stealth you can employ!
I wouldn't buy DLC as this is already a short game, but I'd be interested in a more rounded and longer sequel if there's one in the offing. Makes me hope Red Dead Redemption is coming to PC after all!

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a dumbed down version of Amnesia: The Dark Descent (which was a dumbed down version of the Penumbra games itself).
TDD was still a good game and some of its changes were improvements over Penumbra (less clunky controls to name just one).
The same CAN NOT be said about AMfP: The developers managed to remove everything from the game that made its predecessors fun without adding anything new in return, leaving behind only an empty husk of a game.
There is no exploration in AMfP because it's extremely linear with virtually no alternative routes whatsoever.
The hand lamp burns on forever and the inventory has been removed completely, so there's no resource management throughout the game either.
The very few puzzles in the game are barely worth that name; they are almost insultingly easy and rarely more than using a picked up item at the end of linear corridor #134.
On top of the game's linearity the monster encounters are, for the most part, heavily scripted and mostly consist of monsters moving in the shadows far away from the player - there are less than a handful ares in the game with free-roaming enemies where the player can actually get hurt.
The following paragraph is about game mechanics, not AMfP's story. It can still potentially spoil the game's beginning to some degree, I guess. Therefore I put it in spoiler tags; you might want to skip it if you're planning to play the game sometime.
So, to sum it up: there is not much actual gameplay in Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, it is hardly a game at all.
That doesn't
has to be a bad thing. The same thing can probably be said about Telltale's The Walking Dead, but TWD makes up its lack of gameplay with a very well told story.
However AMfP isn't very good storywise either: It's full of horror-pulp stereotypes, making it very predictable, and towards the end the story gets completely lost in a pile of pretentious symbolism.
Not much is missed by skipping AMfP completely. If you liked TDD and haven't played the Penumbra games, better go for them instead - they are a lot better than this new game.
Also note that AMfP was not developed by Frictional Games (who made Penumbra and TDD) but by The Chinese Room who apparently moved towards making console games by now (figures). So waiting for Frictional's game SOMA, which is currently in devolpment, could still be worthwile if it turns out closer to the games they made themselves.

I completed Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs in 2.9 hours, including restarts, pausing for breaks, and setting up my stream.
This isn't a horror game nor is it a puzzle game. The extent of the 'puzzles' in Machine for Pigs is finding the correct lever and giving it a swift tug. There, puzzle complete. Unlike the previous Amnesia game you cannot pick up in game objects other than chairs in a few areas. The developers disabled the ability to pick up objects - very hastily I might add, as you can still knock things over with chairs and easily cause other "nailed down" props to glitch out. Throughout the game the ambience tries to be spooky but due to the limitations of the game there is no sense of danger. When you are confronted with the monsters you'll laugh or even stare with your eyes half-open at the pathetic excuse of a threat. They are slow and give you plenty of opportunity to run away, and its not very hard to just walk around them when they see you. The new 'lamp' in the game flickers to notify you when a monster is near, which might've worked in a game like FEAR when the atmosphere and the script were above average, but not in a poorly written, poorly built game like this. They took out the paranoia features that the first game had, as well as the tinderboxes and lamp oil. The player doesn't even have any health potions, or any item to retrieve for that matter, which means there's no reason to explore the map other than to look for scraps of paper with sappy dialogue. I expected this game to be an excellent addition to the Amnesia universe, but TheChineseRoom failed in every possible way to make this game worthy of its title. Might've been better if it was designed as a standalone game instead of being directly related to Amnesia. (Note: same universe sequel, not story continuing sequel. Barely any crossovers. Absolutely no reason to have Amnesia in the title.)
I really hope TheChineseRoom learns from their mistakes with this game.

NMRIH. Sometimes, I wish there were more zombie games like this one. There are many positives to this game, but there are also some bads about it too. On a list of some of the good things about this game, it has a pretty good "zombie." What I mean by that is that the zombie isn't like some superhuman monster from World War Z, but is a little like the moving corpses from The Walking Dead (with the occasional runner). Also, the zombies can sense you within a certain range, which makes perfect sense. The game also keeps the legent of the zombie alive by making it to where if you get bitten, you only have a matter of time before you're one of the flesh-eaters. Another thing is the cruelty of this game towards the player. I for one absolutely love it. One reason that I love it is because when you're playing in amultiplayer match and you get bit, there are some choices that you've got to make. You can either turn the gun on yourself and save everyone at the cost of yourself, they can kill you before you turn, or you can try and bide your time with the "Phalanx pills" to help you live a little longer, or you can turn and watch as what could be the catalyst of your team's fall. The game has a very good way of using guns.  It uses a very realistic way of tailoring the gameplay with these amazingly made weapons. The weapons have mostly realistic with gun flashes, mostly realistic sound affects, and the ability to check the amount of ammunition in the firearm whenever. Another brilliant part of the game is the player's capability to board up windows up using the hammer and boards, which is very useful at times. There's also the healing. It's a pretty straight forward system. Bandages tostop the bleding and first-aid kits to recover lost health. The game also comeswith a pretty good amount of levels that range in difficulty based on location and what type of mission it is. On top of all that, the game has pretty dang good voice acting. Lastly, the game has a decent melee system. The weapons that are large, heavy, and powerful affect the stamina of the player more than the smallerand lighter weapons. The weapons that are more cumbersome than the other weapons also affect the player's ability to run for longer durations and can swing only a few times.
The negatives, however, can affect gameplay rather significantly. For a start: the zombies will sometimes grab you through walls (like closed gates that can't be struck through) and bite you while you can't break free from them killing you. The zombies will also tend to double strike the player like in Call of Duty Zombies, which can be very annoying.  Also, the .22 caliber and 9mm caliber pistols don't kill a zombie with 1 bullet on headshot. They take 2 or more bullets. It's understandable for the .22, but the 9mm caliber is definitely capable of killing a zombie with 1 shot to the head. There's also the player's stamina when it comes to the sledgehammer. The player can take 2 swings with that weapon with FULL stamina and be completely exhausted. The average person can swingthat more than 2 times without breaking a sweat. The fireaxe is also nerfed.  The zombies that run are so quick that when they turn quickly, they seem to skip a few feet. They also run faster than the player can sprint sometimes. Lastly, sometimes when shooting a zombie with the .308 rifle, sometimes scoring a direct headshot on the monster won't kill it. These cover most of the problemsI have seen and encountered in my share of playing.
Overall, I think it's a pretty good game. 8.5/10

Plantera is an idle game, which means that the game will somewhat progress while you do nothing and even, up to a point, when it is closed.
Idle games have to walk a thin line between making the player feel useless (in which case the game is actually a screensaver) and having very little idle progress (in which case the game is not much of an idle game). Plantera works that thin line rather well, giving the player incentive to interact with its colorful garden, but also progressing on its own.
The point here is to grow plants and raise animals. You can reap the results yourself or let your blue workers do it for you. Critters (rabbits, foxes, wolves and birds) will try to snatch your stuff, though thankfully they never attack the animals, so they never take your progress back. You can either scare the critters away by clicking on them or invest in scarecrows and dogs.
If you've spent time on idle games like Cookie Clicker, Time Clickers and the like, you will probably like Plantera. Just beware that the game is on the short side.
If you've never played an idle game before, I would advise you to try some of the free ones to see if you like the concept before buying one, Plantera included.

Hi rez kinda suck at balancing games, I get its difficult but their style is to make something and then nerf it into the ground. The recently released roman goddess Terra is a good example, Terra is only useful in competitive team games because playing her properly requires a lot of team coordination, if you don't have that team then terra is a waste of a player. They nerfed her 4 times since she was released and didnt touch what made her worth getting in competitive, only made everything else worse, all they needed to do was reduce the amount of cooldown and mana refund her ult offered the team, that was it and she was balanced but they took literally everything else and drove it into the ground. Now she cant do any damage, her crowd control isnt that good (yeah there is a root and a stun but they are too short for anything other than pro teams to make use of), her heal isnt potent enough and lasts too long as well as scaling poorly with power, the monolith that causes the heal can be destroyed far too easily.
Matchmaking, its not the worst system in the world but it really punishes playing alone as you can get put in situations where its 5 solo guys Vs a clan which is more or less a gauranteed loss if the clan are even remotely capable of playing as a team. The game balances based on your win-loss ratio or something with special consideration for kills, this system favours assasins and kill stealing more than playing the game well, it can also force you into teams where the other players are way better than you and you become the weak link in a chain and teams where you are the only good player and cannot drag your team to the win and theres nothing worse than being stuck in one of those situations where you are way out of your league because despite the average skill level of each team being the same one guy on one team is responsible for most of the skill (or lack thereof).
The community, its a free to play game where you can chat via keyboard. This always results in an insufferable community that will do ridiculous things like send death threats for not following the pro leagues meta in a casual game, it doesnt matter if the meta is right or not or even how well you perform, you will still get called a peice of♥♥♥♥♥♥for it, theres no real consequence for quitting out mid game and because of this people will quit for being beat ONCE, ONCE FFS these people cannot handle being beat despite it being a part of the game. People will also♥♥♥♥♥♥on you for choosing items that they arent familiar with, actively discrouraging creative thinking and counter building. You can even get♥♥♥♥♥♥on for being focussed, a good strategy for handling high skill players is focussing them and forcing them to be useless early on and if that happens to you your team are MORE LIKELY to call you♥♥♥♥♥♥than to take a second to realise the other team are throwing everything they have at you and not eveyone else. They won't adapt to the situation or take advantage of the fact the other team blew their load on you or anything useful they will just ♥♥♥♥♥ and often times quit, and then theres instalocking, you get people who actively refuse to play with the team in a team game, 1 isnt too bad but you get 2-4 instalocking players and its a recipe for disaster, they will also blame you for their failures despite them being the ones doing nothing for the team and they throw games because of these ♥♥♥♥ing hissy fits. The community also has trouble adapting to changing situations and many players are quite predictable, if you can adapt to how others play and spot the patterns its easy to do♥♥♥♥♥♥like approximate where players with invisibility abilities will go while cloaked (I am very good at that and its always hilarious owning some guy who thinks no one knows where they are), its easy to tell who will become the assasins number one target and its easy to tell when the other team will make a move to try and surprise you.
It's inpenetrable to new players, between the poor balancing, constant tweaking, high skill ceiling and awful community its pretty hard to get into the game and enjoy yourself.
In summary I more or less just went off at how ♥♥♥♥ing awful the issues this game has can get. It's worth playing if you can get some mates together and form a clan but if not skip it entirely.

This game is exactly what I expected of the studio that brought us Bastion.
A fresh and intricate method of gameplay is combined with SuperGiant's penchant for excellent narrative to make Transistor another stunning and emotional game. The game features a fresh visual style distinct from it's spiritual predecesor, and an immersive, gameplay-driven story system allows you to uncover deeper truth about the world of Cloudbank simply by trying all the game has to offer.
The game maintains new game plus, as well as the challenge modes from Bastion, and once again features the musical talent of Darren Korb, and the voice of Logan Cunningham (Rucks) as a dynamic duo, bringing a familiar yet distinct feel to the game that will please SuperGiant veterans and new players alike.

The 2nd game from Super Giant Games in my library and with it the affirmation that if their company continues to produce such high quality games I will always buy them ASAP. Transistor is an unusual game- it's jarring- from the start to the finish both in story and in gameplay. It takes a bit to get into and the ()Turn fucntion for combat is at first really difficult to grasp and it kinda feels like cheating; but as you delve further into the game it's charms really hook you and the combat system feels intutive and moldable. The base-story is a bit vague but if you read the character bios and unlock all the details (by equipping each Transistor'd person's tactic into each slot ~Primary, 2nd, Tertiary~ systematically) the charcter links and ergo-story seize more depth. Overall the art astounding- the enviroments are a bit bare but that comes with the plot- and it get addictive to play when you have a good idea of how the combat works and challenge yourself by allowing 'the System' to use 'Limiters'.  I would highly recommend this game!

This game is sick, I personally enjoyed it.  Graphics, gameplay, controls are very good.  I would rate the game 9/10 because its kinda short, 4-5 hours but if you play the extra challenges and go for a second run then it will be more hours, no duhhh.
Like the idea of mixing your power up perks, not really a based turn game in a way.  You got limited mobility (dont get me wrong you can still move, but when planning your attack you have limited time) which you should take advantage and plan your attack, you cant spam your power ups.  Each power up has different abilities, it can serve straight up as a power up or serve as an attachment or as a passive perk.  Mixing your power ups is part of the fun, you can become badass if you used them well.  "With power, comes great responsibility."
Overall game is very balance, kinda short (hoping future DLC can change that), OST is amazing, graphics are great.  Final rating 9/10, would highly recommend.

I loved bastion, so I decided to buy transistor. After playing both, Supergiant games has become my new favorite game development team.

I bought the game because of the great reviews and I was not disappointed. It had a great, and different, play style. The game itself is visually stunning and the story is fantastic. It's definitely worth the money I payed for it.

Another quality title from Supergiant Games.  Yes this game is just walking around killing things, and yes on the surface that sounds remarkably unremarkable.  The real innovation here is the combat system and the way you earn and use new abilities.  Finding just the right combo that is both effective and fits your play style is where all the fun is.  By placing them in different slots you unlock more of the story behind the characters, which in addition to the optional challenge stages is a great way to encourage you to try new combos.  This games puts the fun() in function().  Hats off.

Transistor is one of those rare games that gets it right in every aspect. The visuals and sounds are simply exceptional, while the world building, character progression, and combat system rank among the best that I've ever seen. Expect to hear this game mentioned frequently in Game of the Year discussions.

The storytelling in this single player game is definitely a successor to Bastion. The tactical gameplay really shines with a mix-and-match ability system emphasizing planning under pressure.  If you're a fan of the movie Tron, the visuals are stunning.  If your looking for a good isometric tactical dungeon crawl with a great story, you cannot go wrong with Transistor.

I beat this game in a single four hour sitting. That was even when I took my time and explored.
This game did not live up to it's predecessor at all.
To start with, many of the great items and mechanics of the original were removed, including
tinderboxes, lantern fuel, sanity and the inventory. Without the fear of losing all your sanity, you lose a lot of the fear from the original. "Should I use this tinderbox now, or save it for later? When will I find more fuel for my lantern?" Those thoughts were constantly in my mind in the original, making me fear what lies ahead in the darkness even more. Another major problem were the monsters. They were not scary, and quite frankly, they kind of made me laugh at first. You also don't see them very often. When you do, you MUST sneak past them, there are no wardrobes to hide in if you're spotted. The wardrobes and most doors are locked, leaving a very linear game. No exploring whatsoever. Finally, the story is very predictable, and not overly intriguing. Yes it had it's moments, but it just seemed kind of messy. The music was the only saving grace of this game. It was haunting and beautiful, especially one of the final songs in the game. Overall, this game was a large disappointment and I'm not sure I'll be playing it again in the near future.

If you want you can pluck trees and pick up plants yourself, or let your helpers do the work for you while you watch or build and invest in new plants. The helpers will even continue to work while you are not playing the game, and some new gold should always be waiting for you on your return!
It is good to keep your eyes open though as sometimes some mean critters will invade your garden. Hunt them out yourself or invest in a guard dog to keep the order.
Go up in level to unlock new plants, bushes, trees and animals and continue to expand and improve your garden!

This game is exactly what I expected of the studio that brought us Bastion.
A fresh and intricate method of gameplay is combined with SuperGiant's penchant for excellent narrative to make Transistor another stunning and emotional game. The game features a fresh visual style distinct from it's spiritual predecesor, and an immersive, gameplay-driven story system allows you to uncover deeper truth about the world of Cloudbank simply by trying all the game has to offer.
The game maintains new game plus, as well as the challenge modes from Bastion, and once again features the musical talent of Darren Korb, and the voice of Logan Cunningham (Rucks) as a dynamic duo, bringing a familiar yet distinct feel to the game that will please SuperGiant veterans and new players alike.

The 2nd game from Super Giant Games in my library and with it the affirmation that if their company continues to produce such high quality games I will always buy them ASAP. Transistor is an unusual game- it's jarring- from the start to the finish both in story and in gameplay. It takes a bit to get into and the ()Turn fucntion for combat is at first really difficult to grasp and it kinda feels like cheating; but as you delve further into the game it's charms really hook you and the combat system feels intutive and moldable. The base-story is a bit vague but if you read the character bios and unlock all the details (by equipping each Transistor'd person's tactic into each slot ~Primary, 2nd, Tertiary~ systematically) the charcter links and ergo-story seize more depth. Overall the art astounding- the enviroments are a bit bare but that comes with the plot- and it get addictive to play when you have a good idea of how the combat works and challenge yourself by allowing 'the System' to use 'Limiters'.  I would highly recommend this game!

Tree of savior is a curious creature, it feels a bit like a breath of fresh air in a crowded and uninspired MMO-space, but at the same time it is also crucially recreating an almost ancient model from the Ragnarok Online era. There is a lot to love in this game, the warm, hand-drawn art direction and extremely wide class options are instantly appealing. One thing I particualrly enjoyed was the absurdly archaic inspirations they used for many of the game's more unsual jobs. The Divedirbys, for example carves various holy statues in battle, and is based on an actual real world profession. Many other jobs draw from disparate cultural sources including ancient korea, feudal japan, and wide swaths of middle aged cultures in the baltic regions.
However, the game is not without faults. It lacks a strong narrative backdrop, and even major questlines are riddled with poor translations and mark-up errors. Town hubs can become almost comically overpopulated, though players can usually fix this by changing instances. The underlying gameplay can also grow repetitive, and consists largely of grinding on the same chump monsters as you cut a path to large boss encounters. With a group of friends, this gameplay is a great backdrop for social engagement, but I can't imagine it would remain fun for long as a solo experience.

Call of Juarez is a criminally underrated shooter. All the weapons feel authentic and are a blast to use, I mean, who doesn't love dual weilding six shooters? The game takes the form of a story being told by an old bounty hunter telling tales of the good ole days to the locals. Because the game takes place as a memory, and memeories can become distorted (especially after a few drinks) some zany things will happen that you wouldn't expect to find in a western. The humor in this game is perfect because it doesm't try to hard to be funny like Saints Row or Borderlands, but all the humor comes from the backround commentary of the bar patrons, which all ties in perfectly.
The game does have a bullet time system which I personally didn't rely on much, however is a fun and handly feature. XP works in a very arcade style manner where you gain more XP for every chained kill and more for trickshots. Leveling up has a three tree based level system where you can choose to level either long range, dual weilding, or close range skills. After progresing a certain distance in the certain skill tree, you will be rewarded with a jewled legendary weapon of the appropriate skill.
The only thing about this game that made me not want to play or progress was the boss fights. The boss fights were either giving a single opponent way to much health and a big gun or a quickdraw duel. The quickdraw duel consists of trying to use A/D keys to position your hand, while simultaniously kepping your cursor over your opponent, followed by a reflex test. Even worse was the mexican standoff duel in which you must switch back and forth between whoever was looking at you.
Overall, Call of Juarez is hands down one of my favourite shooters in regards to both gameplay and atmosphere and the best part is IT'S A GODDAMN UBISOFT GAME WITHOUT UPLAY! Definitely worth you fifteen dollars.

Rome 2 in its current state has some really fun features and some serious problems that continue to plague the game years after release. On the whole would not recommend, see below:
Pros:
-very cool/authentic historical setting
-amazing combat animations and finishers
-interesting and varied formations
-new province system that adds an extra dimension to regional management
-AI is somewhat improved since launch
-unit collision feels much better than launch, no more mosh pits (generally)
Cons:
-pathfinding for units is pretty atrocious sometimes
-siege and naval battles are glitchy, buggy, and difficult to enjoy due to aforementioned problems
-faction units lack much diversity for a setting like the Ancient World
-graphics can be pretty bad in some spots, even with settings maxed out
-random/arbitrary frame rate drops
-Grand Campaign is NOT fun due to constant annoyance of unrest in cities/provinces
-AI diplomacy is still broken (as in most TW games)
Long story short, if you're still dying to play Rome 2 (even though its been years since its release at this point), you may be able to get some bang for your buck if you get it on sale. Looking back, however, I wouldn't pay any more than $10 for this game.

Compared with Rome I, this game has many advantages. While playing in the battles is a bit different and takes a lot of getting used to, the strategies you'd use in earlier tw games taking place in ancient or medieval times are fundamentally the same, so it's not as if basic aspects of micro management that we all loved in Rome I in that regard are gone.
Campaign is amazing, provided it's modded. That's not to knock down the plain campaign that the game comes with, it is still a decent and fun struggle to do a lot of awesome things, like diplomatically, economically, and militarily interacting with a very, very diverse array of factions which are dispersed throughout the map and armed with key advatanges that seem faithfully historical for a video game. I love the amount of detail into units, buildings, economics , and politics put into this game, as well as the number of minor factions especially.
However, to a very hardcore tw player, it can get a little too easy, especially if you use a powerful empire. I strongly recommend using the steam workshop to download mods which increase AI aggression, increase the AI's likeyhood to actually use its elite units and best buildings, and make the AI have more diplomatic/strategic common sense (not declaring war and then offering a peace treaty within the same 2 turns, not attacking a giant city with 5 units, ect.) One great mod is an overhaul coming in 5 parts called Divide et Impera which is popular, but i prefer to keep the base of the game in tact and tweak the AI's behavior only slightly.
I haven't delved into multiplayer too much, but it looks solid, and the factions appear to be less "useful" vs. "useless" oriented than in Rome I, which basically made more than half the factions useless for multiplayer combat against those picking factions like the Romans, with some exception depending on the rules players chose to play by and money sets. If you love Hellenisitc factions, they hold up much better. Babarian factions also sport much more effective infantry from a wider selectin of possible factions.
I give this game a strong 8/10 / weak 9/10 only because the campaign could use a little work, but mods are easily able to fix all of that.

Transistor excels in so many ways, I don't even know where to start.
It essentially accomplished what a game means most to me: innovative gameplay mechanics, good storytelling, and state-of-the-art visuals, design, and music. But what makes Transistor stands out so much is that it demonstrated immense strength in all of the areas.
At first, it seems like a generic hack-and-slash game (that is, you simply walk around and beat things up with your "skills"). That's not how half of Transistor works. Later it will reveal a new mechanic that allows you to literally pause the game and plan out your next actions. This is the true beauty of Transistor: you get the action-packed combat mixed together with a strategic problem-solving manoeuver, allowing you to experiment on how you can chain together different moves, and knowing which combo is best used for which situation.
In Transistor, you get to equip 4 "skills" at a time, known as Functions. Functions works in such a way that each function could be operated either as an Active slot, an Upgrade to enhance your Active Function, or a Passive slot that grants you certain perks in combat. Once you get a number of Functions, the possiblities of Function combinations are endless. This is where Transistor truly shines, and after finishing this game twice, I have probably yet to discover hundreds of other possible Function combinations to work on.
Supergiant Games is renowned for its stunning visual art and unforgettable soundtracks, and Transistor is the best example you can get. All the background art you see in the game is hand-painted, and every music piece is woven seamlessly to the game. Besides, Supergiant Games made a really sweet move of creating the main character as a singer. Almost all the elements of the game revolved around her music — your character lost her voice and you're determined to get it back, you get to hear her humming to her own tunes, and you could unlock in-game soundtracks which you can play anytime. Basically, music is an integral part of Transistor, and Supergiant Games did an amazing job on this.
Transistor's backstory may seem mediocre at first, but everything slowly unravels, and it all builds up until the last chapter (watching the end credits broke my heart into pieces). The story was presented in such a way that you have to head to different spots along the landscape and get a hint of what's going on. Even each Function actually originates from a character, so each Function has a story to tell. In order to fully appreciate the story, I suggest you inspect all the Functions and every nook and corner you find (or simply head over to the wiki, everything is there). There's also a sword that talks. Nothing is better than a talking weapon.
I believe that Transistor is the hallmark of an innovative game produced by creative minds. It's not something you get to see very often in these few years, so I fully recommend it to anyone who loves games as a means of entertainment and artistic expression.
TL;DR, Transistor excels in every aspect, innovative and refreshing game mechanics, great artistical value, and nothing beats a talking sword.

is everything that an indie game should be; bold, refreshing, and memorable. The setting is Cloudbank city, a futuristic, high-tech metropolis that one could say gives off an impression similar to that of
's Midgar. You play as Red, a famous singer who, along with the mysterious sword known as the Transistor (and the voice that talks to her through it) travels to hunt down the mysterious group that tried to murder her immediately before the game's opening.  Combat unfolds utilising a mixture of real-time and turn-based elements as you fight against a force of robotic adversaries collectively called the 'Process', and character progression occurs as you level-up to unlock new 'functions' to use in battle, which can be assigned as either abilities, passive effects, or enhancements for other functions. As well as an intriguing story and competent gameplay system,
also features a beautiful art style and an extremely memorable soundtrack that features vocal themes which directly tie into the game's story. If you’re looking for a big-budget, AAA title, then
may not be for you. However, if you’re looking for an extremely well-made and memorable game with an engaging story, setting, soundtrack and set of gameplay mechanics, then
is well worth buying.

A game from creators of Bastion. Oh, what expectations I've had for this one. Obviously had the preorder with the soundtrack going and played it day one. And what a strange experience it was. I like most aspects of the game, and yet I wasn't inclined to play it at all next time, so I finished it only now (2-3 months later?) by forcing myself to do it which is pretty sad, because the main story is actually VERY short. Without much of side "challenges" (which are decently designed but most of the time force you to play with predesigned powers ("functions") installed and it was pretty unfun for me, because I like to design my own tactic in this game) the game takes around 3 hours to finish. With getting "some" challenges done it goes up to 4-5 hours. Nevertheless, I don't think this gamelength is really acceptable, so that's a sure "con" for me. Now some pros and some more cons.
Pros:
-The music. It's very good, wouldn't expect otherwise from Darren Korb. While the game was sitting idle in my library, the soundtrack I have purchased got it's share of plays in the last months. Just like in the Bastion. One thing I would say it feels a bit lacking of electronic elements, which would be suitable in this setting.
-The art is impeccable, with great love to detail. Just like in Bastion.
-The setting. Very strange, interesting, kind of unique. Just like in the Bastion.
-The "functions"-system. Robust and full of variations, makes for good replayability and interesting levelups.
For some cons:
-The story. Very basic, not trying to hook you in at all. Mostly it goes by like "whatever, I am here somewhere, go on now". There's not much happening at all, the synopsis of the story would take approximatly 1 page after it's all done. I mean, I don't  belong to the type of players, who cna't play a game, which is weak on story, but I require at least good gameplay to have interest in it.
-The gameplay. Repetitive, gimicky and boring overall. The "planning thing" is gimicky, overpowered and breaks the flow. The regular mode makes you feel seriously underpowered and is  a bit of a cluster♥♥♥♥. After I've found the "right" functions combination, all of the fights where just a grind. In combination with the first flaw - it is why it feeled like I don't want to go on (I just couldn't figure it out in the first hour yet).
-The sword. He is so whiny and emo it makes me want to smack him and tell him to grow a pair. While he is the 80% of the means how the story and setting is conveyed to player, in the end I just wished he would shut up -_-
Overall, you might want to check it out at your own risk, but this is no Bastion.

I don't know what is with this game but it is magical.
Basically the game is about you being a border guard checking papers at a border between two fictional nations. It all gives the impression being in some sort of eastern-European state during behind the iron curtain during the Soviet era. Your task is to either admit och reject those who seek to enter based on the papers provided and the requirements set by your superiors. You simply scan these papers for faults. You have to do this fast enough to feed your poor family as the time is limited and you are paid per person reviewed. All errors lead to a salary reduction. Sometimes you stand between wrong admitting a person who just wish to be with its beloved, sometimes to accept bribes and sometimes you choose between aiding a terrorist organisation or fact the consequenses of not doing so.
I suppose it is all the context of the game that makes the magic. You strangely enough get sucked into it.

If they made the game exactly like the Aliens (1985) they would win the golden Xenomorph, of that I'm sure. Compared with Rome I, this game has many advantages. While playing in the battles is a bit different and takes a lot of getting used to, the strategies you'd use in earlier tw games taking place in ancient or medieval times are fundamentally the same, so it's not as if basic aspects of micro management that we all loved in Rome I in that regard are gone.
Campaign is amazing, provided it's modded. That's not to knock down the plain campaign that the game comes with, it is still a decent and fun struggle to do a lot of awesome things, like diplomatically, economically, and militarily interacting with a very, very diverse array of factions which are dispersed throughout the map and armed with key advatanges that seem faithfully historical for a video game. I love the amount of detail into units, buildings, economics , and politics put into this game, as well as the number of minor factions especially.
However, to a very hardcore tw player, it can get a little too easy, especially if you use a powerful empire. I strongly recommend using the steam workshop to download mods which increase AI aggression, increase the AI's likeyhood to actually use its elite units and best buildings, and make the AI have more diplomatic/strategic common sense (not declaring war and then offering a peace treaty within the same 2 turns, not attacking a giant city with 5 units, ect.) One great mod is an overhaul coming in 5 parts called Divide et Impera which is popular, but i prefer to keep the base of the game in tact and tweak the AI's behavior only slightly.
I haven't delved into multiplayer too much, but it looks solid, and the factions appear to be less "useful" vs. "useless" oriented than in Rome I, which basically made more than half the factions useless for multiplayer combat against those picking factions like the Romans, with some exception depending on the rules players chose to play by and money sets. If you love Hellenisitc factions, they hold up much better. Babarian factions also sport much more effective infantry from a wider selectin of possible factions.
I give this game a strong 8/10 / weak 9/10 only because the campaign could use a little work, but mods are easily able to fix all of that.

Transistor brings more of the amazing atmosphere and ongoing narration that people loved in Bastion, with an even more incredible soundtrack. The combination real-time/turn-based combat allows for deep strategy and will keep you switching up your selected functions (and the functions that modify them) to find a play style that suits you best.
It is sadly quite linear: all battle encounters are static locations (though the enemies can change based on your level) and there are only one or two very small optional areas. And, unless you missed a few corners of interaction or side rooms with static art (like the opening image,) the only reason to play again is for the sake of achievements; there's not even minor alternate endings like Bastion. (And, when you see the ending, you'll probably wish there was.)
That said, the positives of combat, music, and story vastly outweight the negatives of linearity and low-replay value, and I highly recommend this for anyone looking for a short, strategic brawler or just more of what they loved from Bastion. The soundtrack itself is excellent all its own, so even if you don't go for the game you should pick up the soundtrack.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, the much anticipated indirect sequel to Frictional Games' blockbusting indy horror hit The Dark Descent. Bringing in the writing power of TheChineseRoom (makers of Dear Esther) and delaying the game's release in order to better meet the expectations of the consumer base it was widely expected that aMfP would be a smash hit...
In reality, it's very disappointing.
The first of many flaws is the absolute removal of almost all the interactivity that made the first game so immersive, the player can no longer pick up/throw objects like in The Dark Descent, making the game feel so much more restrictive alongside it's extremely linear level design.
Secondly, the challenge of the game is almost non-existant with the unnecessary removal of the Insanity mechanic, and the light has unlimited use, these two poor choices of gameplay make aMfP seem more like a cheap Slender ripoff than anything that can rightfully bear the title of an Amnesia game.
Finally, the story is nearly the polar opposite of The Dark Descent, instead of being compelling and interesting the story for A Machine for Pigs is drab and uninteresting, completely failing to capture my interest and leaving no memorable moments (they resorted to using the "creepy little children" archetype, a telltale sign of desparation for a scare factor).
Since I loved TheChineseRoom's previous game, Dear Esther, and I greatly respect their ability to convey story, I left A Machine for Pigs feeling all the more dissapointed. Frictional Games and TheChineseRoom let the Amnesia fanbase down, and should have payed more attention to what made The Dark Descent the king of the horror genre.
So no, I do not recommend A Machine for Pigs.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs was published by Frictional Games and developed by The Chinese Room and YOU WILL SEE AND FEEL the difference. The first Amnesia was published AND created by Frictional Games. Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a great horror game, but not as great as Amnesia: The Dark Descent. This has several reasons:
1. You have unlimited light
2. No health is shown, but mosty 2 hits are enough to kill you.
3. Everytime you meet an enemy, your lamp and the lights nearby start to flicker. So you will be warned if something dangerous is near you. That's the point I have to critisize. A horror game shouldn't warn you of horror things, it must surprise you! If I get warned all the time then I won't be so scared because I know some pig is waiting there. I want to move without knowing what awaits me in the next corner.
4. No inventory for items, because you don't have to activate your brain and collect and combine different items anymore!
-> 5. Really easy puzzles, you can't compare it with the first Amnesia.
6. The story in Amnesia: The Dark Descent was better and a little bit longer than in this one. You just play a psychopath who has deep psycho-problems with himself... The whole game is about himself and his noob-life.
But now to the good points:
It is still a very good horror game. If you loved Amnesia: The Dark Descent, you will like Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. But the first Amnesia was a lot scarier and harder. Anyway, definitely a good game and I hope the next Amnesia will be developed and published by Frictional Games. :P

Reign of Kings is a sandbox survival game where you have to collect resources and interact with other players in a small island.
Pros:
-Provides interesting shenanigans with other players (You can capture other players and put them in a jail or execute them.).
-It has an interesting twist: Players can try to ascend to the throne and become kings and queens of the server, thus taxing other players resources and getting acces to some fine equipment.
-Has fairly large crafting system.
-You can actually siege other players' buildings.
-Game had few bugs or there were very minor bugs (except in combat).
Cons:
-The playable area is way too small. You can explore the whole island pretty much in two hours and that means that you will run to the same players all the time.
-Lone wolfs don't have a chance in this game. The best resource-gathering places are dominated by groups of players.
-The combat is just terrible. It's extremely buggy and if you choose to make a short character you have way better chances to win fights since you are so hard to hit.
-The game has actually very little things to do if you are a new player or a lone wolf. You can't really do any cool sieging by yourself now can you?
-The resource grinding is real

Factorio is a great game and I do recommend it, to a certain point. I've gotten to the point in my life where video games just don't feel the same anymoire, and it takes a really amazing game to get me addicted and playing for hours without getting bored. Factorio was that game. I played it through the night and didn't stop, something I haven't done for over a decade. There is always something to do, always something to keep up with and manage and, while it can be overwhelming at times (especially when your base starts being attacked by aliens A LOT), is always satisfying in the end. Also, the learning curve is very smooth in the beginning. Crafting is simple and the machines you use to build your base are easy to use in creative ways. HOWEVER, the farther you make it through the game, the steeper the learning curve gets. I look at all the new things I need to craft and I don't know how any of them work. Yes, I could look it up and learn every single thing to learn about this game, but to me, that overwhelming learning curves ruins the experience and turns me off to playing the game again.
TL;DR: The game is amazing. When you build a world, you most likely won't stop playing for at least the first six hours. After that point however, when your world becomes more advanced and you get closer and closer to end game, the learning curve steepens tremendously. Whether it's worth it to you is your choice, and I may come back to learn everything (that's how truly addicting this game is), but for right now, the curve is too much.

Ok, hear me out: the premise of this game is paperwork, and a lot of it, but it's awesome. No really, it's awesome. Glory To Arstotzka.
Papers, Please is a truly remarkable little game created by a single man, Lucas Pope, who has previously created many freeware titles with a similar look and feel to them. Papers, Please has you being randomly chosen as the chief inspector of the newly opened border to the
glorious country of Arstotszka, your family has been moved to a class-8 settlement and you will need to balance how quickly you get people through your border with making sure that you are only letting through people with 100% valid paperwork to get paid and to support your family so they don't die cold, hungry, and sick. Which seems easy enough, but as the border becomes more and more strict and as the game adds more and more rules to watch out for it can become quite the challange which requires a lot of observation to do your job right. Alongside this, the game will offer a lot of moral dilemmas of desperate people who want into your country who
you shall not approve under any circumstance unless they have the correct paperwork.
The game's story is told very behind-the-scenes and you might not even notice how expansive the story is until the end of your first playthough, with the game having twenty different endings to get to depending on the choices you make and the people you do and don't let through. The game, like some other games of Pope's, seeks to make a political statement about security, violation of privacy and rights, and unjust censorship.
This game is in no ways pretty, the look is dark and dystopian, and the world barely has any color in it, but it's all made this way to help suit the style of the game and also to not blind the player with too much information. It allows you to easily see if a picture is false and if there is something wrong about someone's papers, such as a forged seal.
Overall, the game is very good at what it does and I believe that it actually is worth the ten dollar price tag, as it has a lot of replayability to see the different endings, and the game also has an endless mode. Frankly, there is so much more I could talk about in this game and why it's genius but it would spoil much of the experience, it's really a game that you have to play for yourself.
Now,
Papers, Please.

If you have watched the Alien movies before or even played the other Alien related games (AvP) this game is a perfect addition to the franchise and a must play for any fan. The game looks really REALLY good and has not aged at all despite being released 3 years ago.
It's super cinematic and feels like playing through an Alien movie.
The campaign is 16 hours long and while I didn't get bored of it by the end it did feel like a very long game and I did want to get it done and over with by the last few levels.
The Storyline follows the events after Alien 1 and you play as Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley's daughter who is searching for what happened to her mother.
Alien: Isolation is primarily a survival horror game where you hide from Aliens, other people and Androids (well not really androids they are pretty easy to get around, unless the alien is also around...). You do end up getting weapons like a revolver, Shotgun, Flamethrower and Nail gun as well as the ability to craft weapons like pipe bombs and Molotov’s but they are only really useful in their own specific way. ie. Flamethrower scares off the alien, Revolver and shotgun kill Humans and Androids.
Nothing can kill the alien... I tried and failed.
The game has some of the best sound I've heard in a game of this type. Every bump and alien scream in the distance has you constantly spooked and on edge. Watching your motion sensor while an alien runs around in the vents above you and hearing the pounding of its feet as it moves over you is a really immersive and terrifying experience. Even the squeaking sound your shoes make when you spin around is on point and adds to intense horror experience.
The game has plenty of scary moments but the one issue I found with the game was that some parts of the game where the alien constantly attacks you get really old and the alien no longer feels as scary as it should (for that part of the level atleast)  and you end up just figuring out the correct path you need to take to avoid sudden deaths and knowing where the alien drops down.
Especially if you have Molotov’s and the Flamethrower to defend yourself.
The only DLC I'd recommend is Crew Expendable & Last Survivor. They are 2 missions from the end of the first Alien Movie where you have to trap the alien and when that fails, blow up the ship. Kind of adds a face to some of the events that were done off screen or skipped over.
Keep in mind they are $7 on their own so you'd be better off buying the Collection if you wanted to play these 2 DLC missions. The 2 Missions are only 40 minutes - 1 hour long.
The rest are Survival maps which are just do a bunch of things within the time limit and avoid the alien. This has already been done 100 times throughout the campaign so unless you’re a diehard fan that needs every ounce of content from the game, pass.

Alien: Isolation is a really good game if you are a fan of the Alien franchise. The positive aspects of the game include the retro look (e.g., all the consoles in the ship are big flashing light buttons, attention to details from the original movie for ship design in general, all of the UI menus match up with the movie). The game plays out like you are interacting with an actual Alien movie and the story ties really well into the franchise.
The only cons I have right now are that your objectives are no always entirely clear, there is a lot of dead time when you are hiding from threats (locker to locker as you move room to room) which gets a bit stale, and the increase in difficulty is normally just that the threats can sniff you out faster / better.
I am definitely going to continue playing the game, would recommend fans pick it up, but likely will not replay it due to the cons listed above.

It's difficult for me to write a review of this game. See, I bought it out of a passionate love for Supergiant Games that came forth from playing their first game, Bastion. Now, as this was my motivation, I think it's fair to speak it in terms of its merits relative to the game that caused me to purchase it. Overall, I say that I recommend the game, but that it isn't worth the money for the amount of gameplay you get.
Visuals:
As in Bastion, the artwork was stunning. In fact, this is the main element in which Transistor far surpasses Supergiant
Games's first title. Nowadays, it's difficult to find a truly beautiful game that also plays relatively well. In Transistor, the city of Cloudbank is beautiful, filled with bright lights and dark shadows, each skyline and city street more breathtaking than the last. This was the most impressive aspect of the game, in my mind.
Audio:
Again like Bastion, the audio was excellent. However, for a game whose  main character is a singer (even though she has lost her voice), I saw very little focus on the musical aspect of the game. Unlike in Bastion, where I found myself seeking out and listening to the music after playing the game, I was not captivated. I was disappointed by this, but still found the music to be very enjoyable. I wish that you had the option to listen to the music you unlocked outside of the enclosed zone (that would've been very nice).
Gameplay:
This is the part that most disappointed me. I saw a lot of good ideas in terms of combat in Transistor. The ability to place any skill in a primary, secondary, or passive slot allowed for a lot of different and interesting builds. The idea of the Turn() was pretty cool, as well. However,
I always found myself flailing around after using it, avoiding conflict until it recharged, then immediately using it again. This was not fun for me. It had a couple of good ideas, but some of them were poorly executed, leading to an unsatisfactory combat experience.
Story:
I'm kinda on the fence about this. The characters seem interesting, but again, in relative terms, it wasn't as good as Bastion. There was not enough detail given. In bastion, the story revolved around a core of a small number of characters, who were characterized by their actions and reactions to objects and events. You were told enough to keep you on your seat, keep you guessing, and keep you invested. The characters seemed to matter. With Transistor, I only cared about the two main characters, and not as much as I did with Bastion. Again, disappointment is the main feeling. They could've done better.
Value:
I don't think the game is worth the cost. I spent $15 on about 4 actual hours of gameplay (I had 6 on record because I left it open to go eat), which is not okay. Most $60 games offer at least 1 hour of gamplay for each dollar spent. I felt cheated, to be frank. I had fun, but it wasn't worth it. I'd recommend playing it, but perhaps not purchasing it.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs: Not quite as scary or fun as its predecessor, A Machine for Pigs still is a well-made horror game. Its atmosphere, sound design and graphics overall are really well done and the story told by The Chinese Room here is quite interesting as well. For $20.00 USD you really could do a lot worse, and A Machine for Pigs is certainly great quality for its price. The short comings are the fact that it is part of a series and with that comes some basic expectations which are completely removed in this installment. You won’t be dealing with insanity, inventory, lamp oil, tinderboxes; basically you won’t worry about much in this game aside from the monsters. Your lantern never runs out of energy and puzzles are fairly easy because you can only interact with so much.  You can definitely tell they focused more on the story and background than on anything else since most of it is removed. The other minuscule annoyance comes from the frequency of notes in the game. There are a ton of them, the font used in-game is sometimes a pain to read (this comes down to the individual) and a large portion of the game seems to rely on these notes.  Overall, A Machine for Pigs is a decent horror game and a good first attempt by The Chinese Room, but as an Amnesia title it is definitely a step backwards and fans of the series will walk away wanting more. This is a bit tough since the game is of great quality for the price of admission but it comes as a tough full on recommendation for  fans, and newcomers would be better served to play the previous installments before playing A Machine for Pigs.
-Middle of the Road from Royial

Plantera is a casual garden simulator with some very cute graphics and characters in the game. The game is very addictive and fun to play, but only really for a certain amount of time depending on how much you enjoy playing this type of game.
This game is probably the most calming and relaxing game that I have played in a long time, for a casual game this is what you are really looking for. This game does that and more to make the game a very calming and relaxing experience throughout your gaming time. The main mechanics of this game are rather simple, plant different fruit seeds and wait for them to grow and collect them for money. This is basically the entire game, as you collect more money you will level up and earn more plants to grow that will give you a bigger profit but will cost more. You can also expand your garden to be able to plant more and gain more money.
As you play through the game, leveling up and expanding your garden you will gain a worker who will harvest the fruit and vegetables instead of you clicking them yourself. This comes in especially useful if you aren't actually on the game as they harvest when you aren't even on the game, but more about that later. As well as planting crops you can also purchase animals that will produce profit for you, such as chickens that lay eggs, pigs that dig for stuff, cows that produce milk and so on. Getting a variety of these will increase your profits to plant more crops and purchase more animals.
Now, like any garden there will be pests that will try to steal your crops or kill your animals such as, birds, rabbits, foxs and so on. You can prevent this by purchasing scarecrows and dogs that will scare away the foxs and rabbits to keep your garden safe from harm. It's worth noting that only these pests will come when you are on the game itself, so it isn't that big of a deal.
The game itself can be left for a certain amount of time within purchasing upgrades. There are two types of upgrades, one that will increase the value of the harvest you get and the other will increase the time that your workers will work when you are not in-game. This can really help you with just leaving the game for a couple of hours and doing something else. Although with the more plants you buy will increase in price and therefore you will have to leave for a longer period of time in order to gain that money to harvest more crops. This does string the game out a bit longer than is needed, but I think that's the point of casual games nowadays.
The graphics of the game are just straight up cute, each character has a small animation that will correspond to their own personal behaviour. Such as the pigs that dig will have a small digging animation, the workers have a small harvesting animation. It's all very nice for a while, but then it does get a bit repetitive after a little while.
+ Most casual and relaxing game I have played in a while
+ Variety of crops, trees, bushes and animals to provide a profit
+ You will have to keep pests away from your harvest, adds a little more depth to the game itself
+ Worth the asking price for the game
+ Nice cute graphics throughout the game
+ Nice animations
- Not much variety in gameplay, but that's to be expected with a garden simulator like this
- Crops and trees start to become crazy expensive, meaning you will have to leave the game longer for more money. Alternatively you can buy cheaper stuff but won't gain as much money.
Plantera is a great casual game that will keep you coming back to the game every now and then throughout the day. Depending on if you get satisfaction out of clicking and harvesting the fruit manually or like to leave it for others to do will really depend on how long you will actually play this game. The game has some great and cute graphics, only recommended to those who enjoy very casual games that you only really come back to every now and then throughout a few days.

An above-average survival horror game with an excellent recreation of the atmosphere and visuals of the 1979 sci fi classic, Alien. A must-play for fans of the franchise, although clearly (and refreshingly) tailored specifically towards fans of the original.
As far as survival horror games go, it's nothing exceptional (outside of presentation) but the first 2/3rds of the game are a joy to play through. Unfortunately the game starts to drag in the last third of the game after an arguably unnecessary continuation of the plot is forced upon you. In its final hours, the game begins to pay more homage to the widely popular 1986 sequel, Aliens. While I get that the developers were probably trying to tie the two films more closely together, it still felt lackluster compared to what came before it in earlier sections of the game. The final act is a bit of a mess with an ending that leaves you wanting more, and not in a good way.
On another note, I see a lot of people talking about this titles as though it's a genuinely terrifying experience. As a fan of horror games, I don't consider this game to be anywhere near the scariest the medium has to offer. To a newcomer, it may seem terrifying, but it's no Silent Hill 2. It's not comparable to Amnesia, PT or Resident Evil HD either. While there is an inherent terrifying thrill of attempting to evade the Alien's detection, and an immediate wave of temporary unnerve when you realise it has seen you, it quickly devolves into a fairly predictable scare-fest that loses its touch after a few deaths. Luckily the constantly developing plot and the wealth of visual spectale keeps the game entertaining even when the standard scares are losing their staying power. Although there are a few well paced scripted sequences that are quite effective at causing a good spook, the game's terror element is at its absolute best when the Alien is above you in the vents, not when it's actively stalking you through the hallways.
That said, it's a great introduction to the survival horror genre and It's absolutely a game with replay value. Don't expect to feel like playing through the game twice in one week, but it will draw you back in like no other game when you're in the mood for Alien-related gaming content.

It seems unfair to rate this with regards to Bastion at all, as this game is so ridiculously good. A near-perfect storm of gameplay, storyline, and art, it is hard not to consider Transistor both art and entertaining, white-knuckled challenge incarnate.
Gameplay is interesting, unique, and thanks to the difficulty system (which does bear comparison to Bastion-- if it ain't broke, after all) it takes a long, long time to get old. NG+ introduces even more challenge in the form of tougher enemies as you proceed, and augmenting them just adds to the fun. There's little difference other than that, however, save for a few little cute changes toward the start. Well, it'd be tough to call the first change cute. More like chilling, in context of the storyline.
The story is heart-wrenching, even for those who are jaded with overly bittersweet tales. It simultaneously makes you laugh and grit your teeth while rolling you through the entire spectrum of emotion, from happiness and laughter to utter bloodrage. There were points in the game where it was very, very easy to draw forth and feel the same emotions as the characters-- something I personally haven't experienced since Homeworld.
The art is beautiful, bar none. The backgrounds are amazing, the minimal but expressive cutscene animations are dead center, and the enemies are unique and imaginative while still retaining a vivid fear of their power as you progress through the game. They are identifiable instantly and their design works beautifully with their combat styles.
And of course-- the music. It is very, very hard to review this game without talking about the score, as it is integral to the atmosphere and the story itself. The soundtrack is worth listening to all on its own (much like Bastion!) and is well placed to evoke response.
There are very few complaints I can offer-- the story, despite feeling
short at 4-6 hours of gameplay without counting NG+, felt like it began and ended on appropriate and perfect notes. If you don't enable some of the more interesting difficulty nodes, the combat can get a bit stale. Once you find a combo that works, you can get away with spamming it endlessly, even on the bosses. These are tiny complaints, though, and I am far more than willing to forgive them in light of the monolith that is the rest of this game.
In all, Transistor is the second in series of top tier results for Supergiant. They promised a game of Bastion's caliber, and both succeeded and surpassed all expectations. Easy 9.5/10.

I'm going to start off this review by saying that Transistor has an amazing world. I love it. The colors, the shapes, the Process, the computer lingo, the voice acting... Everything about this game's visuals, audio, and gameplay is absolutely top-notch. If you're the sort of person who likes games with incredible locations, buy this game.
However, there is a problem: the story. Or maybe it's just the way the story is conveyed. See, you play as a singer who has lost her voice. You're guided by a talking sword called the Transistor. Thing is, the Transistor doesn't state your goals very clearly, and provides little to no explination as to why you do the things you do. It feels as if the Transistor was on a mission of some sort, and you just happened to step into it and get in the car, there's no time to explain.
So if you like settings which blur the line between the online and outside worlds, buy this game. If you like interesting, strategic gameplay, buy this game. If you like beautiful, well-thought out worlds, buy this game.
If, however, you want the game to make any effort to tell you about the world, or what's happening in it, or why you're doing anything at all in it, don't buy this game.
6/10. The setting is amazing, but I didn't have any clue what was happening until the very end, and not in a good way.

When a friend asked me what Transistor was like, I said it was like Bastion, but moreso.  Initially, I wasn't so certain as to whether or not this was fair to Supergiant's second game, but the more I thought about it and the more I played, the harder the patterns were to ignore, to the extent that it may even be called a design aesthetic.  To cover the traits shared by both...
*  A stylized, eye-catching isometric world (Transistor specifically is Klimt and Mucha taking on cyberpunk)
*  A well-promoted, atmospheric soundtrack with solid vocals
*  A central hub to refine combat talents, listen to music, reminisce
*  A somewhat unique combat system that heavily involves customization of weapons
*  A means of tweaking difficulty by changing enemy behavior and PC limitations
*  A plot that is concerned with the excesses of technology
*  A bit of a political agenda (Bastion is about colonialism, Transistor, about individuality, dystopia, and the banality of a world that tries to please everyone by consensus)
*  A thought-out, built up world supporting the story
*  A strong, nearly intrusive narration
*  A silent protagonist trudging through a landscape
Where they share influences, they also share flaws.  Weapon customization isn't easily tailored to enemy groups (it's randomized in New Game+, it can't be) and some combos are game breakers.  My favorite setup, which was like tazing someone into quicksand and then golfing a live grenade into their gut, was to spam Void(Get + Purge), then Load() + Breach(Crash + Ping, aligned with both packet and enemy).  If I didn't get one-hit kills, it was only because I misaligned, and nothing late in the game was dangerous enough to get me to tweak my methods.
The same combat system is just barely interesting and fun enough to sustain itself, considering how heavily the game relies on it.  The puzzle aspect of using Turn() seems particularly underutilized, since you only use it once perhaps ten minutes into the game and never again.  Even something as mundane as flipping off a few switches using Breach() or rapidly navigating around using Jaunt() or (let's not get too ambitious) a stealth sequence revolving around use of Mask() might add some dynamism to gameplay that is otherwise combat-dependent.
The world is well-thought out and also empty.  The city or the immediate location is gestured to in context of a larger world, but the current environment is made to be the only relevant thing and the current environment only very rarely has NPCs to interact with.  Owing to the silent protag/narrator combo, this means that your interactions with the world are limited to the passive storytelling that is the narrator's exposition or your reading of a third-hand account.  Sybil, as the easiest example among the NPCs, has a duality and is complex because we are told that she has a duality and is complex.  We never see her as the cheery social butterfly, we just see her, briefly, as covetous to the point of violence.  In spite of this emphasis on telling over showing, certain details are poorly telegraphed by both games.  In the instance of Transistor, The Process can apparently turn people into The Process, at least once, but no one is surprised or confused by this when it happens.  It is taken as not worth mentioning.
To Transistor's credit, it has resolved the matter of not initially having antagonists.  Transistor does have antagonists.  Sort of.  You know who they are at the beginning and you pursue them and fight them, though the reasons why are ultimately confused or dissatisfying in their results, much like they were in Bastion.  One can have dissatisfaction in storytelling, and I often love movies and TV series that end on bummer notes, but when you're controlling a character, pushing them against various odds to do the thing that their world needs them to do, stories that feel incomplete or under-resolved stand out more.
Adding to this, the New Game+ has less going for it now than it did in Bastion.  At least in Bastion, you could choose among ending options.  New Game+ in Transistor offers three things: the ability to continue leveling and get duplicate functions, slightly more populated combat settings (none difficult enough to turn off any of the limiters), and slight change in atmosphere as signaled by different posters and one altered bit of dialogue.  That's all.  Oh and you get your achievement.  Lovely.
To summarize, Supergiant makes a particular game.  It's arty and appealing to the senses and has controls that establish a baseline level of enjoyment, but there's too much devoted to getting the baddies and since they aren't good at developing a plot or characters, corners are cut and they settle for an experience where they tell you most of what's going on.  In my opinion, a lot of effort that went into conceptually creating a distinctive world ends up going to waste because they're awful at storytelling.  But it's a reliable and somewhat unique type of game and gaming experience, and if you're into that, then Transistor could be a game for you, so long as you only play it the once.  It feels like an improvement on the Bastion model, but its strengths and shortcomings also feel more extreme in part due to fatigue resulting from being the same type of game.

Well, I will try to be as short as possible
Pros:
+ Modding community
+ Good atmosphere, revisited time period
+ Detailed battles with many options as formations, traps, etc, etc
+ Replayable. Different and interesting missions and objectives (up to some point) which are specific to each faction are a sure guarantee that you are going to spend a lot of time playing this game.
Cons:
- After all those patches, A.I. is still incredibly stupid when it comes to battles. It just acts suicidal every goddamn time. It is almost impossible not to win a battle given how easy the AI is to lure into ambush or how it does not attack certain units with their corresponding opposing troops (like cavalry - pikemen/spearmen). Instead, they just rush everything head on, expecting miracles. I really can't comprehend why CA could not implement this simple rock/paper/scissors mechanic in the game after years of patching.
- Lame diplomacy. I know a lot has been written on the topic by what bugs me most, again after years of patching, is the lack to give away a region to anyone - even for free. For example - I play as Rome, maintain good relations with the Raeti and the Nori, I decide to turn my focus to Carthage and Iberia so I rely on my allies to keep my back (with some help, of course). After they lose some of their regions, I decide to intervene with my nearby stack so I recapture a territory that was belonging to my allies just a few turns ago. Astonishingly, I do not have the option to return the region to its rightful owner and instead I have to spend resources and time developing that region or just leave it be reconquered by my enemies (which of course is something I would not want to do). Same happens even if I tried to give the region to a client state/satrapy. On top of it, if playing as some barbarian factions, it is possible to "liberate" a region, instantly forming a military alliance with the liberated faction - which means the option of capturing and immediately ceding a region is somewhere in the game - just not given to us all this time, not even possible to be modded out. Do we need to remind CA how many times in the course of history, after the end of a war, territory was readdressed between belligerents? Instead, in Rome 2 owning a region is only a direct consequence of military occupation. B O R I N G
- Broken trade. Now, again, would someone explain to me why (yes, again after years of patching) the trade issues with Sparta and Dacia were never sorted out? It is not a bug per se, but just an incredibly lacking in terms of common sense and logic game mechanic. For those who are not familiar: the game requires you to have a direct route to your capital in order to trade with a faction. Sounds logical as long as you do not play as Sparta and try to keep Athens as an ally or a client state. Because, if you do play as Sparta, you can go out, capture the entire Mediterranean if you wish, but as long as Athens is not yours - you cannot trade WITH ANYONE EXCEPT FOR ATHENS (or the corresponding faction that owns Athens). What if I wanted to keep Athens as an ally? Nope, you are not even offered to have trade-passing rights, so even if Athens was an ally or a client state - even then you cannot trade with anyone except them. Of course, that would be a minor nuissance if you could change your capital - but then again - NOPE, you cannot do that for reasons incomprehensible by human logic... With Dacia things are a bit less annoying since it borders a lot of other regions. But you cannot trade across the Danube even though historically rivers were used mainly for that - trade. Instead you have to circle around in order to start trading with those factions south of the river (or north of the river if you are coming from the south)
I still recommend the game. I enjoy it. The modding community is great, and the game is quite flexible in terms of modding. However, the issues listed above are sometimes driving me crazy especially knowing that after all this time they still haven't been fixed (and they were all discovered when the game was released). What is even worse, CA has announced that they are not planning in implementing the "give region" option because "it was not historically accurate". Just wtf when it is exactly the opposite.
