This is a great racing game. regardless wether you are a fan of the sport or not this franchise brings a lot to the racing genre a lot of other racers dont and not enough people can witness it because they are turned off from the game if they are not a fan of the sport. Do yourself a favour, if your a fan of racing you have to give this a try and heres why:
The AI is simply some of the best in a racing game, they simply react how you expect pro drivers to react. i tried to fool the AI on a few occassions now when they are coming up behind me i will swerve left and right in a completely unpredictable manor and the AI reacted perfectly, lesser games would have them charging into your rear but on this game it genuinly tried to outfox me and find a way past, i was wowed. then theres the thrill of seeing the AI fight ahead of you and behind, again switching back and forth for position and often times losing control and making bad moves. its what makes the racing a thrill, Project cars had a pretty good AI but it was often times deliberately too aggresive, not so here.
Then theres all the little things you wish would happen in other racing games that never do, for instance in other racers more often than not the only failures you see are your own, the only mistakes you see are your own, the only crashes you see are your own, well here things just happen on track that can change the race completely, safety cars, AI crashes on the other side of the track, AI engine failures. It adds to the realism and feeling you are in a real race and not a time trial with added AI cars as filler.
The career is excellent, monitoring the whole situation has never been so good, almost every component on your car wears out, the upgrade system is now much fuller and worthwhile, the added classic car races are a bit gimmicky but they are there and its the better for it, rivalries feel meaningful and something you want to win.
Then theres the car physics, lets get one thing straight, anybody that says this is more like an arcade racer is nuts, you can customise the experience how you please, turn off all the assists, crank the difficulty and you will be fighting the car on every corner. until a critic tells me they have driven a real formula 1 car i can happily say this is likely the closest experience you can get only without all the neck ache and sweat. Then theres the little details that make the experience stand out, the sound now is very good, the tyres cry in pain when pushed hard, they will grain and show visual wear, the mirrors shake, the rubber goes flying and sticks to your visor, the turbos now sound more like turbos and not a high pitched painful whistle. its just such a well polished experience.
There are improvements that can be made i mean its not perfect, the graphics on PC should be better, theres a lack of antialiasing options, theres only TAA and im sorry but its trash, its the vaseline effect and i dont like it, problem is without it the shimmering on fences etc are terrible so it must stay on, yes even at 4k ( im using a 1080ti ). The other problem is some little quips in the career that had me baffled, so i started with ferrari, i got disqualified from race 1 because my son unpaused the game and caused havok, but my next 2 races were a 3rd and then a 1st, only after my win i was given a written warning off my team to improve my performance or face the sack... right after my 3rd race which was a win, needless to say i was confused, i mean i know as a whole i was underperforming and losing my rivalry with my team mate but after getting a win the warning just didnt fit in very well.
overall its an excellent game that makes great improvements over 2016, it does feel a bit samey samey but theres enough added here to make a much fuller more pleasing game than 2016.
race fans, you owe it to yourself to get invested in this, love or hate the sport this is a thrill ride.

This chapter in the Amnesia series is definitely going to upset people expecting The Dark Descent 2, but if you can separate the two games you'll appreciate them both for what they are; Amazing survival horror experiences.
A Machine for Pigs (AMFP) relies less on chases and monster stalking to create its tension.  That's not to say there isn't any, but much less than Dark Descent.   AMFP goes for it's horror in it's atmosphere and writing, letting your imagination paint the disturbing pictures of what our character has experienced.
Since so much of AMFP story and horror is fleshed out in reading notes it doesn't surprise me that people are giving it so much hate.  It took me 6 hours to finish the game without getting stuck too long on any "puzzle", so when I see people claiming to "beat" it under 3-4 hours it's no wonder they aren't enjoying it.  I'd wager they speed run through every area and don't bother reading any journal entries.  They're only giving themselves half the experience.
Perhaps The Chinese Room should have preceded the game with the same disclaimer A Dark Descent used:  Do NOT play this game to Win.  Let yourself be immersed and enjoy the experience.   People that enjoy reading horror storytelling will enjoy AMFP, while others looking for more adrenaline pumping action may want to look to Outlast.
The Chinese Room took a step in the right direction with AMFP.  While the puzzles in AMFP were simplistic compared to Dark Descent, they fit perfectly into the level design and story, and offered a degree of interaction that was completely void in Dear Esther.
I highly recommend this, but with a huge disclaimer - Do not expect Dark Descent 2.

I was so looking forward to this...
When I heard that Frictional were teaming up with The Chinese Room (of Dear Esther fame), I was expecting something pretty epic.  With Frictional's immersive gameplay and The Chinese Room's decent story writing and presentation skills, this seemed like a match made in heaven.  The reality, however, was that development was handed over lock, stock and barrel to The Chinese Room.  The result is not an Amnesia game, more "Dear Esther: The Horror Story".  To say I was disappointed would be the understatement of the century.
The Dark Descent was one of the few games I enjoyed more for its gameplay than the story.  The monsters terrified me and the entire atmosphere of Castle Brennenburg filled me with a sense of cold dread and impending doom.  A Machine for Pigs felt like a different game entirely, with only mere vestiges of the Amnesia formula that I adored.  The gameplay consisted mostly of walking around, reading notes, listening to gramophones and pressing a few buttons/pulling a few levers.  The Pigs did not scare me in the least, they just provided an annoyance that I had to evade; unlike the Grunts, who scared the living hell out of me and made me want to hide until they went away.  The game is more about seeing supposedly "scary" stuff happen, rather than experiencing it yourself.  It seems like they were so proud of their story, that they removed almost all elements of gameplay so you would not get distracted.
Overall, I would not recommend this game to fans of the original Amnesia and the Penumbra games.  While it might appeal to fans of Dear Esther, and games of that ilk where story is the sole focus of the game, it left me wanting much, much more.

The date is December 31, 1899. You play as Oswald Mandus, a wealthy English businessman and a loving father, who has recently returned from a trip to Mexico. Sick and feverish, Mandus is startled awake in the middle of the night by the sound of his children calling out for him. Following the echoes of their voices, Mandus enters the cellar of his house. If only he knew what he would discover down in the depths.
A Machine for Pigs is probably best described as an indirect sequel to The Dark Descent, and though it shares the Amnesia name, the developers are not the same, and jumping in with the expectations of it being the same game will only leave you disappointed. A Machine for Pigs is by no means a bad game, but it certainly is different from its predecessor.
Gameplay-wise, the most noticeable changes are the many elements that are absent compared to The Dark Descent, most notably the sanity meter and inventory. Rather than picking up items and combining them to solve puzzles, you instead must physically carry around anything that you need, and can only hold one item at a time. While this does make for much simpler puzzles overall, it also makes the game feel more immersive. There's no pausing to combine items while a monster chases you down, everything is real-time. Other than those changes, however, the game plays just like Frictional's previous games.
Atmosphere is a large and critical element in any horror game, and few developers know atmosphere better than The Chinese Room, most well-known for their game Dear Esther. As you travel from your cozy mansion, to the graveyard of the church, to the industrial bowels of the Machine, the atmosphere is persistent, realistic and very intense. The monsters, though there are relatively few that pose a real threat to you, are gruesome and terrifying, and the infamous Amnesia invisible water monster even makes a return in a new form.
However, where A Machine for Pigs truly excels is in the story. Like The Dark Descent, you start out knowing very little about yourself and your surroundings. But as the game progresses, you learn more and more, and the plot twists and turns as you uncover more about what is really happening. As you descend farther into the Machine, you discover journal entries and voice recordings revealing the story, but only at the end does everything tie together. This form of storytelling has a way of pulling the player in, giving them clues to let them piece the story together, while making them want to keep playing so they can see if they were right all along. And the ending is nothing short of satisfying. Assuming you pay attention to the notes and conversations along the way, the game's conclusion leaves you without any big questions, and wraps everything up very nicely.
As I mentioned, this game is not by any means The Dark Descent, so playing it and expecting something just like it will not leave you with the same sense of satisfaction. A Machine for Pigs is a very good game, and if it weren't for a few small issues (namely some graphical problems and simplistic puzzles) I would even call it great. And for the $20 price tag, it's certainly worth it if you're a fan of any survival horror games. It won't make you soil your pants like Outlast and it won't make you go insane like The Dark Descent, but A Machine for Pigs certainly has its place in the genre.

A spiritual sequel to one of the greatest horror games, it dissapoints in quite a few key areas, improves in some, but overall delivers on the core idea of a hellish descent into madness in a very special way.
The industrial hell that you explore is particularly striking, and contains moments of pure marvel and disgust.
The sound design is fantastic, and had me jumping at shadows all the way through.
The music is also a big highlight, and although it is used sparingly, it is particularly effective in evoking dose chills.
When compared to the first game, a few things are immediately apparant: removal of the inventory, removal of resource management, and removal of the sanity meter. While I have a sneaking suspicion this may have been due to a large outcry of people 'running out' of light sources in the first game, it might have just been a design choice, who knows. But I do feel that a lot of the tension is removed along with these systems, which is damn a shame.
The puzzles also suffer due to the lack of an inventory, restricted generally to an immediate component search to fix whatever machine has broken down. At no point is there any real challenge, unlike the first game which I remember had me stumped on at least a couple.
The use of monsters has also been peeled back in a way. They will run by as means of scaring you initially, later on they serve more to illustrate certain story points. It is actually rather rare to be put in any direct confrontations in this game, and  even rarer that any amount of stealth or hide-and-seek is required. This is the biggest dissapointing aspect for me, as hiding from the monsters in DD was much more pants-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ scary than just running away from the scripted manpig sequences.
One thing I think the game improves on is mindgames. I can't be certain, but I'm pretty sure that sometimes an areas makeup, (such as doors or other props) have shifted around (then again, it could have been all in my head, but if so, you can chalk that up to the palpable atmosphere). An early revelation in the mansion is also particularly effective in putting you in the paranoid frame of mind of the protagonist Mandus. Some other unique scares or tricks the game throws at you really helps to mix it up and distinguish it from dark descent.
The story is pretty interesting, and some of the notes are rather disturbing, or striking, especially with Mandus's own twisted vision of mankind. However don't expect anything spelled out for you, or for there to be some great revelation.
Overall I'd say that the game is well made, if a little dissapointing. Certainly if you enjoyed Amnesia DD, Dear Esther, or even both, you'll definitely find something here. If you hated one or the other, then probably not ;)

Think of this game as having your own Michael Bay movie; lots of explosions, lots of violence, helicopters in tunnels, cars in low-earth orbit and every gas station & oil platform has enough explosive potential to stand toe-to-toe with nuclear weapons.
The bad part is, that this includes a Michael Bay movies storyline; flimsy, poor and somewhat-mandatory if you want to actually finish the game. The character development is appalling yet totally not the reason why anyone wants or should buy the game to start with. Still, you need to progress the 'story' to disable superweapons protecting command centrals, at which point you'll have to drag yourself from cliche to cliche...
Also, this game has been both blessed and cursed by the influences of Michael Bay's Indian cousin in the physics department; Michael Singh. Blessed, because it's hilarious to be able to go all-out Bollywood and string a tank up against a gunboat using your own personal steel-wire-at-a-distance-despenser and watching both of them explode violently or having two military vehicles somehow embedded into your own, which ends up with an hilarious-if-proportionally-too-large explosion, taking out all three vehicles and nine enemy soldiers and sometimes yourself. The bad part? This also happens during those tedious missions where you have to escort some idiot; who now has two military vehicles glitched into his truck, all of which are about to blow up and cause you to fail your mission.
Lastly, the game is basically a cheap port. You can expect all the glorious performance slump, controller 'features' and stability issues you can get from a cheap port. Get it cheap; it's entertaining enough to play for less than 10 euro or so, at which point the shoddy port job and horrid storyline don't really matter anymore. But not worth it at the full price.

Ok, so take what I have to say with a grain of salt, as it may sound outdated, or a little odd depending on who you are.
I got this game, on day 1 for its console release, specifically PS4. Over the summer of its release I acquired atleast 100 hours and grinded the living hell out of this game. The main experience in this game is its PvP, which is essentially total war, with many repeatable quests in the middle. Something to keep in mind though, is that this game is not a game to be played alone. This is at its core, an MMO, despite it doing a lot of things that make it non traditional, for example, its heavy restriction on what abilities you can use, and by that I mean the count of them you can have. You get two hot bars after getting to level 15, that you switch in between and that also switch your in hand weapons, however the amount of abilities you can have is 6, one of them being your ultimate. So in total you can have 12 abilities, and you can string together any combination of the sort, its very limited when compared to other MMO's that can allow you to have every number and F key on your keyboard bound to an ability.
The games content its self is very big, however due to this being an MMO, you'll never be able to get an attatchment to a character, at any point, unless you want to waste time and sit through dialogue which makes progression feel very halted as you could be spending that time skipping through it all to finally turn in the quets and get the XP, and thats all the motivation you really get to do quests, no story arcs that you'll feel like you have the time to get invested in because the MMO style of the game encourages you to skip through dialogue and just finish the quest. And there are quite a few arcs to enjoy, but you'll never enjoy them.
There are also plenty, and I mean, PLENTY of dungeons to go through and complete which have there own little side quests, that do a very good job at motivating you to do them for the loot and XP that they will trade off.
Verdict: Grab a few friends, agree to grind the hell out of the game, and enjoy it for what it is, an MMO.

Man, I really didn't think it would be hard for this game to please me. So that sword looking thing you see the main character with, is more of a wand, bummer, I like swords. The combat offers so many cool unique things to play with, sadly it is also slow, clunky, and thoroughly unsatisfying. The games flavor is largely rooted in refernces to programming language. You collect Functions as you progress and by using them directly, or to modify other functions you assemble your pool of attacks. This sounds great, and it is. However the animations are so slow, conversely enemy attacks are lightning fast. The pace of a battle is basically using a quick attack while you position yourself to use the "Turn()" system. This system freezes time and lets you queue up actions. This is where your slower more devastating attacks become usable. Most of the strategy comes down to bringing the moves that will maximize your potency in Turn() while having a plan to survive while you wait for Turn() to recharge.
Sometimes you will find yourself dying almost instantly, many deaths feel cheap, and a few encounters I just rammed my face into a few times before just quickly winning it. **Before you waste your time with your L2P sentiments, let me inturrupt you. That is not a defense of poor game design** Of course one can get good at any game, but if that journey is unsatisfying one won't be very motivated to do so. This game would have been better off fully turn based as it's real time elements are unpolished.
The art is beatiful, the voice acting convincing, and the overall flavor of the world is enough to draw you in initially. However, like many of the more notable story driven indie games, this one has the typical vagueness you've come to expect. While this vagueness is a great way to dive into the story at first, sticking to it through the end doesn't leave the audience smitten with curiousity, it just reveals a world with little to say.
I can't recommend this game at full price, but if you want to play something a little different than your endless stream of shooters and mmos, and free to play nonsense this will satisfy an evening, though it will frustrate you with it's puzzling combat design choices.

Really beautiful game. Visuals and audio are top notch. Gameplay is a good mix of action and strategy, and very challenging. The gameplay isn't straightforward either, you really have to think about how you plan to tackle a situation. You can select 4 skills to use in battle, and as you progress through the game, you can combine those skills with other skills to make unique and interesting combos. No one will play this game exactly like another player, as this system makes the combat system extremely customizable. The story is also very well done, not giving away too much as to have the player piece things together themselves. Don't wanna spoil anything. I recommend picking up the bundle that comes with the soundtrack, as the music in this game is beautifully done. Darron Korb shows off his diverse style once again, this time tackling electronic and jazz. This contrasts his more folk/western/blues enspired music from Bastion. Ashley Barrett returns with vocals, and as before she sings beautifully. She isn't just a singer though, as she is the voice of the main character, Red.
Highly recomended for anyone who loved Bastion, loves music, and loves a good action or strategy rpg. The story is great, the visuals are beautiful, and the music is both moving and flowing. Gameplay is a lot of fun and extremely strategic while at the same time filling that action craving you may have with a very open combat system that really pushes experimentation. I can't recommend this game enough.

At first glance fiction of the old west, particularly the game fiction, could strike you as rather stale. The dog eyed tropes of showdowns on Main Street at high noon and dynamite laced fire fights through the old mines seem to perpetually resurrect themselves like the uninspiring zombies of a genre long past its relevance. However like the zombie genre, there can always be room for reinvention.
The Call of Juarez franchise noticed this a while back when its western setting began to wear thin and has been in a constant cycle of reinvention ever since - Most notable being ‘The Cartel’s admirable but failed attempt to translate the genre into a gritty modern context.
In this sense Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is initially somewhat of an enigma. Without switching up its genre trappings in any obvious way, it still somehow manages to feel like a breadth of fresh air. Moreover, we see that rather than dancing around the clichés, Gunslinger has actually dug in and entrenched itself in the pulpy fiction of the old west. It gets away with this by cleverly framing its story arc around the rather dubious recounting of past glories by shady outlaw figure Silas Greaves – That is to say the game doesn’t tell his story – it tells the story of his story! This sleight of hand rather brilliantly comes to define the whole tone of the piece freeing up the plot and gunplay to really revel in a special brand of heightened reality.
Most immediately noticeable is the games beautifully measured visceral feedback. The guns are weighty, the shots are loud and the impacts produce a glorious crimson spray. This is a game that really wants you to enjoy the connection of a well aimed shot, going so far as to slow-mo the dispatched enemies bodies (300-style) as they flail gracefully into the ground.
Visceral reality extends into the environment as Silas recalls traversing a diverse array of locals, made unexpectedly exotic within the confines of this North-American genre. The recounted narrative then builds on this diversity by lending a unique brand of playfulness to the level design: Details of the story can be brought into question, and in response the narrator often bends or twists the nature of the playable reality without warning. As Silas haphazardly revises the flow of his story new paths can materialise, various characters can be swapped out and entire sections of the level design can be replayed along an altered narrative. This surreal manipulation married with the superb visual design creates a crisp, graphic and slightly oversaturated world that ends up feeling genuinely unique.
The rich landscape is not for idle rambling though as the campaign bolts from the starting line and then continues to ride at break-neck pace through the remainder its ripping yarn. Even the plot, quick-fired at you through in game narration and sideshow cutscenes serves more to set the roguish tone rather than attempt to construct any kind of complex narrative progression. In this and many other ways Gunslinger proves to be a master class on the good application of brevity. Slogging and grinding are most certainly off the menu for this insulin shot of action gunplay - Most should finish satisfied but with a healthy hunger for more!
And that’s the joy of Gunslinger - everything about its design has been streamlined to suck you into the zone of it pulpy hyper-realised action core. It’s a game that can genuinely brand itself as gun-running-fun and it has done this by releasing itself of many of the overreaching expectations other games in its category of man-shoot live or die by. Expectations perhaps generated by the traditional triple-A price point that Gunslinger has deliberately dived below.
While the fiction of the old West has long since developed into well trodden territory, its popularity can always be traced back to the youthful pleasures of heroic conflict by way of cowboys and Indians. Simple stuff really – morally unburdened heroes in a savage unpredictable frontier free to carve a path of righteous violence through an ensemble of joyfully hateful villains.  In returning to these roots Gunslinger has excelled in giving us an unapologetic slice of gunpowder-fuelled catharsis, once again making the old west feel new. YE-HA!

I don't really have much to say about Plantera, and that is probably my biggest criticism. For $2.99 there really isn't much on offer that can't be found in a similar free title. The game feels incomplete and a quick browse of other titles from this developer suggests that is a trend in their games.
The plants and animals in Plantera can be unlocked within the first two hours of gameplay. All that remains beyond that point appears to be grinding achievements. Gameplay consists of planting an orchard and collecting gold by clicking on fruit, or by idling the game to allow workers to collect it automatically. The garden can be expanded but continues to get filled with the same plants and animals. It would have been nice to more fleshed out gameplay. Perhaps a greater number of units, or the addition of quests/daily goals to achieve.
If you like clicker games and have exhausted the rest, or you're looking for easy achieves, you could probably do worse than Plantera. If you're looking for a worthwhile experience it would be best to skip this title.

Emily is Away is a free to play, amospheric, retro, indie simulation that, despite being a short game, it's really good, and has a lot of story, and can be replayed to get different responses. It is a great game. 10/10 would play, (and get sad), again.
Emily is Away is a very story driven, sad and emotional game in which you talk to a friend from high school to the end of your college years, Emily. Everything you send her will impact the story in one way or another. For example, going to the party in your high school years will trigger events that will differ from if you hadn't gone to that party. It is a very well played game, and I really like it. It shows the problems, and joys, that occur when hitting college, such as love, and how to comfort someone, (someone being Emily), when they are going through hard break-ups and difficult times in school. However, this game couldv'e worked REALLY WELL if there were alternate endings. This is the one thing I dislike about the game, because there are so many ways the story couldv'e ended: the traditional Emily gets back with Brad (or Travis, depends on your actions), Emily starts going out with you, or Emily stays single.
Overall, this short Indie game was really fun to play, and could benefit from a second game - Emily is Away 2. There are so many more choices that I could've picked, that would've made me selfish and mean, (I choose to be a kind, loving, understanding freind). I recommend this game to everybody. (Please make an Emily is Away 2. Please).

Where should I start? The game is so huge there's endless things to talk about. Please know that I own all DLC, and keep that in mind as you read this review.
Size -
The scale of this game astounds me. I've been playing for 19 hours so far, much of which has been flying around sight seeing, and I've discovered at most 20% of the map.
Story -
So far I've completed only a fraction of the story. However, it seems to be a well put together plotline about a dictator assuming control of a group of islands known as Medici.
Gear, gadgets, etc -
When JC2 came out, it was revolutionary. The parachute/grapple combo was unique among games, and topping something like that is quite a task. However, JC3 has managed to do just that - I won't give away any spoilers, but just know that movement around the map will be fun and challenging
Progression -
One of the things I didn't like about JC2 was that when you started the game you had all of the gear you would get. In JC3 you unlock gear as you go, and are able to do challenges to upgrade that gear. Once you get several of the upgrades, the game dynamic becomes quite unique and enjoyable, with limitless ways to cause chaos.
Graphics -
The graphics in this game are GEORGEOUS. They definitely can hold their own in the modern world of graphics. The scenery and water are especially beautiful
Performance -
Despite the georgeous graphics, optimization is strong with this game. I maintain a steady 80-120 FPS on max settings. No noticable drops or stutters, even during the most chaotic explostions.
Soundtrack -
The soundtrack on this game has astounded me. The music selections almost always match what's going on in the game, and they are very beautiful pieces. I've enjoyed turing the SFX and voices down and simply listening to the music while traversing the map. Couldn't ask for better music.
Controls -
The controls in this game are easy to learn, but hard to master. It's difficult to say more without giving away spoilers, however, cars seem to handle well along with helicopters and (spoiler)

However, some aspects of the game are hard to master, which creates an enjoyable challenge. My only qualm is the plane controls. Perhapse I'm still inexperienced with flying planes in this particular game, however, it isn't easy to do at all, and seems to be slightly counter-intuitive.
Overall, this game is wonderful! I would highly recomend it.

Long review here, but there is too much to leave unspoken about Factorio. I'd be doing the developers a huge injustice if I didn't elaborate just how much technical genius they've crammed into some 700MB of game.
Think of Terraria really quick: Small in file-size, to-the-point gameplay/design (no pretentiousness or wishy washy story), and an utterly stupid amount of content crammed into a sub-1GB game. Factorio is following the same path in early access, and its quality is FAR above other titles in the same state, hell even finished games. It's like a Voltron formed of addicting game types: Citybuilder, Tower Defense, "Clicker," survival, and even a little RTS.
Gameplay involves building a big♥♥♥♥♥factory and ultimately using it to construct a time consuming and expensive rocket to launch into space. You start with hand tools and work your way up from there, climbing an excellently-diverse and well-paced research tree, with upgrades and unlocks that alter the design and gameplay around everything you've built. There is almost no laziness in the upgrade system. The 100+ unlocks take a lot of work but most of them add something significant to gameplay, which can alter the factory, your character, or your arsenal for the better.
As you expand, you will naturally want to automate all the tedious tasks so your character's inventory and build queue will be freed for more important work. The maps are limitless in size and you will be forced to branch out to find more ore and land to exploit.  There are nests of enemies everywhere that will swarm and attack your factory as it creates pollution, and over time they will evolve into bigger and more lethal forms. The devs did not skimp on the combat element in the game and have included a selection of of multiple guns, turrets, fighting vehicles, combat robots, and fallout-style power armor with half a dozen upgrades to help mitigate the threat.
That's about it for gameplay, but I can't stop there; most of my praise for the game lies in its technical aspects. A lot of indie devs don't think about this as much as they should and it's good to see a team hit all the good points with a game they obviously put a lot of thought into.
1. Choosing sprites over models was genius, as it A) makes this game performance friendly for almost any computer, and B) seems to pay homage to the once-dead pre-2001 graphics of Command and Conquer and Total Annhilation. The sprites are a refreshing change from models, are beautifully-detailed and very well animated. The music is excellent too, very soft and fitting for a game you'll be losing so much time in.
2. The game starts right up and is responsive all around. Maps generate ridiculously fast and you can just drop right in within 15 seconds of starting the EXE. There is an adjustable map generator (Tiberian Sun style, sans map preview) AND an editor for those who want absolute control.
3. The UI, hotkeys, and interaction in the game is clean and efficient. Also, the general speed of your character actions. If you place a part in the wrong place, it picks right back up regardless of how big it is. If you place something wrong, you don't have to pull it up to rotate it. Just rotate your tile and place again. It's a small design detail but makes a huge difference with keeping the pace of the game, IMO.
4. Multiplayer is so solid it's almost indistinguishable from single player, performance wise. Your single player file can be used for multiplayer and vice versa. Saves are uploaded to all players that join and are neatly packaged in .zip files in your appdata folder. Factorio does not crap up your system with multiple directories (looking at you, Ubisoft).
5. I ran into my first bug (a strictly aesthetic one) after 30 hours of gameplay and have yet to see any more at almost 70 hours.
6. There is a demo. A good one. In 2016. Too many games try and sell what should be a demo as "early access." That alone says a lot about the devs.
And that's about it. Thanks for making it to the end, here. Get this game. Just be prepared to lose a good chunk of your life in it.

How can a sequel with limited gameplay, fewer puzzles, and a linear design possibly make it on my recommendations? Keep in mind that I have played through Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and while I loved its abiliy to freighten me, it never did much of  anything else. A Machine for Pigs horrifies me through its sound design, its symbolism, and its beautifully written plot. It is unfortunate that some aspects have been removed; having no inventory and less interaction with objects does weaken this title. However, this horror game does something I've never seen in the genre. It forces me to witness the psychological behavior of its characters. It has a central dehumanizing theme to society that I can empathize with. In short, it is art. But it is not just art for the sake of being only for the artistic eye, it is a game that proves how it, and others like it, can be seen as a new artistic medium.

This game was created by the developers of Ragnarok Online. The art direction, the sprite based characters, the addictive-feeling combat, and the gorgeous 2D/3D graphics that give you a sense of life not found in many MMOs nowadays. That being said, it is nothing like RO in its current form. That's not a bad thing, I just hope IMC realizes the reasons why people stuck with RO for so long, the most important of which was probably:
War of Emperium: open world pvp designated to certain maps, with the chance to take dominion over one of many castles that also acted as homes for your guild. Designed in such a way that even typically non-pvp players would join in as a social event.
IMC as a developer genuinely seems to want to do well by this game, but oddly enough they seem to be confused as to what direction they want to go with this game. Several betas later, they still have the same bugs, fps drops, and abuses going on since alpha. I'd really like this game to do well, but to take it to the next level of a game that most people stick with past lvl 75 will take incentivizing leveling and endgame play, more than just "oh look you can do the endgame dungeon!" and "guild battles with no reward except wasted time and resources!"
Give it a try if you are looking for something RO-like, but realize that it is still very early for this MMO to be getting any real review as it is truly, very much in beta if not alpha in spirit. Though people may not like my review, it is but a simple truth that this MMO needs much, much more in all aspects before it can be considered even capable of judgment.

I bought this game during a steam sale because of the absolutely glowing reviews it had:
“One of the best shooters to come out in recent years.”
“Don’t mistake price for quality - this is a top-notch shooter.”
What?!?
Was there some kind of dearth of FPS games in May of 2013 that I wasn't aware of that would make this steaming pile of cow dung somehow rise to the top of a very short list?
Ok ok, let me start over:
The Good
-  The Graphics were actually nice to look at.  Given the fact that there aren't a whole lotta old western video games out there, I don't have much to compare it with.  I mean, it's no ALIEN Isolation by any stretch of the imagination, but I wasn't turned away by the visuals at all.  Some parts were even downright nice to look at like the swamp level.
-  The Story is fun and entertaining.  Honestly, this is the only reason to play this game.  Crank the difficulty down to zero and sit through the old man's story.  I honestly saw part of the ending coming a mile away, and most reasonably intelligent people will too, but the way it's told is great.  There's still one twist you won't see coming cause there's no clues along the way, but it's not a rug puller and makes the ending entertaining.
-  The name dropping is great.  This is an absurd revisionist history of all the old west personalities that you've ever heard of and some you probably never knew existed.  For instance, I've watched a lot of westerns in my younger years and never once heard of George "Flat Nose" Curry in my life.
The Bad
-  The game is 100% on rails.  There's a couple of times where you can leave the trail, but there's no point unless you're really tied in knots over collecting all of the secrets hidden in the game world.  I wasn't.  I knew this going on though, so if I was giving this a point rating, I wouldn't deduct points.  It aint exactly advertised as open world.
-  Weapon variety is terrible and honestly I didn't notice any difference in using either of the 2(3 maybe?) types of pistols I could find.
-  The point system and skill upgrades are mostly pointless with 1-2 exceptions.  Hell, I didn't even remember the skill system until about 3 missions into the game and by the time I went to apply skill points I had six of them saved up.  I honestly could have gone through the entire game with all but one skill upgrade which was the extra ammo skill, and probably didn't even need that one.
-  Extremely short game.  I beat it very quickly and my playtime only looks longer cause I took the dogs out a couple times while forgetting to pause.  It tuns out to be a blessing though, because if I had to put up with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ moving and shooting mechanics for any longer than it lasted, then I would have quit, watched the ending on YouTube and uninstalled.
The Ugly
-  Movement.  I never felt like I was a person walking around in this game.  I felt like a ghost with no legs floating along the ground with a disembodied hand floating in front of me holding a gun.  The normal walk speed felt like jogging and the run speed felt like I had cheat mode turned on.  Sidways movement is just as fast as forward and backwards.  No one walks backward or sideways that fast.  Hell Usain Bolt himself couldn't sprint sidewas as fast as Silas Greaves.
-  NPC's are playing on god mode.  They can sprint to a tree, aim and headshot you from across the map.  If I take my time to make the same shot, then I'm rewarded with "Long Shot!", but apparently all shots are close range for them.  I died so many times from some guy running who suddenly stops and takes a snap shot at my skull.... game over.
- Lots of little annoying bugs.  Bad guys dying and hanging in the air dead.  Shoot a few of them several times thinking they were still alive.  Stuck on the environment a couple of times and had to reload the level.  Bad guys showing up, but the stuff they're hiding behind not showing up.  I'm thinking I'm headshotting them, but when I get closer the grave stone they're behind suddenly pops into view.  Just buggy overall.
-  Last but not least; the shooting.  How in the world anyone thinks this is a good shooter is beyond me.  It's straight point and click with no skill whatsoever.  I headshotted, and I'm not even exaggerating here, a good 75% of all enemies in every mission.  It was absurdly easy to walk through the game headshotting everything.  No bullet drop, no hand wobble while aiming, just straight up point and click.  Add to that the "concentration mode" and no challenge is too hard. Surrounded by 20 bad guys and you're on the low ground?  Hit concentration mode and headshot 15 of them quickly.
Overall, I just can't recommend this game.  Even at the super cheap steam sale prices.  The story is entertaining, but you can probably find a Cutscene video on YouTube and skip having to suffer through the shooting gallery bits all for free.

Let me just start by saying I love Dark Souls, and Souls-likes in general. That said, this game screws up nearly as many things at it improves from the first.
Pros
* The combat system is vastly improved (for the most part)
* Combat is not as sluggish as in Dark Souls
* Stamina matters, and shields are more useful
* Most weapons are viable in PvP
* Connections happen more quickly and reliably
* Powerstancing adds a lot of depth to combat
* More builds are viable
* Leveling is faster, making an item dupe glitch unnecessary
* Spellcasting takes less level investment, making more mixed-casting builds possible
* 4 ring slots
* 70% equip load before fat-rolling
* 3 weapons slots per hand
* Weapon improvement/infusing is much simpler
* Gestures can be rolled out of and generally look better
* Parry timing makes much more sense
* PvP parries are now possible
* More infinite in-combat items than Dark Souls (gold pine resin, etc)
* Invasions no longer require a living boss
* Less lag-stabs
* Free humanity shrine
* Enemies stop respawning after 15 kills
* Name-engraved ring makes multiplayer easier to coordinate
* Pyromancy now scales with both intelligence and faith
* Hexes are pretty well balanced
* Some textures look great
* Water effects are generally very pretty
* The lore seems less interesting on the surface than Dark Souls', but once you get to the bottom, it actually ties into the first game really well
* One of the endings is really satisfying and ties up the Dark Souls series lore nicely
* Every stat matters, making stat investment much more involved
Cons
* Wheel skeletons are back
* Player poise is meaningless
* Every movement, no matter how tiny, causes huge amounts of motion blur
* The infamous 60fps durability bug
* The geography seems just string together at random. At one point, you go up an elevator into a city sunk in a sea of lava... what?
* Every enemy turns to face you constantly, even during attacks. It's especially problematic with bosses. Instead of feeling like you're fighting something colossal like in Dark Souls, it feels like you're just fighting constant hackers.
* Soul memory makes it hard to coordinate PvE with friends (the Agape ring takes some of that away)
* Every enemy deals insane poise damage and pretty much never flinches
* The boss music isn't as unique or interesting
* Leveling up and upgrading the estus flask at the Emerald Herald takes way too long
* Combat is tipped so far in enemies' favor that a lot of late-game PvE feels purely luck-based
* Any enemy with range has a huge advantage over you from the get-go
* Exploding undead are more-or-less undefeatable with a slow weapon
* Level design is uninspired
* Most areas are so tedious to complete they feel like Blighttown/Izalith all over again
* There is even less explanation of what to do than in Dark Souls - you're just told your end-game goal in the unhelpful form of "find the king". It would be like if the only direction you were given in Dark Souls was "open the Kiln"
* Textures are hideous in many places (Iron Keep, Tseldora)
* Enemy homing magic tracks you to the ends of the earth
* Collision detection is worse than in Dark Souls, if you can imagine that. Fire is especially terrible, hitting through several walls at its worst
In short, this game is great for PvP. The PvE, however, is tedious at best and mind-numbingly frustrating at worst. Get some friends together and it'll be a great deal easier, but in the end Dark Souls did PvE better in every way.

Not necessarily a bad game as some gamers declared it. Quite contrary, this is one of the most atmospheric horror games. It doesn't rely on cheap scares or excessive gore, instead it will slowly get under your skin dragging you inside it's horrific storyline. Yet there is a lack of true paranoia and that claustrophobic feeling from Dark Descent that would really improve the overall feel. Still, the experience is spooky and the story leaves some interesting topics for discussion.
The developers (TheChineseRoom) excelled with what they do best - level design and storytelling and I'd love them to continue their cooperation with Frictional Games. With someone else being in charge of gameplay and puzzles, that is.
Compared to Outlast, Machine for Pigs is more cerebral and atmospheric experience. If you're looking for something more than jumpscares in a horror game, this is a series to play.

If you are a fan of The Dark Descend be ready to be disappointed by A Machine For Pigs. Much of previous game mechanics has been taken off in order to increse focus on the plot. Buy it only if you like nice storyes and atmosphere, if you look for a real horror story look somewhere else.
Biggest disappointment of 2013.

A completely different experience from "The Dark Descent", the true king of indie horror games. A:AMFP focuses completely on storytelling and has deep messages underneath.
Enemy encounters (which was a base element in the previous game) barely happen and even if they do, they're just not as scary as we want it to be. We can't hide in closets, creatures won't break doors and we don't even have a sanity meter at all. By not having to gather lamp oil, tinderboxes or health potions, the whole concept of the exploration factor of survival horror is killed.
But what do we have left? It's evident that more was taken away than what was added (like the flickering lamp when monsters are near), but I still can't hate the game. The dark and twisted story makes you think, the cold atmosphere keeps you on edge and the sound design, the music, the voice acting is just amazing.
If you liked "Dear Esther" (the previous work of thechineseroom), you'll be in a hell of a ride! And those, who expected more (like me), well... Try to look at it from a different angle. You may even suprise yourself.

Clever and fun. A great diversion when you need something less demanding of your attention than your usual more serious fare. I've had fun playing it without spending a penny on the available microtransactions.

Game Feelz:
Not a game for its story, but written well enough that it doesn't detract from the rest of the game. Recommended if you're looking for a game to fill time, without too much personal investment, or if you're looking for something with relatively easy 100% achievements (~10% of players global with total achievement completion).
The variety of usable units/characters cover most playstyles, and the obtainable equipment further broadens availability of playstyle accomodation. Minimal character/npc interactions after tutorial; conversations are limited to bosses before their first kill and the wizard.
Overall, the game can be "enjoyed at your own pace," as long as you're willing to leave it running for increasingly lengthy amounts of time. Several points can be considered as having "beaten the game," depending on the tenacity of the player. If attempting to fully complete all aspects of the game, note that some items are restricted to Christmastime, and some cosmetics are only obtained during Halloween.
If you're just looking to beat the first boss, you can make it casually in a handful of hours. Beating the final boss will take a bit longer (around 10-12 hours casual gameplay), and fully unlocking everything will take several hundred hours and plenty of time spent optimizing use of prestige bonuses/team setup/equipment usage.
Good as a strategy/endurance game, lacking in almost any sense of story.
Game Mechanics:
Upgrades can be purchased for real currency or obtained via general progression.
PC port from mobile.
Recruit a squad and head into a cycling dungeon, fighting through waves of 8 normal fights, a midboss, and floor boss, until reaching the level boss. Find better equipment, recruit new fighters, and make your team more stylish after every run.
Prestige to start earning exclusive boosts to team stats and individual character stats.
Game is mostly played afk, with emphasis on team setup and strategy.
Offline gains are limited to gold (with ingame purchase of bank upgrade), no dungeon progression or loot.
Typical elements of turn based combat used in Soda Dungeon: variety of items/weaponry that can be used to improve casting/physical abilities, dodge chance, critical strike, damage reduction, and damage reflection.
Prestiging will remove items, gold (ingame currency), and sodas (used to unlock usable characters), but will NOT remove essence (currency to improve prestige upgrades), tavarn upgrades and VIP upgrades (used to expand character recruitment/general QoL improvements).

before you go on reading: there is a demo version kind of hidden in the factorio game page in the store. it's only about 300mb in size so if you start downloading now you should be ready to go by the time you're done reading this. it's only the tutorial missions and obviously your possibilities are very limited but it's enough to get a perfect idea about how this game works.
at first glance it looks like just another survival game.
but it is NOT!
of course there is gathering of resources, base building, research, crafting and all that stuff.
but here is the twist: it's all about automation, optimization and logistics.
you will use your pickaxe in the first minutes of the game to get some basic stuff but after that? never again. unless you want to. it's not about you turning 2000 iron plates into 1000 gears with your bare hands. that takes forever. instead build a factory that does the job for you. in the meantime you can do other useful things. for example build more factories to do even more work for you. of course the production gets more complex over time and you need to move resources and products around your base using conveyor belt systems.
sooner or later you will most likely run out of resources in the starting area so you need to expand. trains are in for the job. but you will need train stations to load and unload your trains. fully automated of course.
and when a train arrives and the ore pours into your furnaces, the belts fill with iron and copper plates and your huge base comes back to life again and starts producing useful stuff...nerdgasm i tell you.
or when you tinker around with your factory for 30 minutes just to make everything run that 1% smoother...nerdgasm again!
later in the game you get construction and logistics robots. the logistics robots add a little bit more flexibility to the usual conveyor belt transportation and they supply the player with whatever they order them to fetch. the construction robots fly in and place or remove whatever structures you want them to.  you can even create blueprints of base layouts and construct or deconstruct parts of your base or whole outposts in seconds.
guess what? double nerdgasm!
like i said: automation, optimization and logistics.
if that is your kind of game then this is the most fun you can have with your pants on. but you can always play naked if you want to just to cover that option as well.
now go and start the demo. NOW i said!

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a Western themed First Person Shooter from Techland and published by Ubisoft. It is the fourth game in the Call of Juarez series, however experience in the previous games is not necessary to enjoy the gameplay and storyline. This is the first Call of Juarez game I have played, and I don't feel like I was missing out on anything by skipping the first few.
The gunplay in Call of Juarez Gunslinger is fast and hectic, but very enjoyable. The controls are tight, and even when the game throws an overwhelming amount of enemies at you, between the bullet time, three gun types and dynamite, you feel like you have all the tools you need to take down the entire Wild West. That's pretty much what you are doing here, with a body count approaching the thousands by the end of the game.
The ridiculous body count fits in with the story, however, because the plot is framed around a tale an oldtimer is telling to those gathered in a bar. Apparently Silas Greaves was responsible for taking down nearly every famous outlaw in the Old West, and you get to relive the story as he tells it. Within that framework comes some neat tricks, as you will replay sections of levels with slight differences as it is misremembered, and new paths will open up before you as they spring from memory. The whole story takes on the feel of a tall tale, which seems fitting for a game about the Old West, where legends and tall tales are aplenty.
In addition to the normal gunplay, there is a duel mode as you finally come face to face with each of your foes. It does an admirable job of adding the tension that duels must have built, as you must keep focus on your enemy while making sure your hand is ready to draw. If you enjoy the duels, which I did, there is a duel mode where you can face all your enemies again, with a leaderboard to track your score against friends.
The graphics and sound exude style. The characters are all very well designed, and the environments are very enjoyable. Cutscenes all have a storybook feel. The voice acting is stupendous, and often humorous as you listen to the audience argue with the storyteller. I was expecting something good in these departments, and what was delivered is great.
Overall I completely recommend Call of Juarez Gunslinger. It will take about 5 hours to complete the main story mode, but the price point fits that length. This was a budget priced title, but many aspects of it feel AAA in quality. I had heard good things about this game, but it exceeded my expectations.

It's hard to know what to say about this game, but I'll give it a shot...
First, let me say that if you enjoyed playing Ragnarok Online, you should also like this game.  The game has a serious feel of a Ragnarok clone, even to the point of having most of the same classes, abilities and such.  This said... it doesn't diffrentiate itself enough from Ragnarok Online for my tastes.  Or at least, not in the correct ways.  TONS of design flaws (open pathways that are inexpicably blocked by invisible walls. bad, sometimes painful, engrish throughout most of the game.  Bots are on thier way to being out of control).  Zero character customization outside of wearing funny hats or different job outfits and hairstyles.
...but for all the negatives, IT'S STILL A DECENT GAME.
Positives:
++Gorgeous environments
+cute character graphics
+++fantastic music
+++NOT pay 2 win!  Everything that gives advantage in game is available IN GAME.  Only small boosts and cosmetics are behind a Paywall.
+multiple channel instances to all maps
+So long as you contribute a decent amount of damage vs a mob, you'll get drops.
Negatives:
--Not much story to this RPG.  What is there is fragmented and disjointed.
-Engrish makes it difficult to follow what story pieces you do get.
--maps are pathed very strangely, forcing you to travel over areas that sometimes seem impossible and othertimes stop you from walking down completely open pathways.
-TONS of grinding
-EVERYTHING asplodes.  Did you just kill that roach with your wooden sword, lil girl? *Cue screen shaking, loud explosion as bits fly everywhere*
--------BOTS ARE GETTING OUT OF CONTROL!  You need to be at the physical location of the bot in order to report them as a bot and only way to do this is to right click them and choose "report bot".  Thankfully, most bots are easy to identify: multiple characters continuously running a 2 or 3 point path in single file, ignoring thier own hp and attacking everything in sight, all characters swinging thier weapons simultaneously at times as well.
----Apparently, this game is vulnerable to hacks.  Not only is Botting a problem, but there are alot of exploits and hacks in the game where people can delete other people's guilds.  And apparently, the dev's answer to this is ignore it or remove it.  (there was an exploit where people could duplicate items via the buyback from NPC vendors.  So the devs took this function out months ago and never returned it.  THERE IS NO WAY TO BUYBACK ITEMS SOLD TO NPC VENDORS)
---Character customization is almost non existant.  Most of the hairstyles for the males look like they belong on the females while the females only get long and poofy hairstyles. BTW: want one of the BETTER looking Hairstyles?  PAYWALL!
--Community is already getting toxic in shout chats.
Honestly, my only real gripe is that this game is showing all the signs of going down the road Ragnarok Online did.... Eventually, prices will be insane, bots will be nearly a 3rd of the population and the population will be mostly antisocial and toxic people that believe that if you're not playing your character a SPECIFIC way and not wanting to solo the entire game, then stfu and gtfo.
I recommend the game if you're looking for something to pass the time.  The game has some very strong aspects.  But if you're reading this in 2017, unless they make some MAJOR changes to the game, I'd advise to not bother.

Before playing this game, there is a few things that you need to understand.
#1. This game is currently in open beta. That's right, currently. Which means it's unfinished. There are bugs, there are glitches, there is lag, the class structure is unfinished. The fun of playing a game in open beta is that you're there to watch it evolve and be part of that in some small way. If you come in with that understanding, have some patience, and a sense of humor, you'll do fine. Work around the issues, report the major bugs so IMC is aware (they do weekly maintenance and do fix issues), and have fun.
#2. There's this thing called the internet, where jerks, whiners and scammers thoroughly enjoy screwing with people, lying to people, and ruining your day. This is not new, a-holes have been around longer than the internet, the internet just allows them to spread their a-holery beyond their immediate vicinity. The internet is full of scam artists at worst, and opportunists at best. Even the nicest people in real life can become an opportunist a-hole on the internet. Seems like a simple concept, but seeing the constant outrage in the forums shows that people somehow aren't aware of this. If you can accept the reality of the internet, don't fall for scams, and avoid the trolls, you'll be fine.
#3. Everybody's got an opinion on how things "should" be, the "right way" to play classes, set up stats, and reach endgame. That's great. Have your opinion. Do what you think works. Research stuff, see what other people are doing, what they feel works for their build. But play the game for yourself. There are more than enough classes, skills, and combinations to try and have fun with on your own, without depending on someone else's "correct" build and then screaming bloody murder when that build doesn't work for you. Ultimately it's up to you to find what works for you.
#4. Don't act like it's a waste of time to learn to play the game. Treat your first characters like practice runs so you can figure out what skills you like, what attributes help you, what matches your gameplay style. And other aspects, like how the collections work, how to get exp cards by getting 100% maps and killing tons of monsters, and that you don't always have to repair every piece of equipment. I've restarted from the beginning twice because there were things I didn't learn or understand right away. I don't see those starter characters as a waste of time, I spent my time having fun playing the game, learning the game, and doing stupid dorky things in the game.
#5.
is a very good source of information, but is not completely comprehensive. A lot of the information is from the closed beta in Korea, which for all intents and purposes is not the same game. Things have changed, some monsters don't exist, some items don't exist, some maps don't exist. This is where you (as a player) can help everybody by posting a simple comment confirming that you got that drop from that monster, or found that monster on another map that isn't listed. Or you can keep that coveted information to yourself, totally your call.
Things that make me happy:
The artwork - GORGEOUS! I love the backgrounds, it's easy to get lost in the details, it's a very visually stimulating game.
The music - is awesome! I love that each map has different music, that all of the music is well composed and in many cases fits the "mood" of the area (love the metal during boss fights).
The cuteness and doom - The characters are cute, the outfits are cute, the monsters are cute (in some cases ugly-cute), EVERYTHING is cute. I enjoy cute, and also blowing things up, so this is a big draw for me. And the story is pretty dark, you spend a lot of time dealing with graveyards and creepy-cute.
The grinding - This is an epic grind fest and I really enjoy that aspect. I don't expect everyone to agree. You grind for levels, materials, experience, silver, and you have fun making things explode.
I'm brutal - I enjoy being an epic killing machine that makes things explode. You don't have to wait long to feel like an epic killing machine. The first 100 levels you feel like an unstoppable whirlwind of destruction. It gets more difficult later.
The challenge - Oh, you'll get there. That moment where you go from epic killing machine to "What just happened and how am I dead!?" and realize you stopped using tactics or moving around because you didn't have to. Well, now you have to change it up, move around, maybe focus on other stats for a bit. Killing things takes effort all of a sudden. At which point you finally feel like you got past the tutorial to the real game.
The issues:
Yeah, you thought this was all rainbows and sunshine, didn't you? You were wrong. I'm not some deluded idiot who can't see problems because I'm blinded by cuteness, I am ultimately a realist and I know there are aspects of the game that need attention.
Server stability - The server I'm on has not been hit nearly as hard as SEA or SA as far as stability is concerned (lately), but pre-free to play wasn't always perfectly accessible for us NA servers either. I still get booted about once a day when the servers are busy. Commanderloadfail will always be my most loathed and feared enemy. There is no escape and rarely a workaround when he slams his error message onto your screen when you were JUST TRYING TO GET TO TOWN! Sometimes he trolls the dungeons, sometimes just a specific location, but he is always waiting to kill your fun when you least expect it. LURKING! Sometimes he is a precursor to an epic server fail or emergency maintenance, at which point IMC beats him into submission.
Bots and goldspammers - An addition to the aforementioned "internet," bots are a staple of annoyance in any online game. If there is any form of trade, opportunist goldspammers will follow. Period. They♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. Not because the bots farm areas where I'm trying to quest, not because the discourse on global chat is interrupted on a regular basis, not even because it creates a third party pay to win system that offends me on a personal level, but because the programs they run bog down the server and contribute to lag, rubber banding, and that interrupts my gameplay. I hunt down every one I can find to report and block them. IMC has been working on it, there are ban lists that come up on a regular basis on
.
Lag - I'm not a fan. I hate having to wait 20 seconds for the NPC to register that I turned in a quest and give me the next one. Not constant, but often enough to bother me. Another one of those things that comes with more people playing the game. Always seems to improve a bit after each maintenance and regress on weekends. It helps to change to less busy channels or move to less populated maps, much as it annoys me to leave a quest unfinished, even temporarily.
Glitches and mistranslations - Oh there's plenty of them. They can be really amusing or really frustrating depending on what's happening. Sometimes the transition between cinematics and regular game fails, and you're stuck restarting a quest. Some descriptions on things are incomplete, or missing and just a line of code or "Defeat %". It's beta, they're working on it. Expect glitches.
Personally, I really enjoy the game. I've had close to 300 hours of fun with this game already. Are there issues? Yeah, but it's beta, so it's expected to be incomplete. If you walk in thinking it's complete, you'll be disappointed. There are workarounds all over the place, and enough love for the game that people regularly post helpful tips and tricks for framerate issues or settings adjustments to reduce lag. There are really nice and helpful people who answer questions in global chat all the time. There are far more positives than negatives, and the negatives are either inevitable or work in progress. I think it's fun, you might too.

A Machine for Pigs is to The Dark Descent as The Omen is to The Exorcist. As far as horror at its most basic fundaments go, one could even say that it is "merely" unsettling as opposed to downright terrifying. That said, The Omen is my favorite horror film of all time as it is what I consider to be a class act, and what A Machine for Pigs lacks in immediacy it makes up for in spades with an industrial atmosphere that takes you to a place of darkness that feels hellishly real.
The scares are more subtle, the story is better written, and the sound design is some of the best seen in the medium. Jessica Curry's score is instantly iconic and legitimately bone-chilling, setting off each of the game's virtual spaces with just the right accent of terror. However, if you come to the experience expecting The Dark Descent 2.0, you'll come away very disappointed, as A Machine for Pigs is shorter and more mechanically stripped down. It's also not as terrifying, as only the first enemy encounter is really effective, though I believe that this was the intent of developer The Chinese Room, as there was just no way the story could have been told as effectively if the enemies were designed and portrayed any differently.
At its worst, A Machine for Pigs feels like a simultaneous step backwards in the gameplay department and evolutionary stride forward in storytelling within the medium, but at its best it transcends encompassing the sum of its parts and delivers a heightened emotional experience. If what you want is a good horror story with philosophical underpinnings and an eye and ear for real creepiness, then this game will fit that niche and then some.

Transistor is staggeringly beautiful. All of the art, the setting, the music, the writing, all of it. It's also a pretty big departure from Bastion, which was made by the same developers. Yes, it's the same perspective, and there's an ever-present narrator, and the protagonist is mute, and you can increase the difficulty in a piecemeal fashion. The similarities end there. While you can play Transistor like an action game, it really requires more strategy than that. It has an active-pause system, where you can pause the action, plot out a set number of attacks or movements, and then unpause to see the results. The main loop ends up being pause, attack, run, which leads to a lot of guerilla tactics, more than straight out blasting enemies.
The ability system is also super interesting. Every ability, whether it's a straight attack, or a cloak, or a bomb, can be used as-is, attached to another ability to lend it different qualities, or set as a passive bonus to yourself. This leads to a ton of combinations of attacks. Some work better than others, but they all feel unique. The limits to the system is that each ability has a memory requirement, and you have a memory limit. So you can stack up on a couple heavy hitters, but you limit yourself to a small number of attacks or bonuses. Likewise, you can have a full complement of attacks and bonuses, but you'll be lacking the most powerful of them.
The one complaint I have is that the story is less straight forward than most video games. That doesn't mean it has a bad story, or that it's incomprehensible. It just takes more attention to the details than most. By the end, you'll probably get the gist of it, but expect to be a little disoriented.

Alien: Isolation is a survival horror game set in a sci-fi setting. And it is damn good.
Set in the aliens universe you play as Amanda Ripley trapped on a Space Station. Your hunted down by Andriods, other humans, and of course the Alien. Most of the game involves sneaking around and avoiding the enemies to get to your objective. In that sense the game is fairly monotonous in that sense but it does make the game very tense.
The game can be difficult, but it does feel fair. You are given tools to fight back which are all very useful in certain situations. While you are given weapons its important to note that the Alien is immune to almost all of them. It however can be scared off by the flamethrower and molotov. Don't let that lul you into a sense of security, because he will come back to that same spot soon. The Alien by itself is terrifying, you will constantly hear it move around and climb around in the vents above. The AI of the alien itself is terrifying as it will often move around near you, and show up even at certain points when you think it isn't there. There are also points in the game where you have to deal with humans and andriods. These areas are more open as you can fight your way through them. While the combat isn't incredable it does enough to change the pace of the game that adds a some variety to the gameplay.
The game is beautiful as it fully captures that retro sci-fi film. What I mean by this is that game is full of 80s green text computers, retro space ship interioirs designs. While there are parts where where you backtrack through the game, theres enough variety in the game, with the latter parts of the game changing a lot from the begining. The few outerspace moments in the game are amazing as well. The game itself contains the collectables many of which are audiologs. While there nothing new or inovative I found the logs to be quite intresting.
One thing I would like to note is that this game is well pretty long. While I don't think that its bad to get more content for what you pay, it can make the game feel a bit repetative. The ending is a bit strange as well. It took me about 20 hours to beat the whole game and as I haven't even touched the DLC.
I did run into some techincal issues when I first started playing which was fixed by turning down the graphics and setting the game to windowed borderless.
Overall I would have to give Alien: Isolation a 8/10 as it provides a scary horror exprience with a beautiful setting and atmosphere, while being limited by some repatative objectives and areas.

*** EARLY IMPRESSIONS - NOT FULL REVIEW ***
These impressions are designed for people who have played F1 2016 and want to know if it is worth the upgrade.
First up, the car handling. It is so much more fun to play than F1 2016 - largely due to updating the driving model to match the new technical specifications in the 2017 season. We've heard the real life drivers say how fun the new spec is to drive, and that is certainly represented in the game. You realise pretty quickly that you can carry considerably more speed into corners, as well as push the car harder when exiting. It really has more of a "hold your breath" sense of dare when you aggressively attack corners and I have caught myself giggling a few times when a daring maneuver pays off. That said, you still have to learn the limits of your car or you will be punished for taking it over the limit.
Secondly, performance. (For reference I have an i3 6100, 16gb of DDR4 ram, Radeon RX 480 8gb GPU, 256gb m2 SSD, Logitech G29 wheel). For some reason, F1 2016 always threw random frame rate drops at me, regardless of what graphical settings I was using. I'd be coasting along at 85 FPS and then suddenly the frame rate would drop for a second to the sub 50s, which affected my driving performance. I was desperately hoping that this would be fixed in F1 2017. And it has! The game not only looks better than last year, but it also seems to look better while not decreasing the performance compared to F1 2016 and most importantly, the random frame rate drops are gone. I'm so happy about this. It's smooth as silk.
Thirdly, career mode. I put plenty of hours into career mode last year, and while it was great, it was crying out for expanded depth. I've only done one 50 percent length GP for Haas so far, as well as the first invitiational event, but I can already see that they have injected it with more life and depth. The tech tree looks seriously cool, and you are really going to be able to develop a car over the long run that suits your particular driving style. The invitiational event was also a nice little distraction, and it was great to drive (and hear the roar of) a V8 classic). They aren't just reskinned cars, the driving experience is very different, and very fun.
My biggest gripe with F1 2016 was the difficulty settings. I (and many others) quickly found myself stranded between two difficulty levels (e.g. expert too easy & master too hard) and it was impossible to find a middle ground that provided a challenging but fair racing experience. I am thrilled to say that Codemasters have listened to the feedback and provided a 1-100 difficulty sliding scale that allows fine-tuning. It only took me a couple of free practice sessions to find my perfect challenge level and as a result, my first grand prix provided a very fun and competitive midfield race as you would expect from a Haas car this season. Of all he great changes Codemasters have made this year, this is oddly the one that I am most happy about. Such a small tweak makes all the difference.
So to answer my point at the start of the review... is it worth the upgrade from 2016. YES! YES! YES!
If Codies put this much love into the 2018 edition, I will happily upgrade again!

More of the same. With shady business practices this time round.
Remember having a DX11 setting's for your games? Well, FROM Software is charging full price for having DX11 support as a whole seperate game. No i'm not joking. Quality of Dark Souls 2 aside, i simply cannot support such a move, especially when the results of the DX11 version is so minute. It sets a dangerous precedant for PC gaming if it is supported. Imagine Fallout 4 being sold in DX9 and DX11 versions seperately. How about a DX12 remaster? Its a low move, and there is barely enough added content to warrant its price. On to the actual game, which ISNT BAD.
If you liked Dark Souls 1, this is pretty much the same game in a different environment, but this time theres fast travel and the game does have a connected sprawling world. Which is a shame since that made the first one so much more memorable and cohesive as a whole. Gameplay wise i have to say the hitboxes feel a little cheaper this time round, especially with the larger enemies, and the enemy design isnt as inventive.
Its just armoured knights in many different variations, it pales in comparison to the variety we saw previously. The story too, ends off similarly, and the journey there, along with the music is nowhere near as emotional.
Overall, if you just want more Dark Soul gameplay, its still here, its just uninspired with its weaker lore and atmosphere, and feels like a large DLC that isnt as good as the original.

Pros:

- Simple gameplay (once you get used to it)
- Lots of options to progress
Cons
- Addictive game play (as in, you start playing and many hours later you realize it's only a few hours until you're expected at work, oh boy)
- Steep-ish learning curve
