Alien: Isolation is a survival horror game set in a sci-fi setting. And it is damn good.
Set in the aliens universe you play as Amanda Ripley trapped on a Space Station. Your hunted down by Andriods, other humans, and of course the Alien. Most of the game involves sneaking around and avoiding the enemies to get to your objective. In that sense the game is fairly monotonous in that sense but it does make the game very tense.
The game can be difficult, but it does feel fair. You are given tools to fight back which are all very useful in certain situations. While you are given weapons its important to note that the Alien is immune to almost all of them. It however can be scared off by the flamethrower and molotov. Don't let that lul you into a sense of security, because he will come back to that same spot soon. The Alien by itself is terrifying, you will constantly hear it move around and climb around in the vents above. The AI of the alien itself is terrifying as it will often move around near you, and show up even at certain points when you think it isn't there. There are also points in the game where you have to deal with humans and andriods. These areas are more open as you can fight your way through them. While the combat isn't incredable it does enough to change the pace of the game that adds a some variety to the gameplay.
The game is beautiful as it fully captures that retro sci-fi film. What I mean by this is that game is full of 80s green text computers, retro space ship interioirs designs. While there are parts where where you backtrack through the game, theres enough variety in the game, with the latter parts of the game changing a lot from the begining. The few outerspace moments in the game are amazing as well. The game itself contains the collectables many of which are audiologs. While there nothing new or inovative I found the logs to be quite intresting.
One thing I would like to note is that this game is well pretty long. While I don't think that its bad to get more content for what you pay, it can make the game feel a bit repetative. The ending is a bit strange as well. It took me about 20 hours to beat the whole game and as I haven't even touched the DLC.
I did run into some techincal issues when I first started playing which was fixed by turning down the graphics and setting the game to windowed borderless.
Overall I would have to give Alien: Isolation a 8/10 as it provides a scary horror exprience with a beautiful setting and atmosphere, while being limited by some repatative objectives and areas.

More of the same. With shady business practices this time round.
Remember having a DX11 setting's for your games? Well, FROM Software is charging full price for having DX11 support as a whole seperate game. No i'm not joking. Quality of Dark Souls 2 aside, i simply cannot support such a move, especially when the results of the DX11 version is so minute. It sets a dangerous precedant for PC gaming if it is supported. Imagine Fallout 4 being sold in DX9 and DX11 versions seperately. How about a DX12 remaster? Its a low move, and there is barely enough added content to warrant its price. On to the actual game, which ISNT BAD.
If you liked Dark Souls 1, this is pretty much the same game in a different environment, but this time theres fast travel and the game does have a connected sprawling world. Which is a shame since that made the first one so much more memorable and cohesive as a whole. Gameplay wise i have to say the hitboxes feel a little cheaper this time round, especially with the larger enemies, and the enemy design isnt as inventive.
Its just armoured knights in many different variations, it pales in comparison to the variety we saw previously. The story too, ends off similarly, and the journey there, along with the music is nowhere near as emotional.
Overall, if you just want more Dark Soul gameplay, its still here, its just uninspired with its weaker lore and atmosphere, and feels like a large DLC that isnt as good as the original.

With almost 200 hours in game I'll say that the concept is great and very fun at times.  However, unless you are online 24/7 or have an international guild, you cannot maintain a base.  My friends and I have build good multi layered cobblestone+ bases that are completely leveled when we log off and go to sleep.  A steel crest with 6 layers of cobblestone will not prevent it.
The developers need to come up with a solution for the middle of the night base destruction.  For instance, in real life if you were asleep, and someone attacks your base, you'd wake up.  But when you log off the game and go to bed, you're screwed.  There is no balance for this.  It's simply not fun to spend a week gathering stone, iron and wood to build one of the strongest bases in the game just to have it all wiped out because someone else doesn't go to bed the same time you do.
Ideas:
1.  How about Once a person logs off, the block hit-points are incrementally increased by a factor of 120.  Each hour you are offline they decrease by a factor of 5.  So blocks with normal hitpoints of 3000 would have 360,000 for the first hour - 180,000 hit-points 6 hours later and 3,000 hitpoints after 24 hours.  This would help both the legitimate seasoned players as well as the new players defend against griefers and midnight attackers.
2.  Implement a killcam so if your base is leveled in the middle of the night, you can at least see who did it and how they did it.  I have a sneaking suspicion the last base level was not legit and possibly a hack.  My friend said they used gunpowder kegs (which is currently disabled in this version of the game.)  But there's no way to know because there's no telling what happened.  Hint: even in medieval times people would know who leveled a town.  Why not in this game?
So unless you like gathering resources and building bases just to have them destroyed immediately I can't recommend this game in it's current state.

For a little known company, this is an absolutely incredible piece of work. I'd score it about an 8/10 overall, a fantastic piece of work with a couple of little mistakes but nothing else.
The graphics are incredible, storyline interesting and pretty historically accurate (where applicable), the guns were an absolute joy to use (except the ranger, with which i could hit a grand total of f**k all with), even the characters were well written. The whole idea of the character you're playing as narrating the story as you go along, while the world changes around you, sometimes in particularly hilarious ways, is inspired. Particularly the mine scene, i won't go into details because it has more of an affect on you if you don't know what's coming.  And the ending was a particularly nice touch to the whole thing.
The only negatives i could pick out are thus : Sometimes it can be a bit difficult to stay on track, you can get lost very easily. A couple of places are a little buggy where one wrong move can kill you, on the train i believe was the worst. The Ranger wasn't a particularly effective weapon as mentioned before, and i found that there weren't many times where you could use a shotgun effectively. And the little historical secrets were often put in similar places, making them slightly too easy to pick up if you have the right skill, but these are all minor niggles in what's an exceptional piece of craftsmanship.
My favorite part of the whole game was the Silver Shotgun, that thing is pure eye candy, it's worth going down that skill tree just to see it.
If you're umming and ahhing about buying it, just go for it, it'll be the best £12.00 (prices as off 03/01/2015) you ever spend.

Long review here, but there is too much to leave unspoken about Factorio. I'd be doing the developers a huge injustice if I didn't elaborate just how much technical genius they've crammed into some 700MB of game.
Think of Terraria really quick: Small in file-size, to-the-point gameplay/design (no pretentiousness or wishy washy story), and an utterly stupid amount of content crammed into a sub-1GB game. Factorio is following the same path in early access, and its quality is FAR above other titles in the same state, hell even finished games. It's like a Voltron formed of addicting game types: Citybuilder, Tower Defense, "Clicker," survival, and even a little RTS.
Gameplay involves building a big♥♥♥♥♥factory and ultimately using it to construct a time consuming and expensive rocket to launch into space. You start with hand tools and work your way up from there, climbing an excellently-diverse and well-paced research tree, with upgrades and unlocks that alter the design and gameplay around everything you've built. There is almost no laziness in the upgrade system. The 100+ unlocks take a lot of work but most of them add something significant to gameplay, which can alter the factory, your character, or your arsenal for the better.
As you expand, you will naturally want to automate all the tedious tasks so your character's inventory and build queue will be freed for more important work. The maps are limitless in size and you will be forced to branch out to find more ore and land to exploit.  There are nests of enemies everywhere that will swarm and attack your factory as it creates pollution, and over time they will evolve into bigger and more lethal forms. The devs did not skimp on the combat element in the game and have included a selection of of multiple guns, turrets, fighting vehicles, combat robots, and fallout-style power armor with half a dozen upgrades to help mitigate the threat.
That's about it for gameplay, but I can't stop there; most of my praise for the game lies in its technical aspects. A lot of indie devs don't think about this as much as they should and it's good to see a team hit all the good points with a game they obviously put a lot of thought into.
1. Choosing sprites over models was genius, as it A) makes this game performance friendly for almost any computer, and B) seems to pay homage to the once-dead pre-2001 graphics of Command and Conquer and Total Annhilation. The sprites are a refreshing change from models, are beautifully-detailed and very well animated. The music is excellent too, very soft and fitting for a game you'll be losing so much time in.
2. The game starts right up and is responsive all around. Maps generate ridiculously fast and you can just drop right in within 15 seconds of starting the EXE. There is an adjustable map generator (Tiberian Sun style, sans map preview) AND an editor for those who want absolute control.
3. The UI, hotkeys, and interaction in the game is clean and efficient. Also, the general speed of your character actions. If you place a part in the wrong place, it picks right back up regardless of how big it is. If you place something wrong, you don't have to pull it up to rotate it. Just rotate your tile and place again. It's a small design detail but makes a huge difference with keeping the pace of the game, IMO.
4. Multiplayer is so solid it's almost indistinguishable from single player, performance wise. Your single player file can be used for multiplayer and vice versa. Saves are uploaded to all players that join and are neatly packaged in .zip files in your appdata folder. Factorio does not crap up your system with multiple directories (looking at you, Ubisoft).
5. I ran into my first bug (a strictly aesthetic one) after 30 hours of gameplay and have yet to see any more at almost 70 hours.
6. There is a demo. A good one. In 2016. Too many games try and sell what should be a demo as "early access." That alone says a lot about the devs.
And that's about it. Thanks for making it to the end, here. Get this game. Just be prepared to lose a good chunk of your life in it.

This game is kind of a dissapointment but it's also kind of great at the same time. It's an interesting work from a game design standpoint and an actually pretty engaging work of fiction and world building. However, it fails as a surivival horor game however because it simply isn't a suvival horror game. Like this developer's previous work (Dear Ester), it is more of an interactive work of fiction that you only interact with in a purposefully minimalist way, than a video game with defined rules and game systems. If you are looking for something like The Dark Descent you will probably be dissaponted but if you like a more psychological and gothic horror piece with vague musings on English victorian era industrialism that views human workers as mere utility then you may enjoy the experience. It's not a wholly new idea to explore in science fiction but Machine For Pigs does it in an engaging enough way that I enjoyed it and even got an emotional response from it. Plus there is some really nice aspects to it, including an amazing score, great sound design and a nice artistic visual design.
So yeah, it is what it is, and it isn't the Dark Descent, not a game you will be screaming into your face cams for youtube, but it is an interesting game and one worth taking a look at or talking about.

This is a really fun game that delivers, it keeps the same similar feel as the previous Amnesia title but with a completely different setting which was very welcoming in my eyes. The single player story was entertaining throughout and the puzzles were smoothly done to maintain a very flowing gameplay experience. Everything looked disgustingly gorgeous as well throughout the campaign and except a few textures that i personally would wantt a bit sharper up close when playing the looks of this game is great, so along with the sound work. Not only were the sound effects great but how the sound was used around you I do approve of, and in dark areas you rely as much on your hearing as your vision.
CONS:
However I do want to leave some cons in here, if you've played through the first Amnesia, this one feels a bit lacking when it comes to encounters of patrolling npcs in dark areas, there could've been more situations of this in my eyes since this is probably what most people remember the other game for. Though the story is just as solid if not better excecuted in Machine for pigs, you do feel like there could've been just more gameplay avoiding and sneaking past npcs and everything feels a bit too straight forward at times which might actually make it a bit shorter than it could've been, and the game lands in on about 3 and a half hours worth of playthrough, which I'd personally consider a bit too short to leave a greater mark.
Another thing to note that doesn't have to always be bad but does change the mechanics of the game, is that the inventory system is completely missing in this game. This leaves out things like looking for items to carry and craft, to find and fill on your oil in the lantern etc. This was a what I'd consider an important aspect of the game to make it what it was, and without it, it just feels thin.
CONCLUSION:
The game is a great game by any means, and it remains on top of the line when it comes to horror/adventure games worth playing out there, but if it comes to the question "Is it better than Amnesia: Dark Descent?" My answer is,  No, it probably isn't. But if you enjoyed any of their other games I'd suggest getting this in no time since the pricetag is not too bad, and Linux support is great as well(Yes mac is for it too but who'd want to play on such crap anyway).

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a bit of a mixed bag. On the one hand, it delivers in terms of storytelling and atmosphere, with impressive use of symbolism and creative storytelling, as well as amazing audio effects and distinctive visual design to boost atmosphere. On the other hand, it isn't very scary or tense at all. Enemy presence has little impact, the player is rarely in any actual danger, and most enemy encounters are utterly unremarkable. It feels like enemies were only included because of an obligation, not because they wanted to deliver a horror game.
Gameplay was dumbed down considerably, with many mechanics being removed and nothing being put back into the game. There's much less object interaction, the game is several hours shorter than the predecessor, and it's a bit more linear.
Given the amount of delays this game had, I can see some people expecting more out of it and being disappointed. But, like I said, it's a mixed bag with both good and bad. The good does outweigh the bad, atmosphere and storytelling are what the game went for, and that's where it delivers. But it is a letdown as a horror game, and this cannot go unnoticed... or unpunished.
Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is yet another minimalistic, story experience on the resume of thechineseroom. They seem intent on making only these types of games, like Dear Esther. It could have been an excellent horror game, if thechineseroom wrote the story and basic script like they did, while Frictional Games did the actual gameplay.

Keep an open mind when going into this game. If you go in expecting Amnesia: The Dark Descent 2 then you'll ultimately be disappointed, but if you approach it in the spirit of Dear Esther and Korsakovia with a side order of Amnesia then you'll be more likely to gain something from the experience.
Very atmospheric, thanks mainly to the incredible sound design that sounds like something ripped out of David Lynch's Eraserhead and The Elephant Man. Plenty of scares, but perhaps not as much real danger or a sense of urgency as the narrative otherwise implies.
The narrative is largely driven by notes and audio logs, so if you miss some of them (easy to do) then you may find yourself missing a few pieces of the puzzle.
The end sequence is way too long and protracted (I found myself rushing through the last hour or so) but everything that comes before is well worth experiencing.

There's a remarkably good shooter hiding inside this over-the-top satire of hypermasculine action films and jingoist nationalism. Think Contra plus Team America, add a tiny dash of Super Meat Boy, mix it up with a ton of characters who all play a little different, and you've pretty much got it. But this game is far from the dopey fratfest you might initially think it is.
Would-be game designers should pay close attention to how the first few levels function like a tutorial, minus the modern crutch of beating you over the head with distracting instructions. Once you've figured out the simple core mechanic, the gloves come off.
While it's challenging (often one hit kills you), any frustration you might initially feel is quickly mitigated by a clever secondary form of progression as the game keeps killing you over and over: your tenaciousness is rewarded by an ever-increasing cast of characters to play as. These aren't just reskins of the exact same game mechanics; each has a different power set and requires a slightly different approach to any situation. Moreover, many of them hide interesting twists and secrets to their gameplay you probably won't uncover until several times into playing them. These little discoveries can completely alter the way you play the character, making Broforce a surprizingly strategic run-and-gun.
All of this would make a solid, if somewhat forgettable shooter. But then there's the crazy boss battles. And the co-op. And the custom campaign. And the Level Builder. And the likelihood of future expansions.
TL;DR? Do not pass up a Steam sale on this. Heck, the online co-op makes it worth full price. Do it.

Many games advertise "tough moral choices w/ consequences", few actually deliver on their promise. This one certainly does.

The human element.. the struggle.. the oppression..
After playing this game for only an hour, I have never felt so invested in such an elaborate game that feels so.. real. (and you're just sitting in a border patrol booth the whole time!) Not only must you take careful precision in deciding the fate of desperate immigrants, careless citizens and cunning terrorists, but you must also do this as quickly as possible to earn the proper cash to pay rent and feed and hospitalize your own weak, precious family. You are literally playing with people's lives here!
With this combination of panic-driven motivation and life-like themes of nationality and humanity (and even a set of memorable characters!), this masterpiece is certainly one to purchase if you want to try something that feels a little more human and igniting than your average title.
Will you seperate families for faulty documentation to feed the starving family of your own?

This is a silly little game which will suck you in, and make you spend hours playing it. You play the role of a border agent who is responsible for letting people in to a soviet era country. The game starts out simply enough where you just allow locals in, and deny foreigners access, but the difficulty ramps up quickly, where you need to start checking for forged passports and other documents.
There is a bit of a story line which I've only gotten a glimpse of. There are also some moral decisions to make as to whether or not to grant access to people, who don't have the correct documents but claim that they are in danger. Do you risk your limited income to possibly save someone, do you take a bribe from a smuggler, or do you play by the rules?

A surprisingly complex and morally ambiguous game, in the best way.  There is a distinct subtleness to the gameplay -- balancing your own moral code against the needs of your family and the time management aspect of the game.  Definitely worth a try as long as you enjoy non-standard games.

Excellent game, with an awesome soundtrack.  The only flaw this game has is being far too short.
The game mechanics are a new spin on a typical "pick your own abilities" system.  The combat can also be switched between real time and a mode where you can pause the action and plan your moves ahead of time.  Each has their own pros and cons.
Would recommend this game when it goes on sale for 50% or more due to how short the game actually is.  It does have a New Game+ mode though.
Also to note, if you hold the "Tab" button while playing, the main character will hum along to the song being played (unless the song has actual singing lyrics).

Transistor is a highly innovative and unique title which defies convention. The combat system, art style, storytelling and atmosphere are totally unlike any other game I have ever played. There are some technical similarities with Bastion as it is the same developer, but having played both they feel completely different.
Ashley Barrett and Darren Korb return with a superb soundtrack that feels integral to the game (with the protagonist herself being a singer) and this is demonstrated through the wonderful 'hum' system which activiates during 'turn', a tactical combat mode which allows you to pre-plan attacks and execute them at super-speed. Nothing is cliche or obvious in the world of Transistor and for this reason I can't really sum it up or describe it coherently!
The only thing I will say is that it can be a bit challenging to get used to at first, but for £10 during this weekend deal it is an incredible experience, if a little shorter than some other titles. The 'Narrator' voiced by Logan Cunningham (whom you may know from Bastion) is a big highlight,  but I won't spoil anymore, just buy it and play!

Let me start by saing the default controls in this game are absolute garbage.  If you plan on playing with a keyboard the awkward setup will have you constantly moving your hands from mouse to keyboard because you can't rebind the keys & the default is something I've never seen a game do on a PC.  Z is attack, WASD are skills & arrow keys are movement but you can't use the UI without the mouse so what the hell is the point of this?  Constantly moving your hands around is ♥♥♥♥ing annoying & uncomfortable. The game has controller support which helps but you still have to switch between the controller & mouse in order to use the UI or hit RB+X constantly to use a very slow moving cursor that constantly resets it's position each time you use it.. You can rebind them, which I only found in the menu just recently & there is a MOUSE mode option that switches everything to standard WASD movement.  Why it isn't the default I will never know.
You start the game choosing between 4 basic starter classes.  Swordsman, Archer, Mage & Cleric.  The first advanced class option is available at level 15.  I chose the swordsman since it's my default starting choice for most RPG's.  You have 2 experience bars.  One for your class & the other for your level & each time they fill up you get a point for skills & stats.  Stats are basic STR, DEX, INT, SPI, CON.  They do what you think they do if you're familiar with RPG's.
When you make your character you can choose their gender & hair style.  That's it.  No hair colors, no body types, no face types, no hair colors, no skin colors, no clothe colors, etc.  Everything is sold to you in the cash shop because, why not?  Also, if you ♥♥♥♥ up your build be prepared to either start over, deal with it or pay real money for a respec scroll.
The biggest complaint I have with the gameplay besides the controls is there is no collision detection between you & enemy NPC's.  So, playing as a melee trying to attack at awkward set angles is even more tedious when enemies keep running through me.  Enemies will sometimes even run away which is even more annoying for a melee like me since you run so god damn slow & they run at least 2x faster than you do so you gotta chase them down every single time.
This has to be put in it's own section because it's just plain stupid.  So, you learned a new skill by spending a skill point.  You can upgrade that skill you just learned by spending silver at an NPC.  Simple right?  Well it would be if you didn't have to wait a mandatory cooldown after spending that silver to learn it.  This can range from 5 minutes to over an hour depending on the skill & the level of the attribute upgrade.  Absolutely no point in making people wait for upgrades & yet this game does it.  It wouldn't be a huge issue except you can only learn one skill upgrade at a time.  So, yea.  Imagine having enough money to upgrade a skill from rank 1 to rank 10.  Now imagine waiting 5-10 minutes for every upgrade to actually happen.  That's over 2 hours of waiting.  And then you have another skill you want to upgrade after that.  Another 2 hours.  It's stupid as all hell.
The game is pretty & the artistic style is very well done.  Animations are nice & fluid while the art style is cel shaded 3D mixed with hand drawn 2D sprites.  It all goes together very well.  Another game I've seen that used an art style like this was Wakfu & that game also looks amazing.  It would be much more enjoyable if the FPS didn't constantly stutter, though.
So I got far enough into the game to check out the crafting system & it's kind of an odd one.  So you can buy recipes or find them in the wild or off of quests.  You need materials to craft the item obviously & you can theoretically craft anything you have a recipe for, HOWEVER, one of the ingredients IS the recipe itself.  So, once you craft said recipe it's gone.  You need another recipe to craft it again.  That's just stupid, especially when the recipe is listed in the journal once you pick it up.  It's the equivilant of having a cookbook to show you how to cook & throwing the book into the pot with all the ingredients.  It makes no sense at all other than to give you more reason to grind to earn another cookbook every time you want to cook something even though you have another perfectly good cookbook that can't be used for some reason.
Yea, I'm fine with figuring out stuff on my own but like I said, some things aren't explained or just have straight up misinformation on them. Like "Right Click to add to the Adventure Journal" or "Recipe's are learned once you use them". Flat out misinformation. You can't learn recipes at all (not in the traditional sense anyways & everything you pick up is added to the journal right away. I had to figure that out on my own because the game flat out lies to you & not in a Dark Souls kind of way, either. Then there's the 2h swords, they have a description that says, "Level 15 Swordsman Required".  What that actually means is, "2H Sword Skill Required."  You can learn the skill but you need a specific advanced class to learn it.  Basically vendors lieing about their products to get you to buy them only to find out you can't use it.
Negatives aside I am still enjoying the game because I like the class system but I can't recommend it because it's just so broken & it's using the usual BS F2P Monetization that I oh so love to hate.  FPS constantly stutters & can dip below 10FPS.  Constant lag & rubber banding.  I even had a glitch that forced me to restart the game to fix it involving an elevator in the first dungeon.  Another situation where there was a gold spammer spamming so much my FPS dropped to about 5 & I couldn't move.  If you try this game just be prepared for a lot of lag & constant BS from the usuall F2P garbage.
Now don't get me wrong, I want to like this game.  I like the graphics, custom classes & once you get used to the controls (or figure out there's a mouse option) they aren't that bad.  It's everything else that makes me think this game is garbage.  The obvious cash grabbing, the waste of time skill upgrade system, the stupid crafting system that requires multiple recipes even though you have the recipe in a journal, etc.  It's just bad man.  Bad game design in general meant to pad the experience.  If they ever get rid of all the BS, fix performance issues & glitches I'll gladly swap my recommendation.

is everything a fan of Ridley Scott's 1979 original
could want, perfectly encapsulating and highlighting the feeling of total dread and hopelessness across its 20-some hours that its source material understood so well.  As Amanda, Ripley's daughter, you are forced to undergo trials of psychological and emotional torture as you try again and again to evade and defeat the ultimate monster.
In addition to nailing the mood of its inspiration,
also incorporates the famous production design into both its level design and player UI.  As any
fan can tell within two minutes of playing the game, the game's developers remained strikingly faithful to the visual language of the original film, replicating its bleakly industrial space ships and hopelessly complex computer systems.  This 70's vision of futuristic computing carries into the UI as well, an aspect of the game that grew on me despite it being a nuisance to others.  The game offers very little guidance when it comes to your UI, and for the first few hours, it feels dreadfully complex and horribly implemented.  By the end of the game though, you are able to navigate it with speed and efficiency, learning with practice how to search desks, craft items, and operate machinery the fastest possible way.  The map is another common complaint, but I found it incredibly useful from getting to one area of the massive Sevastapol to the next.  Checking my map became a frequent and necessary habit, and learning to understand what it is telling you at first glance allowed me to avoid as much unnecessary contact with the Alien as I could.
All of this effort on the developer's part would be for naught, of course, if the Alien and game itself failed to induce fear.  I'm thankful to say that this is completely not the case, and anyone who says otherwise is either lying or really is not afraid of anything.  For the first two hours of the game, I was having a blast, walking through the nearly empty Sevastapol without a care in the world, enjoying the level and sound design, almost completely forgetting that I would be face to face with a Xenomorph shortly.  When the Alien finally came into play in Mission 5, dropping down from the vents in a spectacularly terrifying entrance, I was stunned and all my previous "enjoyment" of the game went out the window.  I died within 10 minutes of that first encounter, ripped viciously out from under a hospital bed and greeted by the Alien's double jaws of death.  That was the first time I had to put the game down for the night, thoroughly shocked by the Alien's fearsomely cunning AI.
I had been playing
a few weeks before buying
, and though the former definitely had my heart beating out of my chest much more than the latter,
truly made my sleep uneasy, and that's more than I can say for any video game I've ever played.  It's also the only game that I can remember individual missions of (5, 10, 14, and 17) for being so dread-inducing and difficult in its tasks and level design.
It's been said ad naseum, but I can't think of any better way to close this review: if you want to experience being trapped in space with Ridley Scott's Alien, hiding and fleeing from a beast that outclasses you in every way, you will appreciate (not enjoy)
for the terrifying piece of media that it is.

I'm going to say right off the bat, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
It nails the atomosphere of the original 1979 movie Alien in all the right ways. There is not a single moment im playing this game where i dont feel like im in the film. Everything to the music, the noises from everything to the doors to buttons and alarms. Even the padded white walls are there.
It is the most Authentic Alien game ever made, it is true to the franchise where others like Colonial Marines or AvP completely fail and fall short.
The best part about this game though is by far the Xenomorph. It is on point and scary as hell. Its unpredictable and will become smarter the more you evade or drive it away. It isnt just some monster that is on a set path you can avoid by sitting in a corner and waiting it out like its metal gear solid.  It will actively hunt and ♥♥♥♥ with you in all the ways a horror game will.
There will be times you will go through the game without any problems or seeing the xenomorph with it only running through the vents making noise and other times will just flat out relentlessly not leave you alone checking every nook and crany for you. These are not set events either, the times when it leaves you alone it may very well do the exact opposite on another playthrough or if you die and go through the same part twice.
The Xenomorph also looks extremely authentic, its big, its fast, and its mean. It drools and drips acid when shot and even has an extremely long rubber like tail that drags on the floor behind it wherever it goes (a tail which if it happens to brush up against you while cowering under a desk will immediately alert if to your presense and ♥♥♥♥ing eat you)
Gameplay wise this is probably THE best horror game on the market, it is an extremely well done cross between Amnesia: The Dark Decent and Dead Space. Meaning unlike Amnesia you CAN fight back and use weapons, but unlike Dead space this usually is not your smartest option.
When dealing with the other humans and androids on the space station combat is an extremely effective way to disperse of the enemies, but it is also like ringing the dinner bell. Anything louder than a mouse fart will have the Xenomorph dropping out of the vents saying "SUPRISE COCK♥♥♥♥"
You can also use this to your advantage too however, many a time ive come into a room with multiple hostile humans and if i bang on the wall with my wrench the Xenomorph will drop in and start slaughtering all of them, meanwhile theyre busy and i can get by unscathed.
Overall anyone who likes horror games, the original alien film, or both i highly reccomend you buy this game. You will not be dissapointed. I have found nothing wanting.

Short Version: Very Fun but linear, and only ~10 hours. Not graphically fantastic, but great artstyle. Guns all feel nice, as well as the environments. Enemies are varied, as well as bosses. Duelling is difficult, but often far between luckily, and each level feels different. 8/10, very very fun way to kill 10 hours, and good replayability.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger (or Gunslinger from now on) is effectively a rail shooter, so gameplay wise it's not particularly innovative. In short, follow the path, shoot the dudes, rinse and repeat. The western theme makes for some great style, especially in Gunslinger's comic book-esq Artstyle and some interesting levels, such as those in a Goldmine, a Swamp, and a whole-town shootout to name a few. There's a few different guns from which to choose from, you get a primary weapon, Double-Barreled Shotgun or Rifle, and a secondary which you can single or dual wield from the short-ranged Quickshooter or Sawn-Off Shotgun, or the mid-ranged Six-Shooter or the long-ranged Ranger, in addition to some Dynamite on later levels. There's a skillpoint system, and generally you'll level up once a level or so, and there's a variety of upgrades for Short Range, Mid Range and Long Ranged combat with some Weapon Upgrades when you've invested enough points. Towards the end, you may feel a bit overpowered, especially with a new game + option, but Gunslinger's difficulty isn't particularly high to begin with, except for the totally evil duelling, where you need about 3 eyes just to be able to do it decently, and feels a bit token just because it's a Wild West themed game. In addition to your guns and dynamite, Gunslinger also gives you two extra toys: Sense of Death, and Concentration. Concentration is bullet time, but is very useful when things get a bit hectic. Sense of Death has a 30 second recharge that allows you to dodge a lethal bullet if you lean out of it's way. Useful certainly, but you'll probably die a lot from misjudgement.
While Gunslinger isn't particularly innovative or exciting in Gameplay, it makes up for it, strangely enough, in story. Gunslinger follows an old man who wonders into a Saloon of a sleepy town one day, claiming to be the legendary Bounty Hunter, Boba Fe-I MEAN Silas Greaves. The alleged Mr. Greaves then tells some stories from his Bounty Hunting days to the few folks in the saloon, which are the levels we play in game. Where Gunslinger really makes this effective is some excellent narration, seriously the voice acting is beautiful, take my word on it. But Gunslinger has another ace up it's sleeve. The narration follows you outside the cutscenes to the levels, and on several occasions, time will rewind, the level reorganise and plot details change, it's some excellent storytelling.
But as usual, Gunslinger is not perfect. It's not particularly difficult, and the extra ammo upgrades are kind of useless as you get showered in ammo. A lot of enemies are very difficult to see, and misjudgement from sense of death will be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ The duelling system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and the final 'plot twist' is a bit predictable.
While not the greatest game ever, Gunslinger is probably the most fun I've ever had with a game. Not only is it an excellent narritive experience, but it's just fun in a kind of mental/badass way. How many games can you name where you can become a magical shotgun wizard, where you dual-wield Sawn-Off Shotguns, with no reloads and increased damage in bullet time mode, and clear out an entire bank of thugs in the middle of a whole-town shootout? None other, than Call of Juarez: Gunslinger.
8/10 - Not particularly innovative, some dodgy textures here and there, and a poor duelling system. But some simple and rewarding gameplay combined with beautiful setting and level design.

The quick-draw gunfight mechanic is really well done, among other postive things this title has to offer. Comparing Emperor Edition to the 1.0 game is like day and night. It took them a year but at least they fixed the game.
This game offers many unique factions to play with (I ll go to the DLC policy later) and the vanilla factions are a nice mix of hellenic eastern barbarian roman and carthaginian culture.  The time period is in my opinion a great playground and every campaign (while your early tactics are similar for the most part) is different. For example one time i saw the Etruscan Empire sacking Rome and on an other campaign they got rekt by turn 5. This makes for the most part the game fun to play and it offers a unique challenge everytime.
Now going to battles. The game engine is faulty yes, but the issues were at last fixed. Some problems are the game engines fault not the developers fault. For all of you complaining they cant use the engine from Medieval II and Rome I they would basically use a 10 year old game engine.  The warscape engine suits archers peltasts etc very nice but the cavalry fights in particular are a bit clumpsy. The infantry fights look much better in comparison to version 1.0 but it seems that there was margin to improve. About OP units and OP strats, they exist in pretty much every game, this is how it works. This is where modders step in. CA doesnt have endless time for balancing tests etc they need to release a new game in a certain period (Many people see SEGA as the issue here i am not oging to talk about that).
Now coming to DLCs. In my opinion a big reason this game recieved a lot of hate. You make a game in the ancient time and we have to pay for the Greeks? Well not all of the Greeks we got the Diadochoi for free which had the most power in the hellenic world during the time period the game is set but its still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. If you dont like a DLC just dont buy it dont spread s*** to Hades and back. Yes you can see me criticizing the Greek States DLC but you need to understand that CA is business. And they (just like all other companies) want to make money. DLCs such as Nomadic Tribes and Black Sea colonies are in my opinion a good idea they are just new unique factions with not so good rosters so if you play TW competitevly you wouldnt be in a disadvantage because you couldnt play as the Attalid Pergamon(Derpamon).
Coming now to modding of Rome II. PFM and Assembly kit are very user friendly programms(although PFM likes to crash). There have been many overhauls from complete to campaign ones. And if you see the overhaul-fix mods as a bad thing you are wrong. Mods exist to make the game even better so that the casual player can experience a better game. CA is there to fix the problems, mods are more of a help to the problem fix.
UI.
The cards are not exactly brilliant(Hard to distinguish first cohort from eagle cohort at a quick glance if you are new for example), but they work. And yes there are mods that change them incase you dont like them.
The lists on the campaign map (forces provinces etc) are an awesome new feature allowing you to see the positions of your armies and agents at a glance.
Now naval battles.
Yes even in emperor edition are buggy but if i am not mistaked in Rome IIs days the naval battles were the best we had even with the bugs but you need to take into account the fact that naval battles were something of a new thing back then and as with new stuff, it takes some time for them in order to be optizimed and provide you the ideal gaming experience. Αlso naval battles in napoleon and shogun didnt feature ramming and boarding it was all about cannon fire. Altough i still would have liked to see the rows behing useful(Eg they were used to defend against ramming ships to lower their speed)
But but but but...
If you have played older Total War Games like Medieval II or Rome I you may find the game "too simple" (eg the buildings) Sure its simple for an experienced player, but players new to TW series need a place to learn the game and in my opinion it does that well.
And if you think that Rome II is inferior to Rome I i will agree with you. BUT BUT BUT....

Right so, Alien: Isolation
I'm going to say right off the bat, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
It nails the atomosphere of the original 1979 movie Alien in all the right ways. There is not a single moment im playing this game where i dont feel like im in the film. Everything to the music, the noises from everything to the doors to buttons and alarms. Even the padded white walls are there.
It is the most Authentic Alien game ever made, it is true to the franchise where others like Colonial Marines or AvP completely fail and fall short.
The best part about this game though is by far the Xenomorph. It is on point and scary as hell. Its unpredictable and will become smarter the more you evade or drive it away. It isnt just some monster that is on a set path you can avoid by sitting in a corner and waiting it out like its metal gear solid.  It will actively hunt and ♥♥♥♥ with you in all the ways a horror game will.
There will be times you will go through the game without any problems or seeing the xenomorph with it only running through the vents making noise and other times will just flat out relentlessly not leave you alone checking every nook and crany for you. These are not set events either, the times when it leaves you alone it may very well do the exact opposite on another playthrough or if you die and go through the same part twice.
The Xenomorph also looks extremely authentic, its big, its fast, and its mean. It drools and drips acid when shot and even has an extremely long rubber like tail that drags on the floor behind it wherever it goes (a tail which if it happens to brush up against you while cowering under a desk will immediately alert if to your presense and ♥♥♥♥ing eat you)
Gameplay wise this is probably THE best horror game on the market, it is an extremely well done cross between Amnesia: The Dark Decent and Dead Space. Meaning unlike Amnesia you CAN fight back and use weapons, but unlike Dead space this usually is not your smartest option.
When dealing with the other humans and androids on the space station combat is an extremely effective way to disperse of the enemies, but it is also like ringing the dinner bell. Anything louder than a mouse fart will have the Xenomorph dropping out of the vents saying "SUPRISE COCK♥♥♥♥"
You can also use this to your advantage too however, many a time ive come into a room with multiple hostile humans and if i bang on the wall with my wrench the Xenomorph will drop in and start slaughtering all of them, meanwhile theyre busy and i can get by unscathed.
Overall anyone who likes horror games, the original alien film, or both i highly reccomend you buy this game. You will not be dissapointed. I have found nothing wanting.

Let me begin by saying that I'm a big fan of the genre. I'm a huge sucker for 2-d mmos. Ragnarok, runescape, maplestory, elsword, etc. They give me a sense of control I could never experience in a 3d game.
Is the game fun? Eh.
It's a game that makes me want to keep playing. There's tons of things you can optimize: hats, stats, gear, gems, skills, class choices, collections, achievements, exploration, crafting, secrets, movement tricks, I could go on and on. It's a game that's simple on the surface but extremely deep. You will spend hours playing this game without being in front of a computer.
Pros
At it's core, it's all about the grind. Hate it our love it, you will eventually have to buckle down and do it. I have no problem with this, but others might. Personally, I think the game does a good job of making the grind more enjoyable. A variety of monsters have rare, valuable loot that make you feel like it was all worth it. Crafting requires recipes which are dropped by monsters. Then collecting the items needed to craft that item is like completing a quest and getting a reward. Craft enough to fill out your journal and you can get adventurer points and experience. Gameplay is highly skill based, requiring both knowledge and a bit of finesse. The game is optimized for keyboard controls, so your skillshots can only be aimed in 8 directions. There are still cursor target skills that are better for mouse players, yet still comfortable for keyboard. Also supports gamepads.
Mehs
Some may feel that the game feels too hand-holdy, but that's common for theme park mmos. There's also a very high level cap of 280 that is expected to grow to 600 in the far future. If you're in a rush to hit cap, it will take you at least a month. Some p2w features like putting random stats on hats that would normally all have none. All the hats and the premium membership can be purchased using in-game currency from the marketplace, negating the p2w aspect. Add-ons made by users are also available, improving the quality of life of the game.
Cons
Bugs are present, just like in every other game you're played. Translations are done by volunteers so there are some mistakes in the text that may bother grammar nazis. Bots are somewhat common like every other f2p mmo, but you can block them with an add-on. Some classes are horribly balanced, but that may change as new ones get added. Lag and poor netcode are the biggest offenders. You don't need a good connection to play, but you will be heavily disadvantaged.
Personally, I love this game to bits. Though many of its positive features are personal likes, those who aren't fans of the genre will have a hard time enjoying this game.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger (or Gunslinger from now on) is effectively a rail shooter, so gameplay wise it's not particularly innovative. In short, follow the path, shoot the dudes, rinse and repeat. The western theme makes for some great style, especially in Gunslinger's comic book-esq Artstyle and some interesting levels, such as those in a Goldmine, a Swamp, and a whole-town shootout to name a few. There's a few different guns from which to choose from, you get a primary weapon, Double-Barreled Shotgun or Rifle, and a secondary which you can single or dual wield from the short-ranged Quickshooter or Sawn-Off Shotgun, or the mid-ranged Six-Shooter or the long-ranged Ranger, in addition to some Dynamite on later levels. There's a skillpoint system, and generally you'll level up once a level or so, and there's a variety of upgrades for Short Range, Mid Range and Long Ranged combat with some Weapon Upgrades when you've invested enough points. Towards the end, you may feel a bit overpowered, especially with a new game + option, but Gunslinger's difficulty isn't particularly high to begin with, except for the totally evil duelling, where you need about 3 eyes just to be able to do it decently, and feels a bit token just because it's a Wild West themed game. In addition to your guns and dynamite, Gunslinger also gives you two extra toys: Sense of Death, and Concentration. Concentration is bullet time, but is very useful when things get a bit hectic. Sense of Death has a 30 second recharge that allows you to dodge a lethal bullet if you lean out of it's way. Useful certainly, but you'll probably die a lot from misjudgement.
While Gunslinger isn't particularly innovative or exciting in Gameplay, it makes up for it, strangely enough, in story. Gunslinger follows an old man who wonders into a Saloon of a sleepy town one day, claiming to be the legendary Bounty Hunter, Boba Fe-I MEAN Silas Greaves. The alleged Mr. Greaves then tells some stories from his Bounty Hunting days to the few folks in the saloon, which are the levels we play in game. Where Gunslinger really makes this effective is some excellent narration, seriously the voice acting is beautiful, take my word on it. But Gunslinger has another ace up it's sleeve. The narration follows you outside the cutscenes to the levels, and on several occasions, time will rewind, the level reorganise and plot details change, it's some excellent storytelling.
But as usual, Gunslinger is not perfect. It's not particularly difficult, and the extra ammo upgrades are kind of useless as you get showered in ammo. A lot of enemies are very difficult to see, and misjudgement from sense of death will be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ The duelling system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and the final 'plot twist' is a bit predictable.
While not the greatest game ever, Gunslinger is probably the most fun I've ever had with a game. Not only is it an excellent narritive experience, but it's just fun in a kind of mental/badass way. How many games can you name where you can become a magical shotgun wizard, where you dual-wield Sawn-Off Shotguns, with no reloads and increased damage in bullet time mode, and clear out an entire bank of thugs in the middle of a whole-town shootout? None other, than Call of Juarez: Gunslinger.
8/10 - Not particularly innovative, some dodgy textures here and there, and a poor duelling system. But some simple and rewarding gameplay combined with beautiful setting and level design.

This game may offer a short experience, but it is a really fun and well-done shooter nonetheless. As your character narrates the various adventures he has taken as an outlaw, YOU control the adventure in the first-person and often have to play out the story and then backtrack to how the story really happened (after someone in the bar you are presently at rudely interrupts the story and says "that's now how it went down"). This way of storytelling is the main positive for this game as it is truly unique and really well done (and humorous)!
The sound, graphics, and gunplay also add to the enjoyment of this first person shooter as they are also well done. The character progression in the game also adds to the game as you gain XP to level up, allowing you to spend points on different skills such as close-range or long-range shooting, unlocking better guns and making you stronger and more powerful.
I had no issues with the enemies or the boss-fights overall, and I did like the duelling (where you face-off with your enemy, focusing in on them, then drawing your gun before they shoot you in the face), although I did find it tedious at times trying to dodge their bullets if I was too slow. Having said that though, it was probably me just being too slow ;)
There is also an arcade mode (though the main story mode was very arcade-y as multipliers and getting the fastest time possible were key in levelling up your character) which makes for good replayibility, though it is not my cup of tea. This will allow for leaderboard-rivarly-goodness though, so if you have some friends who are also willing to play a fantastic FPS set around the late 1800s and early 1900s, I'm sure you will have fun!
But, if you're anything like me and would just prefer to play the main story mode of this game (whilst maybe dipping into the arcade mode just for a little taste), I'm sure you will have a blast with this game! However, it is a short experience, so picking this up during a sale would be a wise decision.
Enjoy :)

Plantera is a nice (and cute) twist on the standard clicker game that eventually (after two hours) just falls flat due to the lack of 'content'.
The idea of the game is really rather unique and the execution is solid. The music is pleasant (up to a certain point) and the graphics while being simple have a certain charm to them. The premise of the game is simply to build a garden/farm and harvest the crops. To do that you get little blue helper blobs that automate the process and have to fend off meanies that want to steal your crops. Otherwise it's the same 'click on something to get money' routine.
By gaining more money you level up and get access to more plants (and some animals). You also have to extend your garden to have more space to grow more plants. Alternatively you can also spend money on some extras like scarecrows, guard dogs or a permanent gold multiplicator. One rather 'unfortunate' update that you can buy that way is the time that your blue helper blobs will work while being offline. It's a bit like the game knows that it doesn't offer much and artificially makes you come back to it more frequently until you threw enough money at an otherwise completely pointless update...
The real problem of the game is the lack of variety. There are three categories of plants with five plants in them each and four animals that you can get. You unlock the lot within the first hour of play and afterwards you just deal with more of the same. There's one (overused) 'easter egg/cameo' special event, but there are no other specials to see or look forward to. The game play is bland even for a clicker. There no strategy or tactic at all. It's just waiting to get enough money to buy more things to get more money.
It's a nice idea, but it's worth a dollar at best. You'll get an hour or two of fun out of the game until it becomes utterly repetitive.
P.S.: I'm grinding for the last achievements that's why I have way more than two hours playtime, but I don't recommend doing the same.

It was always going to be difficult to follow in the steps of Demon's Souls. The game was more than a mere flash in the pan; it changed expectations for what an action-RPG could be. Instead of simply having statistics that amounted to nothing, the game put emphasis on skill, memorization and strategy as well as allowing gamers to level up their characters. It felt like a true evolution of a stagnating genre.
Then the psuedo-sequel happened with Dark Souls. While it wasn't as fantastically original as it's forefather, it contained a world design that rivals most open-world games. Giving players ultimate freedom in exploring an intertwining map while doing nothing to ease entry for new-comers, Dark Souls was commended for being brilliant in design and tactful in execution.
Expectations were obviously skyhigh for a sequel. When a proper sequel was announced, everyone went crazy. We weren't getting a spiritual successor, but a true Dark Souls game. Then the announcements started coming in. The game was being "made more accessible"; Bandai Namco were going for the "Call of Duty" crowd; DLC was being worked on; gamers let out a sigh that their hardcore series might be coming to an end.
While Dark Souls 2 is definitely easier than either predecessor, I would be hard pressed to call this game easy. If anything, progressing in the game world is a bit more convoluted than either Souls game before it. Combat might be less threatening, but figuring out where to go next becomes a challenge.
Dark Souls 2 has a much larger map than the first, but a lot of the areas link in multiple ways. This game takes the idea of Dark Souls open map and expands it into the size of a small country. It takes countless hours to explore every nook and cranny; by extension, this feels like a true adventure.
The game's narrative also takes a more guided approach. While things are still cryptic in nature and left open to interpretation, it is much easier to find concrete information within the game. While most of this was done in a patch with the release of "Scholar of the First Sin," the game does feel more directed and straight forward to digest.
The weapon and armor descriptions also make more sense. You aren't left to your own devices to discover how to properly wield any weapon; the game now outlines what your statistics do and what each weapon needs before being properly handled. It makes for a game that definitely feels more accessible to a crowd of gamers who don't want to study every small detail.
Then come the boss battles. The AI seems a bit stupid in this first release, but enemies still hit hard. You won't find as many memorable battles in Dark Souls 2 as the first or Demon's, but you also won't breeze through any of them. Without proper skill or dedication, expect to get stuck on Dragonrider.
The combat has become incredibly versatile as the series evolves. You are given more tactics to unleash upon your foes and each playstyle blends better. Using magic while also holding a melee weapon is feasible. Dual wielding makes a welcome entrance in a manner that isn't completely nonsensical. Even archers can stick to solely bows and bolts and end up completing the game.
Weapon and armor degradation is a bit different, though. This ends up feeling like a mistaken concept. Your weapons automatically heal with each rest at a bonfire, regardless of whether you have repair powder or not. If something breaks while in battle, then you need to visit a blacksmith. Until then, your arsenal feels a bit brittle.
It's a strange change that I don't quite understand. While it must be to pressure you into making more precise strikes, I feel like the developers took the idea too far. I shouldn't have to worry about my weapon breaking when I've stopped at 3 bonfires before a boss.
Another change comes in regards to Soul farming. The game actively discourages it by removing enemies from an area after you've killed them 10 times. I actually think this is fantastic. Having to slog through the same foes time after time when dying in an area sucks. You can't deny that, either.
It brings up the idea that you may end up unable to progress because you're too low of a level and the enemies are gone. The Souls games are based more on skill then anything, so I don't even think this is a scenario that would likely happen. If it does, I guess you're SOL.
But since melee combat is so powerful, I'm not quite sure if you'd ever find yourself stuck in a rut. It's really easy to circle most enemies and backstab them. It makes the game feel less rewarding at the end of it all. I know this was a side-effect of changes and wasn't intentional. From Software has never backed away from creating tense and difficult scenarios.
Dark Souls 2 also sees the return of a centralized hub area, similar to the Nexus in Demon's Souls. You do everything here; upgrade your character, upgrade your weapons and armor and embark on quests. Since you can now fast travel to each bonfire, I don't have a big issue with this change. That is never gets explained is shocking, but I suppose being new to the series wouldn't cause issues.
Fast traveling is also fantastic. While it has the downside of making me forget how each area links together or where specific landmarks are, it helps a lot in moving between areas. This comes up during the end game where you need to collect specific items from around the game world.
It also is handy for finding items for armor later on. I collected a lot more sets than I ever have in previous games thanks to this feature. I know it might make the game less organic, but I didn't mind too much. I was just so happy to be able to explore other areas and I made finding each bonfire a quest unto itself.
Length wise, this is the shortest of the series thus far. I managed to beat the game in around 34 hours. That isn't exactly quick, but I never really got stuck with any combat situations. Because of the improvements done to the game in particular areas, it just ends up being an easier experience.
Maybe without any prior history with these games, Dark Souls 2 would be an exhilirating challenge. For series veterans, it's mostly just a new area to explore with a lot of hidden goodies. It makes for an enrapturing quest that I feel was well worth the time and effort.
Even with some negatives, Dark Souls 2 is a great game. Through and through, I would recommend this to everyone. Temper your expectations returning gamers and prepare to die, new ones!

I am a huge fan of the Elder Scrolls games. I played Oblivion and Skyrim both on console and have played Skyrim, Oblivion, and Morrowind on PC when I got one. I have Morrowind and Skyrim on Steam so look at my hours and you'll be amazed. However, I was not excited for ESO when it was first announced and didn't touch it for several years. However, a few months ago it was on a sale and I decided to pick it up. The game isn't as bad as I inititally expected and I actually found myself having a good time. However, this game is not enjoyable for the same reasons that the single player Elder Scrolls games are. Do not go into this game expecting a single player Elder Scrolls. The game's quests are hollow and the world feels like a MMO. Because of this, the world does not feel like an Elder Scrolls game. However, it is pretty awesome to see many parts of Tamriel never seen in the games (except for Arena). The gameplay can be sort of fun however you need to have friends to play with to really enjoy this game. The expansions are money grabs but are cool additions to the game and the end-game content is pretty good with solid PVP and dungeons. I was surprised to find that ESO wasn't the awful game that so many die hard Elder Scrolls fans claim it to be. If you have a friend to play this game with and go into this game with an open mind I think it can be very enjoyable. 7.5/10.

- Nicer feel in terms of handling, cars feel more grippy and responsive (just like their real life counterparts this year)
- Amazing attention to detail in the car models and sounds
- The career mode animations look much better, driver models in general are much improved
- Much better R&D system
- New practice programs like Race Strategy (much better than Tyre Management... ugh)
- No game-breaking bugs on launch... fantastic!
- None so far
I would definitely recommend this game, so far it has been a solid improvement over F1 2016 in all categories.

I was about 10 hours into Alien: Isolation. The idea that there may not actually be a xenomorph on the station was creeping into my mind. I entered a common hall and spotted the elevator I was looking for, but the vents seemed awful noisy. Then it dropped from the ceiling. The sound of it hitting the floor betrayed it's weight. I hid, began sneaking to the elevator, then heard it climb back into a duct. I noticed my breathing was heavy, and barely muted the pounding of my heart. I still felt in control, but ridiculous for being so worked up over a game.
I activated the elevator switch in the back of the box, then turned to face the door. Why didn't I hear it?! No thump, no screech, just a silent ominous barricade hunched outside the elevator. All control was immediately lost. It stared at me, chuffed, and seemed to shift It's weight. The elevator dinged, the doors slowly closed, neither of us moved an inch. I didn't even draw a weapon. I moved to the next floor in silence.
I was sweating. A visceral fight or flight had been activated. I had to turn off the game, had to go to bed. Nothing in real life has ever crippled me like that. Thank you Creative Assembly for certifying my mortality.

Westerns are a touchy subject for me. I never desired to marathon through spaghetti westerns or the American classics involving smoking guns in the title and the action sequences. I was lost when actors donned makeshift rope and cast iron armors at high noon. As a matter of fact my introduction to the setting was Red Dead Redemption on the PS2, so naturally my critical eye was ruined with a glorious example of how a Western SHOULD be made.
Even though it's a few years old, the game still looks great.
Yet those precedents didn't prevent me from enjoying Call of Juarez: Gunslinger by developer Techland. I hadn't known many of the historical outlaws that were referenced, and was not familiar with the character tropes that scattered the mythology. I was good at arcade shooters though, and by the time I was done, I was thoroughly engrossed in the story of Silas Graves. Playing the part of a great mercenary and involving myself in the legendary stories made everything feel larger than life.
There are a great many details that are paid attention in Gunslinger, but few stand out as amazing decisions on the developers part. The well balanced combat, bullet time feature, duels, and arcade style all stood out to me as the best part of the game. The rest of the game was very well put together, had a quality finish and a narrator that was very entertaining. The narrating is done by the main character over a game of poker and a few drinks, so while you're shooting away at outlaws and Apaches, you may be stopped to make corrections in the story. Set pieces fly from the sky, the ground opens up, and enemies are replaced or multiplied on a regular basis. This keeps you on your feet and makes the game much more interesting than most story-based shooters that I've ever played.
The narrative can be both engaging, and erratic at times.
That being said, the quick bait-and-switch of the narrative combined with the quick reaction required to create combos makes for frantic game-play. It is not constantly frantic however. The fights are placed well apart so the attention required to create massive combos is staccato and focused in intense portions that are manageable. Narrative is delivered mostly in the slower gaps between combat so you don't miss any important story elements. Still though, the combination of arcade gameplay and the constantly changing landscape and narrative is fresh and personally I laughed every time my slightly sloshed memories were changed.
There are likely 2 ways that you might approach Gunslinger. The game encourages long-distance cover to cover sniping, and quick running reactive close-range game-play. The best part is that both are viable, and you aren't incentivized or punished too heavily for choosing one over the other. The bullet time feature is one of the ways they balance this. There is both a bullet time feature for combat, and a final bullet survival dodge that is activated when you are about to be hit for the last time. So you don't have to worry while your bullet meters are filled when you can run and gun. However you are risking life and limb once you dodge the bullet (literally) and need to recharge those meters!
These duels really make you feel like you're racing to draw.
This design choice both makes the stories more faithful to the stories of larger than life personalities and makes sniping and close-range combat both rewarding and effective. Instead of applying MORE armor like most games do, they increase or decrease these bullet-time features to give closer-combat more flair and effectiveness.
After playing this game for just a few days, regardless of how high I am on the leader-boards, everything becomes smooth and natural. Bullets fly, enemies fall, and my tally increases. I am not the best in the world, but it feels as though I am the best in the world I am playing in. This feeling that the game bestows on it's user is unique and gratifying. The only word I can use to describe it is "bad♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Yes, I feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥after playing Gunslinger.

- The mechanic of the story telling is fun and original.
- The duel mechanic is simply brilliant. It's simple, yet, not easy. And you really feel like you've won the duel when you finally do.
- The skilling system works really well and is balanced. You can pick your play style and skill up accordingly.
- Great graphics.
- Awesome soundtrack.
- 2 additional game modes. Arcade (score points over set levels) and Duel (self explanatory :)
- Lever action riffle!!!
What can I say? I love this game!
Definitely Recommended!

Elder Scrolls Online or ESO is an MMO from the game series Elder Scrolls. If you haven't played a MMO but have played other Elder Scroll games just know that this is a tad bit different than what you are use to.
ESO gives you full freedom of your character;
Want to be a sorcerer tank? No problem.
Want to be a night blade healer? You can make that happen!
Of course there is min-maxing, how to get the ultimate heals, the ultimate dmg with this and this class. If thats what you like. But you can also tailor fit your character to work FOR you. And nobody will go protest or refuse to take you to a dungeon because you're not using x skill.
Economy in ESO is unlike most MMO's, there is no one Auction House but guilds bid on Guild Traders making guilds more of an importance than just a group of friends.
The only negative thing about ESO is if you're very poor. Not only is it buy-to-play, it also has dlc's. The DLC's is worth the money, you can buy them in the crown store and unlock them for your account forever. Or you can become a member of ESO+, ESO+ is a subscription type which in my opinion is fairly cheap. You can choose to sub for 30, 90, or 180 days. And during those days you get access to a few features. One of them being an material bank which makes life a lot easier. The other being access to all DLC's.

+ Fair sub model
+ Freedom of character/skill/builds

I highly anticipated the release of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs ever since I played through the first Amnesia and found out it was awesome.
But Amnesia:AMFP was not scary. And I mean over the four or so hours it took me to clock this game, I can count the number of times I actually had any sense of fear on one hand. It had almost no puzzles, and while the story was alright, it really didn't grip me. If you want to play a game just for story, you might as well play Dear Esther. But then again, if you want a good story. WHY NOT READ A BOOK OR WATCH A MOVIE!
Somewhere between the first and second hour I discovered that boredom had set in. And I was doing a speed run of the game. Which is never really any good for a horror game. People should be scared about what is around the corner, NOT RUNNING HEAD FIRST ROUND THE BEND IN A FUTILE ATTEMPT TO CURE THEIR SENSE OF BOREDOM.
Ultimately, People play Amnesia:AMFP to get scared. And yeah, some people would be scared by this game. Without a doubt. But it's not as scary as the original. For a start, the AI is laughably easy to avoid and ignore when compared to Amnesia, which is just pure awesome in a horror game. I mean, people are naturally scared of things that are difficult. "oh no, I'm so scared of this exam coming up", "Careful of those creatures, they'll smash you up". So if people are naturally scared of things that are difficult, or dangerous or powerful, then this begs the question: WHY THE HELL IS THE AI SO PASSIVE AND WEAK? What were they thinking? Without the threat of the AI I don't think there is anything else scary about this game. I mean the only other thing that could kill you is fall damage.
No puzzles and no credible threats makes Jack a dull boy.

The game is not worth the 12 euro I gave for it for the story and graphics, but I'm sure it's worth the effort the developer put into it, considering the game is almost a year late!
If you like scary games, then this is probably not the game for you. It concentrates on instant shocks rather than atmosphere. It lacks the ambience in most parts of the game, but you are able to hear the soundtracks in the rather important parts.
Lots of puzzles, but they are easy enough to figure out.
The game is VERY metaphorically! Basically everything is considered a metaphor for something else, so beware of that!
My recommendation for the game:

I'm disappointed I ever played this game, let alone sunk eight hours into it.
This is a briefly entertaining microtransaction game that would be appropriate on a browser on Armor Games but isn't what you expect from Steam. In keeping with typical micros, the game is a little fun but not too fun, otherwise you wouldn't be constantly pressured to spend money on it. You're invited to spend at least a dollar on fifty different things, and the only micro aspect they removed when porting this to Steam is advertisements (presumably because Steam won't allow them, thank goodness).
The game is somewhat fun for a little while but gets repetitive quickly. It's designed to be played for a very long time with a limited set of graphics so that the creator can maximize profit from microtransactions.
It's free to play, but it isn't even worth installing. For anyone looking for a review of the game, go no further.
This game is an early access game, we are all gamers here and we all have a clear idea what that means. There are problems, there are hackers and there is content that just isnt finished yet.
Saying all that - This is probably one of the most polished early access games i have played in a long time. The content is that of which i expect a final game to have. It has crafting, mining, building and clans. What else could you possibly want?
It is true that people can just come into your area and eff up your base if you are not online. This is a problem and i seriously think that the system should be re-worked in some way but i dont have anything in mind so lets continue.
Starting at the begining:
- I started playing the game with 2 other friends, so from the earliest point we were already ahead of people who like to 'lone wolf it'.
- We started on a server and instantly set out to find resources and food.. Both came quite easily.
- We built a crappy base and then worked our way up into a more sophisticated one.
- We continued to sell our services as sell swords to the whole server and sometimes worked for mulitple kings in order to obtain certain resources when we wanted them.
- We did this for almost a few hours every night - During the day we all work so this was the only time to game.
- And then....
- Nothing.
That is the final tale, no more enemies came to seige our castle we had built. No grand battles were had. Nothing.
Other then that, the game got kind of boring after the 30 hours we played for and we just stopped. There are people who are correct in saying its way to easy for people to destroy bases and everytime you leave your PC you have an anxiety attack thinking that when you get back it will be destroyed but its all fairly fun and easy to build back up.
If you buy this game, be aware what you build WILL be destroyed. Nothing stands the test of time in this game and sometimes thats a few minutes or over a week. Its all pretty luck based on who finds your base and what they want to do..
This is a good game. Its fairly well polished now so not many problems there. If you have a high end PC it will run it perfectly and if you have a mid range you might lag in some spots.

Cons.
