I'd like to start with the fact that all the "official, at launch" reviews do not represent the game because they really did improve the game compared to beta and early game.
This review is also my humble opinion.
I have not much PvP experience so I am only going to speak about PvE ( dungeons, trials, quests, main story,..). I also have more hours played, because I used to start the game without the steam launcher)
Besides that, this game is IMO not playable without addons.
But using MINION, the addon manager, your life really gets so much easier (e.g. mini map)
They give a list of most downloaded addons and you can update them easily by just pressing a button.
So DO NOT FORGET to install minion!!!
One of the best things of ESO is that they really put a lot of efforts in the storyline and lore of the quests. No such things like you "slay ten wolves and the next quest you have to slay 15 imps.
There will always be grinding, but yea that is MMO right? :)
Max level is 50, then you start with Champion Points(CP) your gear will be maxed at cp160 and your character cp600.
The main story is really epic and is a solo storyline.
They really blasted me away with that! But no spoilers here!
What I like the most are dungeons and trials.
Everything in normal mode is quite "easy" (depends on your level of course), except the DLC, they are a bit harder.
In veteran mode you really need to know the mechanics  of bosses and you can't just burst your way through it.
That makes it really challenging.
Trials are dungeons with 12 people.
I did a few trials, (the easy ones, in normal mode) and that is playable without much tactics.
But again trials in verteran mode with 12 people requires a lot of coordination. This is also real end game material.
Being in a guild makes this game really worth it. This counts for every MMO.
So as you start, join ASAP a guild that you think seems fun. You can join up to five guilds, so just accept invites and start playing with guys/ girls from guilds.
Find another beginner, quest together and ask help from more experienced players. In a good guild, they are eager to help.
Most have  Discord with nice chat and voice features.  After a while you start to know the people and you really will keep playing more and more eventually.
DLC:
Every few months ESO publishes new DLC.
This consists mostly of dungeons and/or trials or new skill lines like the thieves guild and the dark brotherhood.
The thieves guild is my favorite DLC, because who does not like to steal in elder scrolls?
Really cool quests and dailies.
Morrowind:
It adds a new class ( which is real cool) : the warden and gives you access to Vvardenfell.
I think this is a DLC marketed as an expansion and find it too expensive, nevertheless I bought it, because yea I really like the game. :)
A  lot of people are nostalgic and do not mind paying around 40 euros.
ESO ONE TAMRIEL:
THe best update they ever did.
Why?
Before you could not see your friend or enemy :) from another faction and now they do, which increased the player base gigantic. You will never feel alone in ESO, especially now with Morrowind, but also with the new players batch from two months ago, when the game was F2P for a period of time.
Besides that, it scaled everything to max.
This means that a lvl 10 can play with a cp160. Because his gear, damage,.. got scaled to max.
You won't be as powerful as a maxxed character, but it gives you the opportunity to play with friends that are much higher/lower level. This  update is a real GAME CHANGER.
Homestead:
Adding houses in ESO.
It is something you do not need to do, but you can.
And if you can, why not?
It adds more gameplay to the game, because now you can build/ buy stuff to furnish your house and you will start to invest gold in it and be proud of the result, for sure!. Furnish your house, the way you want, invite your guild members and friends, and have a party. You can even force your friends to build furniture and decorate it in your house.
They also have a useful aspect:
You can add crafting stations, a merchant and a banker  in your house, so it actually becomes a pitstop between dungeons to sell/ desenchant your loot. It is really useful!
The community:
A lot of games face real problems to achieve a decent community. I am looking to you CSGO, LoL, COD :)
ESO has a nice mature community.
Most people are friendly, and willing to help each other out. Even just random people in zone chat.
Even in dungeons, when things don't work out as planned, if someone is getting angry or is losing hope, he just leaves instead of flaming.
I can imagine in PvP that it can be a different story. But i could not tell you.
ESO+ (price varies from 11 to 13 euros/ month depending on how long you take subscription):
Is it really needed? NO, Not at all
You receive:
-Full access to all DLC game packs
- around 1500 Crowns per month
-Access to Craft Bag for the duration of your membership
This is the best feature. If you really get into crafting and gathering resources, I do believe it gets inevitable to not have
ESO+. It can but it won't be easy to
-Costume Dyeing at Dye Stations throughout the world: really cool feature!!! :) but you need to unlock the dyes by
achievements and playing the game. Which I also like.
-Double the amount of Furnishings and Collectibles you can place in each of your homes
-Double Bank Space=> this is a new feature and adds value to having ESO+. I do not deny that.
-10% increase to Experience, Crafting Inspiration, Trait Research, and Gold Acquisition rates. I think that is a fair
percentage.
Things I think need improvement:
- There are still bugs, but that is normal.
- The dungeon finder was broken for a very long time, and that is something that can not be accepted. (but now they  fixed it). But it seems that ESO really struggles with fixing bugs.
- The mailing system, you always need to relog to receive your mail.
- The buying system: if you buy something from a guild trader, you get it in your mail box and again you will need to
relog. They should just put it in your inventory immediately imo.
- Some people are sceptic about homestead and also the crown crates, that ESO starts to ask more and more money, also
with Morrowind pricing.
- Every monday morning there is maintenance and you do not know how long that will take.( It can be hours and hours :))

Conclusion:
You can play it without subscription, but it makes life easier for crafting.
It is not skyrim, the mechanics and combat will feel more like a MMO.
There are bugs that you have to cope with.
How more xp you get, how more fun it will be with dungeons, trials, PvP and so on :)
But the ONE tamriel update made it much more fun for low levels. GAME CHANGER!
If you hesitate, then maybe wait for a deal, you can buy it for around 10 euros in sales. Believe me, that is a real dealbreaker, only if you  want to play the "single player" main story line for example.
if you have any questions, also for beginners, if you need help, PM me or comment here, I am always willing to help you guys out!

Starting off in this game I was quite curious. It brought me back to those nostalgic games where I was a teenager again. I was back to those days of instant messaging, the old sounds, and the old aesthetics right before my very eyes. It was a very surreal feeling that I could not get past. The old avatars just added to the overall charm as I was whisked backward into those eary years of my adolescence. It all felt so genuine which is what really gave me an unnerving feeling. You had your friends, and your best friends. Those people who you would stay up into the night and talk to nonstop. You would type things out, read it, and quickly go back and change it. The way this game was built was ingenius. It gives the illusion of choice, suspends your disbelief, puts reality on hold, and at times convinces you that you are talking to an actual person. Throughout the game I had forgotten that it was all a game. She recognized me by my name and it presented me with choices that I would use in conversations. This whole game flows beautifully and really makes me think. I mean we have all been there. We have missed out on talking to someone from our past and than it finally happens and it is just not how we think it we be at all. It is tragically beautiful and that is exactly why I love this game. This is one of those game where you absolutely need to play, no justice can be obtained by watching someone else play it. The best way to describe this game is a side-scrolling, simplified, idle/clicker version of harvest moon. You choose what to plant and your helpers will harvest for you or you can actively click to harvest for yourself. The money earned from harvest can be used to expand the garden, increase the value of your harvests and increase the time your helpers will harvest after you close the game. There are also various garden invaders that will try to steal your harvest, but you can hire guard dogs and place scarecrows to scare them off. The more of something you have the more expensive it is to purchase the next of that item which promotes diversity in what you put in your garden. You also gain experience from harvesting to level up and unlock more things to buy or increase the value of harvests along with getting more helpers to harvest for you.
I loved playing harvest moon and always wanted to play it on PC, this definitely scratched the same itch and is a very zen experience as you tend your garden. There is a slight learning curve with having to use the trash can and click on the little plant sign and then click the other trash can in the top left corner to remove plants, but once you figure it out it's pretty easy to manage your garden. Once planted things won't die and the harvests will never rot so the only way to lose anything is from the invaders which can be defended against using guard dogs and scarecrows. I have really enjoyed this game so far and it looks like I have plenty of game left to play, at this price point you definitely get your money's worth.

Some people may not like it because it took away the sanity system and other things that some claim made Amnesia: The Dark Descent a masterpiece, but I say I must disagree. Both games have their merits, and I feel that the lack of tinderboxes and other changes made to this game are for the better. This game is a very visual experience, much like Dear Esther--as such, you need some time (given to you via the never-extinguishing lamp in this game, which Amnesia: TDD lacked) to take in your surroundings, listen to the wonderful music, and absorb the images, textures, and placements of certain objects. There is much foreshadowing just in the placement of certain objects and in the order of the notes (which tell the story) found throughout the game. A chilling story that draws you in, Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is arguably more like Dear Esther in that it is less interactive than its predecessor. If that's your thing, then this game is for you. If you prefer more action and hate games like Dear Esther, then, this game may not be for you. It is quite different from the first Amnesia, but I personally found that to be a welcome, refreshing change. After all, there are already tons of custom stories for the first Amnesia out there floating around.

There is something enormously satisfying , after laboring to harvest resources by hand, to finally automate the task. And that is exactly what Factorio does. You start with a pick digging up rocks, then you build a drill to do it for you. You run around to pick up the drilled rocks ( I know theyre minerals Marie) then you build belts to bring everything to you. You take all the rocks to build gadgets, then you build an assembler to do it for you. Over and over this simple formula repeats until youre launching rockets into orbit.
Getting into the groove with Factorio can take a bit longer than other games however. It takes time to figure out what everything does and how to apply certain machines into the factory chain, and even tho the tutorial communicates a good deal of information and mechanics you will often find yourself outside the game looking for answers. But this is also part of the fun and you will soon find yourself tweaking designs and rearranging layouts for maximum efficiency and aesthetics.
Factorio is a unique experience, it takes elements from many genres. It's a builder like Sim City thats thrown in co-op multiplay so you can build a factory with a friend. There are tower defense, puzzle solving, economic logistics and even incremental game mechanics very smoothly functioning in concert. I have been gaming for almost forty years and have not come across anything quite like it. There is just the right amount of challenge to reward, of simplicity to complexity, of minimalism to eye-candy and of value to dollar. If you enjoy builders, get it. If you enjoy puzzle-solving, get it. If you like spinning plates and eventually would like a flying robot to spin plates for you...Get. This. Game.

If i recommend it? If you are a masochist, yes. Most definitely then. We all know those passages in games, where you just play and play and die and die all the time. In Dark Souls 2 you will experience like 100 times more. The good thing is, you get even punished for that. The game will reduce your health points for every death you encounter. At some point you will only have half of your health points left. You can only change that if you becoe human again and the items for that are rare and costy. So you have to choose wisely.
The enemies are strong and unforgiving. A lot of traps and huge bosses who punish one wrong move with insta killing you are awaiting you. Every time you die the enemies respawn. Other than in Dark Souls 1 they won't respawn forever. After 10 times they are gone forever. So no Souls farming.
Aprospos souls. The soul mechanic are still llike in Dark Souls 1. You kill enemies and get souls. It is basically the currency for everything. You want to increase your strength? Spend souls on it. You want to buy a weapon or ring? Souls! You need to repair? Souls.
If you die. You lose your souls. It is up to you to go and collect your souls where you last died. If you die on the way. You lose them forever. So you better be careful :)
The combat is kinda simple. You can lock on to enemies and then it you can choose from 4 different attacks. one hard and one fast hit for each hand. If you wear a shield you can either block or bash. All the different weapons (there are a ton of them and all upgradable) have a different move set. You should experiment with that. Not always the weapon with the most damage is the best choice.
The load is important as well. You can be the tank that wears big armor and big weapons, but that makes you slow. YOu can be also be the rogue or something in between. You can dodge then instead of block. You can also be a mage. A lot of possibilites there.
The story... *sigh* I admit i'm not the best in English, but i guess even if i were better i would never really got it. Maybe i'm just stupid- Don't know. It is a mystery to me tho.
The NPC's are decently voiced and well written. The dialogue is very good most of the time. The sound overall is pretty simple but it feels right this way. Loud music would have destroyed the dark atmoshpere.
The Bosses are impressive. A large variety lies ahead of you. Each needs a different strategy and all have dirty tricks in their sleeves :)
The graphics... yea. They are old. If you are a graphic ♥♥♥♥♥ you should look for mods. The game doesn't look that bad, but you can clearly see that it isn't the newest nowadays.
The Multiplayer. The fact that you can stop the invasions of other players in Dark Souls 2 is a great feature. Invasion means, that other players can invade you and you have to fight them. But that is not all. Friends can always help you or sometimes strangers over their help. This is a good part. It is up to you personally if you like to fight other palyers or if you completely concentrate to explore the world. There are also PvP arenas. Overall the MP isn't a must anymore, but if you have friends who need help or who could help you or if you like to show you are the strongest it is a nice option.
Can't really criticize anything on this game. Had no crashed or other bugs while playing. The lack of Journal makes the traveling or the quests a bit confusing, but nothing you can't handle. You just need to pay attention to what your NPC friends say :)
So if you like a real challenge and you can handle frustrating moments. You should buy it.

There are a very few Wild West or Western shooters in video game history and Call of Juarez: Gunslinger pulls it off in all places. Gunslinger is the first game I picked up for the Call of Juarez franchise as I haven't play the others. As far as I can tell from reading user reviews and critics, Gunslinger returns to its Wild West roots with excellent gameplay fluency, occasional humor, storytelling, and mechanics that stands out absolutely terrific.
The story is short, which may take you 6-9 hours, depending if you are looking for "Nugget of Truth". The storytelling narrative is actually worth paying attention to unlike most AAA titles in the market which pulls out huge price tag just to experience a mediocre story.  For the default price of $15, Gunslinger is an outstanding price if you want to experience the story (or the jack of all trade is the -75% discount for USD $3.75). In terms of gameplay, the mechanics feels really, really smooth and presents a cinematic experience as if you are watching a "widescreen" version of a video game. Each weapon you possess and handle feel power to it, with a touch of authenticity. The best gameplay mechanics would be Concentration and Duel. Concentration is basically slow motion which can highlight enemies, bullet projections, and slows dynamite throws so you can shoot it. In the other hand, Duel mechanic is the ultimate Wild West simulator where you and your AI opponent goes face-to-face in a standoff. The best tension in the game.
Other game modes are presented in the game, mainly Arcade Mode and Duel Mode (which you go face-to-face against 15 antagonists from the story). These two modes are really enjoyable and worth playing if you want to rank against other Steam users to see who's the best of the best. Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is overlooked and underrated which is probably because of the mediocre franchise. However, Gunslinger stands out in sheer awe in terms of players who had experience the franchise from the first game. For many people who haven't play Call of Juarez and want to experience it, like me, Gunslinger is a must own purchase. One of the most underrated games for 2013 and the current gaming generation. I strongly recommend this game for its Western authenticity and immersion.

I'm not going to make a very in depth "review" here, but I suppose it wouldn't hurt to throw in my two cents to try and help the game out.
I've looked through the reviews and a lot of what I've seen in the reviews, I've had no problem with at all. I'm a US player connecting from the West Side and I don't know if that has anything to do with it, but the most I've ever experienced is a slight delay in dialogue and attack registry. I mean like, half a second of lag, so it isn't bad at all. This is also true for friends I have in Texas and Illinois though, so I know that I'm not some special individual, my friends  don't experience any of the problems either so far. The Dungeon bugs, I don't know about those yet because I haven't done any dungeons, but I'll update when I do. If you've played any MMO's before then you know gold sellers are a thing. If they still bother you buy now then you might as well just stop playing MMO's in general, but I would recommend learning how to get over it. I haven't really cared so far about the marketplace and I honestly don't think it's necessary for any success in it either. I also don't know about the whole, world bosses being camped thing, however it's not hard to go to a different channel, or come back on at a different time. Next, I've seen a lot of people talking about how toxic the community is, but I've played on both the Orsha and the Klaipeda servers and I've seen none of this either. Again, I state that I have run into pretty much ZERO problems that other people seem to be running into. My biggest concern for the game atm right now I would suppose is the need for slightly better optimization. The game runs fine, but it does have it's moments of ridiculous frame drops, but they're both bearable and most of the time, lag caused by an overflow of people being in one channel and one zone. Which of course you just fix by going to a different channel. There are enough channels. Trust me. You'll be fine.
I might as well stop it here and recommend the game. I've had a lot of fun playing it so far and I feel like it will be a game I enjoy for a quite some time. Besides, it's free to play so you might as well jump in and just try it for at least an hour or so to see for yourself.
HOWEVER!
If you do plan on playing this game, I would HIGHLY recommend playing it with some friends. For example our healer pretty much does little-no damage, but his heals are a godsend. Our tank does moderate damage, but his health... yeah he will never die. pros: background and atmosphere has been ramped up on this sequel, starts off with a spooky tone that transitions into a horror tone, thought provoking topics, engineering puzzles but they seem too easy, and good soundtrack
cons: majority of the gameplay compose of nothing but hold down "W" and watch scripted events (like Dear Ester), it takes a while for the game to hit a significant turn. It takes around 4 hours to finally face a scary and imposing adversary. Then the game ends before 5 hours. My biggest gripe is the dumbing down of game mechanics, everything from inventory to the sanity system have all been removed. Ive spotted derpy enemy AI, some horrendously lazy texture work, and experienced frame rate drops.
Overall, if you thought The Dark Descent was too terrying and stressful, then try this game. If you didn't think The Dark Descent was terrifying and challenging enough, you might find this game a hit or miss. As the game stands, Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs has my recommendation for what is has to offer. Not the sequel I expected, but its still worth a look.

Alright. Before I go on, I will start by saying this is an excellent game in its own right, and it is very much worth playing, the vast majority of my concerns for this game stem from comparing it to it's predecessor. But more on that in a moment.
What I liked about A Machine for Pigs:
The music. Music in games is always a big factor for me, and this soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal. I adore Jessica Curry, and her work here is just as well-crafted as in Dear Esther. It absolutely defines the atmosphere, and complements everything going on in the game wonderfully.
The atmosphere. Very, very well-done. The game starts in a very domestic atmosphere, which has it's own nightmarish qualities, and eventually segues into this vast demonic machine complex which is confusing and oppressive, and I love it. Very dark, very tense, very good.
The plot and themes (mostly). [POTENTIAL SPOILERS] The plot of this game draws a lot on the concepts of the first. Self-induced amnesia, in an attempt to undo the unspeakable deeds the protagonist has committed, nothing new. But it is the context in which this is done that sets it wildly apart. Whereas the first game has the protagonist a victim, slowly turned psychotic in his work, this one has the protagonist as a monster on such a larger scale. The themes of industrialization and dehumanization are fascinating, and portrayed in very unnerving and gut-wrenching modes. I say that I mostly liked the plot, however, because I am utterly baffled by the ending. Maybe I'm stupid, maybe I wasn't paying close enough attention, but I just did not understand it at all. I feel like there was some huge twist and it was completely lost on me.
What I did not like:
Other elements of the plot [VAGUE SPOILERS CONTINUE] were poorly delivered, jarring, or incredibly predictable. Twists and revelations fell flat because you had seen them coming from ten miles away. I'm not sure if the character of Mandus is in massive denial or if he's just that dense sometimes, at the repetition of certain elements of the story. Overall the story really felt incomplete.[END SPOILERS]
Removal of literally every gameplay element from the first game. Your lamp is unlimited, tinderboxes are not a thing that exists, you have no health or sanity bar. I think the sanity thing is the worst offender. There is now no consequence for looking at monsters, which destroys half of their menace, there is no consequence for sitting around in the dark the whole time. And now that your health regenerates, there;s really no sense of desperation if you come away from a creature encounter poorly.
The horror. It was weak at best. I was infinitely more unnerved by the themes, setdressing, and practices of Mandus' processing plant than I was by any of the game's overt attempts to scare me. I think the moment I realized this was going to be disappointing in the horror department was my first concrete encounter with a monster. I saw it turning a corner and I froze and put my lamp away, all well and good, got the adrenaline flowing just like old times, but then I go down to where it is, and after hiding in the corner trying to get past it, it sees me, chases me into a dead end, and proceeds to..... do nothing? I'm not sure if this was scripted so that your first encounter with a monster was tense but safe, or if it was just a glitch. Either way it ruined the scariness of the monsters from then out.Even after that though, the monsters are unresponsive, slow, and generally less than terrifying. There were a few moments of true terror in this game, but they were few and far between, and not due to the monsters at all.
Overall, I have some very saddened disappointment toward this game. I expected it to be everything the first was, if not more, and that was my mistake.
Regardless, it is an excellent game, especially viewed in it's own light and not in comparison to it's precursor.

I have to recommend that you DON'T get this game, not if you liked the first Amnesia and are expecting more. Gone are most of the game mechanics from the first game: hiding from abominable creatures, scavenging for lamp fuel, and choosing when to keep that lamp lit or deal with the eroding sanity effects of the darkness. All that is kept is the general mise en scene and the periodic acquisition of notes filling in story details. Sadly those details are so dripping with poetry and convultion that they rarely add up to anything making much sense. Visually the game is virtuall unchanged from the original and still seems to be using utilizing now ancient Source engine. Here too they've managed to strip away some of what the original game brought to the table by covering the entire screen with a procedurally generated fog that serves only to muddy every single view in the game. Even after removing the fog (via save file editing) it's obvious that The Chinese Room (in taking on stewardship of the property) misunderstood that "dark" means shadows and not, "there's no strong light sources anywhere, ever." I found myself squinting my way through the game's 5 or so hours and lamenting that I could never quite see what appeared to be a somewhat detailed and visually interesting world.
I could have given A Machine for Pigs a pass for getting rid of the horror game play elements of the original Amnesia as a trade off for a deeper narrative experience, but unfortunately the game fails to succeed in this task. The end result is not quite Dear Esther and not quite Amnesia and sadly not worth your time.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a kind of a mix between the previous Amnesia game and Dear Esther, and the resulting product is certainly not everyones cup of tea. The game is a very streamlined version of Amnesia with all of the survival and most of the horror elements removed. However what remains is kinda very good but not reminicent of the previous game. You just kind of walk around and listen and read the well written story while listening to the excellent sound design and soundtrack. There are some enemies in the game, but they don't look very threatening and you can easily outrun them. The lack of threat and pressure is a major letdown, and while the sound design is impressive, it is at best only unnerving and not at all scary.
In true The Chinese Room fashion the game is also very artsy and pretentious and it is very lacking in its forms of engaging with the game world. That might annoy some people who just want to play something with more clearly presented story and substantial gameplay.
I myself enjoyed most of the game, and I was kind of expecting something like this when I heard The Chinese Room is involved. You just need to tackle A Machine for Pigs with an open mind and not expect it to be like the original Amnesia, and maybe you'll find something to enjoy in this game.
The game gets a recommendation from me, but only barely.

Now this game has ALOT of DLC which can be interpreted as P2W "OH THE DLC HAS BEST GEAR I HAVE TO PAY THEREFOR P2W!!!" Allow me to give a rebuttal: thats not entirely true. I have the DLC's and use gear from the base game, most every set (as a certain guild member has taught me) is completely viable. It's just not the "meta" or not as practiced. But ive seen a beekeeper set tank beat out a min/max'd plague doctor warrior poet set tank. Ebon set is gud too, btw. TL;DR with this section< Game is NOT P2W (PS. I dont have ESO+, the banker, or the merchant that follows me, all 3 basically make it so you dont have to go to town while grinding/farming. QoL upgrade more than anything).
Furthermore COSMETIC THINGS ARE OPTIONAL D:< (low key salt given I bought a house in game for over 1mil gold, fun to decorate, but its sole purpose is vanity xD)
Crafting!
Crafting breaks down into several categories: Blacksmithing, Alchemy, Provisioning, Enchanting, Tailoring, and Woodworking. Now each has its own place in certain builds: really plays on the idea of “PLAY HOW YOU WANT” and it means it. If you want to be a mage, or archer, (you can also craft shields) woodworking is great because you can use wood to craft yourself staffs or bows with wood you collect by wandering the open world (which is something I’ll try to get to later on if I remember). I’d categorize Alchemy and Provisioning as the two “non-gear” related crafting systems.
Alchemy is potions, buffs, poisons, etc. Same thing’s potions have done in previous elder scrolls games. Ingredients are the biggest Problem for me here. But I’ll talk about that in the later part where I mention foraging. You can make a potion to increase critical rate, increase dps for a moment of time to take down that one boss, share potions with your mage friend to buff their spell critical damage, give poison to your assassin friend to maim your opponent, a stamina regen potion to your DPS dual wielding friend to make sure he can do enough damage to the boss. Buff yourself however you want!
Provisioning buffs your stat max for a limited time (limited not being a mere 5 minutes, but around a half hour or greater. Up to 2 hours from what I’ve seen). Magika, Stamina, or Health can be buffed, so can Health Regen, Stamina Regen, or Magika Regen or any combination of these things. I believe up to 3 stats at a time may be buffed. Im a provioner, it makes you synergize well in a team of strangers. Eg, “You need a magika buffing fruit dish @random mage in dungeon?”
Blacksmithing: Crafting heavy armors or melee weapons is what this tree is for. Not to complex. You can upgrade your gear with rare items you can get from refining raw ore, or from deconstructing items of the rarity you wish to upgrade to and getting a %chance drop of that item,
Enchanting: The SLOWEST to level without a friend. Ultimately useful. Not much to say, but it does require alot of inventory space. You need THREE GLYPH TYPES. Square, triangle, and circle, square determines level requirement.
Tailoring (clothing): make light armor, or medium armor!
Woodworking: make bows, shields, or staffs.
All six can make furniture for homes. All six have their place in the game. Choose whatever you want an if you don’t like it, guess what? YOU CAN RESPEC! Another benefit of being able to craft whatever you want ties into the market. You can be hired for your crafting services if you want to, more RPG elements that encourages use of the MMO genre. I LOVE this.

Questing
The questing is something I have a love hate relationship with. Now there is so much in this game your not gonna spend all pf your time doing questing what with the foraging, dungeons, dolmens, PvP, random people who challenge you to duels, and general social activity that comes with a MMO. Now, sometimes if all you do is questing, it can get boring by just having to go to point A complete action 4C, then point B and then point C, talk to person A_16 and then return home. Sufficed to say, it follows a formula most of the time. But the game is FULLY VOICE ACTED and the writing is GOOD (mostly). Usually. It is an RPG the choices are seldom and rare, but they do make you “characterize your character” as a person.
Furthermore, you can say that the quests rewards aren’t always great, but choices ultimately don’t matter for it. But there is a sort of permanence with choices I love about this, I did a quest early on at some religious temple. Guards and civilians will thank you for your actions, it’s great! It makes you feel like you’re in the world your creating. Similarly, if a quest, perhaps, involves calming the hostile wildlife, and you complete it, the wildlife are no longer hostile in the area! I adore this. I Could go on, but this review is already CRAZY long and I have more I want to talk about.
TL;DR for this part is: quests can be a bit repetitive, but it's not the only thing to do. They're fun overall.

Basically, ALL ENEMIES scale to you at your current level. It's pretty awesome and gives you freerange to do whatever you want whenever you want. No level locks, only level locks are no dungeons unti level 10, and second weapon hotbar unlocked at level 15. Furthermore, some content is next to impossible until higher levels as well. Despite that, theres alot of content at every level (eg Mages/Fighters Guild Questline, Dolmens, Dungeons (on normal), etc.)

Idle games occupy an interesting position in the video game climate. Most of us don’t really think of games like AdVenture Capitalist or Cookie Clicker as core video games, or even really recognize them as games at all. They’re really just distractions, nice ways to pass the time and still feel like you’re accomplishing something thanks to ever-increasing numbers, enticing you to get the higher amount of points your heart desires while waiting for your download to finish or microwave to beep. Little distractions, usually cute, and always a good way to fight off the always approaching threat of boredom. The issue is when an idle game manages to screw up even those basic fundamentals and becomes a bore itself.
Plantera has a charming aesthetic that makes for a nice screensaver and nothing much beyond that.

On starting the game, I was pleasantly surprised by the sheer number of digits and names that had to be cross-checked and I was enjoyign my first day as a guradian of the Democratic Republic immensely before the day ended and I was forced to return home to my parasitic family. This opened up the second key part of the game, being depressed as loved ones die because you, as sole family provider, were too busy apprehending criminals in the name of mother
Arstotzka. This in the end turned out to be very useful as one family member dying really frees up funds to pay for medicine or expensive crayon sets and keep the others alive.
As the game went on I found that a significant amount of nothing happened, which really livened up the experience and made me wish that exciting things like dening people entry would happen less frequently, however I then began to see the value of things happening in video games as it helps to compartmentalise the long stretches of enjoyable bureaucracy.
In conclusion, more games need to make me feel completely bored and slightly depressed, then maybe they too could have as much praise as I'm dropping onto Papers Please.
Also Papers Please is what we in the industry call "enjoyable", we also say that it "contains gameplay" which may sound strange in this day of 10 minute long cutscenes, but surprisingly it actually contributes to the experience if the player is occasionally allowed to take control of the protagonist.

You need a keen eye to pick out the discrepencies of official government documents, like travel passports, permits, vaccine charts, I.D. cards, etc. You can detain suspicious individuals who either are smuggling contraband, possessing forged documents, or being on the wanted crinimals list. The "Ministry of Admissions" can somehow sniff out "every" protocol violation you make and will give you citations, they become more severe with each violation on the given day.
Worth the money if you have a high level of intellect and patience.

Amazing. This game is a tedious yet heart warming yet makes you want to have a heart attack as you wait for a violation. This game takes place in a made up country called Arstotzka, and you are a person pulled in the labor lottery to work at the new border checkpoint. Though at first it seems very simple elements are quickly added to make you decide between speed and quality, and the wrong choice could get you exacuted. Random events happen throughout the pre-made story to make you go against or for your country. Also you meet intresting characters that you see time and time again and make you smile and you are evaluated on how well you do your job, needless to say you will probably be told you are scum several times over each day. There is a struggle that feels almost too real in this game where you are trying to make ends meat, making almost nothing and supporting an entire family on that. There is far more i could say about this but in the almost ten hours i've played already i know this game is like non i've played before.
If you like being challenged, experiancing something new, or even deciding who lives or dies. This game is for you. If you want a unique game that will challenge you to add to your library, Welcome To Arstotzka.

When I saw this game advertised I was excited.  I loved the first one.  I eagerly started  playing and realized nothing was happening.  I did not encounter a dangerous monster until a couple hours in.  I even laughed at it.  I see people argue that this game has horror elements towards others that found it to be weak.  Abrupt loud noises and a flickering light while something runs by is not scarey.  If it does not cause you anxiety to walk around that dark corner without fear of having your face ripped off, it is not scarey.  This game was not scarey.  I roamed the halls generally care free with a flashlight that never died, health that would renew and a serious lack of danger to worry about.  It had some decent story elements, and a lot of detail went into the machinery, but the game itself was just not fun.  If you have not played the first one, please do not buy the 2nd.  I wouldn't want you to miss out on an actual good game because of utter disgust for "a machine for pigs".

This game is amazing. It is soo much better than The Dark Descent in a lot of different ways. One thing that really made me happy when I played the game was that unlike, The Dark Descent, in A Machine for Pigs there is electricity in the building! So there's always light (unless the lights go out). There is no sanity meter, so being in the dark will not harm you (Unless there's mosters lurking in the darkness). They still have a lantern that you carry around, but unlike the oil lantern in The Dark Descent, you now carry around an electric lantern that never runs out of fuel. This makes the game a lot easier and more fun to play because you are focusing more on the actually story rather than the survival of your character, including: trying to find oil and tinderboxes. I would recommend this game to anyone who liked The Dark Descent and if you haven't played that, then I recommend it to anyone who loves to be scared and likes to play horror games.

Hmmm...  Machine for Pigs is amazing looking, and has great pacing and atmosphere.  It addresses a lot of the problems I had with Amnesia the Dark Descent: the poor hostile NPC design has been replaced with something much more impressive and frightening, and the occasional cramped and badly designed chambers (most notably the ending) have been replaced with massive vistas reminiscent of the ending of Portal.  The problem is that it isn't really a game anymore; it is more like an interactive story or experience, and a fairly abstract and repetitive one at that.  I like it as a work of art, but the puzzles were both poorly defined and too easy, the NPC interaction was unfulfilling, and it has little replay value.  I finished the game in a little over 5 hours.  $20 is a bit much; I would wait until it drops below $10, possibly below $5 if you aren't into horror.

Words cannot describe the beauty and philisophical nature of this game, the atmosphere is intense, the gameplay is solid, and the story is immersivley dangerous. Get this game now, no excuses, you need it like you need air.

Do not expect this to be anything like The Dark Descent, or you will hate it. The stories of the two games are indirectly connected, but that's it, they are completely different games. This one is much more like Dear Esther, in terms of gameplay. That made me skeptical at first, but if you can merge with the story and the atmosphere, A Machine for Pigs becomes nothing short of greatness. The storyline is about social darwinism and makes much more sense than the one in TDD, I also found it to be very emotional thanks to the superb voice acting.
Do not buy this if you're looking for jumpscares and all those things that modern horror games promise, this one has something different to offer, and it's worth experiencing.

*Maximum of five characters can be used
*Arena battles with good rewards

Cons:
*Mid-way through the game is extremely booooring
*Transferring to new Dimensions resets almost all of your progress!
*Few monster types (See the same faces of them monsters)
*Needs lots, and lots of grinding
*Some character classes are seemingly worthless *coughs*
*Most upgrades are toooo expensive, "cha-ching!"

All-in-all I wouldn't say it's a bad game. Just a normal F2P game with 'in-game purchase'. Looking forward for more fun and helpful game updates. Keep up the good work, cheers!

This game does an incredible job of making you backtrack through certain areas, without making you feel like you have ever been there before. By utilizing enemy types and their placement, it forces the player to take different paths through seemingly familiar areas. For many people, this backtracking took away from their experience, saying that "it made the game carry on too long" or "it was just padding without designing anything new". I completely disagree. Seeing familiar areas later in the game with new threats and subtle changes add to the experience and effectively enhance the suspense when an area that was once safe now bears many dangers. It also forces the player to explore the beautiful station more, too. Hiding from enemies and luring others to their doom is refreshing and being vulnerable to almost everything on the station is thrilling. Lots of in game controls use lots of different keystrokes to unlock making opening a new latch a bit of a speed-puzzle when  certain death is right around the corner.

Name: Plantera
Developer: VaragtP
Release Date: 28th January 2016
Plantera is a very simple and addictive click based game, where the basic objective is
to construct and enlarge your own garden. As your garden grows, you collect more coins
which allow you to further improve your garden. Boosters can be bought with the coins,
which allow higher value of produce, the ability to collect coins when the game
isn’t running for long periods of time and dogs/scarecrows to scare away the
critters trying to steal your produce! Though I’m not usually a fan of clicker games
i thoroughly enjoyed this one.
Gameplay in Plantera is relatively simple in that you build a garden, collecting coins in
in order to buy more land, plants, animals and boosters whilst warding off
critters who are trying to steal your produce. As more coins are collected you are
able to expand the land, thus expanding your garden size and capacity. As you expand
garden size, you obtain more helpers; round little blue creatures whose job it is to
harvest plants and gather coins.
Controls are very simple as the main premice is just clicking, the only other buttons used are the arrow keys to scroll across your garden.
The graphics are great. The colours used and the nice little cartoon creatures all fit in perfectly with the games theme and while the games upbeat soundtrack fits it very well, it can be extremely repetitive (it’s just the one song played over and over) and can be a little annoying after a while.
This is a small and fun game with easy to learn and addictive gameplay, controls that
make it so that any aged person can enjoy

There is something enormously satisfying , after laboring to harvest resources by hand, to finally automate the task. And that is exactly what Factorio does. You start with a pick digging up rocks, then you build a drill to do it for you. You run around to pick up the drilled rocks ( I know theyre minerals Marie) then you build belts to bring everything to you. You take all the rocks to build gadgets, then you build an assembler to do it for you. Over and over this simple formula repeats until youre launching rockets into orbit.
Getting into the groove with Factorio can take a bit longer than other games however. It takes time to figure out what everything does and how to apply certain machines into the factory chain, and even tho the tutorial communicates a good deal of information and mechanics you will often find yourself outside the game looking for answers. But this is also part of the fun and you will soon find yourself tweaking designs and rearranging layouts for maximum efficiency and aesthetics.
Factorio is a unique experience, it takes elements from many genres. It's a builder like Sim City thats thrown in co-op multiplay so you can build a factory with a friend. There are tower defense, puzzle solving, economic logistics and even incremental game mechanics very smoothly functioning in concert. I have been gaming for almost forty years and have not come across anything quite like it. There is just the right amount of challenge to reward, of simplicity to complexity, of minimalism to eye-candy and of value to dollar. If you enjoy builders, get it. If you enjoy puzzle-solving, get it. If you like spinning plates and eventually would like a flying robot to spin plates for you...Get. This. Game.

Transistor is about blank canvasses, and what you paint on them.  The gameplay alone has literally more options and combinations than you have time in your life to try out.  The story is in pieces, but not by accident - you are the one who needs to splice it together, and fill in the blanks.
Transistor is a demanding game even in the short time you need to play through it, and not simply for its technical challenge.  It asks of you to create an experience for yourself that transcends just playing out the main character's journey.  In fact, I'd argue that you are not playing as Red.  You are playing as the Transistor itself.
Also this game is super duper gorgeous!  Definitely check it out, even if you don't want to exercise your imagination.

Death in video games is something that usually has little impact upon a player. You routinely kill thousands upon thousands of virtual foes and death or failure means teleporting back to a checkpoint. But here, death and failure are extremely psychologically taxing. The sound of a printing citation telling me that 5 credits would be deducted from my pay because I misprocessed someone was a sound that I dreaded and made me flinch everytime I heard it, because it meant I wouldn't be able to cure a family member of disease. A friend died and I replayed a day 6 times over just so that I could save him, because he was the only friend I had. The pixel art faces that come up to your door begin to feel more human than most video game characters rendered in 3D. This game is a masterpiece.

Been on the game before they opened to F2P, so far, I can say that the game needs some work.
Going to do this with pointers, so people understand why I gave the thumbs up to it.
Pro's
1 - Old School Graphics(2D art type?) Nostalgia, Brings back the memories of Ragnarok Online for those that played it, most of the design decisions are remarkable very close to what RO had back in the day.
2 - Quests/Open to explore, you have the base main quest you can follow, gain XP and learn the ropes that way, from there you can either jump into grinding(some people like that) and grind for your levels, aka why I said "open to exploration", and there's the "Hidden quests" on each map you have a set of quests that aren't that hidden, where by simply talking with the NPC's the quests are there, I found one or two quests already on a few maps that are triggered by items or simply by walking into the area, very interesting concept.(you can chose to do these or skip them.)
3 - Combat/movement mechanics(a breath of fresh air.) in this day an age where most of the mmorpgs movement and combat mechanics are simply doing a copy paste of the base system we had with EQ, some others going the point and click route, the fact that you can play the game almost not touching your mouse, using the keyboard or the same with the gamepad, its different, new, to me at least.
CONS(this is subject to change)
1 - F2P, so its currently with the usual stuff you see on popular mmorpgs, full of bots running around grinding to make "silver"(the currency used to pay repairs and do other stuff like buy equipment.), the usual standing bots on towns selling Silver aswell, bare in mind that IMC is doing their best to keep the game free of this plague, but we all know its a fight hard to win, or loose.(more methods to combat this are being thinkered by the Dev team from the information provided from them to me, so its something to keep an eye out.)
2 - Lag/server issues(this may change, the game just launched, its normal that EVERYONE wants to give it a go, and with the Bots/gold sellers in the mix, you can imagine how the servers struggle, may change like I said with time, once the hype dies, the server machines get upgrades and more servers pop up.)
Now the question everyone poses, is it worth to give it a go and play? in my opinion, yes, if you like anime style graphics(2D?) and grind mechanic ala Ragnarok Online(you can choose to do quests tho if you feel bored, and you will.) its the right game for you, if you are unsure if yer going to like it even after reading all of this, I'd say still give it a go.
One thing I must say is that, "reviews" by other people should be taken as opinions, when the game can't be branded good or bad, instead of going for the reviews of other people, TRY THE GAME!
You never know, you might find something you find interesting to play huh?

When the end credits rolled, I let out a breath I had been holding for 10 hours and muttered, "wow." Call of Juarez: Gunslinger was crafted with love. Whomever wrote the story deserves special recognition. The shooting feels great, the bosses are challenging, but not infuriating, and the upgrade system keeps the whole experience fresh. Even if the all else was total garbage, the thing that hooks you is the story, not so much the narrative itself but the narrator and how the story is told.

Don't let the price tag fool you, this is a full blooded, entertaining as hell first person shooter. Having no idea what this series is about I jumped into this one after hearing of an arcade-style adventure, and I was certainly surprised by the amount of content packed into this game. You can play through the fourteen level main campaign detailing the exploits of Silas Greaves, a fun adventure with the occasional slip-up (where do I go, some occasionally ridiculously hard fights, especially in the 360 degree arenas). You can go through arcade mode, racking up points to upgrade your weapons and compete against friends on the leaderboards. Or you can run through all the stand-offs in the game (and then some) in a gauntlet-style challenge mode.
I had a lot of fun playing this game, finding that there's a lot of replayability in finding all the hidden items and powering yourself up, as well as the fact the game is just plain exciting. As a newcomer to the series, I had a ton of fun and can't recommend this enough.

An underappreciated gem; Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a colourful, arcade-like run-and-gun through a realistic western setting. This is no Red Dead Redemption, and nor should it be. This game will pit you and your side-arm against legions of enemies, with little more help than a crosshair. Emphasis is made on skill, while technique awards you meter for bullet-time, and the rest is up to you.
Gunslinger is no Doom, so don't expect an armoury at your disposal. You get a primary (shotgun/rifle), a secondary (pistols/sawn-off) and dynamite, with upgrades to your effectiveness along three paths, focusing on pistols, rifles or shotguns. More improtant than the sattisfying splatter of your guns hitting their marks, is the unique as-it's-being-told mechanic of the story. There is a constant narration, a la Bastion, with time-skips, re-takes and other embelishments as an old man tells his story.
CONCLUSION: Gunslinger is a beautiful, linier shooter, that will leave you wondering why no other western-based games have managed to capture the raw simplicity of gunning-down bandits like this one has. It's not particularly long, but offers plenty of replayability due to its arcade format. I whole-heartedly recommend this solid, fun game.

This is a good game! It captures the feel of the Wild West well, takes you on a journey through the legends of the famous Wild West figures and has a great sense of humour while having a good story of revenge/redemption with some unexpected twists and turns. The gameplay is fun but challenging enough to be satisfying. Handling six-shooters and a small variety of other weapons feels weighty and realistic. The art design is a bit different. but works very well given the genre and humour.  I did need to search how to make a couple of tweaks to reduce the black-border and change the FOV but once done, the game runs well and looks good even on older set-ups. It is fairly linear but the variety of locations manages to keep it fresh most of the time and only a couple of the levels actually make you feel like you're being channelled along a set path. Shootouts in towns, log-mills and mountain passes all work well and are well designed to give the illusion of space and choice to choose your path. The skill tree adds some variety. And the quick-draw one-on-one shoot-outs actually take a degree of hand-eye coordination skill and quick reactions that can be frustratingly challenging on higher difficulty settings. I'd recommend this game, particularly at sale price as a fun, not too taxing but nonetheless satisfying immersion in the Wild West.

I actually think it should have gone further, because some elements remove me from the experience so their voice actors can have a talk at the player. There is also a dispiriting lack of chases by monsters. So why did this game take two years to make? Because it's a finely crafted experience, one with excellent design and unrelenting dread, the kind that actually creeped me the ♥♥♥♥ out instead of vaguely irritating me. Even the jump scares, an incredibly worn out cliche, are done effectively and with reason. So if you need your sanity meters, chases around the dinner table with monsters, and are not willing to sit down and actually listen to what the game is trying to impart, consider playing something else. Everyone else: The sequel to Amnesia is here.

A highly streamlined experience when compared to its predecessor. Many of the mechanics were eschewed in the name of simplicity and focus on the narrative.
The tone and world are darker and far more real than A:TDD. However, it wasn't as terrifying to play.
The environments were lush, beautifully rendered/realized, and felt appropriate and real at all times. The sound design is fantastic, and the story is wonderful. Given the direction by The Chinese Room, it is easy to see why the focus shifted to the narrative over scares/gameplay.
If you want to be creeped out and exploring a tragic, dark vision of late 19th century London, this is the game.
Amensia (s) are more about story, the universe of the game, and the whole feel. The games take the time to pace things, and to allow you to fully immerse yourself in the universe they've created. The feeling of constant dread was much thicker in Amensia (s) than I ever got from any other horror game. Listening to the final plea of the antagonist in A Machine for Pigs, hearing the gut-wrenching emotion of the antagonist begging him to go through with activating the machine, just... What an amazing moment. The story disturbed me. I continue to think about it, and I revel in re-telling the story to others.
That is what makes Amnesia different. It sticks with you longer than the "Summer Blockbuster" type horror of other games. When I leave the worlds of other horror games, they leave me as well.

They've removed tinderboxes, oil (lantern has infinite oil or something like that), the inventory, and a lot of interactability with the enviornment. Monsters are less frequent, and those who appear are easy to evade. It's not good compared to The Dark Descent.

The Chinese Room has an excellent writer (or writers), of this I have no doubt. A Machine for Pigs burrows its way into Victorian fear of its own industrious brave new world, the hallmarks of futurism, and existential musings on the nature of man and evil. All of this wrapped in grimy, visceral prose, much akin to the machinery the player stalks the bowels of.
But it feels TCR overstepped their creative boundaries into what drew people in Frictional's previous titles Penumbra and The Dark Descent completely. Gone are the inventories, the limited resources, the ever-growing insanity. Your light never fails, you never need to drag an object more than twenty feet, and death is only a temporary setback. It feels almost as if Frictional had very little to do with it, aside from the Amnesia brand name and some input on nasty monstrosities out to eat the player (And these moments are very few). You will spend a lot of time walking around and listening to talking. Doesn't that seem familiar, now? Dear Esther was an experiment, one I feel failed, but dragged kicking and screaming into this long awaited project. I think Frictional were tossed to the side as nothing more than code monkeys, with the rest of the design process dominated by The Chinese Room. Do not seek a survival horror, here: Whatever plans for it have been buried by script dictation.
It's not all bad, though. If you do want the thick atmosphere of rusted, Victorian machinery, the trudging through the catabolism of our species as the anabolism of it stalks you, and finding out just what those colourful piggie masks are all about, I suppose you could do a little worse than spending the tenner to find out just what exactly lies deep beneath that meat packing plant. But if TCR want to create Dear Esther, then try to inject that piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥into Amnesia, then I'm going to hold it to the same criticisms: What is it, in the medium of videogames, that I could not have experienced or entertained from a good book, or an elaborate theme park ghost house? If you want to challenge the medium of videogames, you're going to have to do better than this. Take responsibility for your crusade, don't drag another's projects down with you into pretense hell.

Ok then. This won’t be simple.
Why this won’t be simple? To put it upfront: Because Transistor is complex in a way you rarely see, even in AAA productions. All elements and systems of this game are interlocked, none works autonomous from the others in any way. To achieve that, Transistor uses a borad range of synergies between the involved media. Be it moving pictures, unmoving pictures, music, sounds, voices, literary content or game mechanics.
How to unravel the whole to make clearer what I mean… Let’s choose the following as a starting point: Transistor basically consists of two games. One is a research game, very broadly similar to “Analogue – A Hate Story”. It’s about collecting more and more fragments of information about different people in the game’s world to assemble a coherent picture of events over time. Events that lead to the state the world of Transistor is in and help clarify it.
The second game is a (tactical) combat game that is about eliminating various combinations of different enemies using smart combinations of specific abilities. The well-planned use of abilities is emphasized by a turn based/real time hybrid combat system that allows the pre-planning of a limited amount of actions in freeze time in certain intervals.
Those two games are connected, or merged, via the Function-system. The mysterious eponymous weapon integrates the digital remnants of passed away citizens of the city Cloudbank, baroque-futuristic metropolis in the decaying/transforming claws of the “Process”, as so called “Functions”.
Functions have strong meaning in both constituent games at the same time. In the combat game, they function as abilities that can be employed offensively/actively, or passively, as upgrades/modifiers for other active Functions or as buffs.
Use in one of the three roles unlocks one of three fragments of information in the research game-part of each function, each disclosing details about the biography of the person the function is based on.
Through this synthesizing system the two games described above are allowed to interact with each other and become mutually motivating.
The muteness/silence of protagonist Red in combination with an extremely external, exposition-free, narrative style and the sparse commentary of Red companion who is trapped in the Transistor, lead to an information-vacuum that drives the player to search for new or further details which he can find in the research game. To get new information, he has to recombine his Functions to switch the role of each one. This created new challenges in the combat game. Those challenges motivate the player to  play with different new combinations, which in turn unlocks new information.
In this way the literary narrative of the game is directly but alinearly interlocked with the mechanics-based progress of combat.
The conflict between fragmentalised information, constant change/continuous recombination and stringent structures/regular patterns permeates not only the two games and their synthesis but also the visual and sound-design, is rooted directly in world and story of Transistor.
Cloudbank, stretching out along skewed perspectives, assembled from 2D, isometric and 3D, is a kaleidoscope of glaring colors, ornamented, sometimes old, sometimes new, sometimes European, sometimes Asian, styles of architecture. Broken time and time again by the calm cubic white of the Process.
A grassroot democratic digital Utopia formed by permanent change in the constant flux of currents and trends.
The music a dreamy melancholic contrast bath of harmonic and depressing sounds. Sometimes just ambient background, then almost downright narrating.
And in all those things Transistor is also something else, in a very special, not often seen way.
Metaverses, Hyperreality, absolute connectedness, digital transcendence and transformation, ubiquitous fragmentation of personality and world as a leading theme.
Eclectic hectic, skewed, often changing perspectives in the visual style.
Told from the perspective of an artist. Hard-boiled and noir tone in visual style, music and the raspy dark lines of the protagonists companion.
External, exposition-free narrative style, highly reminiscent of a “show, don’t tell” dogma. Large parts of the story unfold alinearly (especially looking at the time axis).
Transistor is Cyberpunk. And not just in the sense of prop-Cyberpunk that wraps time-tried adventure stories into implants and matrices.
No. Transistor is 1980s manifesto-Cyberpunk.
Unconventional, dense, vibrating with ideas and references, pumping the relation between human being and technology as overarching motif through its every vein, without ever being judgmental, without moralising.
Behind every corner lurks a detail, behind every detail a train of thought begging to be followed, in every design decision resonates the whole world of Transistor.
Everything is stylistically, thematically, narratively interlocked.
To play Transistor feels like reading a good book. And that without it ever having to try to copy or mimic the literary arts. Quite the opposite. The game is so integral in the whole construct and its impact here, that it is hard, in many respects, to try to analytically cut it out.
I may slip into latent euphoria here, but be it as it may. In my eyes, Transistor is nothing less than an exemplary masterpiece of this medium. And maybe I could make clear why I think that way, at least a bit.

Transistor, SuperGiant's follow up to the incredible Bastion, somehow manages to improve on their previous offering in every conceivable way.  I'm going to avoid spoilers in this, so I'll be mindfully vague at points.
The music is amazing.  I mean, if you just set it out on its own and listened to it, it is brilliant.  However, more than just that, the music is integral to the plot.  They use the music to tell the story via lyrics.  At times plot and music is blended so well it leads you to question whether they are diegetic or non-diegetic, not unlike brilliant pieces of film such as
.
The graphics are aesthetically wonderful.  Myself, I've never been a big proponent of attemps to use realism in gaming, I far prefer a well done art style that fits the world we're playing in, and style is something that simply oozes out of Transistor.  From the usage of vibrant colours juxtaposed against stark white landscapes in later games to the deco styling prevalent throughout, you will drool over this game if you have any love of comics, art, or cartooning.  Absolutely wonderful.
The story is a strong narrative told in an unorthodox way.  I'll be honest, this won't be for everyone.  The story isn't spoonfed to you, you need to work for it a bit.  You have to unlock all 3 facets of all your functions, read between the lines of conversations between characters, listen to all the terminal reports and only then, at end game, do you really start to pull everything together into a functional whole.  If you take the time, however, it does make it worth your while.  The game paints a stark portrait of Orwell mixed with Huxley to create a world of immediate and meaningful gratification that overwhelms the populace's drive for freedom and the ability to stand against a tyranny, whether purposeful or merely incidental, from the people who control it.  Hardly new or different in terms of a story, but told very well and in an interesting way.
This game easily creeped into my top 5 of all time, can't recommend it heavily enough.

Transistor is a game developed by Supergiant Games, who are well known for their stylistic action game Bastion.  Transistor definitely borrows from Bastion's strongest suits; notably it is brilliantly compsed and absolutely beautiful.  The story is extremely esoteric (certainly moreso than Bastion), but not unsatisifying.
Where it differs from Bastion is mostly in gameplay; Transistor still is still an action/RPG where you traverse levels, attack bad guys, and level up, but the game plays much slower almost as a strategy game would.  Enemy encounters are isolated and you can use a "Turn" to essentially stop time and plan out your attacks, which will then carry out in nearly zero time.  Just like Bastion, you're offered a plethora of ways to deal with enemies.  Instead of weapons, you use "functions", which are essentially castable spells and abilities   Each ability can combo with other abilities to alter them, or can be used in a passive slot to provide a permanent buff.
The result is an insane amount of combinations, and you are incentivied to explore them because using abilities in different ways unlocks more information about the story and the characters which are a part of it.  In Bastion I found myself finding a weapon that I really liked and sticking with it for the rest of the game (even though many weapons are equally viable).  The story mechanic in Transistor subtlely pushes you to try different combinations, and in doing so, you often stumble into even better combinations that you probably wouldn't have realized existed otherwise.
All in all, I highly recommend Transistor.  Most fans of Bastion should enjoy it -- although the amazing art and music is immediately noticable, it is definitely a slower burn in terms of gameplay and the early parts of the game take a little while to get into.  As more abilities and the true nature of the game unveils itself though, it is very well executed and an absolute joy.

They do happen, chase scenes, but the ultimate creep factor of this game comes from the accumulation of the notes, journal entries and audio logs and what they ulitmately mean. A machine for pigs does have entertainment value. I played the game from end to end (all 5.8 hours of it) and it was interesting to make guesses as to what's actually going on and getting more and more clues.
However, that about sums up the game. You can leave your light on from start to finish if you wish and there's no inventory. The scare factor is 2/10 (the game features about 4 or 5 enemy encounters, but they're just anthropomorphic pigs with bad pathfinding, so when one appears in front of you, you lead them in a circle and continue (which is one of the problems: the game is almost entirely a linear walk through rooms, it never locks you in the dark with something scary or such). All puzzles are object fetching (reaching their highpoint when you have to fetch two things instead of one).
I don't regret this buy, but it is more of a playable fan-fiction story inspired by Amnesia than anything else. "The Dark Descent" was much smarter about how it tried to invoke fear (eg. the water chase, the wine cellar, the vivisection room) and it had clever puzzles. Frictional Games should have taken this game from "The Chinese Room" in its current state and then built their own scares and puzzles into it because what I see could have been an excellent foundation for a real Amnesia 2.

There are certain parts of history that seem like an endless supply of ideas for new stories and settings, and the Wild West is one of the greatest examples to prove that point. Call of Juarez Gunslinger uses that exact period in time to tell a great, believable and unexpected story using a combination of fictional stories and characters with actual events and legends from the American West. You play as Silas Greaves, one of the few fictional characters created to fill the bucket of an already enormous cast of Wild West legends, such as Billy the Kid, Jesse James or the Sundance Kid. The story unfolds as Silas Greaves tells more about his adventures to the young and old adventurers alike, listening to his stories at The Bull's Head Saloon. His narration is part of what makes this story so unique, as things will happen and events will chance according to the story he tells you and the interaction he has with the other characters taking part in the conversation at the saloon, adding things according to how they recall it happened or approving of things that Silas says, adding more context to the story. While the story is relatively small, taking around six hours to complete, the places you visit and enemies you will fight will make each moment of it feel memorable and unique, as you will one moment go head to head against one of the Dalton brothers, only to face Jesse James himself shooting a gatling gun your way the next one. In the same manner the locations will differ, offering a new and refreshing experience with each chapter, taking you from a vast canyon to a cave, only to then end up on a moving train, being a part of one of the biggest events in the American West history.
In a crowd of modern military first person shooters, Gunslinger manages to stand out by using intuitive and easy to use mechanics that reward you based on how you play and give you the option to choose in which direction you want to go forward. This feature comes as a result of the skill tree, that allows you to unlock a new skill each time you level up, which can be done by collecting enough experience of course. Depending on how you play and manage your abilities you might earn you more or less experience, but the game never stops you from earning more, even after you get to the end of the game, as the New Game Plus mode will allow you to start a new game with a different difficulty level while carrying over all your unlocked skills and remaining experience points. There are two main abilities that will be unlocked from the start, with the option to improve or modify how those work and how long it takes for them to charge, and using them in an efficient way will prove to be the key later the game or in arcade mode if you're going for the highest score. Bullet time will slow down time, highlighting the enemies ahead of you and giving you a better chance at scoring headshots and combos, while bullet dodge will automatically activate when you are low on health and about to get hit by a fatal bullet, allowing you to move left or right in order to avoid it. Aside from the campaign, the arcade mode works in a similar way, allowing you to choose at the beginning of each level a specific loadout and unlock more skills to use with that loadout and improve the possible outcome as you play more and earn more experience.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger might not be the best looking game out there, but its unique art style does a great job hiding that, as the game's art style comes pretty close to what you would see on the cover of a dime novel, and with Silas' constant narration of the story, the entire game feels like you were actually experiencing the wild stories of the west seen through the eyes of Silas Greaves. The visual effects, while not stunning, manage to mix in with the scenery in a way that makes them feel natural and a part of the environment, even if some times they are out of place. The highest detail was of course put into the wild west legends themselves, making characters such as Jesse James look stunning and closely to what you would imagine him to look like if you were to stand right next to him.
While it might not be as memorable and big as the soundtrack of other western themed games such as Red Dead Redemption, the tracks that are here manage to always stay in the mood with the action and when one of those rare moments of less shooting and more beauty comes along, there is always a good tune to add to the view. The voice acting is excellent and while some of the characters which are only part of Silas' story and do not actually stand with him in the saloon rarely speak, the ones that do take part in the dispute happening at the saloon over facts and how things went down are treated with a high quality voice that makes them come to life, with the honorable mention of Silas Greaves himself which is the narrator for most of the stories.
The campaign can be completed within six hours, but the fact that the story has two possible outcomes and that the New Game Plus mode which will unlock once you have completed the game for the first time allows you to start a new campaign and keep all your progress at the same time makes this experience be worth at least another replay. Aside from that you have the Duel Mode which is a recollection of all the duels throughout the story where you can improve your reaction time and compete for the highest scores, and Arcade Mode which is all about the leaderboards and the stars you can earn. There is no multiplayer mode, but with all there is to do as it is, you can easily spend around 15 hours in the game without even realizing it.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is one of the best western experiences to date, and while it not might be as full of content as other titles on the market, it manages to tell an interesting story by using actual Wild West legends in combination with some newly created characters that have their unique personalities and role into the story. Aside from that, for the 15 bucks you pay for the game at full price, you get at least 15 hours of pure entertainment and maybe even more if you're digging the arcade mode and aim for a top position on the leaderboards.

A saloon? Check. Cowboys? Check. Guns? Check. A badass grandpa telling a story about his youth? Check. Gatling Guns? Check. Did I mention cowboys? Oh, I did. Next one, bounty hunting? Check. Humor? Check. Replayablility? Check. Duels? Check. Great story? Check. Well, I think that pretty much is all you need to know about this game.

If you enjoyed playing Red Dead Redemption for its narrative and the Dead Eye Mode, you'll really enjoy Call of Juarez Gunslinger, as the game features some interesting Mechanics, as the Concentration Mode which is similar to the Dead Eye Mode; or there is the Sense of Death: While your are near Death, you can dodge  the one Bullet that will kill you in Slow-Motion !!!
The Story itself is told by Silas Graves, a former Bounty Hunter who fought with and against various Legends of the wild West like Billy the Kid, the Daltons etc. Almost in every Level, youll have to Duel with some of those Legends; again the Duel Mode is similar to RDR, too. But with some differences: You need to hold your Hand above your Gun in order to pull faster than your Opponent, also you have to keep the Crosshair on him for more Accuarcy, as the Enemy can kill you easily if you miss the shot.
In CoJ Gunslinger, you are able to earn XP by performing various Actions like shooting enemies in the Head, penetrating Shots or performing Kill-Combos; the XP can be spent in three different Skill Trees: Akimbo, Rifles, and Trapper (Shotguns).
So if you want to play more Wild West themed games, CoJ Gunslinger is a must have !!! ( Its 1 Mio. times better than the crappy the Cartel game)
