Gunslinger is the lastest from the Call of Juarez series made by Techland, developers of Dead Island.  This time, the series brings you back into the Old West and it's a damn good thing too.  The art style of the Old West is cell shaded, though with a nice realistic approach.  The action is as fun as it gets, and can get tough, especially on the harder levels.  The story tells the tale of an old man looking to get revenge on the one who shot and killed his brothers and tried to murder him.  On his quest for revenge he meets some of the greats from the Old West History books (i.e. Jesse James, Billy the Kid, Sundance Kid and much more).  The action is top notch and is especially well showcased in the arcade mode.  There's a slow-mo effect that helps with your aim and making the intense action sequences possible to get through.  It's well implemented and not too gimmicky.
The tale of the protagonist is not a great tale, though it is interesting, and what makes it super interesting is the fact that it is related through a very well voiced narration as you play the action.  Think, Bastion the RPG game.  Same deal.  The narration really helps keeps things interesting, in perspective, and exciting.  There's nothing like shooting someone in the head and having the narrator describe what you just did, or having someone ambush you and have the narrator talk about the ambush.  Also, because the story is being told as if it was the present, sometimes the story will get corrected and the truth will be told. Are you a human being? Do you like explosions? As in "Michael Bay"-level of explosions? Do you love action movies where the heros shoot first and ask questions later because they're that badass? Do you love games where you can literally shoot your way through anything - and I do mean
?! Do you love over-the-top American badassery? Then join the Broforce and become a legion of 80's and 90's action-heroes who've been lovingly renamed with "bro" somewhere in the title. Gender, genre, and age are no object here - if your favorite action hero is in the Brofore, they're a bro.
Ranging from the serious, like The Brofessional (Professional) with his mostly one-hit kills and the hard-hitting, resurrecting Brodock Saints (Boondock Saints), to the over-the-top, like Rambro and his classic run-and-gunning and Bro Lee with his insane, time-defying punches, it's all here, and they all play completely differently!
The maps are all destructible - everything which isn't required for sane gameplay, like checkpoints, can be destroyed with enough firepower. This creates some cool solutions to normally-problematic enemy placement. Can't face off against that horde of mechs head-on with your current bro? Just tunnel your way behind them! Got some heavy-hitting foes you don't want to get up close with? Send some explosive barrels falling on their heads!
Furthermore, the campaign, which lovingly rips on America's former "preemtive strike" attitude, ramps up the enemies and bosses you encounter, with special, one-life challenge maps unlocking powerups upon completion.
The challenge maps deserve a special mention, as they either highlight the abilities of a specific bro, or they teach you about the powerup you're about to unlock (sometimes both). These force you into a variety of playstyles, like "speedrunner" or "stealth explosive takedowns" (stealth being silent in
game? U mad, bro?).
While you can play through the complete campaign without the story mode via "Arcade" mode, you won't be able to unlock powerups, some of which are quintessential to the experience.
If it sounds like I'm in love with this game, I am. This is the most metal video game I've ever played - and this is just from the single-player experience! I'd love to play this with my friends and share the over-the-top Americaness with them.

No More Room in Hell uses the Source engine and the graphics as well as gameplay are quite simple and basic but to an tolerable extent. It has a few creative but simple aspects to it which make it more fun and worthwhile though in my opinion is only so when played with friends.

- Minimal bugs and glitches

Con's :
- Dwindling Player Base / Privatised Servers ( Only a Con for Solo players)

- Rare map bugs and mission glitches
- Occasional Weird hitboxes

In conclusion, I would only reccomend this game if you're looking to have a few laughs and giggles with a bunch of friends. Otherwise I wouldn't reccomend this game for those who are looking for a graphically advanced and story based game.

I find myself having to give this a negative review, despite kind of enjoying the game, for a few reasons.
I wont bother saying much about the graphics, it's a free game so don't expect too much.
Now first of all the difficulty. it seems almost impossible to do single player. It says up to eight players and it MEANS up to 8 players. If you are going in with a small team and are new (or are just going in single player) then be prepared to just die either through♥♥♥♥♥♥♥game mechanics or bugs.
The bad mechanics consists of the WORST hit boxes known to any game ever created. Distance required to hit an enemy with melee is sporadic at best, not even dependant on the type of weapon as they are all the same. Fun knowing that a tiny kitchen knife has the exact same range as a bloody sledgehammer but you still have to change your swinging distance all the time even whilst solely using one weapon. Oh and as added fun, the enemies hit range is actually longer than yours. Because that makes every bit of sense.
Weapon damage is stupid to. Okay so I one shotted a zombie in the head with a sledgehammer. Okay yes that is believable. Oh it takes me three hits to do the same with a machete. Wait what? Now I'm no serial killer *shifty eyes* but I know for a fact machetes are more effective than that against someone's head.
Oh and you want to shove them back do you? well good luck with that, if ANYTHING is behind them, even a tiny bucket or another zombie then they wont get pushed back. Just so you know, physics doesn't actually work like that in the real world. You shove someone into someone else and there is a good chance the pair will fall over. So physics is another thing the game fails at.
Your invisible stamina bar is a joke. It doesn't seem to have an actual level to it and is completely randomized. Swinging a weapon at one point can get you in a good number of hits, and yet another time (with no added effects like damage taken) you try it and can get in about two swings before your gasping like a chain smoker. Remember the earlier machete rant? Well it seems pointless to use when you are out of breath after killing a single zombie.
Carrying weight is another bit of crap. Despite having a decent sized backpack my character seemed to neglect to ever use it. I can shove WAY more into any backpack I've ever had than this game seems to indicate.
Jumping seems like an added afterthought by the developers. Seeing as 99% of objects in the game can't be jumped over. I can't jump onto this table but I can jump onto these boxes that are way higher and are definitely not as accesible? Wow! Amazing! It's actually almost as if the developers themselves don't know what jumping is and how it works. Have they ever done it themselves in real life? Does not seem like it.
Now let's talk about the infinite spawning zombies shall we? Yes you heard me right, INFINITE. The instant you get into a "larger" area of a map, the zombies just keep spwaning. Now I wouldn't really mind this, makes it more challenging, but as stated before YOU HAVE. NO. FRIGGING. STAMINA. And as it takes 3.8 million swings to kill a single zombie...well you tell me how you are meant to push through a horde? the moment you have killed one another spawns. And by the time you regain your stamina that zombie has rejoined the current horde. oh and you've been pushed back about 7 metres too. Have fun advancing. (less of an issue with 8 players yes but single/ a couple of players and well...good luck with that)
Oh and doors make no sense either. It is entirely random which doors you can and cannot close (for zero given reason) after you open them and apparantly the zombies are also smart enough to open some doors but can't open others. Not even vaguely linked to which doors you can close either. Some I can close they can open. Some I can close they cannot.
When using a gun, that is IF you have one and have been blessed by some developer created higher power to find ammo for the actual ♥♥♥♥ing guns the game spawns in the level (it is mostly randomized), always use iron sights. A bit of a given as shots wont be accurate. That is just how it is. Buuuuuuut when you aren't iron sighting and you point blank shoot a zombie with a shotgun and the bullet marks appear on the wall about 60 or so degrees to your right instead...well yeah even that aspect is totally broken.
And now a very quick session on some bugs. I've had random occurances where the game has taken away my respawn tickets for no reason. Without even dying I've suddenly been notified that a ticket has been used. By who? I was playing solo and am still very much alive.
Random occurances also happened where (again, without dying, still having respawn tickets and without running out of time) a notification pops up telling me the survivors have been overun and making the level restart. Oh and once this happened when I was three feet away from the exit. Thanks game!
Checkpoints themselves are bugged. Sometimes when I die I will respawn at a one checkpoint. Sometimes I will randomly respawn at a totally different checkpoint, but my personal favourite is the one where it decides my respawns aren't good enough and just ends the level with the "have been overrun" message.
There are probably more occurances to scream about but I'm currently trying to recover from the game auto ending my level when I was at the end. So I'm too annoyed to remember the rest.
All this being said though you CAN have fun with the game, just do so with a full team of people. Because you wont have fun on your own.

PLAY. THIS. GAME. Supergiant has hit another home run with Transistor. Not only does it have a gorgeous style and an addictive soundtrack, the combat is interesting with variable play styles and the challenge level is easily adjustable. The enemies evolve and make you adjust combat strategy as you play.
However, this game should come with a warning that it will rip your heart out and eat it in front of you with a glass of wine and a side of scalloped potatoes. As you learn pieces of the lore in interesting slices, you'll see the ricness of variety in character's lives which makes the sadness all the more tragic. Your only companion/narrator is the soul of Red's lover trapped in a sword, whose love for Red is utterly sincere and true without going into glurge or being sickeningly saccharine.
The villains are also compelling in ways that present them as people who have done terrible things, but are probably doing the right thing.
The world is ending, are you truly saving it?

If ever there was a game that flaunted its squandered potential, it is Transistor. What exists in Transistor is a duality of very captivating plot and brilliant-fun game design alongside dully written paragraphs of texts and tedious groan-worthy moments of play. Conceptually, Transistor presents a lore rich world with gameplay options that are variable enough to suit the player's desires and offer a huge variety of play. In practice, Transistor's plot is delivered to the player in a scattershot and confusing fashion, with text logs providing most of the lore and significant interactions of the game. In play, Transistor's multi-faceted system becomes either exploit-a-strategy to win or get destroyed. Environments that the game tells us are really interesting end up feeling more like arenas for the next fight, and the entire game gets wrapped up in moving from arena to arena, hoping the plot will become more accessible by the next big fight. The beautiful art direction and captivating soundtrack offer just that more of the tease of what Transistor could have been. For its low price, it's certainly worth enjoying what Transistor is--a touching, sometimes-confusing romp through a cyberpunk strategy combat world.
That is one beautiful game!

I remember few games that made me cry. Really few. To be honest, you really dont expect that from a game. Supposedly, you play it to have fun. That´s the main reason you play games, right?
There is another reason why we do play them, however. Experience. Trying new things has always been a driving point for many things, games included. Art can be summarised as feeling new experiences, something niche that produces certain feelings. That´s a bit how I feel about Transistor.
Can´t really say much about the game that hasn´t already been said. It is simply a work of art. Even with all the commotion with the city dissapearing, the Process killing everyone and the entire world coming to an end, I couldnt help but feel that the love story between Red and the man trapped inside the Transistor was one of the driving points. I felt Red´s pain, not being able to talk or see his beloved. I also felt his pain, being trapped and alone. The connection between those two was incredible, both in the excelently realised combat and the wait time in between areas.
That´s why I cried... the ending, not to spoil it, will make you consider to what extent the love to another being can drive us to commit certain actions. Red will stay in my mind as one of the most powerful "humming" characters in the history of gaming... that´s the least she deserves.
Thank you, folks at SuperGiant. For having created something that will stay in my memory for the longest of times. And for making me fall in love with your worlds. Thank you so much.
And, to Darren Korb... Kudos for making music that stays. That´s something that cant be achieved by mere folk.

From Supergaint Games (the same people who brought you Bastion), comes he Sci-FI Acton RPG Transistor, a game that feels like a more futuristic Bastion but with a futuristic setting and with a silent female protagonist named Red, with the narrator taking the form of the talking sword she carries with her (that has he conciousness of a man close to Red) as she peices together what happened to her as well as what is happening to the city of Cloudbank. The game's soundtrack fits in perfectly and is really quite amazing. The game gives the player the job of trying to peice together the stpry as it unravels through voice recordings, terminal messages, and exchanges between the characters. The game can be played with a gamepad but i found a mouse and key to suit better for gameplay. The combat system is complex in the sense that Red has the ability to stop time with ()turn and allow her to plan movements, attacks and combos with limitations of course. Take too much damage and a function you have equipped will short circuit, casuing you to return to another user terminal to try and recover it after a battle. Having all your functions destroyed ultimately cuases death. Each function can be equpided to the Transistor for a main attack, another function for an added effect, or to Red herself for a buff like extended health. The fuction system provides different styles of gameplay and different powerful combinations. The versitility of how these functuions are equipped add to the story becuase the functions, appart from being attacks and various buffs, are actually the essenses of some of cloudbank's finest. The more you use a function in a different slot, the more you'll discover about the person behind the function. The game does a great job of haing the player peice together what is going on, tagged along with a great soundtrack, gorgeous graphics and snazzy voice work make a great game. BUT the game feels just a tad short...that's what made me a little disapointed..so while the game is good, it is recomended to buy during a sale :p

Another great game from the makers of Bastion. Excellent gameplay coupled with a one of a kind narrative makes this mysterious story both quite memorable and replayable. The soundtrack alone makes this game worth at least one play through if not more. Transistor has a very neat way of introducing challenges as well as altering modes of difficulty through "limiters," these are sort of down-grades that can create a challenge, but reward you with greater experience. The higheryour level, the greater number of "Functions," or abilities you have at your disposal. While some abilities may not seem very useful directly, they usually have a benefit ifused passively. Utilizing different combinations of abilities allows for a wide range of play-styles and tactics. Transistor has such a great take on gameplay mechanics that it is entirely refreshing and a lot of fun. Considering the above, the one minor drawback, to me, is how vague the world is. However, I can't really consider that a negative, because the world of Transistor and everything in it can be open to interpretation. GIven this I think Supergiant has accomplished a pretty awesome feat, making the player use their imagination in both the gameplay/strategy as well as the story they've told. I highly recommend Transistor to just about anyone.

This is one of those games you have to experience to truly appreciate, as it is fairly unique. I wouldn't say it's a "fun" game, that's not really the point, but it is enjoyable and rewarding once you learn the rules. That being said, there are definitely some humorous moments that break up all the seriousness.
The game has a certain grace about it, it's very small from a content-perspective, but has enough variety to keep you on your toes. Without spoiling anything, there are several moments that will likely surprise you and you'll realize the developers really put thought into this. Even the standard game over screen is a mix of sadness and humor.
For better or worse, the game doesn't tell you much, which is nice because you learn and experience on the fly but that also means it takes some time to get the hang of, and definitely multiple tries to beat the campaign. Also, a few things seem arbitrary (example, closing/opening the shutters seems pointless?)
Some of the "find-the-difference" details require a very specific cross-match, and takes some trial and error (or internet searching) to learn what needs to go with what.
On a final note, holy crap is that country's financial laws harsh: I only owe $5, please don't throw me in jail!!!

Another entry in the Amnesia series, however this time developed by the makers of Dear Esther. Not really all that scary when compared to the harrowing experience of its predecessor, Amnesia: Dark Descent, or the pure terror of the recently released Outlast, A Machine for Pigs deals more in psychologically disturbing stuff than in-your-face boogeymen and buckets of guts.
It's only halfway successful though, since I didn't really enjoy it as much as the other games I've mentioned. The story is intriguing, but the puzzles are way too easy and enemy encounters are few and far between. Graphically, the Frictional Engine is starting to show its age as well, however sound design and music are great.
Overall, A Machine for Pigs is a slight disappointment, especially if you're expecting a ride similar to the original Amnesia.

Hunting games have been intriguing me for a while, and after much research I decided to get theHunter (others either have ridiculous bugs or are too old etc..).
I'll start with the most debated subject about this game in the reviews: The economic model. I don't get people putting negative reviews only over an economic model, because if you put aside this point, the game is absolutely fantastic.
It says Free to Play but if you want to enjoy the game, I won't lie, you'll have to put some money in (there are ways to not give a dime, but it's really not worth the time).
I had some money to spare, so after trying out the free version of the game, (which gives you a really great preview of what you get) I bought a subscription to get all the licences and be able to hunt every single species.
Graphics: They're actually pretty good, it may not be a challenger to AAA's games but it is really pleasant to hunt on the maps available. I still didn't try them all, but from what I saw, they're pretty "unique".
Gameplay: It's clearly not meant for everyone, but you don't need to be a hunter in RL to enjoy this game. I have no experience in hunting, and still I find myself drawned by this game. Everytime I launch it I go for a few missions and I always end up saying one more hunt, only one more. I think it's fair to say it is pretty realistic, you can't run and find yourself in front of a majestic deer. That is not going to happen. You have to find tracks->follow them, hear calls->locate it and when you finally spot your prey, you can lure it if it's out of range or take your shot if you're able to aim it properly. BANG! I hope you didn't miss it, cause if you did miss it, you're up for another stalking time.
If you killed it, you can walk up to it and check if you did a clean shot. There's a scoring system attributing points accordingly to where you shot the animal, if he died instantly etc. If you managed to do all this perfectly, there's not better reward. I messed up a few shot during my game time, and I didn't feel satisfied, even tho I tracked for a long time, it didn't matter, I didn't kill it right. FAILURE.
Sound: Ambient sound is really great, really makes you feel you're deep in nature and animal calls are really great aswell. God those hog screams are ♥♥♥♥ing real.
Multiplayer: Haven't really tried this, only with a few friends, but I saw there are some tournaments, seems pretty exciting !
Conclusion: If you like hunting or the idea of it or just want to try something different just give it a try, it's free to try ! I almost have 17 hours and I only had the game for 3 days, I'm completely hooked, this game is definitely a niche game and is way too underrated.
I'm literally thinking of becoming a hunter in RL now ! Thanks Devs :)

I'm gonna try (and likely fail) to keep this short n' simple, and hopefully not fill this review page with another poorly written review.
Basically, this might be the greatest zombie FPS ever made (so far).
I'm not overexaggerating here.  The atmosphere is INCREDIBLE, with a great soundtrack that goes beautifully with all of the death and wonton destruction you'll find in the many official maps that comes with the game.  The zombies capture the creepy, uncanny look of George A. Romero classics like "Night of the Living Dead" perfectly, with their rotting flesh and undead shambling.  Mechanics like limited ammuntion, limited medical supplies, and infection make it a true zombpocalyspe experience.  There's no safehouses.  No ammo piles.  No machine guns and auto shotguns.  Just you, whatever supplies you've scavenged up, and whatever location you've fortified up.
There's two gamemodes:  Survival, and Objective.  Survival maps are small and force you and a group of other survivors to gather nearby supplies while fighting back hordes of zombies from trying to capture the last bit of safety left.  Objective maps are large, and you need to (what else) complete objectives to escape before the zombie hordes get you.  In either game mode, safety is replaced with breif respite and a few seconds of life.  Guns are scarce and ammo even scarcer, forcing you to rely on melee combat, putting you ever at risk of one of the shamblers grabbing and biting you.  Infection is certain death:  the only cure is to find a very rare gene therapy syringe, or take a bullet to the brainpan.  Otherwise, your body will rise up and your ghost will watch helplessly as you tear your former friends apart.
There are three types of zombies, with a few subtypes thrown in.  You have Walkers (with the most health and the slowest movement), Crawlers (with the least health and medium movement, but being able to blend in easily), and Runners (with less health than Walkers, but being able to keep up with you).  Subtypes include National Guard zombies (who are impervious to headshots) and Children (who are Runners with less health but being much harder to hit).  Zombies have a tendancy to form hordes and will always go for the nearest target.  Fighting a horde by yourself is near suicide.  Teamwork is needed to fend them off.
Weapon variety is great.  Firearms range from 9mm Berettas and 12 gauge shotguns to 5.56mm M16s and .308 caliber sniper rifles.  Melee weapons range from your fists, to Kit Knives, to Machetes, to Sledgehammers, to the almighty FUBAR.  Everything has its purpose.  Nothing is worthless.  And combat is fluid enough to where anyone can become skilled with any weapon in any situation.
The community is surprisingly tame.  The worst you'll find is the occasional kid who doesn't know how to turn off their mic, or the occasional Brazilian, or the occasional person who uses nothing but guns and grenades.  I've had one run-in with a troll/greifer, and even then he rage quit as soon as he got swiped by a Walker.
And as a bonus:  this game is complete free, if you don't want a copy of the amazing soundtrack for yourself.
My final verdict:  Give this a try.  Please.  You'd be doing yourself and this game a disservice.
Final score:  9.5/10

This game does an incredible job of making you backtrack through certain areas, without making you feel like you have ever been there before. By utilizing enemy types and their placement, it forces the player to take different paths through seemingly familiar areas. For many people, this backtracking took away from their experience, saying that "it made the game carry on too long" or "it was just padding without designing anything new". I completely disagree. Seeing familiar areas later in the game with new threats and subtle changes add to the experience and effectively enhance the suspense when an area that was once safe now bears many dangers. It also forces the player to explore the beautiful station more, too. Hiding from enemies and luring others to their doom is refreshing and being vulnerable to almost everything on the station is thrilling. Lots of in game controls use lots of different keystrokes to unlock making opening a new latch a bit of a speed-puzzle when  certain death is right around the corner.
- 9/10

I remember few games that made me cry. Really few. To be honest, you really dont expect that from a game. Supposedly, you play it to have fun. That´s the main reason you play games, right?
There is another reason why we do play them, however. Experience. Trying new things has always been a driving point for many things, games included. Art can be summarised as feeling new experiences, something niche that produces certain feelings. That´s a bit how I feel about Transistor.
Can´t really say much about the game that hasn´t already been said. It is simply a work of art. Even with all the commotion with the city dissapearing, the Process killing everyone and the entire world coming to an end, I couldnt help but feel that the love story between Red and the man trapped inside the Transistor was one of the driving points. I felt Red´s pain, not being able to talk or see his beloved. I also felt his pain, being trapped and alone. The connection between those two was incredible, both in the excelently realised combat and the wait time in between areas.
That´s why I cried... the ending, not to spoil it, will make you consider to what extent the love to another being can drive us to commit certain actions. Red will stay in my mind as one of the most powerful "humming" characters in the history of gaming... that´s the least she deserves.
Thank you, folks at SuperGiant. For having created something that will stay in my memory for the longest of times. And for making me fall in love with your worlds. Thank you so much.
And, to Darren Korb... Kudos for making music that stays. That´s something that cant be achieved by mere folk.

From Supergaint Games (the same people who brought you Bastion), comes he Sci-FI Acton RPG Transistor, a game that feels like a more futuristic Bastion but with a futuristic setting and with a silent female protagonist named Red, with the narrator taking the form of the talking sword she carries with her (that has he conciousness of a man close to Red) as she peices together what happened to her as well as what is happening to the city of Cloudbank. The game's soundtrack fits in perfectly and is really quite amazing. The game gives the player the job of trying to peice together the stpry as it unravels through voice recordings, terminal messages, and exchanges between the characters. The game can be played with a gamepad but i found a mouse and key to suit better for gameplay. The combat system is complex in the sense that Red has the ability to stop time with ()turn and allow her to plan movements, attacks and combos with limitations of course. Take too much damage and a function you have equipped will short circuit, casuing you to return to another user terminal to try and recover it after a battle. Having all your functions destroyed ultimately cuases death. Each function can be equpided to the Transistor for a main attack, another function for an added effect, or to Red herself for a buff like extended health. Another great game from the makers of Bastion. Excellent gameplay coupled with a one of a kind narrative makes this mysterious story both quite memorable and replayable. The soundtrack alone makes this game worth at least one play through if not more. Transistor has a very neat way of introducing challenges as well as altering modes of difficulty through "limiters," these are sort of down-grades that can create a challenge, but reward you with greater experience. The higheryour level, the greater number of "Functions," or abilities you have at your disposal. While some abilities may not seem very useful directly, they usually have a benefit ifused passively. Utilizing different combinations of abilities allows for a wide range of play-styles and tactics. Transistor has such a great take on gameplay mechanics that it is entirely refreshing and a lot of fun. Considering the above, the one minor drawback, to me, is how vague the world is. However, I can't really consider that a negative, because the world of Transistor and everything in it can be open to interpretation. GIven this I think Supergiant has accomplished a pretty awesome feat, making the player use their imagination in both the gameplay/strategy as well as the story they've told. I highly recommend Transistor to just about anyone.

While the game is very nice to look at, has good music, and the combat mechanics have some cool ideas, I think this game suffers from a lack of good implementation of it's ideas. The story isn't well communicated to the player, and there's zero emotional connection to the characters because there's no lead up into anything. You're just suddenly in the middle of a story that ends in a couple of hours and the only character who has any personality is the unnamed guy in the Transistor. Even then we know nothing about him. Thus, any scene intended to evoke emotion falls flat, because the player has no connection to the characters. (And text profiles aren't really good enough for you to make a connection.)
The combat has interesting ideas, but I feel it has poor implementation in some ways as well. There are a lot of ideas presented but a relatively short time to explore them, as there are only about 30-40 battles in the main game. Many of the abilities seem poorly balanced as well.
Overall I feel they would have done better staying more grounded. The story, characters, and setting make it seem as if it's trying to be an art piece first and a game second.

Are you a human being? Do you like explosions? As in "Michael Bay"-level of explosions? Do you love action movies where the heros shoot first and ask questions later because they're that badass? Do you love games where you can literally shoot your way through anything - and I do mean
?! Do you love over-the-top American badassery? Then join the Broforce and become a legion of 80's and 90's action-heroes who've been lovingly renamed with "bro" somewhere in the title. Gender, genre, and age are no object here - if your favorite action hero is in the Brofore, they're a bro.
Ranging from the serious, like The Brofessional (Professional) with his mostly one-hit kills and the hard-hitting, resurrecting Brodock Saints (Boondock Saints), to the over-the-top, like Rambro and his classic run-and-gunning and Bro Lee with his insane, time-defying punches, it's all here, and they all play completely differently!
The maps are all destructible - everything which isn't required for sane gameplay, like checkpoints, can be destroyed with enough firepower. This creates some cool solutions to normally-problematic enemy placement. Can't face off against that horde of mechs head-on with your current bro? Just tunnel your way behind them! Got some heavy-hitting foes you don't want to get up close with? Send some explosive barrels falling on their heads!
Furthermore, the campaign, which lovingly rips on America's former "preemtive strike" attitude, ramps up the enemies and bosses you encounter, with special, one-life challenge maps unlocking powerups upon completion.
The challenge maps deserve a special mention, as they either highlight the abilities of a specific bro, or they teach you about the powerup you're about to unlock (sometimes both). These force you into a variety of playstyles, like "speedrunner" or "stealth explosive takedowns" (stealth being silent in
game? U mad, bro?).
While you can play through the complete campaign without the story mode via "Arcade" mode, you won't be able to unlock powerups, some of which are quintessential to the experience.
If it sounds like I'm in love with this game, I am. This is the most metal video game I've ever played - and this is just from the single-player experience! I'd love to play this with my friends and share the over-the-top Americaness with them.

So just to be clear, I was offered a steam key to look at/review this game, but this review is a completely unbiased opinion.
The truth of the matter is, I went into this game honestly not believing this was something that would be for me, but I like to keep an open mind.  But even if a game is specifically not catered for me personally, I believe myself to have an open enough mind that I can see whether a game is good or bad based on its own merit and the market it is trying to appeal to.
The gameplay was surprisingly addictive, once I got the farm really beginning to take shape, leveling up and getting access to new items to plant/use.  I liked that there would be different creatures that would attempt to thwart my plans of growing a great farm.  Admittedly, when I first started the game, I thought again that I wouldn't like it and would be done with it right away.  And then an hour passed, and I still wanted to play.  And then two hours passed, and I was still playing.  It's incredibly addictive and easy to play.
I enjoyed the music of the game as well.  Light in tone, it kept the right mood as you clicked continuously to earn that gold.  Granted, I believe it was just one song on a loop, but that's perfectly fine.  And who knows, perhaps there will be an update with more music added, as I see there are updates being added from time to time, including one recently.  But even if not, I believe it more than satisfies the mood within the game.
Are there features I would like to see added?  Well, I didn't get crazy far into the game, but I would love to see perhaps a day/night cycle.  Perhaps some various weather patterns?  Maybe these things are in the game already, so I apologize if I didn't get far enough to witness them, but if I were to ponder on features I would love in this game, I think that would give it an added variability that might be interesting for the player.
This game is something that surprisingly gave me a good period of enjoyment, and at the end of the day, that's what games are all about.  Entertainment and an escape from the real world.  It accomplished its goal, and I think a lot of people could enjoy this game if/when they give it a chance.  My biggest suggestion is play it for an hour or so and then make a decision.  The beginning game starts off slow, but then things begin to pick right up.

A clicker game disguised as a cute farming game.
You can build a berry bush, garden crops like carrots, and plan different trees. You can also adopt cute animals, like a happy Sheep. All the fruits, berries and crops, and whatever the animals will give you, earns you money. With the money you can upgrade your things to become more valuable, like the apple tree is less valuable than the cherry tree. Every time you make a tree of the same kind, it will cost more the next time, and actually get really expensive over time if you plant the same tree. That goes for everything in the game.
You got happy little blue 'Helpers' that will help you collect all the fruits and berries for you, and they will also keep working if you're going offline. Expanding the farm will automatically hire another Helper, and levelling up hires a Helper too sometimes. However, some evil animals will try to disturb your Helpers! Rabbits will try stealing carrots, Birds will try stealing apples, Wolves will scare away your farm animals. You can counter them by clicking on them, buying guard Dogs that barks at them, and recently you can buy scarecrows to scare away the Birds!
There is no "end game", as you can keep grinding, levelling up and upgrading your farm to make more money. I got to level 100 and got all the achievements within a day, and I consider the game completed. But I still launch the game and upgrade things here and there. It's a really good clicker game worth the 3 Euro I paid.

Plantera represents developer
's third game released on the Steam platform. Like the developer's other game
, it is also a clicker game. This one is in a slightly different form, and that's of a form where you tend to a farm, buying plants and animals, picking up the fruits and loot that they give you, and scaring away animals that steal your fruits.
(
)
* Cheery graphics, slightly close to, but not entirely, retro-style
* Soundtrack (or rather only one song) fits the mood that the game is trying to project
* There's been a few updates since the release, which adds a bit of content - it's a good thing and hopefully this continues. Adding Loot Hero as a cameo character was a nice touch, I liked
even though it was short!
* Compared to other games, the price point is relatively cheap!
* And lastly, unlike other clicker games - NO MICROTRANSACTIONS!
* You won't take that long to get 100% achievements in this game, especially if you aim for the "plant 100" achievements specifically. It's really a few hours of active clicking, and after that more hours of idling.
* No brain required to play this game, even though at the higher levels your plants and animals get upgrades - I mostly stuck with the most expensive plants/animals throughout instead of trashing them to plant the less profitable ones again.
* You only gain a maximum of 1 level while the game is closed, which means you have to check in after a while to get the gained level and make sure the EXP gained does not go to waste.
* EDIT: I completely forgot to mention that the sound cuts if you click out of the game. This explains why my video above loses audio all the time, since I click out of the game window to type in chat.
* EDIT 2: The UI will take some getting used to, but after a while it's helpful for when you want to select a specific plant/animal to trash.
* Unlike most other clicker games, you have to pay to even play this one
* It definitely feels like a mobile port due to the nature of how you shift to look at the other part of the farm. It REALLY feels at home on mobile!
* While the aforementioned song was nice, after playing it over and over it felt REPETITIVE! I wish there were more songs...
* Honestly I'm not really compelled to continue playing it after 100%ing everything.
Despite the flaws I can't say I did not enjoy this game - overall, it proved to be rather fun and addicting. :)
If you like clicker games and/or getting 100% achievements in games relatively quickly, this is worth a pick up due to the relatively low price as compared to other main games.

Clear cut "clicker" game mixed with a Farmville theme. As expected you start the early game massively spamming your mouse button trying to collect carrots. After upgrading from carrots and gaining more "helpers" (the blue guys that are sorta aimless and don't help TOO much) you begin to realise that you don't end up clicking less but only clicking more. As the trees/bushes both drop fruit it will be stacked quite high on the ground while playing since your helpers are slow at collecting the fruit.
Graphically this game is a sprite based 2D game as most clickers but it has a nice charm to it. The characters are quite cute and the sprites are clear to tell apart with colours being very vibrant. The music and sound effects though leave much to be desired. The same short music loop plays endlessly for the entire game so you will be muting that quite quickly and when collecting fruits and other things they make the same "clink" coin sound every time. This means by mid-game you will be hearing that more than 10-times per second.
Like other clicker games (Sakura Clicker among others) while you're not in the game your workers will still collect coins. This is good but this system is usually easily exploited by changing the computers clock time (may not work on this game). Otherwise this game is a very app-like game with mass clicking which is no suprise since the developers last game was a mobile game.
I'd say for $2.99 this game does not have DLC or any Microtransactions so you can get a full clicker experience here with a new theme and cute art design. If you enjoy clickers than this game will feed your strange addiction 7/10.

After 3 years, I'm still coming back and playing this for hours on end. I finally won my first campaign as Parthia, because I would always just start new campaigns. I'd say the strongest point of this game is the start of campaigns, when literally anything could happen, any AI faction could rise up and become a major player. You can play the same faction infinite times and your experience would be different each time.
However, the biggest problem I have with the game, the reason why I was never finishing campaigns, is how stale the endgame is. It gets super repetitive once there are only a handful of factions left, and there's hardly any diplomacy at that point, just conquest after conquest. The politics "mini-game" seems tacked on, or not fleshed out to its potential. And Diplomacy can sometimes seem strange, factions refusing to trade with you even though you have tons of resources and they have none. Every once in a while a faction will declare war on you right after agreeing to a treaty.
But in the end, the strengths of this game come out on top. Battles are epic, especially when they're between two powerful and advanced factions. The growth system for cities is ingeneous, and the wide variety of cultures at play insure a unique experience for each faction (outside of the Greek city-states). This went from one of the worst Total Wars at launch to one of the best. It's in my top 5, maybe arguably my top 3 with Rome and Shogun 2.
9/10, would recommend.

This is one of the best games of this year so far. In Transistor, enjoy the beautiful scenery as you attempt to make your way through the city, all the while trying to uncover the events that led up to this point. As the protagonist Red, you fight you way through multiple enemies in either of two ways: Analytical or Brute Force. Different classes call for different styles of fighting, all the while being very enjoyable. The visuals in this game are fantastic, and the soundtrack is something to behold in it of itself as Ashley Barrett vocalizes the mood of the game. Overall, I give this a 10/10 and will definitely be revisiting this very soon.

From Supergaint Games (the same people who brought you Bastion), comes he Sci-FI Acton RPG Transistor, a game that feels like a more futuristic Bastion but with a futuristic setting and with a silent female protagonist named Red, with the narrator taking the form of the talking sword she carries with her (that has he conciousness of a man close to Red) as she peices together what happened to her as well as what is happening to the city of Cloudbank. The game's soundtrack fits in perfectly and is really quite amazing. The game gives the player the job of trying to peice together the stpry as it unravels through voice recordings, terminal messages, and exchanges between the characters. The game can be played with a gamepad but i found a mouse and key to suit better for gameplay. The combat system is complex in the sense that Red has the ability to stop time with ()turn and allow her to plan movements, attacks and combos with limitations of course. Take too much damage and a function you have equipped will short circuit, casuing you to return to another user terminal to try and recover it after a battle. Having all your functions destroyed ultimately cuases death. Each function can be equpided to the Transistor for a main attack, another function for an added effect, or to Red herself for a buff like extended health. The fuction system provides different styles of gameplay and different powerful combinations. The versitility of how these functuions are equipped add to the story becuase the functions, appart from being attacks and various buffs, are actually the essenses of some of cloudbank's finest. The more you use a function in a different slot, the more you'll discover about the person behind the function. The game does a great job of haing the player peice together what is going on, tagged along with a great soundtrack, gorgeous graphics and snazzy voice work make a great game. BUT the game feels just a tad short...that's what made me a little disapointed..so while the game is good, it is recomended to buy during a sale :p

Another great game from the makers of Bastion. Excellent gameplay coupled with a one of a kind narrative makes this mysterious story both quite memorable and replayable. The soundtrack alone makes this game worth at least one play through if not more. Transistor has a very neat way of introducing challenges as well as altering modes of difficulty through "limiters," these are sort of down-grades that can create a challenge, but reward you with greater experience. The higheryour level, the greater number of "Functions," or abilities you have at your disposal. While some abilities may not seem very useful directly, they usually have a benefit ifused passively. Utilizing different combinations of abilities allows for a wide range of play-styles and tactics. Transistor has such a great take on gameplay mechanics that it is entirely refreshing and a lot of fun. Considering the above, the one minor drawback, to me, is how vague the world is. However, I can't really consider that a negative, because the world of Transistor and everything in it can be open to interpretation. GIven this I think Supergiant has accomplished a pretty awesome feat, making the player use their imagination in both the gameplay/strategy as well as the story they've told. I highly recommend Transistor to just about anyone.

While the game is very nice to look at, has good music, and the combat mechanics have some cool ideas, I think this game suffers from a lack of good implementation of it's ideas. The story isn't well communicated to the player, and there's zero emotional connection to the characters because there's no lead up into anything. You're just suddenly in the middle of a story that ends in a couple of hours and the only character who has any personality is the unnamed guy in the Transistor. Even then we know nothing about him. Thus, any scene intended to evoke emotion falls flat, because the player has no connection to the characters. (And text profiles aren't really good enough for you to make a connection.)
The combat has interesting ideas, but I feel it has poor implementation in some ways as well. There are a lot of ideas presented but a relatively short time to explore them, as there are only about 30-40 battles in the main game. Many of the abilities seem poorly balanced as well.
Overall I feel they would have done better staying more grounded. The story, characters, and setting make it seem as if it's trying to be an art piece first and a game second.

This is a completely different game with different game mechanics, however, it is still set in the Elder Scrolls universe. ESO is an mmo, so you can expect multiplayer, loot, guilds, crafting, etc.

-There are a lot of maps, you will never run out of new places to go unless you pour your life into this game

-Unlike most MMO's, you can play ESO with a single purchase and get some bonuses if you pay a monthly subscription

-You can switch between 3rd and 1st person on demand

Cons:
-Inventory space sucks early on if you don't pay the monthly subscription

Do you look back on the days in the arcade blasting villains for a high score with nostalgia? Because that is exactly what I first thought of when I started playing through the addictive story. I'll give you my first impressions about halfway through the game right here:
9.5/10. It's great for what it is, and it's really a diamond in the gutter.
At heart, it's an arcade shooter, and that's absolutely refreshing and tons of fun. There's loads of replay value in the forms of little "nuggets of truth," the tidbits of historical info, and the drive to get a great combo going. I would also like to make special note of the voice acting and soundtrack, as they hearken back to proper Westerns in all the ways you'd expect. The soundtrack is really beautiful on occasion. The story is told in the background of your actions, and it's both a good story and a well-acted one. The gunplay is very fun, as is the sense of progression.
However, there are some minor gripes I have with the game:
-Graphical fidelity is all over the place, and there is some kind of weird issue where it looks to be lower-resolution than it actually is, or that could be a fault with the aesthetic that seems to make everything blend into the background. It is either a very pretty game, or a god-ugly disaster depending on the area. There are some borders along the screen, and while it adds to the effect, I want the option to turn them off.
-Duels. They suck, and frankly they don't add much to the game. Good thing you're not doing too many of them, and regular boss fights are actually very fun.
Buy it as fast as you can and get going!

The content gets somewhat recycled but there's enough differences to keep it fresh and the despair dungeon seriously cracked me up.  My only gripe about this game is there's no way to separate the sound and music volumes and the sound volume seems really high compared to the music which is a shame because it has a really good sound track.
Edit for a bit more detail.
Most of the negative reviews are complaining because it's "Not an idle game" but take note!  Those reviewers just didn't give the game enough time.  That or people complain because the bank pays you to be offline but you will very quickly get to the point where the money the bank gives you is negligible so don't listen to those either.
You see there's esentially two parts to this game and this is important to know.  There's the "getting there" phase and the "idle game" phase as I call them.  After you reach floor 100 for the first time you will figure out that this is just the beginning and the wizard can transport you to the "next dimension".  There are multiple dimensions (10 total) and it's also important to know that any gear and sodas you've acquired will be reset to nothing when you hop dimensions.  This makes for a very active RPG like game with not very long "dungeon runs" because you have to re-gear up repeatedly and buy the sodas for new classes again in each dimension until you reach "The warrior dimension" which is the last one.  Once there you will always keep whatever gear you acquire unless you sell it and it's that dimension in which it truly becomes an idle game.  On average I have to start a new run once a day or less.  I've had one dungeon run go for 48 hours without me touching it at all, I'm up to nearly floor 78,000. (77,910 as I write this and counting)  So if you're looking for an idle game just give this one some time and it will be one.
My gripe about the sound volume sticks, which saddens me but at least the file structure of the game comes with the music in WAV files for you to just pull out and play with if you want so that's good but wow do the sounds get annoying fast so I run the game muted 99.99% of the time.  Once in a while I brave the sounds for like 5 seconds until the "nope" moment comes back.
Now here's an in depth list of things that happen when you jump dimensions.
You lose all items.
You lose all sodas.
You keep any VIP unlocks.
You get a new "relic".  There's a relic for each class and most stats.  An example of these is the attack relic you get which raises attack by 2 for every point spent in it.  You get a choice between some relics in most cases, though at certain points you're down to only one choice for the moment until the next dimension.  Class relics are given to you in order for the classes. (Soda Junkie, Ruffian, Conscript, ect)  Each class relic level will add +2 to all basic stats of the class (Attack, HP, Mana) and give that class a new ability.  Sometimes passive and sometimes active. (Soda Junkie is a passive 20% evade chance, Fighter gets a stronger extra attack) This part is slightly annoying considering it takes a while to get the Healer and Knight relics which are very important classes through a lot of the game.
Also starting when you reach floor 150 (in my case this was in dimension 2, but you may be able to unlock this in dimension 1) you get access to the "Realm of Despair" and oh my this is where the funny begins.  All of the monsters have "alternate art" and most of them are hilarious, the top one being the big demon boss/mini boss from the fire area looks like he's in a bubble bath having a great time.  Now the realm of despair is the only place you can get "mythic" level gear and where you'll spend most of your time in the last dimension because unless I'm mistaken the normal dungeon has no... point to it anymore.  And fairly quickly in the last dimension you'll get to a point where the game runs itself for hours on end and you'll never turn off your PC again and Soda Dungeon will always be running.

I played the first Amnesia: The Dark Hellish Scary Doom Game That Forever Scarred My Life Descent for such a long time now, but mostly the custom stories. Thou the campaign was enjoyable as well, the community is lovely strong. A lot of people are basing their review solely in comparison with the first game. Nothing wrong with that. In any case, just a few points to keep in mind.
I enjoyed this game quite a lot. I personally think that handing this to thechineseroom was not too much of the greatest idea, rather, Frictional Games should have done all the work, ALL, and they should have said NO DON'T DO THAT! AND THAT! BAD BAD! Removing elements (Yes I'M GONNA BRAG ABOUT IT BALHBVALH) such as the sanity was something TDD was special for, because it created tension, and so did running out of oil, and what am I gonna do with my life after it depletes, or what if I pass out next to that monster and he sees me and comes towards me then I just shut the computer off instantly, go to my bed and weep and cry ALONE AND FEEL MISERA-....*AHEM*.... that kind of tension is what made The Dark Descent special. You just had no idea what'd you do in that situation, and it was just frightful to be left without any idea on what to do next. At some points I just didn't even want to continue in The Dark Descent, as I was too nervous and scared. (Sh-shush baka, n-not funny).
T-thou the staggering amount of effort given, and the interesting story kept me going and going for A Machine for Pigs. As suppose to the first one, the sound effects are very well done and much more vibrant, and I could say a little about how the game looks, as I felt it was a slight improvement, but that's it. I felt like I was still apart of the game, and not what some people say "a walking narrator". I am easily scared, VERY easily, so the monsters did their job just fine, and so did the lights flickering as they got near and I panicked and cried and screamed for my life. So in a way the fear also kept me going as well. The atmosphere was just brilliant!
So in the end, I enjoyed it, and had fun, and cried in fear. I don't use numbers, but if a grunt or pig monster came and asked me for one I'd immediately shout a 7/10 and then die, thou that really doesn't mean much to me. So, as a 'sequel' to the first game, The Dark Descent is far much superior, but A Machine for Pigs is still a Machine of Terror and dread to enjoy, yet could have been MUCH better.

I felt very underwhelmed about the game, but I'll try and make as unbiased a recommendation as I can.
Pros:
The game keeps the same amount of atmosphere from the first game.
-
The level design is pretty cool, mixing pseudo-industrialism and victorian england together.
-
There's a nice chunk of backstory and fluff, both which I enjoy greatly.
Oh boy, now for the cons:
The constant blue tint when the game wants you to feel spooked gets incredibly grating, making it look like you're wearing blue glasses everytime something scary happens.
-
The way the games story suffers the same problem as Dear Esthers, often belting out incomprehensible "2deep4u" drivel that it tries to mask as dark and deep, which I guess The Chinese Room is to blame for.
-
The game is laughably short, taking a maximum of 2-3 hours to complete.
-
There's barely, if any, real puzzles in the game. Its mostly a walk forward, get blue tinted screen, get spooked, repeat.
-
The enemy design is a huge step down from the first game. I won't say what the enemies look like in AMFP, but the thing that made the enemies in the first game terrifying is that they only looked vaguely human, you had to look twice to understand just what was wrong with them. Comparing the AMFP monsters to the first games monsters makes them look sloppy and unconvincing.
All in all, its not really worth the 15,99€, unless you're determined. Wait for it to go on sale.

After 3 years, I'm still coming back and playing this for hours on end. I finally won my first campaign as Parthia, because I would always just start new campaigns. I'd say the strongest point of this game is the start of campaigns, when literally anything could happen, any AI faction could rise up and become a major player. You can play the same faction infinite times and your experience would be different each time.
However, the biggest problem I have with the game, the reason why I was never finishing campaigns, is how stale the endgame is. It gets super repetitive once there are only a handful of factions left, and there's hardly any diplomacy at that point, just conquest after conquest. The politics "mini-game" seems tacked on, or not fleshed out to its potential. And Diplomacy can sometimes seem strange, factions refusing to trade with you even though you have tons of resources and they have none. Every once in a while a faction will declare war on you right after agreeing to a treaty.
But in the end, the strengths of this game come out on top. Battles are epic, especially when they're between two powerful and advanced factions. The growth system for cities is ingeneous, and the wide variety of cultures at play insure a unique experience for each faction (outside of the Greek city-states). This went from one of the worst Total Wars at launch to one of the best. It's in my top 5, maybe arguably my top 3 with Rome and Shogun 2.
9/10, would recommend.

If this was the game CA released to begin with, it would've ranked up as one of the best in the series. Beautiful visuals and an enormous attention to detail, interesting and varied unit rosters for each faction, a thematic soundtrack, a yuge and engaging campaign map full of dozens of nations and tribes with legit working diplomacy (an enemy of your enemy will actively seek to trade with you or seek a military alliance for example), battle AI that managed to surprise me by using formations effectively and actually trying to outflank me and finally (in my opinion) a more visually interesting and streamlined UI.
It's not perfect by a long stretch; true to the series it can be too easy (especially as Rome) and upping the difficulty doesn't make the AI smarter, it just lets them cheat with more money and better stats, 1 year per turn means your generals drop dead from old age before you've even had a chance to properly level them up, the AI will sometimes not attack you during sieges or tire its units out by running them all over the map for no reason and the performance is pretty awful for a game of its age, although I did find upgrading my Radeon drivers to Crimson 16.9.2  boosted my framerate by nearly 20fps!
If you're a fan of the series but have put off buying Rome 2 because of the awful state of the game at release, you're a fan of the time period, or you just fancy building an empire - definitely pick this one up. Highly recommended.

This game is not what it seems!
Working at a border checkpoint, your job is to ensure each person passing through has the proper documents and requirements to enter your country. But all is not what it seems. With constant fake passports, visas, terrorist attacks and more, this game tests every bit of your moral values.
So you let this man through, but his wifes passport is wrong.They are fleeing their country in fear of death. Do you follow orders and deny her, sending her to an uncertain death? Or do you let her through and take the penalty, even though you need the money for medicine for your dying son?
This game is challenging as fake passports, fake work permits, fake visas and the like, become harder and harder to spot. Plus you are on a time limit. The more you process, the more you get paid then the more money you have to care for your family. (Basics like food, heat and rent!)

I played this game during the beta and was thrilled to find that the full release would be coming to Steam. They have done a great job expanding upon the premise.
While
has you in the role of a border control inspector doing his daily grind, the game finds many ways to make the job tenser than you might think. Each time you verify someone's identity in accordance with the game rules, you'll always be left wondering if maybe, just MAYBE, you screwed something up. New gameplay rules come up every now and again, keeping the rhythm fresh and keeping the tension high. There is also a surprising amount of choices to be made every now and again that will demand your own moral judgement. These bouts of moral choices aren't so much black and white as they are grey and grey, letting some of the game's unsettling political and ethical undertones sink in. The well-being of your family and paying off your bills is a looming concern, giving you much incentive to perform at your best.
Papers also has a lot of character.You'll see very many faces from a fictional, yet realized world. Despite the lack of voice acting, the dialogue is well-written and gives off the pseudo Russian/eastern European accent that characterizes the setting. There are funny bouts of humor amid the rather grim 1980s atmosphere and the game does a good job letting you know that you're part of a very rough region.
The only things I really have a problem with would be some of the controls and feel of the game. It works out 90% of the time, but sometimes the UI gets cluttered with too many different documents to sort through. During your first run, getting the hang of identifying discrepancies might also be confusing. The subject matter may put off some people since it deals with border control, terrorism, and TSA-levels of invasions of privacy in a pretty unapologetic fashion.
Its unwillingness to tone down its, well, tone is one of the game's strengths, though. It's well worth your time if you want to exercise your obervation skills.

Tips
- Be black, this is not a racist remark. Its a fact if you are black you can literally lose someone chasing you when you are 5 feet from them at night time.
- Make your head tiny, bigger head easier to hit
- Use shift+tab then look under guide section and click on the map. This is a lifesaver.
- Do not build next to or on top of resources, people will attack you for this and more importantly know exactly where your base is easily.
- Build in hidden spot that is only a minute or two away from stone and iron

General:

Published by: VaragtP
Developed by: VaragtP
Genre: Casual, Indie, Simulation, Family-friendly
Release Date: 29 Jan, 2016
Create, expand and watch your garden grown in this super addictive and totally adorable casual clicker game.
Plantera is a simple and highly addictive clicker game, where the basic objective is to build and expand your own garden. As your garden grows, you collect more coins which allow you to further boost your garden (and coin collecting efficiency). Boosters can be bought with the coins, which allow higher value of produce, collecting coins when the game isn’t running for larger periods (I can currently leave my game for 12 hours, and come back to a large sum of coins waiting for me!), and guard dogs and scarecrows to scare away the critters trying to steal your produce! Though I’m not generally a fan of clicker games, I have really enjoyed Plantera thus far.
The general idea surrounding Plantera is that you build a garden, collecting coins in order to buy more land, more plants, animals and boosters whilst warding off the critters trying to steal your produce. As you collect more coins you are able to expand the land, thus expanding your garden size and capacity. As you expand land size, you obtain more helpers; round little blue creatures whose job it is to harvest plants and collect said coins.
Plants, bushes, trees and animals can all be placed in the garden to earn coins, and you can also manually click on butterflies and moles to gain even more (the helpers cannot collect these).
Leveling up will unlock different varieties of plants, bushes, trees and animals to add to your garden, and with every purchase of these, the price of each rises.
The controls are very simplistic. As it is a clicker game, you basically do just that; click. The only time you will need your keyboard is when your garden has expanded in size enough that you need to navigate from one side to the other.
Whilst the upbeat soundtrack fits in very well with the game, it is very repetitive (it’s just the one song played over) which can get a little dull after a while.
I absolutely adore the graphics. The colours used and the cute little cartoon creatures all tie in perfectly with the game’s theme.
Though I’m not sure if there is a maximum level (I’m currently level 67), I do believe the repetitive nature of the game may leave little replay value when a certain level is reached.
There is no real difficulty in Plantera; it would be appropriate for all age levels and skill levels respectively. The whole expanding process is fairly linear, thus leaving little room for fail; ie, you will essentially just keep earning coins and progressing no matter how you play it.
A reasonable amount of interaction is needed when you first play Plantera, as you start with a blank garden and very few coins. Once you are able to build it up to a reasonably large size, you will be able to let it idle and check on your progress from time to time, which I think is a definite advantage for the casual player. How involved you wish to get is completely up to you; either click away and earn the coins yourself, or leave it up to your helpers, checking in from time to time to keep the progress going. There are limited variations as to what can be bought currently (4 each of plants, bushes, trees and animals), but that doesn’t affect the gameplay for me personally. The devs are continuing to add to the game which is fantastic.
Really relaxing and enjoyable game. Would recommend it 4 sure.

Put simply, this game consists of encountering some kind of roadblock, finding the usually laughably easy solution to a "puzzle" and then watching as every important door relocks itself behind you. There's also machinery and pigs, all wrapped up in a very dark package. If you were to ask me in person what I think of A Machine For Pigs I'd reply with a shrug and a low non-committal noise, then suggest you just play it.
You know in The Dark Descent how you could pick up all of the random clutter scattered around the place and throw it around or break it? It was a great way to destress yourself after a scary part. A Machine For Pigs doesn't let you do that, the vast majority of the crap strewn around is just for decoration now and can't be interacted with. You also can't throw important items, so if, for example, you had to stick a lever into a hole in the wall, you couldn't chuck it from across the room and feel like a badass. Luckily (or not I guess) you won't need destressing. We'll get to that later though.
Speaking of not picking things up, you no longer have an inventory so you won't be scouring every nook and cranny for tinderboxes or oil. Almost everything's electric now, including your lantern, so there's no danger of running out of light. Not that that would be a problem anyway, but I'll get to that in a sec. On one hand, this is good news because it means you can keep advancing and following the story, but on the other hand not worrying about your oil removes a lot of tension. Remember when you were new to The Dark Descent and you didn't know all of the cheap ways to gain oil and avoid enemies? Those were the days. The lights suffer from the same issues as lights in every other horror game, so you know that if they start flickering it's brown trousers time.
Back to running out of light not being a problem - this is because they've removed the sanity mechanic. In The Dark Descent if you sat in the dark or looked at a monster for too long you'd start losing your mind. This ultimately made it easier for enemies to get you. In A Machine For Pigs, however, you can just sit there with your light off and stare at the enemies until they get out of your way, just like in every other stealth game. The first time I encountered an actual enemy (as in an enemy that can attack you, not just scamper past and disappear around a corner) was in a massive dark room. I heard a horrid noise and was looking around, trying to find out what had made it, when suddenly a pig-monster thing ran at me and spanked me a few times. I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, I "escaped" by turning off my lantern and crouching on the spot. I didn't expect that to work and had already resigned myself to having to restart when the monster strolled off. This brought back painful memories of Call of Cthulhu.
Let's talk about scares. A Machine For Pigs takes the "make a loud noise and shake everything"
route. Now I'm not a game designer or horror writer or anything, I just play games, but this just feels more annoying than scary. The worst part is that whenever this happens the game stops you from moving, so you know there's absolutely no danger because you don't have the option to run and hide. When there is danger, on the other hand, the game makes sure to point you at the enemy during this temporary paralysis, so you know exactly where NOT to go. Thanks game. I don't know, maybe horror games just aren't for me any more.
A Machine For Pigs was meant to be released in time for Halloween 2012, but was delayed until early September 2013. They said that the delay was because they weren't happy with the game and wanted to improve it. What we got was a watered down and honestly kind of dumb game that was over in about 4 hours, so I shudder to think what they had before the delay.
This whole thing felt a bit unfair. I really should have been focusing on what the game DID, not what it didn't do. It's just that everything was done so well in the past. If you want my real opinion, The Dark Descent is better than A Machine For Pigs, and the Penumbra series is better than either Amnesia game. As for the recommendation, do NOT buy this for $20. If you've not got The Dark Descent yet, spend your $20 on that instead, or better yet head over to the Frictional Games store and grab the Penumbra series for $10. It pains me to say it but this was just a huge disappointment.
A pure example of "pretentious indie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" , this "game" is a huge letdown.

Ah, nostalgia. "Alien" was my first R-rated movie.

The set design, the lighting, the agonizingly slow 1970s mechanics, a bunch of freaked-out people with an us vs. them mentality, rogue robots, a mendacious self-serving corporation... oh, and one indestructible xenomorph, and the BAFTA-winning sound design.
This is another one of those games where I died numerous times from suddenly standing there with my jaw on the floor (a Working Joe on fire, walking, with apparently accurate fire dynamics)! My only complaint is what I perceived as a

What more can I say about this highly praised game that hasn't been said around before...?
It's good. It's great. Yes, it has some flaws and glitches (which game doesn't?), but it already is one of my most favourite games ever!
However, it's not really a game I would consider as "seriously challenging."
I finished the campaign on Nightmare difficulty just yesterday and while it can be a good challenge for an "average action-arcade player", I personally wouldn't really call it a "Nightmare" difficulty. There are some parts which are tricky, but if you're an experienced stealth and survival horror genre fan, you're never really stuck in progress and after some change of approach and tactics, while sticking to some basic survival guidelines, you can do it without any serious difficulties and almost always outsmart the adaptable Alien AI in some way.
The crafting resources are abundant even on Nightmare difficulty towards the end (if you manage them rationally). And even though the adverts mention the Alien is not giving you any "second chances" on Nightmare, I think his senses weren't as sharp in some situations as I would expect them to be from an ultimate predator, a "perfect organism"
In fact, I would change the vanilla Normal difficulty to "Easy", the vanilla Hard difficulty to "Normal" and the vanilla "Nightmare" should be Hard. And there should be another ultimate difficulty called Nightmare... for example only with autosaves and no manual save points. You die once - that's it. That would be some serious and satisfying accomplishment!
However I must also say that the difficulty appears to be quite higher in the DLCs, which are mostly smaller areas and the Alien only rarely gives you some space to take a breath, by retreating to the airducts. And you can't save in Survivor mode.
Anyway, despite my nitpicking, I think this is a worthy, if not even essential game for every serious survival horror gamer.

Engineers rejoice. Learn Technology, Automation and Efficiency in one easy to learn package. No? Seriously. this is a hard game to put down.
Let's take a typical late game scenario.
Assembler #28, manufacturing Advanced Electronics (let's call it a PCB) has a bottleneck and it's dragging down the entire electronic circuit assembly line.
I took a look at the insertor (a small robotic feeder arm) sitting idle as copper coils were swallowed up by the identical assemblers before it reached #28. Obviously I need to increase copper coil production.
Soo... I took a look at the copper coil assemblers, already sporting a Tech III speed beacon and Tech III efficiency modules and noticed that the copper plate was in short supply.
Sooo... I took a look at the copper ore smelting furnaces, also sporting (hard earned) Tech III modules and noticed the selectors feeding those were too slow and were skipping every second ore.
Sooo... I upgraded the selectors to fast selectors and solved the problem.
Or did I?
10 minutes later, Assembler #28 is doing it again. I repeat the above mitigation steps and notice the increase in insertor efficiency at the furnaces is depleting the ore feeder line. I have to increase ore production at the mining drills. Obvious right?
Sooo... my first thought is to add Tech modules to increase speed but... because the PCB production line is effectively in stasis I can't make more modules just yet so I have to do it the more obvious way. Add a new mining drill. Right?
Sooo... I went to get some iron plate BUT... there is none free because it's also being used on the PCB production line. I ran down the conveyor belt, scooping up iron plate, made my mining drill, ran down to the ore fields, installed a power line, placed the drill and.... lost power.
Sooo.... While I started to manufacture more panels and accumulators to add more power... the aliens came and with no power on my defenses, it took a superhuman effort to eradicate them using my flamethrower and Power Armor (Mk II of course). My personal construction bots all the while repairing what I damaged with my aggressive flame attack.
Meanwhile.... Because I had stolen the iron plate off the PCB production line the copper coil problem was sorted... at least... temporarily.
Then my sulfuric acid production stopped, which makes my batteries which is used to make my logistic bots that supply the whole higher end production chain... including my research.... because I ran out of..... iron plates.
I'll have to redesign the whole damn thing. Tomorrow.
Or maybe I can just do this little bit now...

Now you have to manage population, population growth, and family/government influence. Unlike previous TW games where your population was really only something that reflected how much money you could get from taxes, in Rome 2 you need population numbers to actually build stuff.
