From the makers of Bastion comes another excellent and original title for gamers to enjoy. Transistor has a lot of class and charm on its own, let alone for people who were fans of Bastion.
Taking a few similar mechanics such as the narrator, isometric realtime battle system, and customizable weapons, Transistor ups the ante by adding new twists to the genre such as tactial mode (which pauses the action so you can plan out a few moves in a chain before starting the battle again), and the higher complexity of weapon customization and the idea of weapons becoming unusable for a few battles in exchange for another health bar. All of these changes work well together to provide a fast pace action game.
The narrative introduces you to a strange futuristic world filled with politics and intrigue. After completing the game however I was craving more. The light between the cracks of the mystery is never fully revealed, which is both a positive and a negative for me.
The game took me about 10 hours to complete for the first playthrough, but not everything is accessible during the first run. A new game + mode is provided to allow you to fully unlock Red's abilities and side missions. I will be returning to this game for a second run when I get the opportunity.

It's a beautiful game, and I'd say the combat is more interesting than in Bastion. In fact, I'd say it's superior to Bastion in all ways but one--it didn't suceed as well at getting me to care. The way Bastion played, and particularly the clever way they wove narrative and gameplay together, really did well at slowly making you care about the world and the characters. With Transistor... I never felt that. I'm not sure I can put a finger on why. Maybe it's because the world is falling apart around you so you have no time to learn how it *used* to be.
Regardless, if you enjoyed Bastion, you'll enjoy Transistor. If you haven't played Bastion... play it first.

This is an excellent FPS with some fresh ideas, a great story, plenty of replayablility and a great sense of humor.  I can't remember the last time I started an FPS and "couldn't put it down" as is the case with this one.
Even the most experienced players will find plenty of fun and challenge here.  The role-playing/skill-up elements add to what would otherwise still be a very good FPS, and the "nuggets" of wild west history are just icing on the cake and all interesting reads.  I actually couldn't wait to read each one after I found them.  Be careful you may end up researching old west history after playing this game.
The boss fights are fought both in traitional fps style, and in old-west style "duels".  The "dueling" mechanics are well-done, a nice change of pace for "boss fights" and add a whole new fun element to the "old-west" atmosphere of this title.

All that is available just in "story" mode, but there are 2 separate "arcade/challenge" modes as well in which you compete for scores.  In "arcade" mode you get to beome a one-man murder-machine as you blast your way through really fun shortened levels from the story mode, trying to gain as many points as possible.  There is a separate XP bank in this mode for each of 3 archetypes you can choose (basically rifle, shotgun or pistol style) and skills in this mode are gained automatically as you complete the challenges, all of which can be replayed infinitely for more xp if you want.
In "duel" mode you are given 5 lives to survive as many duels as possible, all presented in order and taken from story mode.

I'd write more, but I have to get back to the frontier right now pilgrim.  Watch your top-knot and keep your powder dry.

Call of Juarez® Gunslinger is the 4th game of the series. Story-wise it has no connection with the other games, heck you won't even visit Juarez in this game, so I really don't know why they titled the game "Call of Juarez", it could seriously be just "Gunslinger" or something.
There is a new protagonist, Silas Greaves, and there are no other playable characters in the game. Silas is a bounty hunter, and he wants revenge against 3 bad guys who killed his brothers. So, he searches for them killing other legendary outlaws who are foolish enough to stand in his way. Or at least that's what his story is about. That's right, the whole game is a "story by Silas Greaves", which he retells in one of the bars. So each chapter is a flashback from his past, kinda. Such style of giving the story is a bit odd and it oddly impacts the gameplay, for example when Silas says that he was fighting apaches - you fight with apaches in the game, but then he says that they were not apaches, they were just bandits who ambushed him "apache-style" and poof! the apaches in the game magically transform into bandits and the level continues. Yeah, that's pretty funny, but actually I didn't like such things. Because the story is actually series of flashbacks, "in-game Silas", that you play during the levels never speaks for himself. We can only hear the Narrator-silas, who is telling the story. There are many cool bosses in the game, but they are kinda soulless, because Silas never communicates with them directly, we can only hear narrator-silas say something like "...and then I told him to surrender, but he didn't listen, so I had to shoot him." Well, the story is kinda poor if you ask me, yeah there will be an interesting twist in the end, but still. I just don't like this kind of narration. The protagonist is ok, but he is nowhere near Ray McCall (who was a total Badass). The bosses are cool and most of them (if not all) were real people. But in the game they are kinda soulless because most of them never speak and it makes me sad. Also, this special "dark" atmosphere of the first two CoJ games is gone here.
Now about the gameplay - well this is where the game shines. It is an excellent FPS shooter with lots of cool arcade elements. We have our classic slow-motion ability, which highlihts enemies, also there are different QTE moments which look pretty brutal, and there is a decent power-up/level-up system. You can spend your experience to upgrade your abilities of dual pistol wielding gunslinger, close combat shot gunner or long distance rifle using Ranger. Whatever fits your playstyle, amigo. There are very few weapons in the game, unfortunately, we have 3 types of pistols, 2 types of rifles (which are almost the same), and 2 types of shotfuns. Oh and we have dynamite.The levels are quite short, but I was still satisfied with the length of the game. Aside from the main story mode there are Arcade mode (where your objective is to clear the levels fast enough and to have a solid combo-series of kills to achieve a highest grade) and Duel-mode, where you will face all the bosses in a duel, so it's kind of a boss-rush duel mode I guess.
Soundtrack is decent and the graphics are good enough (although I miss seeing my lower body and legs when I look down. looks like Silas doesn't have 1st person model :( ).
VERDICT: "Gunslinger" is a decent western shooter and I definitely recommend it to any FPS or Western lover. But the story is not connected to the previous games of the series and this flashbacks-narration style is not to my liking. I haven't played CoJ: The Cartel yet, but I can definitely say, that the first two CoJ games captivated me more and I had a stronger impression after completing them. If you ask me, Bound in Blood is better than gunslinger in every possible way, although if you look at Gunslinger as a game of its own and not a Call of Juarez game, than it will be much better.

Tl;dr: Assassins are broken and this game was only designed to make money. Too much DLC, used to be more expensive and now I wasted some money. :(
Here's why: Let's look at the classes. Clearly, since this isn't meant to be Skyrim online and instead maybe Oblivion online with a dash of Skyrim in it, you select from a bunch of different classes which I don't really like myself. While this is an Elder Scrolls game where sneaking is very effective especially in Skyrim, I wouldn't say it is in this game. At all. I didn't mess with it much since I really didn't like it, but it seems more like the enemies detect you more the closer they are which makes no sense. I tried to shoot and arrow while sneaking once, and it forced me to stop sneaking which completely breaks the archer + assassin combo I'd always use in Skyrim. There's also the fact that this is an online game, meaning sneaking is never really an option which is why most games have their "assassins" just move fast and do damage. If you want to play as a mage, there's no spells (from my knowledge, I'm assuming they can possibly be acquired through skills) so you use staves, but I hear it's a good class. The others I'm unsure on, but they're all a bit weird and involve the constant use of skills with normal Skyrim attacks which adds more to combat, but also is just more repetitive attacks.
My other reason is money. I heard that this game used to require a subscription plus $60. Subscriptions on a game you buy for more than $20 is ridiculous. In my opinion, even paying $60 for this is ridiculous. No, it's not that it isn't really worth that much, it does have decent graphics and is fairly large, but that's $60 missing some races and barely even being able to get a horse or a pet (that does nothing but follow you). If you want a ride or pet it's extra and expensive for what it is, but that's normal for an mmo, right? No, not really since most others are free or much cheaper. If all this DLC contains a lot of content, then sure, maybe it isn't so bad, but I don't remember seeing Skyrim or Oblivion with Thieve's Guild DLC.

I have played many clickers from clicker heroes, sakura clicker, adventure capitalist, and crusaders of the lost isles. This clicker game was different because instead of clicking in the middle of the screen the entire time; this game allows you to move left and right from plot to plot. This makes improving your farm plots more engaging. It's also sort of an innovation in the clicking game genre. I review games for the genre they are in, and not for the negative reviews that say, "you just click things." That's what this genre is.
+ Innovative sidescrolling for the genre of clicking games
+ Cute graphics which would be good for any age group (unlike some of the ones mentioned above)
+ Achievements occur often and help keep you entertained
+ Music was fun
+ Trading cards
+ Balanced, a lot of clicking games are not balanced in terms of leveling/achievements and time played.
(instead of cons because it's a decent game in the genre)
- No menu / help, kinda have to figure stuff out on your own
- No clear way to see how much gold you make for what type of plant you farm (edit: I found it, blue ? mark icon next to the count, adds to the first point of no help menu)
- Zoom feature to see your whole garden
- Add more types of plants and animals, maybe different buffs as well.
- The way a lot of clicking games become successful is microtransactions. I know people hate them and especially if the game isn't free, but cosmetic changes could add flair into this game. If the cosmetic changes are going to be free, they could be based on level or purchase with gold.
- Another suggestion would be to add seasonal events. Maybe even seasonal vegetables or animals. This would keep players playing even after the game has been resting in the library a few weeks. You could also add seasonal cosmetic changes (see above).
- A way to see level up rewards. The reason this is important is players will have a reason to want to reach a higher level. Even adding in some cosmetic stuff.

Overall, this is a good game for the genre. I'm on the fence about the price of the game though, I usually treat clicker games as mobile game prices. So anything less than $2 is good. With some improvements, this game could become higher than a 6/10. The developer is very active on his/her game's discussion, which is nice.

I know it might not be the same thing as The Dark Descent, but...In its own way...This game has made a huge impression on me due to the symbolism and storyline involving the industrial era and perhaps even today. This is NOT a typical horror game involving jump scares. It's more about figuring out what is happening, what has happened and what will happen, as well as the meaning of it all. In the end, it is truly rewarding.
A lack of inventory system only added to the immersion because there was no extra pause screen to go to try to combine items / use oil or health, or even escape for a moment.
"The party that leans upon the workers but serves the bourgeoisie, in the period of the greatest sharpening of the class struggle, cannot but sense the smells wafted from the waiting grave."
— Leon Trotsky

This game is definately on par with the first game, with a few key differences to be noted before making a decision to purchase this game. Number one is game mechanics, get that out of the way before we go into more important stuff, there is no inventory so to speak, no sanity meter; there's not even really health as you regenerate automatically if you get hurt in any way form or manner. You no longer need oil or batteries or whatever to keep your lantern up, which can really remove alot of tension but sometimes in a horror game you just need tension, you can keep the lantern up the entire time you play the game basically after you find it. Now for the story.
The story of this game is on par with Amnesia on an almost equal scale, depending on weither you are more favorable towards revenge driven or family driven heroes, ithey're both fairly developed, Mandus is much more outspoken than Daniel ever was, which can be a good or bad thing depending on how much you would prefer to fill yourself into the character, he certainly has a personality that really shows itself over the course of the game. Machine for Pigs story is essentially more narrative driven than Amnesia.
Overall I recommend you get this game if you already played Amnesia the Dark Descent, if you haven't played an Amnesia game yet, I recommend The Dark Descent before getting this one as there's simply a few references in the second game that lead back to the first and the horror is alot more -darker- there than it is here.

This game is basically an interactive eBook. That being said, the game's story is pretty fantastic. It unfolds very well in front of you, just at the right pace. If you're looking for a horror game, this isn't really where you should be going with it. Try maybe the first amnesia, or the penumbra games. This game has barely any scares, it just has a constant unnerving feeling from the atmosphere itself. The setting just feels....wrong. The game is pretty short, clocks in at about 4 hours, give or take an hour depending on how long you decide to sit in front of it. It's definitely worth the money regardless.

Simply said: Put away the Amnesia from title and you have a game without complaints.

Atmosphere is not that scary as was in first game either, don't make me wrong, a few first Jump scares got me almost to change my pants but then it became kind of routine, common and expectable routine.
That leads me to kind of short gameplay time which the average player will finish in no more than 6 hours, I am not even sure if I can complain about it because after getting beyond later half of the game it gets a little boring and somehow uninteresting.
The game itself is rather average experience with nothing new to show us compared to previous Amnesia but still worth your time. Try it, then judge it. There is way too much of undeserved hate towards this game on Internets.

(I'll try to keep this spoiler-free) Kind of sad that I finished this game on the very day that it was released. Not a whole lot of hours of gameplay, but it was a few hours of VERY high quality, stylized, atmospheric, and memorable gaming however. I don't like that they don't have an inventory anymore, no health or sanity meter. The lantern mechanic has certainly changed. I also don't think the opposing force of the game is as good as in Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
In my opinion (Yours may very well differ), 'A Machine for Pigs' is better than 'The Dark Descent' in some respects, but in most ways, I prefer the first in the series. I DON'T think this one will catch on as well as the first did (though I've been wrong before, we'll see), however I most certainly recommend it to those who enjoyed the first one! Like I said, it's very memorable, touches on some historical facts of the time, as well as insight into 'future' events, and WILL make you think on occasion. I'm glad I played it, and might possibly play it again some time later on.
Had a few good scary and suspenseful parts in it, and hopefully some talented modders will perform some similar magic for this platform as they have for the last one. As is the game has a GREAT feel/atmosphere to it, I don't think that can be improved upon, however as far as scariness goes I believe we can expect some improvements by the upcoming fanbase. People smarter than I who would know how to create mods and really make people quiver. Come on, give Storpy, Pewds, Markiplier, and the rest of the popular youtube gamers something to scream about ;)
I hope you found this recommendation (and kind of review?) informative! Happy gaming!

Transistor simply dominates. Its addictive and juicy gameplay, soundtrack, and art made my jaw literally drop within the first 20 minutes of playing. The strategic action of the game is completely original and fully-realized, which left me star-struck at the brilliance of the entire package. On a minor hindrance, while the story itself is simple yet satisfying, Transistor could have benefited from a more complete "3 Act" story. It felt like there was a few missed opportunites here and there, but nonetheless, every part of the game was fun and thoughtful. If you haven't played Transistor, buy this masterpiece right now. [9.5/10]

Although Transistor has been reviewed and praised countless times before me, it goes without saying that this game is a glistening gem amiss a sea of franchise sequels whose sheen can be compared to that of rust and decay. But in order to really review this game properly, we would have to start off by comparing this game to supergiants first, and only other shining success of 2; Bastion.
Like Bastion, Transistor's story begins in tragedy, with your main protagonist Red having to run from a group known only as the Camerata, who as far as you know have just failed to assasinate you. Why, you do not know, but in foolishly doing so have given you a powerful weapon known only as the transistor; A sword, posessed by a voice acting as your only aid that holds the key to stopping a mass outbreak of creatures known as the process, who do nothing but kill and assimilate anything and anyone who is unfortunate enough to step in their path.
Overall the story is very, very immersive, and will keep you engaged until it's finale, where my only gripe with this game resides. In comparison to Bastion, Transistors climax is done quite well, but then it just ends in a very somber note with not much rhyme or reason, which in turn makes it a good, but inferior ending to that of it's predecessor. If you are like me who has played Bastion before Transistor, don't be too surprised if Transistors ending feels lackluster in comparison. Despite that though, it's story is still very much worth playing through, if not only once if you are a completionist like me (played 20 hours total, and unlocked all 33 acheivements). If you have not played Bastion before this game, then you will definately get to enjoy the fullness of the games narrative with unbiased eyes, which is probably the best way to play this game.
I definately recommend playing this game at least once through, regardless if you have played Bastion before this or not; it is definately worth every minute of your time.
If you Bastion you'll love this game.

From the makers of Bastion comes another excellent and original title for gamers to enjoy. Transistor has a lot of class and charm on its own, let alone for people who were fans of Bastion.
Taking a few similar mechanics such as the narrator, isometric realtime battle system, and customizable weapons, Transistor ups the ante by adding new twists to the genre such as tactial mode (which pauses the action so you can plan out a few moves in a chain before starting the battle again), and the higher complexity of weapon customization and the idea of weapons becoming unusable for a few battles in exchange for another health bar. All of these changes work well together to provide a fast pace action game.
The narrative introduces you to a strange futuristic world filled with politics and intrigue. After completing the game however I was craving more. The light between the cracks of the mystery is never fully revealed, which is both a positive and a negative for me.
The game took me about 10 hours to complete for the first playthrough, but not everything is accessible during the first run. A new game + mode is provided to allow you to fully unlock Red's abilities and side missions. I will be returning to this game for a second run when I get the opportunity.

Ah, nostalgia. "Alien" was my first R-rated movie.
And this game captures the essence of Ridley Scott's sophomore masterpiece 100%. I mean it's basically a love letter. The set design, the lighting, the agonizingly slow 1970s mechanics, a bunch of freaked-out people with an us vs. them mentality, rogue robots, a mendacious self-serving corporation... oh, and one indestructible xenomorph, and the BAFTA-winning sound design.
This is another one of those games where I died numerous times from suddenly standing there with my jaw on the floor (a Working Joe on fire, walking, with apparently accurate fire dynamics)! My only complaint is what I perceived as a
difficulty spike about halfway through the game (the medical bay, for those who've played it). I mean, the game is challenging anyway. If you're looking for "run, shoot the alien with some amped-up neutron gun, ha-ha!" then this game is
not for you. This is stealth-survival-horror the Ridley Scott way. Soak it up, enjoy, and remember: it's only a game.

It's a beautiful game, and I'd say the combat is more interesting than in Bastion. In fact, I'd say it's superior to Bastion in all ways but one--it didn't suceed as well at getting me to care. The way Bastion played, and particularly the clever way they wove narrative and gameplay together, really did well at slowly making you care about the world and the characters. With Transistor... I never felt that. I'm not sure I can put a finger on why. Maybe it's because the world is falling apart around you so you have no time to learn how it *used* to be.
Regardless, if you enjoyed Bastion, you'll enjoy Transistor. If you haven't played Bastion... play it first.

What more can I say about this highly praised game that hasn't been said around before...?
It's good. It's great. Yes, it has some flaws and glitches (which game doesn't?), but it already is one of my most favourite games ever!
However, it's not really a game I would consider as "seriously challenging."
I finished the campaign on Nightmare difficulty just yesterday and while it can be a good challenge for an "average action-arcade player", I personally wouldn't really call it a "Nightmare" difficulty. There are some parts which are tricky, but if you're an experienced stealth and survival horror genre fan, you're never really stuck in progress and after some change of approach and tactics, while sticking to some basic survival guidelines, you can do it without any serious difficulties and almost always outsmart the adaptable Alien AI in some way.
The crafting resources are abundant even on Nightmare difficulty towards the end (if you manage them rationally). And even though the adverts mention the Alien is not giving you any "second chances" on Nightmare, I think his senses weren't as sharp in some situations as I would expect them to be from an ultimate predator, a "perfect organism"
In fact, I would change the vanilla Normal difficulty to "Easy", the vanilla Hard difficulty to "Normal" and the vanilla "Nightmare" should be Hard. And there should be another ultimate difficulty called Nightmare... for example only with autosaves and no manual save points. You die once - that's it. That would be some serious and satisfying accomplishment!
However I must also say that the difficulty appears to be quite higher in the DLCs, which are mostly smaller areas and the Alien only rarely gives you some space to take a breath, by retreating to the airducts. And you can't save in Survivor mode.
Anyway, despite my nitpicking, I think this is a worthy, if not even essential game for every serious survival horror gamer.

You can play through the campaign, where the game holds your hand and guides you through the steps of making things and producing materials. You'll be done with the campaign and you'll be wondering what to do.
You open up a new game. The game tells you that your goal is to build a rocket. You're given 8 iron plates, 1 burner mining drill and 1 stone furnace. That's it. There's no more help coming. You're on your own.
You use your hard earned knowledge from the campaign to mine stuff, and make more stuff to help build stuff, which then can help automate mining and building stuff a bit more. Then come the aliens, who hate you for polluting their planet. As aliens usually go, they just want to murder you. You'll learn to be a big boy and deal with it and kill them back. You'll be doing a massive amount of work by hand, until you use your brain and figure out a way to automate it. Then you move on to bigger things, and you try to automate them. It just goes on and on and on until you are knowledgeable enough to hate what you've built. That's when you scrap everything and just restart.
The cycle continues, a few restarts later you're good enough at the game to realize how you can scale production up, make a factory that won't jam up and will product end products smoothly. You'll probably launch a rocket sooner or later when you're well into your 100+ hrs of playtime. And then it suddenly hits you, the goal was not making a rocket all along. It was just a glimpse of how big things can get in this game. You keep playing and launching more rockets and making your base bigger. You'll try out some well made and amazing mods that are community made, some of which will drastically change the gameplay, add amazing content or have very good quality of life additions.
All the while, the game keeps you happy. You'll have a great feeling about spending that 20$ for this game, because it has given you so much entertainment and fun already, and will do so for hours upon hours to come.
This game is a classic, absolutely amazing and engaging, and a must have for anyone who is interested in building things, solving problems and playing in a sandbox environment.

You check passports and identification to make sure people can or can not enter the country, your goal; make
money to keep your family alive. This is coming from someone that hadn't obtained the game until AFTER the One Tamriel update and Morrowind release.
That being said after delving over a hundred hours in to this product, I will say that it is a completely different experience than what was reviewed at release. With the update via Thief DLC adding theft and the justice system. To One Tamriel itself allowing you to go to the other lands not integrated with your original alliance questing. To the other DLC such as Dark Brotherhood or the Solo Dungeon DLC's.
If you get Tamriel Unlimited Gold Edition, I personally believe if you were a Skyrim fan you would enjoy this 1000x over in comparison to the original release. If you are a veteran MMO player, you may have some gripes in comparison to the original version of ESO.
If you are looking for long spoken dialogue voice acted, and are here for the Elder Scrolls experience. I can say personally, they have achieved that. Add it with years of creating content and you have a HUGE world to delve in to.
If you are a veteran MMO player looking for level specific zones, and to feel more progressed as you play. That is where the new wall has been created.
ESO has became similar to Guild Wars 2 where the questing itself takes over the progression of questing. They did this to achieve the more "single player Skyrim" feel.
For me, someone that does care about MMO aspects. The missing Auction House aside. It does create a new MMO styled experience that in my opinion is what we will see in the next generation of MMO's much more often. It allows you to do quests at your own pace and you will never have to worry about grinding.
As a Vet MMO player, them removing grinding to me is a god send. I didn't realize how much I hated grinding, until attempting to return to LOTRO after playing this. It becomes almost game breaking irritating after you have become accustomed to the newer experience.
The actual story of the quests, maybe since they are fully voice acted, also seems to be next level over Guild Wars II. I found myself following the story easier, and feeling the impact of twists that are attempted much more than some of the main character deaths in GWII.
For point of reference, I am using GWII due to me having a level 80 in every class. It is my most modern MMO experience aside ESO. So do not take my comments as a insult to GWII, I love GWII. Single Player wise, it just does not hold up to par to Elder Scrolls Online.
I played the PvP experience of ESO, and that is one place it is lacking in comparison to GWII. But instead of it making the veteran MMO players angry, it will make you happy to know that the levels you earned, gear, and so on actually matter a great deal in the ESO PvP.
GWII, became a system that relies on various buffs/debuffs each update to balance PvP across the board.
You will eventually as I am sure ESO end game has to, will have certain advatanges and disadvantages to abuse. the upsidre with GWII however, it is patched often, as well scales the equipment, level, and so on. That way even a level 2, can have a chance at a fully capped char in PvP if the character was built properly.
For PvP it is a matter of preference. I prefer the scaling and changing in GWII in comparison to the MMO heavy version of PvP ESO currently has. There are people however I am sure, with capped ESO characters that feel changing the system demeans their earnings. Which, that is literally correct. I just believe because of that, it isn't top tier as GWII in PvP balance/entertainment.
All that being said, Elder Scrolls Online has become the one MMO I just can't seem to put down. The free range experience a Elder Scrolls brings you with live teamwork on dungeons, and integrated lore you have become a fan of prior to this release places it in my opinion on a new plane/tier.
Other established Single Player games attempting to create a system should take notes on ESO 2017.
If they do, the MMO genre has the brightest future I have seen since the release of WoW after the death of Everquest~.

Pleasantly surprised by CoJ Gunslinger, it being the first game of the series I've played. It's a no-nonsense, single-player arcade gallery shooter that deserves more praise and attention.
Pros:
- It's a Wild West game. Why can't we have more Wild West games?
- Cel-shaded art style looks great (think Borderlands 2 but a little more realistic).
-While levels are mostly linear, the environments are all standouts (the vistas in particular are quite stunning). You get to play through classic scenes from Westerns like moving trains, underground mines, mountain passes and ghost towns.
- Strong story told through first-person flashback narrative. This unique style intertwines fantastically with gameplay. New objects or enemies often appear out of thin air as the protagonist Silas narrates the scene. You might play a section of a mission, only to have to play it again because Silas didn't quite tell his story correctly the first time.
- Solid voice acting throughout help sell the narrative.
- Bullet-time mechanics are nothing new, but they actually work really well for a Wild West shooter.
- Devs didn't feel the need to tack on a watered-down multiplayer mode.
Cons:
- Skill trees and gun types aren't balanced. I went with the shotgun/dynamite tree and it became immediately apparent that close-quarters combat is weak. It doesn't make things overly frustrating or difficult -- and you can eventually unlock all the skills thanks to a new game plus mode -- but I still feel it's worth noting.
- Characters can get stuck in the environment from time to time.
- Enemies are just sitting ducks for the most part. A few run at you aggressively but their behavior could have been more dynamic.
- The duel system didn't really do it for me. It gets easier the more you do it, but I just didn't find the focus/speed system that compelling.
Final thoughts:
CoJ is definitely worth the buy. Great bang for your buck (pun totally intended) -- it can be had for under $5 on sale.

One of the few first person shooters where I would say that the story and it's presentation far outstrip the gameplay, which is a significant achievement when you consider just how tight it is. The actual story itself is not complicated or morally challenging, but the use of an unreliable narrator combined with how the game itself reacts to when he backtracks to redescribe certain details is both amusing and engrossing. It cannot be overstated just how enjoyable the game is for it's presentation alone.
While the gameplay does not push boundaries it is dependable and will prove both challenging and fun. Essentially there are three gameplay types based both on guns and the skills associated with them: shotguns, pistols and rifles. Skills are attained through scoring points which you obtain by killing enemies: pulling off headshots, performing multiple kills in a row, long distance shots, on the run kills will all net you bonuses which are coupled with your combo meter. Additionally you have access to a concentration meter (aka bullet time) and also a cheat death meter allowing you to dodge a life-threatening bullet. This arcade style action is not revolutionary but is incredibly fun.
The story mode also contains duels which are a point of contention for many players. Thematically they almost seem necessary but mechanically they can be a bit of a nightmare, especially if you intend on winning your duels honourably. You have a focus and arm speed percentage which you want as high as possible before you draw but even with high numbers it can end up being a gamble as to whether you get a decent shot off first. The duels later in the game can be quite infuriating as the target moves around or simply draws with very little delay or room for error.
Just a fantastic game from start to finish, with a new game plus mode to offer even more details to the mysterious story. Personal gripes lie with the last level being obnoxious as you're assaulted on all sides, the rifle build/path not being the best and losing save data related to the alternate modes. Otherwise I cannot recommend this game enough, on sale or not.

Here's what you should do if you want a horror game: Go get Outlast. Here's what you should do if you want a TRUE sequel to Amnesia: Go download the mod The Great Work. That mod is more scary and actually relates to the Amnesia mythos. In The Great Work, there's the Orb, the Shadow, and sanity! In this "sequel" there is NONE of that!
I hate kids. Except for Clementine from The Walking Dead because she was WRITTEN well. A game can't MAKE me relate or be sorrowful to any character without ANY ♥♥♥♥ing background. Not only that: the two kids were so poorly designed and in my face EVERY goddamn second that I knew not to care. What am I going on about? The main character has two twin sons who are CLEARLY already dead after 5 minutes of gameplay. (That wasn't a spoiler if you have half a brain.) And we're supposed to feel sorry for Mandus? ♥♥♥♥ that! I knew Dear Esther and Korsakovia were thinking games when it came to a plot, but you don't ♥♥♥♥ing do it half and half! You either go all the way like in those previous experiments or just a little like in Silent Hill 2 or Spec Ops: The Line!
For it's credit, it has great sound design and there's two moments where I felt all "EEEEK!" but those were at the end. Nothing scared me in the least. You're likely reading this review wondering whether you should get this game or not. Sadly I probably cannot answer that question but I can give you my opinion about the game. If you're interested in that then read on.
As with all sequels there are always two kinds of potential buyers: those who played the original and those who didn't. Chances are that whether you're new to this or not you've already heard, read or seen something about DS2. One thing the Souls-series shares is a very passionate community and they are very vocal about the games. I personally see this as a positive sign; it means people care deeply about these games.
Unfortunately for DS2 a lot of negativity takes center stage. This personally strikes me as being somewhat unfair and it's easy to dismiss the game outright because of the naysayers. However what often seems to happen is that many people pass off what is essentially just their opinion as if it is a solid fact. I wouldn't say you should dismiss those people - instead try and read between the lines; perhaps what they consider a bad thing is something you'd like or don't really mind that much. One very interesting thing to keep in mind though: it seems that the majority of the people who greatly dislike DS2 are people who played DS1. Perhaps it is a question of perspective then? I personally know many people who started with DS2 and later played DS1 who greatly dislike DS1. I also know people who played DS1 and later DS2 who prefer the sequel. Personally I still play both games and love them - each for different reasons.
FOR THOSE OF YOU WHO NEVER PLAYED THE ORIGINAL:
I'd actually urge you to read any of the reviews of the first game first to get an idea what these games are generally like. The main reason I suggest this is that DS2 doesn't deviate much from DS1 in terms of general gameplay. But of course you might be here because you are wondering whether you should start with DS2 instead of DS1? Or perhaps you've already decided to completely skip DS1 completely? Both those things are completely fair points.
Let me start out by saying that I believe DS2 is actually harder in the beginning for new players. You're given less Estus flask uses (healing) than DS1 and you loose a fraction of your max health each time you die (down to 50% max health). On top of that DS2 likes to throw more enemies at you at once compared to DS1. All these things combined can easily make for a frustating start for a completely new player - each death compounds your difficulty and the means to restore your lost health are limited at first.
It also depends on why you might be interested in playing a Souls game. If you are really interested in the lore/story I'd absolutely recommend you check out DS1 first. Although knowledge of DS1's story is not really needed to appreciate DS2's story it naturally builds on DS1's lore because it's a sequel to it. And a word of warning: the Souls games are known for their obscurity. Few things are explained to you - most of the story has to be pieced together by yourself. And even then not everything is ever completely clear. Keep that in mind.
If you're here for the gameplay (and by extension PvP) I'd probably recommend DS2. From a mechanical point of view DS2 is more solid with regards to its controls and systems. I can't comment on the balance of PvP (and that's always a great debate) since I personally don't take part in it but this is the general vibe I get from the community.
FOR THOSE WHO PLAYED DARK SOULS 1:
I find it really difficult what to tell you. Not that I find DS2 hard to recommend - I'd say chances are good that if you liked DS1 you'll like DS2. And if you didn't like it DS2 might not be different enough to win you over. But as with so many things in life it depends entirely on your expectations.
If you essentially expect DS2 to be exactly like DS1 in a new package you'll probably be disappointed. Mechanically I'd say most changes are for the better although the introduction of weapon durability and how it is handled on PC is a matter of great debate. The upgrade system has been changed and requires less titanite but is harder to come by early if you need extra, as you can't immediately buy unlimited amounts. Infusions (elemental damage upgrades) has been expanded to include things such as bleed and poison effects.
World wise Dark Souls 1 was a smaller, more compact experience with areas that connected with each other, cleverly looping around with shortcuts you could open along the way. Dark Souls 2 in comparison is bigger; more open and sprawling, spanning a larger area and losing some of the interconnectivity from the first game. One major change, probably due to being the world being larger, is the ability to warp between bonfires from the very beginning of the game.
For as far as difficulty goes: that's a tough one to talk about. If you're a DS1 veteran who could dodge-roll his way easily through the entire game with an SL1 character then perhaps it might not be that difficult for you. Whether that's the fault of the game or the fact that players (you) is now familiar and experienced with the system is probably open for debate. Where DS1 often had singular enemies (or pairs) DS2 often has you fighting groups at a time. The same concept extends to bosses where a fair share of encounters has you fighting 2 or even 3 enemies at once.
Whether any of this appeals to you as an experienced Souls-player is entirely a question of taste. As I have tried to emphasize: these things are often a question of perspective and expectations.
There are things I greatly dislike about DS2 compared to DS1 but there are also plenty of things I think DS2 did better. But as I already said: I love both games and enjoy them for what they both did right - not for what one game lacks compared to the other. You might disagree of course and that's completely fair.

I played Heroes of the Storm pretty intensely, and then League of Legends, before finally settling on Smite. When I first played smite I found it sort of plain and uninteresting. The third person combat didn't quite do anything for me. But once I dived into conquest I found myself enjoying the game more and more. It's in a decent state balance wise. God design is sometimes uninspired but I haven't found a single god that isn't enjoyable to play yet, and I have mastered 45 of the 84 or so gods.
Cosmetics in this game are beautiful, but pricey. Unlocking characters can be done rather easily without paying. I never pay and have unlocked half of the gods in the game, at a rate of one new character every week or two.
The community can be fairly toxic. People say that league is bad but I have had much worse experiences with Smite casual games, as far as toxicity goes. The report system tells you when an action is taken against a player, but what exactly that action is, who knows. I don't think it's anything more than a slap on the wrist, unfortunately.
There is a lot of variation in casual game modes, ranging from arena brawling to a siege mode, to the 5v5 standard moba gameplay, and two more modes, plus a special mode of the day every day. Ranked has a duel mode, (rather poor since the game is not balanced with duel in mind, but small improvements like more bans and some map changes would fix most of the issues.) 3v3 joust, and standard 5v5 conquest. These modes all have a ban phase.
Overall Smite falls a little short of league of legends in complexity (less diverse items/builds for example), but it makes up for this with the mechanical skill you bring to the third person aiming. There are still mechanics like autoattack cancelling/ability cancelling, relics/actives, kiting, freezing lanes (although this is rather different in Smite and generally less useful). Don't let this bit on smites complexity be your takeaway, it is certainly not as simple as heroes of the storm, for example.
Edit: The complexity of this game is about to be ramped up rather considerably with new season 4 relics, items, god changes, and new characters. I would say rather confidently that the game is at league complexity in everything except for god kit design, which is getting there. (all without detracting from the experience of casual non-conquest players.)

I have over 200+ hours logged on RoK now, and I feel like it's safe to write how I've felt about the game so far.
First things first, if you are having a huge issue with the "Asian Hackers" go to a private, no-KOS server and stop complaining.
ROK is incredibly fun, plain and simple. It is a mix of Minecraft, Chivalry, and the gametype king of the hill. You will spend a lot of your early days learning how to gather resources, and fight. But once you get those two mechanics down it becomes much easier to play this game. You will almost certainly become frusturated with how the game plays at first, with how long it takes to gather materials to build structures, and how bad you are at fighting (unless you've played many hours of Chivalry, then you'll be fine.) But give the game time and it will all get easier.
Once you find a group of people to play with, the game get's even better, as the community is a huge part of this game. I would argue that playing ROK of your own is neither for nor plausable due to how often other players will try to raid you.
ROK is early-access, but they regularly update with new features and engage the community with what direction they are moving with updates. Code Hatch is doing an exceptional job with this game.

The Xenomorph!
400 kilos of interstellar apex predator.
This creature starts it's life as a parasite, a facefugger! Once attached to the face of a host, an embryo is implanted into the chest of the victim. Here, one of Nature's rarest phenomena takes place: Horizontal Gene Transfer! Traits of the host are inherited by the Xenomorph, allowing it to adapt to any environment it may be born into.
The embryo gestates for 12-16 hours, and is birthed in spectacularly gory fashion, killing its host and terrifying all others that may be nearby at the time. It is thought this horrifying life cycle has two evolxutionary advantages: A source of food if birthed within the safety of the nest, and scaring away potential threats if born in new environments.
AFter birth, Xenomorphs quicky grow to full size, and they're instantly recognizable with their elongated heads, retractable jaws, and unparalled strength and speed.
There's a Xenomorph on Sevastapol Station, and he's a bad mother! He's already killed dozens of people, and he's still hungry. With every passing minute, he grows smarter and more keen to his surroundings.
I'm gonna sneak into it's lair, and pick a fight with him!

Bastion 2: Electric Boogaloo is a fantastic game, and a more apt name than it should be. That said, while the game has many key similarities to Bastion (art style, certain plot points, music, the same narrator), it also has many key differences, even some more subtle ones in those similarities I mentioned. Most obvious is that it's sci-fi rather than fantasy, the story as a whole is bit more subtle and atmospheric, and the battle system is... turn-based...???
Regardless, it's a ton of fun, the music and art are just as good if not better than the amazing precedent Bastion set, giving us a lot more vocals of the singer behind Build That Wall from Bastion (there's even a hum button this time around! it is the most important button, you can literally have your character hum to the music at pretty much any time), and having a more tech-heavy-feel to it in general.
Point is, it's a fantastic game, buy it 500 times.

Plantera is a fun and colorful clicker game that's different and more interactive than say....Clicker Heroes or AdVenture Capitalist. In the beginning you don't get a lot to work with, you can grow carrots and plant some apple trees and blueberry bushes. As you go along you can unlock more fruits & veggies to plant as you level up. There are also specials you can buy like guard dogs to chase away critters, a clock that lets you earn money for a set time while being offline (although it's more profitable to leave the game running) and a multiplier which increases the worth of everything. Later on you can also expand your property so you can plant more things. It's very simple and there's not much to it yet I found it addictive. I hope the dev has plans to add more in the future.

Gunslinger is a fun, funny, creative and consistently entertaining romp through one old-west shootout after another. While the overarching plot is predictable, it feels like the game is aware of this, and the storytelling is more tongue-in-cheek than serious as a result. The way the objectives and level design change depending on how the story is being told by the game's narrators is creative and engaging. I highly recommend Gunslinger to anyone looking for a fun, but brief reminder that the Western genre is still alive and kicking.

Ok to all the reviewers who have complained that this game is not free to play - please fully read the game description ... which states "Two huntable species (Mule Deer, Cottontail Rabbit, European Rabbit), a weapon (.243 Bolt-Action Rifle) and a bunch of additional equipment are available for free when first entering the game. Additional items such as weapons, species licenses and ammo can be acquired with gm$, the in-game currency that can be earned through play, or em$, the in-game currency that can be earned through winning competitions or purchase for real money. "  No game is ever truly "free to play", the company must somehow recompense the capital they have put into developing and/ or running a game - usually there are shops where you can buy premium goods for real money and/ or a subscription model that allows more full access to features - theHunter is no different!
For free you can hunt mule deer all day long on one reserve ... yes, there are other animals on this reserve which you are unable to hunt without a license however, if you complete the mule deer missions you will quickly start earning gm$ (the in-game currency) with which you can buy licenses for the other animals ... my advise would be if you want to play this game for free then focus on mule deer missions earn some gm$, then buy licenses for 1 species at a time & do as many missions for those as possible.
If however, you can afford to subscribe (which is actually very reasonable), you will be free to hunt whatever you wish as long as you are able to hunt the species with the weapon you have!  I and a number of friends have played many, many hours on this game & we continue to love it!
For me personally I would give the game 9/10 - it is something that I initially downloaded to troll a friend who played, and upon playing I totally fell in love with it & now have a higher Hunter score :P

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, I wouldn't say it's a very good Amnesia game.
If you are expecting Amnesia or Penumbra, Stop. This is not the same type of game.
This is more or less a lot like Dear Eshter, a mod made into game, that is simply you walking around listening to stories by the narrator.
In Amnesia AMFP's case, you are doing very little puzzles and mainly just walking around as things happen, there is really no point in searching for any items, because there are NONE to gather! You are directed to every single object required to finish a puzzle and you don't do much aside from walking around, turn on a valve or two or pull some levers, then walk some more, often the narrative takes control from you, for the sake of telling you the story.
Cons:
- Lack of inventory, there are no items to combine for a puzzle or things to conserve.
- Lack of sanity meter, you don't have to worry about anything.
- Most of the environments were dull and you can't interact with it, 80-90% of the time like in Amnesia and Penumbra. They look good though, but thats about it.
- The flashlight you find is endless, it requires no fuel or battery.
- Exploring in it is kind of pointless since all you are looking for are notes, and if there are puzzles, you mostly find stuff immediately, there is nothing cleverly hidden.
Pros:
- The Score is pretty good.
- Most of the areas had nice-good atmosphere.
- It had very good concepts for the most part.
I would say more about the story and monster, but this remains spoiler free.
Overall, I rate this game 5/10, it's not really a survival horror game, it's just a walking horror tale.

If your looking for a game with a great story to keep you going, then this one should keep you fairly interested for the most part; it has a pretty good start up and keeps you curious on whats going to happen next, so I do recommend giving it a shot if your a story player.

If I had to write down two flaws, one would be that the game feels a bit more grindy as you progress further down the line; but it's not entirely neccesary as you are actually completely capable of taking the enemies that are 10 or 15 levels higher than you, at the expense of being more difficult, obviously.
Secondly, the game has little to no customization for free to play players, all of it's pay for customization of your character; which even that isn't open up yet as they have yet to implement the token functionality yet for free to play.
Other than that, if you got a few free hours everyday, give it a shot, it's F2P now, so, you've really got nothing to lose.

I can not in full faith recommend this game to anyone. The game has some huge fundamental problems.
The game features several different controls depending on how you want to play. It's great that they offer the ability to change on the fly at any point. However, it does come with the problem of things like keyboard prompts appearing while playing with a controller.
The gameplay itself is rather bland. It's slightly more active than a typical M-M-O game, but still lacking. The addition of awful server lag every time I played didn't help in this regard. It always felt like too many people were in a channel even if it displayed the capacity as being on the lower end. Sometimes you would also get thrown into the high capacity ones for seemingly no reason.
Towns have plenty of silver spammers already. The speech bubbles that appear with their world chat spam will cover the UI / menus and be incredibly fustrating to deal with on the first encounter. Thankfully you can turn these global chat bubbles off and save yourself some pain. HOWEVER, the worst part is that the bubbles will actually LAG your game, and what does disabling them do? Only hides them. YOU WILL STILL LAG. I kid you not.
Tree of Savior quickly runs out of quests for it's newbies. Around LVL 30 you'll hit a wall of a lack of quest lines in the starting area of your choice. Now you can go to the other starting area and progress through that one as well, but variety is pretty much non-existant as far as I could tell.
The class system is where the meat of the game is. Plenty of options to choose and pick from.
The game is free though and worth taking a look if you have the data to spare. Honestly to me it's just another MMORPG to throw in the bucket. I'd recommend Path of Exile if you want deep and complex character builds with RPG elements. It's free to play as well.

Engineers rejoice. Learn Technology, Automation and Efficiency in one easy to learn package. No? Seriously. this is a hard game to put down.
Let's take a typical late game scenario.
Assembler #28, manufacturing Advanced Electronics (let's call it a PCB) has a bottleneck and it's dragging down the entire electronic circuit assembly line.
I took a look at the insertor (a small robotic feeder arm) sitting idle as copper coils were swallowed up by the identical assemblers before it reached #28. Obviously I need to increase copper coil production.
Soo... I took a look at the copper coil assemblers, already sporting a Tech III speed beacon and Tech III efficiency modules and noticed that the copper plate was in short supply.
Sooo... I took a look at the copper ore smelting furnaces, also sporting (hard earned) Tech III modules and noticed the selectors feeding those were too slow and were skipping every second ore.
Sooo... I upgraded the selectors to fast selectors and solved the problem.
Or did I?
10 minutes later, Assembler #28 is doing it again. I repeat the above mitigation steps and notice the increase in insertor efficiency at the furnaces is depleting the ore feeder line. I have to increase ore production at the mining drills. Obvious right?
Sooo... my first thought is to add Tech modules to increase speed but... because the PCB production line is effectively in stasis I can't make more modules just yet so I have to do it the more obvious way. Add a new mining drill. Right?
Sooo... I went to get some iron plate BUT... there is none free because it's also being used on the PCB production line. I ran down the conveyor belt, scooping up iron plate, made my mining drill, ran down to the ore fields, installed a power line, placed the drill and.... lost power.
Sooo.... While I started to manufacture more panels and accumulators to add more power... the aliens came and with no power on my defenses, it took a superhuman effort to eradicate them using my flamethrower and Power Armor (Mk II of course). My personal construction bots all the while repairing what I damaged with my aggressive flame attack.
Meanwhile.... Because I had stolen the iron plate off the PCB production line the copper coil problem was sorted... at least... temporarily.
Then my sulfuric acid production stopped, which makes my batteries which is used to make my logistic bots that supply the whole higher end production chain... including my research.... because I ran out of..... iron plates.
I'll have to redesign the whole damn thing. Tomorrow.
Or maybe I can just do this little bit now...
..oo00oo..

You can play through the campaign, where the game holds your hand and guides you through the steps of making things and producing materials. You'll be done with the campaign and you'll be wondering what to do.
You open up a new game. The game tells you that your goal is to build a rocket. You're given 8 iron plates, 1 burner mining drill and 1 stone furnace. That's it. There's no more help coming. You're on your own.
You use your hard earned knowledge from the campaign to mine stuff, and make more stuff to help build stuff, which then can help automate mining and building stuff a bit more. Then come the aliens, who hate you for polluting their planet. As aliens usually go, they just want to murder you. You'll learn to be a big boy and deal with it and kill them back. You'll be doing a massive amount of work by hand, until you use your brain and figure out a way to automate it. Then you move on to bigger things, and you try to automate them. It just goes on and on and on until you are knowledgeable enough to hate what you've built. That's when you scrap everything and just restart.
The cycle continues, a few restarts later you're good enough at the game to realize how you can scale production up, make a factory that won't jam up and will product end products smoothly. You'll probably launch a rocket sooner or later when you're well into your 100+ hrs of playtime. And then it suddenly hits you, the goal was not making a rocket all along. It was just a glimpse of how big things can get in this game. You keep playing and launching more rockets and making your base bigger. You'll try out some well made and amazing mods that are community made, some of which will drastically change the gameplay, add amazing content or have very good quality of life additions.
All the while, the game keeps you happy. You'll have a great feeling about spending that 20$ for this game, because it has given you so much entertainment and fun already, and will do so for hours upon hours to come.

8/10 - Transistor is the first title released by the studio Supergiant Games since their excellent piece of work - Bastion, and just like Bastion; this game has plenty of charm.
Lovely visuals, satisfying music and wonderful voice acting (particularly from Logan Cunningham, the man who played the Stranger in Supergiants' previous game, coming back for another smooth performance) are all to be expected here.
The playtime is about 10 hours. For better or for worse, the story is kept vague throughout. Also - for better or worse - the combat system allows you to stop time in order to plan out attacks. This helps plot out attack patterns and devise strategies accordingly - but on the other hand it can make the combat feel disjointed occansionally.
Overall the game is lovely, endearing and tugs on a few emotional heartstrings. Also the game has a hum button! You have to love a game with a hum button!

This game is both really fun and very beautiful. Mix that with with an entrancing sound track and a setting and plot that unravels as you progress, and you have gold.
Most of the fun is running around mixing different functions to develop your own combat styles in both turns and real time. Despite being a work of art, they did not slack on the gameplay. Between the various combat options and limiters (which ramps the difficulty for bonus experience) you can find a playstyle that is right for you. It manages a balanced difficulty that remains challenging but never overwheling. Whenever you drop to zero health, a function (one of your combat abilities) becomes disabled for a few fights, but you can still fight until you are out of all your active functions and just set up another at the next access point (save points). There are back doors that you can access where you can run through tests, and eventually do practice rounds.
The game's visuals are stylized and I personally like it. It may not appeal to everyone, but art is subjective. The graphics, the music, the setting, and even the gameplay all come together as one cohesive piece of work that tells an amazing but tragic story. It's good enough to play through a second time. It's just a fun experience. Oh and the music... I love it so much that I sometimes play just to listen to the music. It's ambient and yet resonating. It draws you in, and it's great to have Red hum to the background [The game says she lost her voice, but it seems it's more like her words or tongue that she lost].
Great gameplay and design are accompanied here by a smooth pacing. Letting you learn and revealing more and more at a moderate pace, not so fast that you're overwhelmed but never so slow that you're grinding. In fact, you can't really grind; while not a terrible thing on its own brings me to the game's one downside.
The closest thing you can do is the tests and practice battles. You can do the practice battles all you want, but you have no control over which enemies you fight. The tests are fun, but those are a one time deal which is a real bummer since some of them are a lot of fun. I guess you have the option to start over the entire save file, but then you lose out on all the functions you played through to get. Essentially you are locked into the game's pace whether you want to or not. This is not an RPG, you don't grind or explore. It's a story with really fun tactical combats.
It's an astonishing game, and while not long, it is definitely worth the money. Buy it if you're looking for an immersive story with exciting combat, just don't expect a RPG with sidequests or branching storylines.

Plantera is love, Plantera is life

So a few weeks ago i received a code for a game called Plantera on Steam. It's your usual clicker game in which you have to constantly click the mouse buttons until you get carpal tunnel and your pointer finger is crooked for the rest of your life. But Plantera isnt like all the other games where you have to defeat a certain amount of enemies and then get a boss or constantly clicking an item to make your production go up in a game like Cookie Clicker (i've played that game and i hated myself afterwards, dont judge me). In Plantera the goal is to build your own garden packed full of fruits and vegetables. You can grow trees, bushes and use animals to harvest the crops for you. It's perfect for a lazy guy like me because i'm a slave driver and those crops wont harvest themselves.
When you first start out, your garden looks like this. Pitiful, i know. But as time goes on you're collecting coins in order to buy more trees and bushes so you can plant more crops. While doing this you're fending off the woodland creatures such as foxes, birds, moles and other dasterdly animals just trying to take what you worked your little blue rear end off to achieve. There's no mashing in this game as i stated before, as all you have to do is pick up the fruits and or vegetables that your friends dont get for those sweet, sweet coins. MONEY!
As you progress throughout the game getting coins, you're also gaining XP to level up to unlock new plants, bushes and animals. I do want to point out that when you're not playing the game, your worker friends are actively harvesting your garden for you. That's a HUGE bonus for a game like this, i wouldnt have much of a social life if i were doing everything. That's not a knock on the game, this is one of the few clicker games i actually enjoy, i just like the outdoors too and dont want to get addicted, lol.
For a simple indie game, VaragtP did an amazing job on it. It serves it's purpose as a simulation game but the only problem i have is it only has one song throughout the entire game and you dont get any actual in game audio. I would like to hear the birds coming in and trying to steal an apple or a mole coming out of the ground to take a pile of blueberries. I'd lose it if i heard one of the foxes being scared off by my gang of bodyguards protecting my crops AND my workers. It's the little things that put games over the top and make them that much more enjoyable. Again, i enjoy this game. It's addicting in it's own way and the only way i'd probably stop playing is if there was nothing more to achieve. With the ability to buy more space to grow ALL THE PLANTS i dont think that would be possible.
It can get a little crowded and i dont know where to click at times but it doesnt bother me THAT much. All in all, if you enjoy simple games like this then support VaragtP and buy the game, It's like 3 bucks on Steam and it's worth it if you're a fan of the indie game scene. It's not too heavy on your computer so you should be able to run it if you're interested. That is unless your computer is ran by a hamster running on a wheel then i dont know what else to tell you. I give this game a 5/5 and highly recommend it.​

[Western Themed] First-Person Shooter.
You play as the badass Silas Greaves, a bounty hunter with a very long list of hits and a very long list of stories to tell.
The graphics look like they were ripped right out of a story book, and in the most heart-warming way. You can tell Techland put a lot of love into this project, because it shows every step of the way.
The gameplay setting takes place in the past, while the narration takes place in the present as he tells his epic stories to some teenagers at a bar. This let the developers have some fun with the story-telling mechanics, with frequent rewinds and misinformation, making for longer gameplay. You can collect artifacts to read the true historical facts if you wish.
The gameplay is, for the most part, like most first person shooters. But CoJG comes with a fresh twist on gunplay. While old mechanics like the concentration gauge make a warm return, you can now come face to face with an outlaw for a quick-draw duel. Very groovy mechanic, and it definitely makes the whole western theme feel extra solid. You can carry two single handle weapons such as pistols or sawn-offs, as well as a double handed weapon like a rife or shotgun. This installment in the franchise plays a little differently from it's predecessors in the sense that it has an arcade feel to it. Every shot has skill points attached to it, which gains experience points to upgrade your character the way you play. The skill tree is divided into three classes: Gunslinger, Ranger, & Trapper - giving you the power over how to evolve your character.
Normal, Hard, and True West difficulty settings. New game plus is unlocked once completed.

I've followed this game since November of 2014 and have many more hours clocked than my steamprofile says.
This game is best compared to a city-builder. You start off with very little, and end up with you basically owning the world. The building aspect of the game is heavily focused on optimizing your setups. This leads me on to the main point of the game: automating
. You will have to move mining locations when you deplete the ores close to you - eventually requiring you to use trains for transport.
The game has a very nice progression to it, which helps you learn while progressing. Even after hundreds of hours I still don't know the best solutions to a lot of things. This is also mostly because there are none. Every player can have their own playstyle, their own way of solving logistical problems. These aspects are what makes this game great for me.
I'd also like to give a fair warning. If these things interest you, then you will probably have to reschedule your life for the next few months. This game eats up free time faster than you can say "What year is it?"
There are other aspects of the game, such as: combat and general tinkering with the wire system.
The last thing - which I want to mention - is the modding. The game is almost built around being extremely moddable. I can't recall where, but I read a post where (I think) one of the devellopers said that they wanted their game to be a framework for mods.
I cannot reccomend this game enough if you like tinkering with setups, optimizing the processes that are running the factory and just building a giant interconnected mess of a factory that nobody other than you can navigate through.
This game will consume your life if you aren't careful!

Ever wondered what it owuld be like to work for border control? Well now you can with Passport Simulator...I mean Papers, Please! Set in dystopian Artstozka, your job is to check immigrants documentation and decide whether they are to be let into the country or turned away. One of the most engrossing simulation games in recent memory, Papers, Please is all about speed and organisation skills in order to process as many people as possible in a given day.

In
, you are a hapless, hopeless Arstotzkan, forced to continually work at a boring, menial job for very little reward, being penalized for minor infractions and never quite having enough to keep your family fed, warm and healthy. So, essentially, something like the fringes of Russia crossed with every terrible desk job you can think of.
As an unhappiness simulator, it's top-notch. As an enjoyable game, not so much. The art is lovely, and I appreciate that the point of the game is to capture that Eastern European bleakness and force you into a moral corner - but seriously, it just makes for a pretty dull game, especially at the beginning before any kind of plot kicks in. (I'm sure there must be a plot there somewhere, but I gave up after the first few days.)
Plus, I personally found the controls really clunky - why couldn't some of the functions be assigned to keys? Why can't I just keep the drawer with the stamps open? If the devs were trying to make me just as bored and frustrated as my character must have been, then they succeeded, but they failed at making me want to actually continue playing the game.
If you're really patient with details-checking, really into gulags, or don't mind your whole family dying of illness while you claw your way to the top of the border-patrol career ladder, buy this game. Otherwise, maybe look elsewhere.

8/10 - Transistor is the first title released by the studio Supergiant Games since their excellent piece of work - Bastion, and just like Bastion; this game has plenty of charm.
Lovely visuals, satisfying music and wonderful voice acting (particularly from Logan Cunningham, the man who played the Stranger in Supergiants' previous game, coming back for another smooth performance) are all to be expected here.
The playtime is about 10 hours. For better or for worse, the story is kept vague throughout. Also - for better or worse - the combat system allows you to stop time in order to plan out attacks. This helps plot out attack patterns and devise strategies accordingly - but on the other hand it can make the combat feel disjointed occansionally.
Overall the game is lovely, endearing and tugs on a few emotional heartstrings. Also the game has a hum button! You have to love a game with a hum button!
Incredible soundtrack

This game is both really fun and very beautiful. Mix that with with an entrancing sound track and a setting and plot that unravels as you progress, and you have gold.
Most of the fun is running around mixing different functions to develop your own combat styles in both turns and real time. Despite being a work of art, they did not slack on the gameplay. Between the various combat options and limiters (which ramps the difficulty for bonus experience) you can find a playstyle that is right for you. It manages a balanced difficulty that remains challenging but never overwheling. Whenever you drop to zero health, a function (one of your combat abilities) becomes disabled for a few fights, but you can still fight until you are out of all your active functions and just set up another at the next access point (save points). There are back doors that you can access where you can run through tests, and eventually do practice rounds.
The game's visuals are stylized and I personally like it. It may not appeal to everyone, but art is subjective. The graphics, the music, the setting, and even the gameplay all come together as one cohesive piece of work that tells an amazing but tragic story. It's good enough to play through a second time. It's just a fun experience. Oh and the music... I love it so much that I sometimes play just to listen to the music. It's ambient and yet resonating. It draws you in, and it's great to have Red hum to the background [The game says she lost her voice, but it seems it's more like her words or tongue that she lost].
Great gameplay and design are accompanied here by a smooth pacing. Letting you learn and revealing more and more at a moderate pace, not so fast that you're overwhelmed but never so slow that you're grinding. In fact, you can't really grind; while not a terrible thing on its own brings me to the game's one downside.
The closest thing you can do is the tests and practice battles. You can do the practice battles all you want, but you have no control over which enemies you fight. The tests are fun, but those are a one time deal which is a real bummer since some of them are a lot of fun. I guess you have the option to start over the entire save file, but then you lose out on all the functions you played through to get. Essentially you are locked into the game's pace whether you want to or not. This is not an RPG, you don't grind or explore. It's a story with really fun tactical combats.
It's an astonishing game, and while not long, it is definitely worth the money. Buy it if you're looking for an immersive story with exciting combat, just don't expect a RPG with sidequests or branching storylines.

I was pretty disappointed with the length of this game. Was expecting the early reviews to be overly critical of how short it was. I finished the game in just under 4 hours having fully explored the environment and having stepped away from my computer a time or two. That being said, I had a hard time enjoying this game when I started it with thoughts of Amnesia: the Dark Decent in my head. Once I began to think about it as an entirely different type of game, I began to enjoy it a bit more.
There wasn't anything I think the game did particularly well. That's not to say it was bad, just nothing blew me away.
The only thing that really bothered me is that the experience felt entirely out of my control in just about every way possible. Most doors are locked or stuck and only become open when you've clicked the magical button; there is no exploration. The drawers/desks/etc. that are not locked (most are due to reasons) throughout the game have maybe 2 notes in them? If you're going to lock nearly everything why not lock up the 40 empty desks I went through? To add another half hour to the game? With the exception of one "puzzle" in the game, everything is overly simple. For instance, you'll have a situation like... an engine won't start, but rather than get you exploring and worrying about what's after you while you figure out how to restart that engine, the engine and fuel are right next to the button you pressed to find out it wasn't working. In addition to this there will be a big sign that says, "ENGINE REQUIRES FUEL IN ORDER TO START" right above the button, the engine, and the fuel can. The only "puzzle" in the game that involves an answer that isn't immediately in front of you basically spams you with notes, journal entries, and monologue to force feed you the solutions several times before you even get to attempt it to the point that I couldn't take the character I was playing seriously in that event.
The point is, this game has you on rails HARD and it's really obvious. This makes it difficult to become frightened at all due to the fact that shortly into the game you accept that you can't really control anything.
While it's easy to fault the game and it probably sounds like I hated it, the criticism is meant more as a forewarning than anything. If you go in expecting great indie horror, you'll have a hard time enjoying yourself. If you go in expecting a interesting story that isn't really going to blow you away, then here you have a decent way to spend an otherwise boring afternoon.
If you're looking for a cost effective purchase, avoid this game. I'm happy with the near 4 hour experience, but $20 for a game that only lasts for 4 hours, or less, with no replay value is just a bad deal.
