is a thriller based in the Alien universe. And just so you can judge me up front: I've never seen the movies. So I've no idea how faithful it is to the films nor it's canonicity.
In Alien Isolation you play as Amanda Ripley, the daughter of the main character of the movies. And early on she is tasked with retrieving a ship after recovering the flight recorder. Upon arrival, quite expectedly, things are not as well as hoped.
The gameplay is primarily stealth focused, keeping quiet, staying low and out of sight. However, there are blueprints and tons of crafting material to find throughout the ship as well as weapons. Too many weapons in my opinion. You have a number of distractions at your disposal and numerous ways of dispatching or completely avoiding conflict, whether it be from the alien itself, Seegsen working joe synthetics or regular ol' humans. However I'm of two mindsets of this in horror games specifically: Stealth is obviously needed to not only aid in survival but build tension against an unbeatable enemy. But having too many weapons or gadgets can make you lenient on them, perhaps even over confidant removing most if not all tension. Additionally, the stealth mechanic of hiding in a locker or whatever else is also a bit played out.. It perpetuates this sit and wait mentality. Which can be quite filled with tension but overdone.. can be be an exhaustive practice.  – and in this case specifically I felt as though the game drags itself on for far too long.
The alien is a one shot kill which I imagine for most people is fear inducing. However, there are frequent save points and the fact I had no real recourse to fend off the alien aside from my Flamethrower/molotovs earned later on made the sequences when the alien was present more frustrating than tense: Certainly not scary. Early on, the only times I ever felt tense enough to jump were when a pipe burst and a light fell off the ceiling. This isn't to say the game as a whole is devoid of tension rather simply once you learn how the alien behaves its just not that big of a deal. Additionally, it makes a very distinct sound when it crawls back into the ducts. Giving you clearance to move around visibly but still needing to heed audio cues lest you bring back the one shot monster.
I think the tension of it being in space and on a malfunctioning ship, "atmospheric tension" if you will, wasn't used enough. There are a few moments that do use this to its advantage and quite frankly those are probably my favorite moments, leaving me with feeling in regards to the other moments something of a “to be expected, lets keep moving” sort of feeling towards them.
The art design is very well done. The whole 80's retro future aesthetic is in full effect. Tons of space sci-fi jargon is all over the place. Of course space travel will be done with MS-DOS. As if you'd trust anything else anyways.
Nice terrifiying experience.

Ever wondered what it owuld be like to work for border control? Well now you can with Passport Simulator...I mean Papers, Please! Set in dystopian Artstozka, your job is to check immigrants documentation and decide whether they are to be let into the country or turned away. One of the most engrossing simulation games in recent memory, Papers, Please is all about speed and organisation skills in order to process as many people as possible in a given day.

In
, you are a hapless, hopeless Arstotzkan, forced to continually work at a boring, menial job for very little reward, being penalized for minor infractions and never quite having enough to keep your family fed, warm and healthy. So, essentially, something like the fringes of Russia crossed with every terrible desk job you can think of.
As an unhappiness simulator, it's top-notch. As an enjoyable game, not so much. The art is lovely, and I appreciate that the point of the game is to capture that Eastern European bleakness and force you into a moral corner - but seriously, it just makes for a pretty dull game, especially at the beginning before any kind of plot kicks in. (I'm sure there must be a plot there somewhere, but I gave up after the first few days.)
Plus, I personally found the controls really clunky - why couldn't some of the functions be assigned to keys? Why can't I just keep the drawer with the stamps open? If the devs were trying to make me just as bored and frustrated as my character must have been, then they succeeded, but they failed at making me want to actually continue playing the game.
If you're really patient with details-checking, really into gulags, or don't mind your whole family dying of illness while you claw your way to the top of the border-patrol career ladder, buy this game. Otherwise, maybe look elsewhere.

You awake in the middle of an industrious, brave England to the churning of an ancient machine under your very floorboards... and you can't remember a thing.
It would be unfair to call this a "sequel" to The Dark Descent, because it sacrifices almost every aspect of it. A Machine for Pigs, sadly, drops a severe amout of gameplay to focus on it's story. Whilst the story is bold, dark and something that I have never seen before, the gameplay of The Dark Descent would have fitted into this new world the player is thrown into perfectly. The entire game is walking, a few stealh scenes and of course collecting Journal entries. This lack of gameplay isn't something I found bad about the game, just dissapointing.
If you are one of those badass, hardcore gamers, A Machine for Pigs is not for you. It's much more of an interactive novel than a game, as it possses little or no hostility towards the player. You can take pleantiful amounts of beatings from a pig gentleman before you die, and with no way of checking your HP, this is yet another dissapointing factor of the game.
A Machine for Pigs' strong point is by far it's story. It's one of those games that "went there" and wasn't afraid to tackle morality, religion and horror all in one story. The narrative is well paced, with slow but progressive acts seperated by scenes where the player is contaced by a mysterious voice via a phone call. This gives a rough idea of your progress, and what you can expect next. Despite how short the game is (Around 3 to 4 hours, 5 if you get scared easily) the narrative still leaves me satisfied, and the overall journey doesn't come to an anti-claimatic ending. Most of the story is told through journal entries, and without reading them you will be left stumped at the end of the game.
Overall, A Machine for Pigs' story is what earns it a place in my heart. It's not everyone's cup of tea, nor did I think I would be mine, but I would reccomend it to anyone out there who is looking for a great, immersive story experience. But sadly, it's lack of gameplay and desierability to be different, leave the asking price a little too much.

Supergiant Did it again, an amazingly beautiful game, great soundtrack, and fun gameplay.
Transistor takes a more tactical approach to it's battle system than the more chaotic hack and slack ARPG combat of bastion. In many cases you absolutely need to utilize the Plan() system and can't just rage through with a few good weapons like in bastion. The game also has a slightly more mature artstyle, and I enjoy the elements of art noveau and cyberpunk aesthetics strewn about all of the cityscapes. It really is a gorgeous game. The story is refreshing and takes some unexpected turns, and despite it being a bit too cryptic at times, i enjoyed it and thought it pulled together the game well.
My only complaint is the brevity of the game. Supergiant just leaves you begging for more, maybe we'll get lucky and some form of expansion will be added. That said I still do not at all regret spending $15 dollars on this beauty of a game, however short.

I very much enjoyed Transistor. The soundtrack was beautiful and the visuals can only be descirbed as stunnin. To compare it to Supergiant Game's Bastion, the gameplay was alot more enjoyable, the ability to plan your attack and the incredibly array of options available to you made the gameplay highly immersive and personal, leaving you wanting to try every combination, incentivized by the additional bios you can unlock. However, the narration does not compare to that of Bastion's, but the 'dialoge' between the mind inside the Transistor and Red fills the hole quite nicely. However, the story itself also feels a little lacking, especially towards the end. The ending somewhat makes up for this, as it is somewhat unexpected, and cute at the same time, but I felt less invested in Red as I did with the Kid. However, the game was definitely as enjoyable to play through as Bastion, and equally deserves multiple playthroughs so you can keep discovering all this game has to offer. I highly reccomend this game to anyone who either enjoyed bastion or enjoys the art and sound in a game as much as the actual gameplay and story. Supergiant Games shows us once again how video games can be heavily artistic while maintaining complex gae mechanics.

Already my GOTY. Top-notch storytelling and worldbuilding, a deep tactical-rpg system with a head-spinning amount of playstyle customization, and an even better soundtrack than Bastion. Supergiant's outdone themselves.

Transistor is the best game of the year so far. Its narrative, while suffering somewhat from issues of pacing, feels like a breath of fresh air. The art design and sound design is phenomenal; the ethereal atmosphere and bright visuals, combined with the strange soundscape and Darren Korb's outstanding soundtrack, adds up to an experience unlike any other.
What's even more impressive is Transistor's combat mechanics and the way they've been integrated into the narrative. The game rewards players who diversify their combat techniques with further information about the story and the world it takes place in. In addition, the game offers narrative reasons for the mechanics. The mechanics are essential for telling Transistor's story.
Supergiant had a strong debut with Bastion, and if nothing else, Transistor serves to reaffirm the development team's talent and potential. Its fantastic visuals and sound, along with its effective marriage of game mechanics and narrative, add up to an experience that's impossible to forget. Transistor is simply stunning, and one of the best games in recent memory.

Well, anotha clicker game!
And anotha one. Yet this time, its spicier than any clicker game you have ever seen! It looks cute and it is!
Haha, jokes  aside this is a really cute and addicting clicker game! All clicker games are addicting but oh man, this is by far the most addicting one!
You start out with one worker and start building up your estate with some carrots and the first critter you encounter trying to steal your carrots! Don't get scared.. you can bash that rabbit and keep it away from your carrots! An amount of interaction is needed at the beginning of the game as you start planting all kinds of fruits and vegetables, as you will attract all sorts of critters like the rabbit as mentioned, the crow and the mole. Once you reach the animal stage, you'll encounter the fox and the wolf, the point when you need to be really careful if you have no dogs to guard your sheeps and pigs. After you expanded the land enough and you have a nice amount of workers you should put a dog then some more so you can have them guard around while you are away.
Furthermore, there are upgrades like idling and a multiplier for the cash. Both are really important and the base for your economy. Investing in those two will grant you a nice income and you'll get money in no time if you go away and idle.
Grind all the cash and level up, you'll get stars to the plants and animals which will boost the economy some more.
Extremely cute and detailed, aesthetics surely to keep you looking at them for a long time!
The soundtrack is as well cute and it fits exactly to the farm theme, while the sound effects are great too!

Even though Dark Souls 2 is a fantastic game, it is no where close to the near perfection of the original and fails in many ways. Difficulty is not used in the same way. In DS1 every enemy placement seemed to have hours of thought behind it and you never felt like you got killed unfairly. Although, in DS2 I died many times to enemies I had no way of seeing and no chance to dodge the one-hit kill attacks they have. The addition of the life-gem, small items that slowly regenerate your health and can be bought and found on bodies, ruin the entire idea of the estus flask. A lot of the bosses are just humanoids in giant armor and many seem to be rip-offs of DS1 bosses. The biggest way DS2 fails the original is in its level design. DS1 felt like a real place. The placement of areas made sense. If you are at sea-level in DS1 and go up an elevator you will no longer be a sea-level and the environment will reflect that  ect. In DS2 zones are placed all over the place and make no sense when you at the entire map. All of that being said, the game still plays like a Souls game and is still fun and rewarding, just not as good.

Secondly, the engine is similar to that of TES games. No ladder climbing animation. Rigid movement animations etc. But this is easily looked over because it's considerably better than most MMORPG out there. So rest assured, it'll be nice to play.

The game is pay-to-play.  After Zenimax switched from a Subscription platform to a one time payment, they added many new items to the crown store that allows players with real money to get far ahead of those without money.  Thus, new players will find themselves playing for months just to be able to compete in PVP.  PVE, however, is a different story.  From level one, a new player can play with whomever they desire.
This being said, the new Morrowind update finally drove me away from the game.  The fact that the developers tried to force their existing player base into paying another $40 after the base game fee shows that they are focused on money and not on the community.
It was the players who asked for the improvements included within the Morrowind update and it's a real shame that none of them will be able to experience their suggestions without dishing out more cash.

Total War: Rome 2 is one of my favorite stradegy games of all time. The Total War series is a different take on the stradegy game gendre. It isn't about just winning battles, it's also about taking care of your economy and making allies. It is not too political but also satisfies all those questions like: "Where does that guy get all that money to make all of those elephants? I have killed like 5 000 of them already!". Not that I ever wanted an answer for that but I guess it is cool that we now have an answer. Look, I haven't played any previous Total Wars, so heres my list of things why I like this game:
1. Rome. Come on, it's Rome. It means swords and hand-to-hand combat. Javelins and walls. The Antique world facinates me.
2. Emperor Edition. Think about this for a moment: You get the base game plus a free campaign from Creative Assembly, which is basicly them saying: "We know that the launch was horrible. Here,"
3. Great politics. Not too hard to follow politics like the taxation of trade routes or any other formal Jedi business. You can raise taxes, lower taxes, murder political opponents and... thats about it. You aren't rising to power through politics, you are already at the top.
4. Great combat. Hard to explain. It's... it's... combat. How would I explain that? Press this, you can do this, do that etc.
5. UI. PT34 may disagree, but I really like the UI. Everything is nicely placed into the bottom of the screen. Taxes, objectives, diplomacy etc. It is all nicely put together. I can't think of any way to improve it... expect for the occational bug. And shortcut keys to ease the butthurt for PT34. :P

If ever there was a game that would be defined as replayable, this would have to be it. I found myself playing this game in all sorts of scenarios, be it watching videos, playing with friends or grinding on my own, the world of Pandora was always there with something to do. What gearbox managed to do with this game is in my opinion lightning in a bottle. They made something serious yet funny and causal but in depth.
The artstyle of the game is reason enough to buy it. The visuals while some may consider dated in this age hold up so much better than most games of the time. The art direction matches the tone of the game in it's wonkiness and can be distractingly beautiful sometimes.
There are two aspects of this game that have me coming back: the gameplay and the dialogue. Gearbox really found their stride with this game in terms of tone. Each quest is voice acted in a fun way that gives each a distinct feeling. While the gameplay may repeat from time to time, the ridiculous banter coming from the character is always fresh and new in my opinion.
Speaking of gameplay, the game is a blast to boot. You can play however you want with whatever guns you want. The game is so appealing because of its vast diversity in terms of gameplay. While the skill trees from the different classes aren't anything to cry home about (they're actually quite lackluster) each class serves its own purpose in mixing up the gameplay.
The replayability stems from grinding in my opinion, which the game makes a pleasure. It's fun to go back and kill bosses with new and different guns or maybe with friends.
In summation, definitely pick up the game of the year edition as you will be craving more content once you've dried up the main game. Definitely one of my favorites and hope others feel the same way.

Dark Souls II is an amazing experience.
After hundreds of deaths in a time period of 50 hours, I finally managed to defeat the final boss and finish the normal game. The amount of satisfaction you get when the credits pop up is unbelievable.
And apart from the "story" there's much more to discover. It's great to see that shiny orb of loot in the distance, and then to find a way to get to it, sometimes that's way harder than you'd think and it might result in (of course) death.
The weird thing, at least for me, is that you don't get mad when you die. I just thought of it as "That's the game." and I went back, died again, went back, died again, went back, and killed the mofo!
The game really puts your patience to the test and therefore it shouldn't be played if you have a temper. But if you are into challenging RPG games, then you don't want to miss out on this. And remember: Gameplay beats graphics all day every day!

People are being so damn harsh with this game!
I've played 10 hours so far and I'm level 26 and this game is absolutely FUN!
I love the fact that you can talk to every single NPC, there are lots of subquests, the skills are really varied and some require tactics and not just smash and kill, the graphic and music are amazing, I'm basically never bored.
The true grind part is if you want to complete collections but they are absolutely NOT necessary to keep going on with the story so I don't really see why people complain about grind. All games require to kill mobs but BELIEVE ME, I played games where the grind was WAY more serious than the TOS one. (I'll just say Warframe as an example because grind is everything in that game yet I still love it.)
This game is really good played with friends too because if you make a party, quests where you have to collect items become much easier but if you play solo EVERY BOSS I encountered so far was perfectly soloable. Maybe it's because I'm a Pyromancer? I don't think so but if you have trouble it's really easy to make a party and find other players. There are always at least 5 parties in the busiest channels and a couple in the less crowded ones.
Another great thing is in fact, the CHANNELS because if a channel is too crowded or if you can't find the right mob, you can always change channel and find a less crowded one where monsters will respawn.
I've heard many people complain about lag but I'm having no problem so far and my PC is kinda old too. If you experience lag you should change some settings, go to a less crowded channel and close unnecessary applications but, seriously, it's a 2D game, if you can't even support this kind of game just go buy a new PC and shut up!
There are many interesting mechanics that I still didn't even try yet and the game has just been released so I have faith many good things have yet to come but my overall experience has been extremely positive!
I've played this game for a whole day and I absolutely did not feel bored! It's been so long since I last played such a good MMO where the atmosphere and mechanics are so smooth you would just play without stop. (GW2 and FFXIV were my latest favourite MMOs)
I love the fact that there are many subclasses so you can choose your favourite style but BEWARE, the game is not meant for EVERY subclass to be played but instead, it's made so you can create really rounded but specialized characters. You need to decide which classes you want to go for beforehand and you'll find out the gameplay will be very smooth! I was disappointed by this at first because I wanted to play every subclass but then I realized it was absolutely unnecessary because if you take a close look at each class's skills (and NOT ONLY THE ATTIRE because let's be sincere, we all want good looking outfits haha) you'll see you will not want to play every class but instead get better at a couple ones that compliment each other well.
Everyone has it's own preferred build but you can always create a new one. :)
Another thing I love is the fact that you can jump around and some places can be reached only with jumps. The game encourages you to explore all the map to find hidden treasure chests and I think it's amazing because it's not like other games where you could just avoid half of the map and go on. You even have an Adventure Diary (I don't really remember how it's called) that keeps track of everything you did and sometimes you get rewards so everything you do in this game is worth doing!
I guess the only bad thing about this game are the gold sellers but seriously, EVERY GAME has them so just ignore them or just switch to normal chat so you won't read them.
Anyway, I seriously recommend everyone to at least TRY THIS GAME and do not be discouraged by the reviews because it really all depends on your tastes! I was discouraged by the reviews but then I tried the game and loved it so you should too! Trust me! :)
(Besides, I think to better enjoy a game you need to have a bit of fantasy too. If you empathize with your character a bit everything will be more beautiful. If you just call you character "Dumbdog5" and just play to reach endgame and troll people in PvP then of course you won't like the game.)
So rembember, TRY FOR YOURSELF, THEN JUDGE!
I hope you found this review useful! Happy gaming! :D

Reign of Kings is very fun to play. I have actually had quite a few fun times of this, but I want to share my personal favourite;
> I made my character a dwarf with beautiful blond hair and a goatee.
> I spawned on the beach. I had only my primitive club over half my puny size, 2 torches and a few bandages.
> I decided I'd prowl the beach, looking for sleeping people I could pillage.
> Just as I had finished killing a sleeping man, a muscled, tall man in full steel armour emerged from a bush.
> I used voice chat to tell him I was a fresh spawn; that I meant no harm. He laughed.
> He used voice chat. In a disappointingly squeaky voice, he said something along the lines of;
"Dude, you're so small. I could easily kill you".
> I told him that I didn't care that he did because I only had a few supplies.
> He laughed again and gargled, "Okay then. I won't kill you".
> He pulled out a chain and chained me, and started pulling me along the ground.
> My body twisted in painful-looking ways as I was pulled along the ground, almost like a ragdoll.
> Finally, we stopped at a quite OP base.
> "This is my base", said the man, very seriously now, "If you do anything to it I will be very mad".
> He dragged me into a small room with a sleeping roll, then removed the chain from me.
> He made me click the sleeping roll so that I would spawn there when I died.
> "You're my servant now", he laughed.
> He told me that I would get food if I behaved myself.
> His first job for me was an odd one. He had captured another person, and had put him on a guillitine.
> He handed me a whip. "Whip the prisoner", he said.
> I did. Despite the prisoner's pleas, I did it.
> The master (yes, that was what the man was. My master) told me he had enough of the whipping. I stopped.
> The master chopped of the prisoner's head. He told me that as a reward, I could have the prisoner's items.
> The master sent me back to my cell. I now had wood armour.
> A few IRL days later, I joined the game again. It just some happened Master was online too.
> He told me that I needed to cut down some trees for him.
> I thought this would be a good opportunity to run away, but I was wrong because Master was supervising me.
> After cutting down 3 trees for Master, he handed me some rope.
> He told me that he trusted me enough to capture someone for him, and that I had one day to return with someone or else he would hunt me down, bring me back to his base and behead me.
> Well, that got rid of the idea of running away.
> He released me into the world.
> I decided that I had plenty of time to catch someone, and that I could spend some time gathering supplies.
> After spending 5 minutes gathering wood, ore and stone I saw a fresh spawn.
> I ran up to him, telling him through voice chat that I would not harm him.
> I wasn't lying; it would be Master that would harm him.
> I swiftly roped him and dragged him back to the Master's base.
> I found something odd when I got back; the door was open.
> I decided that I would take this opportunity to explore the base, as I had only been in the cell and the torture/execution room which had been right next to each other.
> I guess there's an amount of time or an ability to escape rope through struggling, because the prisoner got up and ran away.
> I chased him, fearing what the Master would do to me, just when I had got this far in the game!
> I lost him, and just as I was returning to the base I saw a sleeping man.
> I happily went up to him and clubbed him to death, and searched his inventory.
> I was shocked.
> I found the Master's FULL STEEL ARMOUR, his sword and some other bits and bobs.
> I realized I had killed the Master.
> I went along happily, free as a bird.
> The Master soon came online again. He started raging in chat.
> I explained to him what happened (albeit with some jests)
> His explanation was that his WiFi connection went dodgy and that he had lost connection while out chooping wood.
> I didn't reply and went on with life until the server shut down.
TL;DR: I was captured by a man who made me his servant and do his dirty work until one day he lost his connection while cutting trees so I found his character asleep and helpless and killed him and took his stuff.

I had rarely heard good things about the Call of Juarez series until Gunslinger which I never heard anything bad about.  After having played it myself, I can safely say that it is a fantastic game and one I've never played anything quite like before.
You play as Silas Greaves, playing through stories of past exploits in the wild west as they are being told by yourself in the present.  This is one of the game's greatest strengths, as the storytelling not only perfectly matches the action, but will also change the environment and even make you replay parts of the story in different ways as various people tell how they've heard the story before.  It may not sound like the best idea, but it plays excellently and I'd love to see more games done in this style.
The other big strength of the game is the gameplay itself.  It does arcade shooting action very well and also includes the ability to avoid death by dodging bullets and slow time down with concentration mode.  You gain experience for killing enemies with a combo multiplier increasing the value of each kill and can use this experience to gain new skills.  Outside of the regular gameplay there is also a rather unique dueling feature.  You will be pitted against a famous outlaw in a wild west duel where you must keep your concentration by keeping a reticule on your enemy while keeping your hand ready to draw.  It provides an excellent sense of suspense before shots are fired and tests your reaction time very well.
Graphically the game looks pretty good with a pseudo-comic style lightly outlining objects in the game.  Don't expect groundbreaking graphics, however.  Sound effects are also quite good and fit the game very well.
On the technical side is the only part of the game I'm disappointed in.  Call of Juarez Gunslinger runs on the Chrome engine so like all other Chrome engine games I have played it won't run quite smoothly.  It likes to drop frames randomly though it will run quite fast.  The game does not respond well to ALT+TAB and will get a visible mouse cursor fairly often when using the Steam overlay.  FOV can be changed through a config file as with other Chrome engine games.
Buy this game, you won't regret it!

I'll be honest. I never got into the call of Juarez series. I only looked into this game because I saw it in an online top 10... and I'm glad I did! Ubisoft did something almost no FPS does, particularly a certain series by EA that's released with incredibly few changes every year...
This game told me a STORY. Literally. I love the fact that as I'm playing, the protagonist is actually narrating. I love it when he goes back and changes the story and thus changes the structure of the level. The shooting isn't particularly difficult. Like most modern shooters, Call of Juarez Gunslinger utilizes the same "Regenerating health" model pioneered by Halo. Even when you do die (and you'll die a lot, as despite regenerating health, you don't have much to start with), you won't go back very far, plus you won't have to listen to the same voiceover again and again since he won't continue the story until you get to the next line of dialog.
The cell-shaded graphics are beautiful to look at: bright and colorful even when you're in the middle of a ghost town in the dead of night. Everything's smoothe and runs quickly. It goes to prove a game's graphics don't HAVE to be hyper-realistic in order to immerse you.

There are a couple intriguing mechanics to talk about. Most notable is the "concentration" system. By killing foes along your path, you build up a "concentration" gauge. At any time, you can press the appropriate button and enter concentration mode, where your enemies are highlighted, and time slows down. A few quick shots will build up your score multiplyer quick, particularly as you become adept at headshots!  The second mechanic is the "death sense" mechanic. After your character has cheated death for a short amount of time, this gauge fills up and will let you dodge a bullet which might otherwise be lethal... provided you hit the right button of course. Finally, most chapters end with a "duel," a classic, spaghetti western-style duel in which you and a famous gunhand (like Sheriff Pat Garett, for example) each get a single shot to find out who lives or dies. Points are scored more highly if you let him draw his gun first, but you can always cheat and draw yours as soon as you're ready.
A few RPG elements are lightly sprinkled throughout the game, as you can build your character into a long-range fighter, a close-range juggernaut, or even a dual-wielding desperado gunslinger. Exploring those options is a delight in itself, so I won't spoil them with this review.
The weapons selection is basic western fare, with a selection of pistols and rifles, and the occasional stick of dynamite filling out your arsenal. But honestly? That's all you need. Most of the attention is on the story, and you feel powerful enough without having a BFG equivallent loading you down.
I haven't even finished the game yet, but I already love it so much, I had to sit down and write this review. I bought it for $20, and it's absolutely worth the money. So if you like shooters, and you like westerns, I'd absolutely recommend Call of Juarez Gunslinger.

Story time (skip to bottom for review summary):
I bought this game because my little brother was playing it and thought it would be fun if we played together. When I finally downloaded it, he had stopped playing because it had become too challenging where he was and he didn't like playing with people he doesn't know online (he does this with most games). So I played it on my own for a while, got frustrated that the raiders kept respawning as soon as you left an area, eventually got bored with it and I stopped playing...until a couple of weeks ago.
I hit a dry spell with Fallout NV (it happens when you are playing on both your xbox (I know, I am a peasant) and on your computer with different variations) and started playing Borderlands 2 again.
For some reason when I picked it back up it became a whole new game for me and I was sucked in. Previously I had not played with others online (and you don't really need to in the beginning) but started to with the fight against Wilhelm. I then spent the next two weeks plugging tons of hours into this game (well, a lot for me with work, and I was playing Payday 2 at the same time due to its free giveaway).
I became consumed with this game, wanting to complete every side quests (I still have one or two left I have to find) and allowing people into my game when I needed help. Then I started seeing people join my games from previous days (I doubt they realized it) and I began progressing through the game with the same people which made it a lot more fun.
When I finally beat the Warrior (so much easier when you have a full party) I became lost. I had no idea what to do now that the game was officially over. I literally typed into the chat to the other players "what now?"
I actually became sort of sad because it was all over and I wasn't sure what to do with my free time.
AND THEN I FOUND MORE STUFF TO DO!
The leveling up never ends, there is in fact another optional boss after the Warrior, and I will never get tired of driving around the desert blowing up raider helicopters and trucks. Also, you can still go join games of others ready to fight the Warrior.
TL;DR
Might start off a little boring but it is an extremely immensive and captivating game that at the end will make you question what you are going to do with your life now that the story line is over (Hint: you will start over with a different hero and experience the greatness of this game all over again).

In a world where Tron meets Fritz Lang's Metropolis, there is a singer who has lost her voice wielding a sword who just found one - the eponymous Transistor. Together they battle a digital menace called The Process in order to...
Well, what do they want to achieve actually? See, Transistor provides two challenges for the player: first, fighting The Process and second, actually understanding what is going on. While some people will hate this minimum style story telling, others will embrace it as another challenge to overcome and will find it very compelling.
Combat, on the other hand, is much more straightforward, deeply strategic and very rewarding. You gain a number of abilities, each of which may be used by itself as an active attack, as support for another ability or as a passive enhancement to your character. Take Bounce, for example. By itself it is an attack that ricochets off enemies, hitting multiple targets in the process. Add it as support to another ability and now this attack will chain-hit. Assign it as a passive enhancement and it will make enemy attacks bounce off of you. Decisions, decisions...
Adding to that is the Turn() sequence, which allows you to pause the game, queue up attacks and actions, and have them executed in bullet-time. Thus, strategy is much more important than good reflexes.
Most important about Transistor, however, is that it is art. Not art as in the "you might lable this as pre-post-retro modernism" sense. It's art because it's beautiful in every aspect. There is a fundamental aesthetic vision that permeates all elements of the game and strings them together nicely. It just works, and it's gorgeous all the time.
That being said, not everything is perfect about Transistor. Gameplay generally feels just a little bit rough. Menus like ability selection are somewhat clunky and Turn() can be hit-or-miss without much explanation. The key mechanic for getting more background info becomes somewhat tedious after novelty wears off, paling significantly in contrast to the Turn() mechanic. Some streamlining might have done wonders, but there are limits for indie companies, of course.
Now, Transistor: The Game might have some issues, but Transistor: The Experience is awesome nonetheless. Visuals, soundtrack and voice acting all weave an atmosphere that carries the game over many flaws. What Transistor wants to do, it does really well.

Transistor is a rather unique game, coming from the developers of Bastion, Supergiant Games. While some may have been expecting a story and gameplay similar to Bastion, it is fortunate that Supergiant Games did not down that route, and it is important to remember the following: Transistor is not Bastion, and Bastion is not Trasistor. That doesn't mean they don't have a few things that are alike, but they are very different games.
Much like Bastion, much of the 'narration' of the game, if in this case it can be called that - is once again voiced by Logan Cunningham, who voiced the narrator of Bastion. Here, though, the voice is much more laid-back and relaxed rather than the rough voice he used before. It works, and helps distinguish his 'character' from being yet another narrator. You'll be hearing him a lot.
The gameplay is quite solid, although, much like Bastion, not too difficult, for some not being difficult enough. To remedy that, there are the Limiters - which act much like Bastion's Idols - which make the game harder. The way you fight in Transistor will rely on you using the functions you have available, and the best thing about them is that they can 'upgraded' with other functions to change their effects slightly or fit into a 'passive' slot that passively affects things. For example, the first function you get, Crash(), does 50 damage and very temporarily stuns enemies. In another function's upgrade slot, it will make that other function temporarily stun the enemy. In a passive slot, it will reduce damage by 25% percent. There are 16 different functions in total, and that allows for a lot of different combinations . This allows you to use whatever functions fit your playstyle. For example, there's one that 'masks' you, making you effectively invisible to opponents, and another that temporarily switches their allegiance from opposing you to serving you. All of these functions can be used inside and outside Turn(), which is a fairly important mechanic: it stops time, and allows you to plan your moves, then perform them in a matter of seconds, but has a cooldown that spans several seconds, in which you can move - but can't use any functions. This helps when dealing with large amounts of opponents, or when you want to backstab them and they just won't stop moving. This also leads to situations where using Turn() wouldn't be necessary or very hard, due to the nature of some opponents - sometimes you will have to wait for the right time to use it, or decide whether to use it at all.
In terms of music, it fits the game's world, and is very good. Obviously, that's no surprise, this being a Supergiant game after all. But it's the songs that have lyrics that stand out. In Bastion, there were only a few, about two or three. In Transistor, there are five. What's even better here, is that you can 'earn' the music to listen to them in what is basically the closest thing the game has to a hub by completing the game's challenges.
Story-wise, the game doesn't give much exposition. Most of the story can be gathered by inferring from what the game shows and tells you through the 'narration', as well as the function files. This is probably where the game falls short for some, as some things are not immediately obvious.

Okay so I'm going to start things off with it's not a bad game. It really isn't. I pre ordered it the second I could and played and beat it on release day and it made me so upset at how short and "non scary it is." Well I decided to try the game again, in the dark, headphones on and the volume up, and I am horrified. This game isn't as scary as Amnesia: The Dark Descent (which is an amazing horror game that anyone should try.) but the game is still scary. It also tells a great and creepy story in such a short time frame (around 4-5 hours).
If you're looking for the inventory system, oil management, and keeping track of your sanity, hell even messing around with the envirionment, it really isn't here in A Machine For Pigs. You can only interact with little things for puzzles (or chairs). The inventory system and the fuel management is gone. Which makes you not have to explore much (besides to do puzzles or find notes). That's one of the bigger gripes with this game is that they took too much away that made the original game what it was for a great story. That and the pig monsters, while intimidating, they really aren't as scary as the grunt, brute, or the suitors from the original game and the free Justine DLC.
Overall if you're looking for a game that tells a great story while getting scared here and there, while looking through the beautiful world of AMFP, you should buy this game.
If you were looking for the game to be♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants scary like the original and like having the inventory system and a more reason to explore you should still get this game just to witness the great story, but prepared to be slightly let down.

When I first heard The Chinese Room was co-developing the game, I was excited. I liked Dear Esther and I thought that style of writing would lend itself well to the Amneisa formula. What I didn't know at the time is that TCR would handle much more than the writing. A Machine for Pigs is Dear Esther: Spooky Slaughterhouse edition, and that is not a good thing. At the moment, the game is a buggy mess. But those issues can be fixed. The more stunning issues lay with the core mechanics of the game, or rather, a lack there of. Lamp oil, tinder boxes, inventory, and insanity are all gone. Any sort of inventory management or resource juggling has been removed. What's left is a theme park attraction where you are lead down a path to Ooh and Aah at things without any fear of consequence or failure. Sure there are spoOoOoky pig monsters, but as you'll see in a video I'll post later, they're not much of a threat. Especially since the protagonist is some sort of immortal. Some reviewers placed this game in the Survival Horror genre, which is really an insult to the genre as there is nothing 'survival' about it. At this point, I don't think it's possible for a game coming out in 2013 to dissappoint me more than this one.
There's a debate on which is the better game; Penumbra or Amnesia. I don't care where you stand on that issue, but if anyone tells you A Machine for Pigs is the best game to come out of the two series, I want you to laugh at them, kick them, stop being friends with them, whatever makes them the MOST uncomfortable. They deserve it.
Also, Penumbra is better than Amnesia. True fact.

Released at the start of 2017, Soda Dungeon is an idle RPG, developed by AN Productions and Poxpower, published by Armor Games. In this game, you must manage your team of adventurers as you raid the local dungeon for treasure.
When I first played this game, simply to grab an achievement to keep my TSA achievement streak going, I rated it very low, only 1.5 stars out of 5. However, I logged back onto it the other day so I could start grinding on it to begin completing it and getting through the achievements and getting things done, and I found I actually really enjoyed it.
This game is incredibly simple; you hire adventurers, you go to the dungeon, the adventures automatically attack and kill the monsters, and you keep going until all of your adventurers are dead. And that’s all the game is, other than selling items and buying upgrades. That’s literally all there is to this game – or you can actually take control of your adventurers, but who really does that in an idle game – but for some reason I’m totally addicted to this. It’s fun to play and the soundtrack keeps it going and keeps it fresh, changing every 20 levels to something new.
Of course, there’s a lot of repetition throughout the game, in monster design – looking through my screenshots alone, you can see most of the monsters are just given a new texture pack for a different set of levels – and it’s all the same thing no matter what, the monsters just get higher HPs. It’s a bit of a down side, with all idle games – I’d love to see one with unique monsters for every level, and not just a new texture pack all the time.
At the end of the day, this is a really fun game to just sit and let burn on it’s own whilst you’re busy doing things – I’ve done it plenty whilst writing reviews today, and getting on with some studying. It works, it grinds well on it’s own and I would definitely recommend downloading it. It’s fun, the soundtrack is fun – and if it gets repetitive, you can always just mute the game. Definitely give this one a go, at least. It’s nostalgic, but modern, fun.

Don't buy this for a story.  The story is simplistic, and the story missions are boring and horribly designed.  What you buy this for is the freedom of movement around this open world.  Slinging yourself from rock to rock, gliding through canyons, accidentally smashing into walls ... every second of that is fun.  Honestly, you can keep ramping up your heat level to 5 stars and have a whale of a time every time.  The side tasks (races, gliding challenges, destruction trials, etc.) are all actually enjoyable - far more so than the main story missions.
Be wary, this does suffer from some really poor choices of keybindings, and some laziness in the port.  Any vehicle with turrets is a nightmare to use if you have low sensitivity - there's clearly something not balanced properly there and there's no distinct turret sensitivity setting.  There are also the occasional game limiting bugs which you'll have to turn to the internet to find solutions for - for example, there's a mission that's not completable unless you disable a certain upgrade that you get early on.
Overall I rate the game positive, as long as you know what you're getting yourself into.  I bought this on a Steam Sale, and would certainly not have paid full price for it given the apparent lack of polish.

Supergiant's second game has much to live up to. Their first game, Bastion, was a fantastic gem with great storytelling and good, if sometimes frustrating, gameplay. So how's Transistor?
It's actually quite different than Bastion, and yet is also similar. The gameplay is no longer a hack and slash spamfest, but a very thoughtful combat system that rewards planning rather than button mashing. Naturally, I prefer this to Bastion and its damned challenges, since i'm not very good at that frantic sort of stuff. You also choose from a variety of abilities for combat, and you can attach other abilities to your "main" ones to make those ones do cool stuff. A favorite example of mine being adding an ability that pulls enemies in and attaching it to a large AoE effect that makes enemies take more damage, giving me this lovely black hole... thing that puts enemies in one place where I can proceed to blast em. Good stuff. :D
So combat is, in my opinion, improved. How about story? Here there is still great quality and that lovely narration, in a different form, like there was in Bastion. It does take some time to unfold however, and until that point you are basically running about killing stuff because... I don't know. Fun? Also the game is rather short, with the main storyline lasting about 6 hours. There are lots of challenges and other stuff, but I cleaned everything out in 16 hours - or about half of my still-unfinished Bastion playthrough. Lastly, the ending was, well, something I have mixed feelings about.

Saying Transistor is a spiritual sequel to Bastion would be reasonable but unfair. The game is a beast within itself. Think equal parts Blade Runner, equal parts turn-based combat with a real-time counterpart (and vice versa), and topped off by isometric RPG beat 'em up. Transistor pits players as red-headed diva carrying an over-sized battle sword. (I like the theory that you aren't controlling the sword, but rather the sword is controlling YOU.) I won't get into mechanics because you can read about them on the store page: The combat is a thinking-man's sport. People may argue that you can spam attacks - and that is true - but if you want to be a master, you have to strategize and think out your movements. For these reasons, the game can be unforgiving to those who aren't as cerebral as the developers. Some fights are just insane and my greatest pet peeve exists in this game: Monsters who spawn more monsters.
Overall, I'd recommend this game.

Transistor has a lot of aesthetic appeal, with nice cutscenes, great looking visuals and well written music to fit the atmosphere of the game. Not only does it just look good and sound good, but the gameplay is outstanding. With the option to use a turn and plan out how to wipe out enemies quickly, or to just use your abilities to run through the battle. As well as the gameplay aspect, the story is enthralling. It sucked me in right off the bat being thrown in the middle of the chaos and not knowing what's happening and why it's happening. Supergiant really knows how to make games. 10/10

Okay, so I write this review coming from the single-player Elder Scrolls games. I have to admit. I had pretty dismal hopes for this game. "An Elder Scrolls MMO? Ugh..." was my attitude going into this and I had heard a lot of negative things about the game.
And yes, I do have my gripes with this game, but overall, I genuinely have enjoyed the game so far. If I had to list my complaints... For one, the combat feels a little awkward in comparison to the single player games, but it's not horrible, two, the fact that races are limited to only a handful of classes which kind of limits you role-playing potential, where role-playing is my favorite thing about The Elder Scrolls. Also, I don't know if this is a glitch or not, but sometimes, I'll have an enemy's health refill at random and they'll run away in the middle of a fight. And my final complaint is that you can't loot all enemies that you kill like in the single-player games.
Now for the positives...
1) The character customization is actually pretty damn good. Not only do you get quite a bit of freedom in character building in the initial character creation, but the sheer amount  of customization you can do in game is pretty impressive, so my kudos to Zenimax on that.
2) While the class selection is a bit limited, you still have the ability to customize your character to the way you want them, which is nice. My Khajiit as of writing this review is a Nightblade, but I'm trying to make archery her main ability, since that's my main playstyle in the series.
3) I like how you can't get awesome armor right off the bat.
4) Soloing the game is possible and the game accomodates that, so it's nice to be able to play the game as a single-player game.
If I had to say one final note... It's... okay as an Elder Scrolls game, but a great MMO.

PLEASE NOTE: You actually have to think for this game, if are looking for a overly easy, absent minded game, find a different game, Factorio isnt the game your looking for at this time. If you are up for some thinking and problem solving, keep reading, if not well what are you still doing here?
Pretty freaking awesome. Its got quite the learning curve (if you dont play the tutorial... I was never offered a tutorial). But watch a few youtube videos on it and you will get it. Its a base building, alien slaying, alien invasion (technically you are the invaders but thats not important), cat and mouse game (aliens and you). Its pretty complicated, but once you figure it out its great. It wasnt so sure at the start, I didnt get to do much cause my friends carried me for a long time (cause they had the good sense of looking up tutorials, which I lacked). It reminds me of starcraft brood war, but only graphics wise. I wish it had better graphics but I guess thats part of the charm. The more aliens you kill, and the more pollution you spit out, the stronger they get, the more frequently the attack waves come, so if you sit in your base 100% of the game you will eventually become overrun (because you will eventually run out of resources, it may be a while but it will happen). It has a interesting tech tree. Some things more important than others *cough *cough lamps. The aliens are actually a challenge. They dont give up till you smash the nests. The longer the nest is there, the harder it is to crack, because it grows. Hatchery to hive (not actual terms) if ignored for too long (or if you just dont find it).
Simple edition: Fend off those filthy aliens with your friends or alone, build a kickass factory that runs itself, Mount a counter offensive, retreat because big worms. build a better base. repeat.
Tips and tricks: Machine gun turrets dont need power, just ammo (however laser turrets dont need ammo but do require power)
Machine guns (machine turrets or handheld guns) are ineffective against medium biters (beefier melee alien). However laser turrets ignore their armor and finish them easily.
Drive zoomed out (like really zoomed out), it will be easier to avoid obstacles, this is more important in cars, not so much tanks (cause tanks plow through everything, cars dont)
Try mods, the modding community for this game is great, they are not too far fetched for the game
Play with friends, its alot of fun (you know as long as you dont invite your friend that likes to troll)
I would give it a buy, its certainly worth 20 dollars, despite not looking it from the trailers.

I want to preface this review with the fact that at the time of reviewing it this game is still in Early Access. That being said the game(for the most part) does not feel like it is in early access.
This game is very good is you like resource management. If you hate that kind of thing you should probably look elsewhere. This includes your time as you will be playing and it will be 8pm, next time you check the clock you realize it is 530am and birds are chirping outside.
Although the graphics make the game look like you're playing starcraft 1 and the gameplay is rather simplistic there is tons of things you can make.
You're goal in this game is to make a self sufficient factory that increases in complexity as time goes on until you can finally make a space ship(which generally signals the end of your playthrough). That said replayability is up to the individual. Some people may want to try again and make their factory more efficient or less polutant(the cause of aliens attacking your factory) but I definitely could see some people may find this game lacking in replayability.
What truly makes this game satisfying is when you complete a section of your factory that automates something you previously had a lot of trouble making. An example being at the beginning of the game you find yourself manually making lots of conveyor belts to move your resources around. Conveyor belts require iron plates and gears(which are made from iron plates). So to make a conveyor your character has to have multiple iron plates(made from smelting iron ore in a furnace) and spend several seconds making a small stack of conveyors. Eventually you will have the iron being automatically harvested, smelted, split into two groups, half of it made into gears and then combined to automatically make more conveyors. It feels so satisfying once you put all those steps together to make something truly automated. And the best part is you design every aspect of the process. You're the one who gets to decide how to lay out all your assemblers and furnaces in the best way to utilize your space efficiently.
Multiplayer is the way to play this game. It is so much fun with a group of friends.
This game will run even on my girlfriends potato of a laptop so if your computer runs it will be able to run this game.
I definitely suggest this game to anyone who likes this style of resource management. Very good game!

There is something totally engaging about this game.
At first I was a little wary of its pixalated art style, but it actually helps to put you into the minimalist and classic mindset that really captures the communist mood. Its soundtrack is just perfect, with the right blend silence and background noise that keeps you engaged as you run through the same actions over and over again.
At times the repetitiveness borders on tedium but the story and the character you are given keep pushing you forward.
Having to make moral decisions that can affect your income for the day with bribes or citations that will then have an impact on your family and their survival is a level of depth I didn't even expect going in.
One thing I will say is that it is not forgiving! The tutorial is not the best, and it really expects you to pick it up as you go and realize what it wants or doesn't want. Sometimes a single letter will be incorrect and you have to spot it or get a citation.
I haven't finished the entire story yet, but I can't wait to see what happens!

Let me preface this review by saying that I am not a fan of stealth games, any game that requires a modicum of patience I usually won't touch. That being said, Alien: Isolation has changed my views on that. Every second spent hiding from hostile humans, Working Joes, and most of all the Alien feels like a fight for survival. The AI for the Alien stalks you from every corner making the game feel tense and difficult without being frustrating. I spent countless times dying only to realize I needed to use stealthier tactics and distraction methods to hold out just to hit the next objective. The game doesn't rely on "scripted" encounters, or normally placed enemies, the Alien WILL find you like Liam Neeson.
While this game does have combat, ammunition is sparse, and it just makes the atmosphere more tense and helpless. The only negative part of this game is the backtracking can get a little bit annoying in the second half of the game. They could have possibly cut some backtracking or a mission or two just to make it a little less frustrating.
-9 out of 10. Great game that deserves a playthrough.

If you are an alien fan, you will love the visuals and feel of the game. I have given it a positive review because of that environment and because I was on the edge of my seat the entire game listening for any small crack or alien scream to alert me that I was in trouble.
That being said, I can't help but agree with people on the problem with backtracking. For the vast majority of the game, the backtracking wasn't a problem because of new equipment that you received that would allow you to divulge on different paths. However, the last few levels of backtracking were just not acceptable and it made it so I didn't appreciate the emotional rollercoaster of a game that I just went through. I don't want to spoil anything, but one level has you go back and forth 4 times in an area that is very linear. It made me feel like dodging the alien the first time meant nothing, as I had to do it 3 more times only with lighting changes.
These issues almost ruined the game for me, but thankfully these problems get overshadowed by the incredible visuals (would highly recommend a rig that can play on max settings), excellent sound effects, and an overall enjoyable horror experience.
TL;DR,
Pros -
Great Visuals
Excellent Sound Design
Great for Alien Fans
Cons -
Unfortunate Backtracking

Okay, so I write this review coming from the single-player Elder Scrolls games. I have to admit. I had pretty dismal hopes for this game. "An Elder Scrolls MMO? Ugh..." was my attitude going into this and I had heard a lot of negative things about the game.
And yes, I do have my gripes with this game, but overall, I genuinely have enjoyed the game so far. If I had to list my complaints... For one, the combat feels a little awkward in comparison to the single player games, but it's not horrible, two, the fact that races are limited to only a handful of classes which kind of limits you role-playing potential, where role-playing is my favorite thing about The Elder Scrolls. Also, I don't know if this is a glitch or not, but sometimes, I'll have an enemy's health refill at random and they'll run away in the middle of a fight. And my final complaint is that you can't loot all enemies that you kill like in the single-player games.
Now for the positives...
1) The character customization is actually pretty damn good. Not only do you get quite a bit of freedom in character building in the initial character creation, but the sheer amount  of customization you can do in game is pretty impressive, so my kudos to Zenimax on that.
2) While the class selection is a bit limited, you still have the ability to customize your character to the way you want them, which is nice. My Khajiit as of writing this review is a Nightblade, but I'm trying to make archery her main ability, since that's my main playstyle in the series.
3) I like how you can't get awesome armor right off the bat.
4) Soloing the game is possible and the game accomodates that, so it's nice to be able to play the game as a single-player game.
If I had to say one final note... It's... okay as an Elder Scrolls game, but a great MMO.

The visuals, story, soundtrack and gameplay are superb. So much fun was had, and so many feels were felt. Supergiant games really know how to make a damn fine game. First Bastion, now Transistor. Looking forward to their future projects!

This game is everything you'd expect from SuperGiant Games, which is great, but also a little disappointing. The artwork, music, story and acting is phenomenal, and the gameplay is rock solid --- just like Bastion, by which I mean that it's great like Bastion is great, but also that it's great in pretty much the exact same ways that Bastion is great. It's not Bastion 2, but you wouldn't know it if it wasn't for the title. I can certainly understand that it'd be nearly impossible for SuperGiant Games to release a game without having it constantly compared to Bastion --- and maybe that's why they chose to not deviate too much from what made Bastion amazing. I don't know. But I have already played Bastion and been thoroughly amazed by it. Obviously a second iteration of the formula isn't going to leave the same impression, and thus Transistor falls a little flat, which is completely unfair to say after using adjectives such as "phenomenal" and "rock solid" about it, but that's the reality. It's a phenomenal and rock solid game that somehow doesn't quite impress as much as you'd expect it to. I'd still recommend it in a heartbeat though. And, I do want to say that the biggest deviation from SuperGiant Games' previous indie smash hit, the combat system, is really, really good and it makes battles feel very futuristic, manageable and awesome.
TL;DR: This game has everything that Bastion had --- and more. And that is, however weird it may sound, probably its weakest point.

This is a weird game to describe. My best attempt is that it's a Cookie Clicker-alike. You recruit characters to go fight enemies for gold, then you use that gold to upgrade the main hub (a soda tavern) with things that increase the amount of recruitable people. There's also armor and weapons, making it more of an RPG. As far as I can tell, your session does not end until your whole party dies off, then you begin the process again. You also upgrade to another difficulty once you beat the big boss you're building up to.
What sets this apart from other Cookie Clicker-alikes is the fact that you can make it as strategic or as automated as you'd like, right from the start. See, there's a button that makes your party auto-fight, which means you can just start up the fights and let it run in the background - there's even an option to make them auto-equip the best armor/weapons. That means you can tackle it as a Cookie Clicker game or as a strategy game. The convenience is brought to further heights when you purchase a warp that lets you pay a reasonable price to jump to the highest levels you were on before you died.
If I had any nitpick, it's that the game honestly doesn't have much of a soda motif, which would have been a very fun aesthetic to see. The tavern's several sodas (which are unlocked to gain access to different types of recuirts) are a small factor here, as is the collectible soda bottles that you get by moving onto higher difficulties. When you remove those two minor things, it kinda just looks like a standard RPG. That being said, I do like the sprite work, and the sound design.
If you like Ragnarok Online this for you, just be ready to deal with the server problems the game is currently suffering from right after public launch.

Sometimes you find love where you didn't expect it. I certainly didn't expect much of a game called "Call of Juarez: Gunslinger", or at least not more than a mindelss little trash fest. Actually the only reason I bought this game was because Chris Fanklin said some things about the story telling that sounded interesting - and the game was on sale.
But now that I've finished the game over the last two days I can barely remember the last time I had that much fun with a game. The action is fast and there's enough variety to keep the interest even for someone like me, who usually doesn't like shooters. I played the game with an Xbox controller and it worked fine (even if it wasn't the most easy game for me).

You barely see a game that in manages to intertwine storytelling and gameplay mechanics in a way that both complement each other. Gunslinger does it with an easy that not only impressed me but could also be a textbook example for the whole ego shooter genre, that seems to be stuck in the same tropes since Half-Life was released over a decade ago.
I didn't expect much from Gunslinger and got a game that impressed me with it's perfect execution of a well thought out idea. It might not be as ambitious as Bioshock Infinite, but it's certainly a better game in any regard.

8.5 / 10 (An enjoyable and fun redemption to the Call of Juarez series)
One would think that after the abyssmal Call of Juarez: The Cartel, this series would have been done for. However, by going with a Wild West narrative, this game is full of flavour. Told as a gunslinger's relating his snipets of his past to an audience, we become engrossed in that tale. At times, sections are repeated to correct facts missing from the legends. The story also adapts depending on how you deal with your shootout duels with well known persons from the wild west. It all amounts to a climax that properly concludes Silas' tale of vengence.
Combat is fast paced and enjoyable throughout the game. With the ability to 'bullet time' on command and given a chance to avoid death when your 'death sense' is full, the player is always given a split second chance to overcome insurmountable situations. Periodic scripted quicktime events are best when done right, but if not, the quicktime event ends, and the remaining enemies can be dispatched in normal gameplay. The ability to fail the quicktime event without resulting in death rewards doing the quicktime right but doesn't punish the player irreversably.
Bosses provide different challenges before you can get close enough to dueling them. (Avoiding gatling guns, Thrown dynamite, arena fights.
Dueling is this games signature as you try to keep a reticle on your opponent and maneuver your hand closer to your gun for when the shootout. Pulling first results in a dishonorble kill (thereby costing you your bounty). So the skill to dueling is to be able to wait for your opponent to pull first, but you kill them first. It is a rather fun and interesting play of skill that also shows the metrics of how well you performed. Higher handspeed results in a faster draw giving you (marginally, but importantly) more time to shoot the opponent. Higher Focus allows you to target the opponent faster and more accurately. And the game also tracks how fast you pulled your gun. Knowing these numbers helps you know where to improve your technique and skill. Truly, an excellent mechanic.
As the player levels up, skills unlock and the player is not confined to any particular track. These abilities provide subtle, but noticable, improvements in your gameplay. As you go through the game, you find secret 'nuggets' which provide details about the persons and places of the wild west era. This is an interesting and educational use of token pickups.
Once you finish the game, a NG+ mode unlocks where you can replay the game with all previously unlocked skills intact. The game also includes a Realism mode (no hud information) called True West Mode to provide a more serious challenge to your gunslinging. From the first time you play and arcade mode and dueling mode are available. These modes are seperate from the main game. The arcade mode builds skills through successful runs with each class used, The mode has a 3 star rating to indicate bronze/silver/gold standings in points (where comboing really pays off). The duel mode runs through 15 consecutive duels where experience with duels really pays off.
This is an excellent FPS with flavourful narratives and environments to play through.  Periodically, enemies can be very difficult to identify from the environment, especially if they seem to have pinpoint accuracy at times sometimes. The final fight be very difficult and chaotic as you have limited cover, even obvious cover gets shot through (feels somewhat like artificial difficulty - looks like it protects you, but does not). But it does lead to an epic shootout in the end.  Very satisfying.

I'm a huge fan of Western movies. Once Upon a Time in the West, The Man with No Name Trilogy, The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, Tombstone, The Wild Bunch, True Grit, 3:10 to Yuma, etc. To me, when it comes to a good Western, I'm not too concerned about the tone or style. I'll enjoy 2+ hours of a Western without a single gunshot just as much one where everyone is getting put down like old yeller.
However when it comes to videogames, I want a lot of action. For the longest time Sunset Riders was the only Western game I enjoyed. I guess I never had the patience for titles like Red Dead Redemption* and...uh...okay well there haven't been a lot of Western games period. I never realized just how barren the genre really was until now. It's really quite strange because with a little imagination, you can do anything with a Western-themed videogame.
So let's look at Gunslinger. As the story goes, Silas Greaves is a man seeking vengeance. In his search for his brother's murderers he encounters many of the legends of the West. Billy the Kid, Jesse James, Butch Cassidy & The Sundance Kid, you get the idea. This can't be just mere coincidence...can it? The storyline is unreliably narrated, with storyline changes affecting progress of the game. Expect to run into situations where you go one way, but then Silas is all "Wait. That's not how it went." and suddenly you're going somewhere else. All told it's very effective and adds a lot to what is a traditional Western storyline.
Speaking of traditional, this game is an arcade shootemup. There are some rare moments of quiet reflection, but you never spend more than a few seconds, not shooting cowboys in the face. The game is divided into several short stages. You run through the various environs, outlaws accost you, you gun them down. Each stage usually ends in a boss-fight. Some of these fights are straight out of Sunset Riders, just in FPS fashion. You've got the guy with the big health meter, he's firing on you from an advantageous position with the assistance of other thugs, oh if only they dropped a memorable one-liner when you dropped them (Bury me with my money...). Stages can also end the old-fashioned way, with a stand-off. In these duels you have to center your sight and steady your hand on your gun. Only the fastest and most accurate draw lives to tell the tale. These are pretty neat, though in the main game there isn't much to set one duel apart from the other. As you progress the outlaws become faster on the draw and move around more to throw off your focus at least.
For the most part, Gunslinger is pretty much a shooting gallery. Surviving dozens of armed bandits is one thing, but killing them stylishly for larger XP bonuses is what it's really all about. The trickier the shot, the more points you receive. Not everyone can ricochet a bullet through a wooden post and into a man's skull in the blink of an eye, but for those that can, it's worth a bunch of points. Trickier shots also reward the player with more concentration. Yes, this is obviously a mechanic with its own gauge at the corner of the screen. Concentration is basically the "slow down..pardner" button. Aside from causing everyone to move at the speed of snail, other benefits such as increased-damage are applied. XP is used to unlock various skills. While they're tied to certain weapons (pistols, rifles, or shotguns) the bonuses are univerally applied.
The first play-through is probably going to take five hours or less. As I said, Gunslinger doesn't fuss around with the details. Multiple difficulties are available, including a bonus "True West" setting. Not only does Silas die a bit easier, he also doesn't get all those helpful UI elements. Even something as simple as a crosshair is straight-up gone. At this point it is definitely to your benefit to take advantage of the New Game + so all of your acculumated skills carry over.
There are two additional modes in Gunslinger. Arcade mode dumps all of the plot, throws in more bad-guys, and changes the skill system. Instead of three sets of skills, you get three classes each with their own set. Getting the high scores practically require that you chain the entire stage. That means knowing where every outlaw is going to appear, reloading at the right moments, and using concentration when absolutely necessary. This mode definitely lives up to its name. It's frenetic and prone to chaos at first, but players will eventually become skilled enough to clear entire levels without wasting a shot. Duel mode is shockingly all about the duels. There are 15 stages and you have a limited number of lives to work with. If you enjoy the duels in the main game, that's plenty reason to consider giving this mode a run-through.
Really though, what I enjoy the most about this game is all the shooting. Actually this game graduates to the level of shootin' game. Gunslinger is at it's best when you're rushing through stages capping everyone with trick shots and looking golden. Unfortunately there isn't the Western equivalent of a "360 no-scope". Still it's one of those shooters that knows how to make a player feel good about killin'. Also I like how there are bonus points for "last-breath" kills. One thing I hate about these checkpoint-based shooters is that they feel the need to obscure the player's vision when they're about to die. Look, it's a videogame, when I'm close to death I want to be able to see everything, not be handicapped. At least Gunslinger gets it right by giving a bonus for shootin' someone while half-blind.
With good story-telling and even better action, Call of Juarez (registered trademark) Gunslinger is definitely worth a look.
*It could be I'm just sour because there's never been a PC port. I really didn't spend much time with RDR on my X360 or PS3.
