In regard to this review, keep in mind that I have not played CoJ: The Cartel. Not that I heard great things about it...
The two other predecessors, however, I have played and finished.
The first thing I would say, if you are a fan of the series, is to divert your expectations. The first two games both were stories that attempted to, and perhaps succeeded, into gripping you into their narrative. A heart clenching story of vengeance and/or a lust for a haunted treasure.
In comparison, Gunslinger's story seems like a mini version of it. A simple adventure about and narrated by Silas Greaves, spoken in the context of a Saloon like he was a Cowboy telling a tall tale.
The interesting thing done here is how the story impacts the game, whereas it's usually vice versa. Your audience at several points takes over the narration for a moment, telling how they heard an event in question went down.
And you play it all out, in a non-forced manner, taking their narrated path through the level. Eventually Silas will cut back in and tell how it really happened, winding back time to let the player cross through the level that way.
It's a very impressive, if not unique way of telling a story in a game.
The story itself, due to this, often comes across as a bit light heartened. It feels like it's lacking that darkness, that grit. But let me tell you, it eventually does come around, as Silas tells the story of his life as a Bounty Hunter in his quest for Revenge, and how he got around on starting in that line of work.
The array of guns may also seem simplified. A total of seven firearms and dynamite as throwables. It seems like that's not much, but for a story of this length, it seems enough. By the time you've gotten well comfortable and skilled, you'll have levelled up plenty and gotten around to a nice build to complement your weapon of choice.
Talking of Levelling, the game makes use of three skilltrees. They mainly befit the Archetypes of Gunslinger, Ranger and Trapper. Which simply means Pistols, Long Range and Shotgun/Dyanimite. Each skilltree awards you with a stat boost and pretty skin of a specific weapon halfway and at the end of the skilltree. Each tree has at least two unique skills that make you an even deadlier man, and the weaker skills tend to have some synergy going with other skills. Again, it's not very extensive, but enough for a game of this length.
Combat wise, it feels pretty good. The guns have weight to them, and fatal hits feel very satisfying. You have regenerating health, but so does the enemy apparently. You can fire two bullets in their chest, but if they find cover, those bullets can be considered wasted.
I played this game on Hard, which especially urged me to make good use of cover. The enemy will not relent, and is quite intelligent compared to some titles. They take cover the moment you are spotted, move to another one if their current one proves not good enough, and they seemingy try to outflank you when they have the numbers. I was kept on my toes quite a bit, and every enemy felt like they could end me very quickly if I didn't pay attention.
Overall, Gunslinger feels like a smaller (not necessarily stripped-down) version of the first game and Bound in Blood. But those were also full titiles, while at the time of writing this game is sold for 15.
So all in all, I would say that, with rational expectations, you'd very well get your money's worth.

This is a weird game to describe. My best attempt is that it's a Cookie Clicker-alike. You recruit characters to go fight enemies for gold, then you use that gold to upgrade the main hub (a soda tavern) with things that increase the amount of recruitable people. There's also armor and weapons, making it more of an RPG. As far as I can tell, your session does not end until your whole party dies off, then you begin the process again. You also upgrade to another difficulty once you beat the big boss you're building up to.
What sets this apart from other Cookie Clicker-alikes is the fact that you can make it as strategic or as automated as you'd like, right from the start. See, there's a button that makes your party auto-fight, which means you can just start up the fights and let it run in the background - there's even an option to make them auto-equip the best armor/weapons. That means you can tackle it as a Cookie Clicker game or as a strategy game. The convenience is brought to further heights when you purchase a warp that lets you pay a reasonable price to jump to the highest levels you were on before you died.
If I had any nitpick, it's that the game honestly doesn't have much of a soda motif, which would have been a very fun aesthetic to see. The tavern's several sodas (which are unlocked to gain access to different types of recuirts) are a small factor here, as is the collectible soda bottles that you get by moving onto higher difficulties. When you remove those two minor things, it kinda just looks like a standard RPG. That being said, I do like the sprite work, and the sound design.

Welcome to Plantera, and not to be confused by the Terraria boss, because this game has nothing to do with that.
Ok for the review:
Plantera is a "click-a-thon" game, where you own a farm of your own, and grow fruits and vegetables. Once they are grown, you click on them to collect them, and you get money to buy more crops for more money. There are 3 types of plants you can have (currently): Trees, bushes, and crops. The 3 types just produce different foods, with not much difference. There are also animals you can have, including (so far) chickens, pigs, cows, and sheep. (as well as a dog, but that works differently.) The animals also produce stuff for even more money. You are not alone however, because there are these blue helpers that, hence the name, help you collect the crops, even when you are not playin! Because the helpers also work when you are not playing, means that Plantera has a phone game sometimes, where you play the game in short periods, and come back every now and then.
Note that Plantera doesn't have an end to it, and there's no objective to the game. You can also unlock everything the game has so far in under an hour, so that might put people off on that one.
The game is for casual people who want to play a game that relieves stress. In my opinion, the way to get more enjoyment is to acheivement hunt this game. (meaning getting all of the acheivements.)
Finally, if that last part sounded negative towards this game, theres this that might change your mind about it. The game is in early acess, and is being worked on a lot. It seems like the people who made this game are working, and releasing new, but small things every week. With the $2 cost, it seems overpriced, but if it get more updates, I think it's worth it, or if there's a price drop.
I give it an 8/10 (right now)

Transistor is like nothing else I have ever played, and it is easily my Game of the Year so far for 2014.
Yes, the game is short (between 4-6 hours). Yes, it's extremely linear. And yes: to some, it may not be as good as Bastion (Supergiant Games' debut title). Though, I would respectfully disagree with those who consider Bastion to be the superior title. In my mind, Transistor is a more focused game that has a much clearer and more confident vision. Just my opinion, though I've heard others describe the game in the same fashion.
A prominent online gaming publication described the game as "intoxicating," and I think that is an excellent word to use. Transistor honestly makes you feel like you've wandered into a state of lucid dreaming. Darren Korb's score is just bloody brilliant. There are echoes of glitch-jazz, bossa nova, hard rock and just about every other genre-fused amalgamation you can dream up. Combat and cutscenes are woven together so tightly you often experience the equivalent of the "just one more page" feeling that comes from reading a good book. Before you know it, you've finished the game and are being asked if you would like to "recurse" through the story. It's a clever and simple way to make the "New Game+" concept work within the world Supergiant has created.
Combat would take a long time to explain and I've never been one to dig into the details of how developers engineer their combat systems. What we have is an elegant combination of turn-based and active-battle mechanics set within battlefields that provide cover and opportunities for player positioning (where you are in relation to the enemy). So, standard RPG concepts like "backstabbing" make an appearance. Every action (apart from basic movement) is oriented around "Functions," which are essentially computer programs that act as either usable attacks, upgrades to those attacks, or passive buffs. Every single Function in the game (there are 16 total) can be used in any of those three capacities. Where things really get fun is when the player is introduced to Function "stacking." Any function can be upgraded with itself. And the results of stacking the correct combination of Functions together can provide for combat moves that are devastating and gorgeously rendered.
I can't count the number of times I've just smiled and shook my head as I watched things unfold. The adrenaline rush from uppercutting an enemy with the Transistor and blasting them to holly hell--effectively splitting them into a explosion of sparks and twisted metal--RIGHT as one of Darren Korb's tracks hits a towering climax is, in a word, "intoxicating".
One final note: I'm a busy gamer, and I'm rather picky too. I NEVER complete games to a 100% achievement rating. Transistor is an exception. I stuck with it and recently mastered everything. That stretched my playtime out to about 18 hours. Not bad at all for $20. But the experience of this game is about so much more than how many hours you'll get to play it. Transistor is an entertainment experience, and one that should be relished and savored as if it were a fine wine.
Seriously, buy it. You're going to love it.

This is one of those games that you've probably heard about or saw in an article but didn't think much of it. However, this game is well worth a look. Supergiant Games does all the right things with Transistor. They've made a neat action-RPG that manages to feel novel and invoke the player with a desire to get more of the game.
The story takes place in a cyberpunk-esque city. You play as Red, a singer who lost her voice, and finds a fancy techno greatsword called the Transistor. The story itself is a bit vague and doesn't spell everything out for you, which is a refreshing take on some of today's stories that are filled with scripted explosions and obvious plot twists. The story kind of unfolds through the action and setting itself, as you see what is happening within the city. Other parts of the story, as well as some interesting side notes, are acquired by checking terminals and gaining bios on the denizens of the city, similar to Bioshock. Also, Logan Cunningham from Bastion makes a return as the narrator, of sorts. All of this leads to an intriguing compilation of a plot that left me curious even after the second playthrough. I even thought the ending was satisfying and bravely done, although some might disagree.
The combat is unlike any I've seen in any other games. Like other action-RPG's, you have skills that you acquire and use in combat and you gain XP for successful combat. However, Transistor adds in a few nuanced features that made me really enjoy the action. For one, you can fight in combat in real-time like normal, but you can also pause the action via Turn() and plot your attacks and moves, then unpause to watch the fury fly. The flip side to this, though, is that using Turn() makes it so you can't attack for a moment. So, you really have to strategize when you want to fight enemies head on or use Turn() to land some precise strikes or flee certain death. Speaking of death, you don't necessarily die when your health reaches zero. Instead, you just lose one of your skills (functions) until you pass through a couple access points. This might sound agitating, but it just forces you to be creative. Say you lose a couple functions that you've been using for awhile but lost them and now you have to switch to some other functions that you've never used. Maybe it doesn't work but maybe you find a combination of functions that work really well. I've done that a few times and it's satisfying to test out new combinations and see them really flourish. Another thing about functions is that you can combine them. Some games say, "you have 12 skills but only 4 skill slots so the other 8 just have to sit there and do nothing." But this game says, "You've got 12 skills and 4 slots, so how about you use those extras to upgrade your functions or give you passive abilities." The really cool thing is that there is an unimaginably large number of combinations of functions that you can use. Want your short range attack to have an explosion that does DoT? Do it. Want a ranged attack to stun your enemy and siphon their health? Do it! You can also assign functions to passive slots that increase general damage, generate a shield, or turn you invisible after killing an enemy, to name a few. Lastly, the difficulty is set to a certain level. So if you get good enough you can just blow through the game. Or you can add limiters that hinder you in some way, but also give you an XP boost. This all adds to some really challenging and satisfying combat.
The art design and music really make this game memorable. The graphics have a watercolor look and make the city look beautiful. If you played Bastion, you may remember the cutscenes that were done in a similar fashion. The city's mood is dark but the art still brings out the lights and life of the city. And the soundtrack is fantastic. Darren Korb from Bastion handles the music well. Most of it is like old rock, electronic jazz, which I dig. Ashley Barrett adds her lovely voice to some of the songs as well. Also, you can press a button in the game and your character will hum along to the song. I enjoyed this too much. I've never bought a soundtrack to a game but I'm seriously considering buying this one.
In general, Sugergiant Games did an excellent job with this game. Everything felt solid about the game as a whole. So, if you enjoyed Bastion or if you want an RPG that has a lot of cool features (which I didn't mention everything!) with an interesting story and a stellar art style and soundtrack, definitely check this game out. If you've made it to the end, thanks for reading my first review!

For all their hundred-million dollar budgets and hundreds strong development teams, it feels as if indie games have all but entirely eclipsed those of AAA developers. Transistor stands at the precipice of this phenomenon, an unprecedented achievement in artistic vision and game design that I hesitate to review for fear of not doing it justice. Supergiant Games, creators of the outstanding Bastion, have not been resting on their laurels, returning after three years with an experience that has completely toppled any expectations I previously had for it, leaving me stunned and in awe at the scope of their vision and the skill in which they execute it. Transistor is, simply put, a masterpiece.
Transistor isn’t the story of a falling city; of the rebel group, Camerata, letting loose a viscous process to annihilate the city of Cloudbank to be rebuilt to their designs. It’s not the story of the many characters filling its voluminous backstory, fleshing out a fascinating futuristic dreamscape that is so similar yet different to our own world. No, it is the story of two people, or more accurately the relationship between a girl and her sword. The dynamic between Red, a singer who has had her voice stolen, and the Transistor, a talking sword now housing the soul of a deadman, is what drives the narrative. Despite Red’s inability to talk, the Transistor’s dialog creates a tangible connection between the two; an emotional tie that makes the continued suffering of Red, and the guilt expressed by the Transistor (who somehow feels responsible for what happened to Red), incredibly real and heartbreaking.
It would be too easy to write Transistor off as using its many narrative tricks to hide the fact that its plot is fairly straightforward, because it’s not about what happens throughout the story, but the relationship between its two leads that makes it so compelling. All too often games will try to force characters to depend on each other, whether through arbitrary mechanics or cliched victim roles, but Transistor sidesteps this issue by having the two characters literally rely on each other to survive. They need each other, and its for this that the narrative manages to create such an effective emotional connection with these characters; similarly causing you to despise those that have put them through so much distress. As simple as it may sound, the nuance of every line and its delivery is no small feat, and a true testament to the writers and voice actors behind them.
I could go on at end for how emotionally invested I became in the characters of Transistor, but it’s the finesse of its gameplay that truly astounded me. Aside from some mild exploration, the experience is entirely focused around its incredibly deep and rewarding combat system, which seems outwardly inaccessible but is shockingly intuitive once you get your hands on it.
Combat can be broken down most easily into two phases: real time and the planning stage. During the former, you can use any of your abilities at will, but enemies in turn can also move and attack, which becomes an issue with the long build up required for most attacks. This is when you transition to the second phase, which then turns the game into a sort of strategy RPG, freezing time and allowing you to plan out your moves (which will then be executed near instantly when you leave the phase) with the only restraint being the action bar which is used up with each move you make. It's not an entirely unique formula, but Supergiant Games has carved out an incredibly fine tuned and complex niche for itself, with the sheer number of different ways you can approach an encounter.
Every action you make is the result of a function you have slotted in, which in turn can then have additional functions slotted on top of themselves, as well as passive functions which give you boosts outside of individual moves. However, none of these are separated into classes or otherwise excluded from being assigned a specific role with the rest of your abilities. This creates an incredible amount of options for you to experiment with, with each function you unlock having three unique abilities onto itself (if not more when combined with other functions), and new functions being added regularly as you progress and level up.
Supergiant has also found a brilliant incentive to getting players to try out new combinations they might otherwise never use, by tying every bit of backstory to a specific function, which then needs to be used in all three slots (technique, enhancement, and passive) in order to unlock all of a character's biography. It’s a fantastic way to almost entirely fix a common problem of getting stuck in a routine of the using the same abilities the entire game, and had me constantly swapping different functions in which kept the combat fresh the entire game (even after having beaten it I haven’t used every combination there is, creating a ton of replay value on top of the already included new game plus mode).
Bastion was an undeniable artistic treat, but in comparison to Transistor it might as well be a rough prototype of a game. The art design of every single frame is unbelievably gorgeous, from amazing architecture and environmental designs, to characters and even the subtle yet beautiful sparks that spring forth from Red dragging the Transistor around. The dark color palette matches the somber mood of the narrative, but it does so without bringing you down with it, leaving enough brightness and pure beauty despite the events happening around you to make you feel like you’re on a vacation to a fantastical city in the sky. Darren Korb once again returns to deliver a soundtrack that surpasses what I even thought he was capable, with a layered and elaborate score that still feels as raw and personal as he's known for.
Transistor left me floored. What Supergiant Games has accomplished is hard to properly put into words, as even with all I’ve said I can’t help but think I’ve barely scratched the surface of the praise I wish to heap upon the game. It’s vision is remarkable, stunningly consistent and inspired in every aspect, achieving a level of excellence that exceeded my already high expectations. It’s undoubtedly one of the best games I’ve played this, or possibly any year, and is an experience that cannot be overstated or should in any way be passed up.

Is Rome II good? Yes, the land battles are fun, there is immense variety when it comes to factions, with diversity in units, the Grand Campaign is highly addictive, and replayability potential is massive, as each culture is different. The graphics are very  good for a 2013 game, especially of this scale, and we can have massive battles with hundreds of soldiers on each side. But it has a number of serious flaws that need to be addressed. Firstly, the performance. While the game is stable and runs decently, it does experience framerate drops during the turns of the other factions, and while zooming in to ground view during battles. Those drops are not horrendous, but my PC is a good one, and this game is old. I have a 960, and it is to be expected that a 2013 game would perform well on this hardware, which it does, but there are a few times when it should do much better. Secondly, the naval battles are just boring. Uninteresting units(merely the army units on a ship), uninteresting ships, and every faction has virtually the same ships. Thirdly, diplomatic featuress are a bit lacking. No trading of provinces, your client states dont feel like client states but just ordinary allies. They are too independent. Logically, they should behave like puppet states but they dont. We should be able to push them around, intimidate them, as after all, they are our client states, and insubordination would not be tolerated by a faction that is so powerful. Lastly, SEGA's dlc practices. Nations like Athens, Sparta are not playable in the base game's Grand Campaign. Not even a single Iberian faction is playable in the base game. These factions cannot be unlocked, they need to be bought via dlcs.  An entire culture, the Iberians, are not playable in the base game. At least Macedon, Seluccid etc are there as playable Hellenistic factions, but there should have been at least one Iberian faction in the base game.
Overall, I recommend this game, because it is extremely fun. But these flaws are not minor and should not be ignored.

The coins unlock many features that are used to limit and frustrate you into supporting the game.  I'm not sure if this is the best tactic, but it got me to buy it.
The crafting, item upgrading, gems, cards and pets are all pretty well done.  Crafting is actually relevant for obtaining some of the best gears.  Upgrading makes almost all peices of gear better in some way.  Gems provide neat buffs depending on the peice and can be leveled up to provide bigger buffs.  I like these systems.
The worst part about this game is bots and how they are trying to handle them.  Atm bots are to a degree ruining certain farmable crafting materials prices by having them constantly farmed.  This sucks but it also makes those mats cheaper for those looking to buy instead of farm, but it makes the farming yourself harder.  The restrictions on trading and the AH can get pretty frustrating.  They were put in to stop bots, but not really working.  They are however semi frustrating to real humans.  All in all though, they have already patched and made quite a few of them better.... provided you are using a token.  The most frustrating part is that you can't move gold between your characters, and if you buy any item off the AH that has no potiential, it becomes bound to that character.  These are not that huge as far as negitive impacts go.
I've only had lag for 1 day.  It was the day they split servers.  Can't really say its an issue at all.
TL:DR
Its a solid start to a game with many many fun choices to explore and play out.  Bots suck, but aren't that big an issue atm.  Alot of the complaints i see are solved by supporting the game and getting an in game Token for premium features.  That doesn't mean its pay to win, just lowers frustration level with trade and item limitations.  Meaning if you don't have a Token you must be patient.

It would seem that Creative Assembly clearly have a lot of love and respect for the 1979 film, Alien.
The atmosphere in this game was incredible, I couldn't put it down. It's not a short game either so you really get your monies worth here. I'd highly recommend this to any horror fan and or Alien fan, it feels like an addition to the universe rather than a sloppily made tacked on mess. It's not the scariest game out there however there are quite a few "Oh crap... ohcrapohcrapohcrapohcrap" moments. There is enough here to be able to enjoy as either a newcomer to the Alien franchise or as a die hard fan.
However a few minor frustrations, some glitchy A.I. behaviour can somtimes take you out of the experience but this is only highlighted by the fact that the game is polished, so take that with a pinch of salt. One thing I can't forgive is that occasionally the zenomorph just knows where you're at, it can be a little cheap and makes encounters feel somewhat random, rather than genuine. I'd like to think i've died by a mistake of my own rather than the game spinning a wheel of fortune. The last issue is that vents and other hiding places require you to press a button prompt to enter. Button prompts work fine for say... lockers, it doesn't work so well for vents. When you're being chased down mercilessly, time is of the essence. The last thing you want is to be awkwardly rubbing up agaisnt a wall shouting to yourself "GET IN THE VENT! GET IN THE VENT!".
These are minor blemishes on an otherwise spotless adventure, I feel like i'm picking at hairs but they're still issues nonetheless. Pick this game up, run for your life for a bit, it's a good laugh.

This action packed game hides a surprising depth and tactical thinking. Solo or coop, it's a blast.
The trailers for Broforce shows it as a fast paced carnage, a run and gun and leave no survivor type of thing. But this is probably not how you're gonna play Broforce. You will soon understand that rushing blindly will probably kill you long before you reach the end of a level. There are tons of stuff that can kill you, and it's usually best to plan your path into the next serie of enemies and explosive barrels if you don't want to get blown to bits.
But that tactical approach is what makes the game fun. Rushing blindly can be fun, and sometimes does work, but if the game had been all about that, it wouldn't be as interesting, and it wouldn't hold your interest for long. The free promo game "The Expandabros" is actually proof of that, it's much more lenient, and you can run and gun through it all, but it soon becomes repetitive and boring.
The tactical approach is greatly completemented by the huge cast of "Bros" that you will unlock as you play the game. Each of them is a spoof of a well known character from Hollywood action movies.
Beside the chuckle you get when you reach the next bro reveal, this allows change the gameplay drastically. All bros have unique weapons and special powers, and you will switch to a new bro everytime you die or liberate one of the prisoners (they act as 1-Up, giving you a free live) spread around the levels.
Therefore, you're constantly switching how you need to approach the game. Some Bros have great range to pick out enemies from afar, others have great power but require to get close. They are probably not balanced, some are clearly better than others, but even an underpowered Bro can shine in the rights circumstances. And in any case, this constant switch of approach keeps the game fresh during the whole lengthy campaign.
Behind it's apparent mindlessness, Broforce is a very clever title, and that makes it a great game, rather than just a flash in a pan. Solo players will enjoy being very tactical to survive, while multiplayers will bring more mayhem but also more leniency in how you approach the game. Both modes work great and are a joy to play.

I decided from the start that I was going to approach this game as though it was single player. I've played a lot of MMOs (taking a break from 11 years of WoW currently) and needed something fresh. This game has been exactly what the doctor ordered. Everything you've come to love in the main Elder Scrolls series is present; a strong main story line, a plethora of side quests that keep you engaged in the world, the little touches out in the world that make exploration a joy. The addition of the MMO element allows for the world to simply feel more populated and "living". Each zone that I discover I spend hours and hours in, exploring them fully and loving every second of it.

The combat system is deceptively simple, and does take some getting used to. With so many skills being attaching to your weapon type or guilds, the different classes can start to feel the same which gets a little frustrating.

Auction houses are sorely missed, relying instead on using guild vendors and trade chat. Bag space is also extremely limited, espcially for horders like myself. At first I was okay with what became a complicated system of mailing things to different alts, but eventually relented and bought the Plus Membership. The shared resources bag that you get with the subscription alleviated that issue.
Overall, a little over 100 hours in to the game, I would give it a solid 7.5/10

Papers Please is a very unusual game. I’m not even sure how I can describe it effectively.
You play as a dude who checks passports for a fictional communist country. Sounds boring right? But so much drama happens. People try to bribe you, they tell you their sob stories, they try to smuggle weapons and drugs, your superiors are eager to punish you for any mistake you make, terrorists ask you for your help in overthrowing the government (and you can!), and if you mess up, either your family will starve, you’ll be arrested, or you might just die in a terrorist attack. There’s tons of different endings, and all of your actions have far-reaching consequences.
I used a walkthrough, because I didn’t find the gameplay very fun, I just wanted to experience the story. But I think the gameplay is supposed to NOT be fun. It’s supposed to be really stressful, and to put you in the shoes of the character you play. And maybe I cheapened the experience a bit by using that walkthrough. Oh well.
Anyway! The story was intense! It makes you really think about what effect your actions will have on others and yourself.

So I got sent this out of the blue, for review purposes.  But first small background; I am very impatient when it comes to games, especially retail I feel like hiding features behind a time wall is padding and a type that should really only be used in free to play games or games that actually have a reason beyond 'its just how it works' like plot or some crap, such as a prolog.
Clicker games aren't something I enjoy really, with few exception (Parodies and the like)
But I do enjoy (mostly) games like Harvest Moon, and Animal crossing where there's farming and more to do.
This takes farming and is the most basic of clicking games, with a graphic style that looks like it was made without much thought, and bores me to death.  The leveling system is poorly thought out giving you only one new item per level with few exception, also I'd rather a proper tutorial than be given a item from a catagory each level, in addition to level you need to use money to buy a item and every time you buy a item the price doubles all the way up to 99 million (I think)
Which needless to say doesn't make sense in a farming game, a genre in which the standard is fixed pricing.  I'd really rather have fixed pricing that you work your way up to rather than waiting for levels to get the item which I could afford to buy a year ago.
Seriously feels like a free to play flash game would have more content than this, even for a price of three dollars off sale I'd avoid it.  If you're looking for a paid for farming game that's not only cute but is in a promising state for the future, I've heard things about Slime Rancher (Though I don't own it myself)  There also seems to be a good lineup for early 2016 as far as big budgets go, and hopefully a couple indie suprises so especially at this time it'd probably be best to save money.

This game is different from any other game in its genre (base-building, strategy, 3rd Person shooter). The level of detail, as well as the extreme playability of this game made it an easy game for me to get addicted to. In regard to this review, keep in mind that I have not played CoJ: The Cartel. Not that I heard great things about it...
The two other predecessors, however, I have played and finished.
The first thing I would say, if you are a fan of the series, is to divert your expectations. The first two games both were stories that attempted to, and perhaps succeeded, into gripping you into their narrative. A heart clenching story of vengeance and/or a lust for a haunted treasure.
In comparison, Gunslinger's story seems like a mini version of it. A simple adventure about and narrated by Silas Greaves, spoken in the context of a Saloon like he was a Cowboy telling a tall tale.
The interesting thing done here is how the story impacts the game, whereas it's usually vice versa. Your audience at several points takes over the narration for a moment, telling how they heard an event in question went down.
And you play it all out, in a non-forced manner, taking their narrated path through the level. Eventually Silas will cut back in and tell how it really happened, winding back time to let the player cross through the level that way.
It's a very impressive, if not unique way of telling a story in a game.
The story itself, due to this, often comes across as a bit light heartened. It feels like it's lacking that darkness, that grit. But let me tell you, it eventually does come around, as Silas tells the story of his life as a Bounty Hunter in his quest for Revenge, and how he got around on starting in that line of work.
The array of guns may also seem simplified. A total of seven firearms and dynamite as throwables. It seems like that's not much, but for a story of this length, it seems enough. By the time you've gotten well comfortable and skilled, you'll have levelled up plenty and gotten around to a nice build to complement your weapon of choice.
Talking of Levelling, the game makes use of three skilltrees. They mainly befit the Archetypes of Gunslinger, Ranger and Trapper. Which simply means Pistols, Long Range and Shotgun/Dyanimite. Each skilltree awards you with a stat boost and pretty skin of a specific weapon halfway and at the end of the skilltree. Each tree has at least two unique skills that make you an even deadlier man, and the weaker skills tend to have some synergy going with other skills. Again, it's not very extensive, but enough for a game of this length.
Combat wise, it feels pretty good. The guns have weight to them, and fatal hits feel very satisfying. You have regenerating health, but so does the enemy apparently. You can fire two bullets in their chest, but if they find cover, those bullets can be considered wasted.
I played this game on Hard, which especially urged me to make good use of cover. The enemy will not relent, and is quite intelligent compared to some titles. They take cover the moment you are spotted, move to another one if their current one proves not good enough, and they seemingy try to outflank you when they have the numbers. I was kept on my toes quite a bit, and every enemy felt like they could end me very quickly if I didn't pay attention.
Overall, Gunslinger feels like a smaller (not necessarily stripped-down) version of the first game and Bound in Blood. But those were also full titiles, while at the time of writing this game is sold for 15.
So all in all, I would say that, with rational expectations, you'd very well get your money's worth.

From the start, the surreal setting and enigmatic characters pull you in and the game continues on a pretty good pace throughout.
The only real downside to this game is that the battles become routine once you know how to defeat the 7 or so major enemies you spend the game fighting through.  The enemies at the end are almost an after thought to let you fully understand the story.
All in all a GREAT game and well worth picking up to anyone who wants a great gaming experience.   I really look forward to Supergiant's future as they seem to be firmly at the fore of creating great games.  8/10

It would seem that Creative Assembly clearly have a lot of love and respect for the 1979 film, Alien.
The atmosphere in this game was incredible, I couldn't put it down. It's not a short game either so you really get your monies worth here. I'd highly recommend this to any horror fan and or Alien fan, it feels like an addition to the universe rather than a sloppily made tacked on mess. It's not the scariest game out there however there are quite a few "Oh crap... ohcrapohcrapohcrapohcrap" moments. There is enough here to be able to enjoy as either a newcomer to the Alien franchise or as a die hard fan.
However a few minor frustrations, some glitchy A.I. behaviour can somtimes take you out of the experience but this is only highlighted by the fact that the game is polished, so take that with a pinch of salt. One thing I can't forgive is that occasionally the zenomorph just knows where you're at, it can be a little cheap and makes encounters feel somewhat random, rather than genuine. I'd like to think i've died by a mistake of my own rather than the game spinning a wheel of fortune. The last issue is that vents and other hiding places require you to press a button prompt to enter. Button prompts work fine for say... lockers, it doesn't work so well for vents. When you're being chased down mercilessly, time is of the essence. The last thing you want is to be awkwardly rubbing up agaisnt a wall shouting to yourself "GET IN THE VENT! GET IN THE VENT!".
These are minor blemishes on an otherwise spotless adventure, I feel like i'm picking at hairs but they're still issues nonetheless. Pick this game up, run for your life for a bit, it's a good laugh.

Papers Please is a very unusual game. I’m not even sure how I can describe it effectively.
You play as a dude who checks passports for a fictional communist country. Sounds boring right? But so much drama happens. People try to bribe you, they tell you their sob stories, they try to smuggle weapons and drugs, your superiors are eager to punish you for any mistake you make, terrorists ask you for your help in overthrowing the government (and you can!), and if you mess up, either your family will starve, you’ll be arrested, or you might just die in a terrorist attack. There’s tons of different endings, and all of your actions have far-reaching consequences.
I used a walkthrough, because I didn’t find the gameplay very fun, I just wanted to experience the story. But I think the gameplay is supposed to NOT be fun. It’s supposed to be really stressful, and to put you in the shoes of the character you play. And maybe I cheapened the experience a bit by using that walkthrough. Oh well.
Anyway! The story was intense! It makes you really think about what effect your actions will have on others and yourself.

"Cause no trouble."
A typical month through the viewpoint of a border agent in Artstotzka. At least, that's on the outside. In fact, this is one of the most interesting months that could happen for your border agent. The plot is wonderfully constructed, with multiple branches and backstories to keep things interesting.  Most of the people you file passports for are dull and boring, but there are a few who make it all worth it. The gameplay is surprisingly fun, as I played it as more of a puzzle game, trying to find the one missing piece in that person's data.
Overall, I would give this a 4 out of 5, and strongly reccommend you give it a try.

Okay, I bought this game because it was by Supergiant Games, because I loved Bastion, but then I fell in love with this game's story and characters. This game is possibly the best game I've played over the past 5 years.

First considered getting this game after finding out it's made by the same people who did Bastion. The soundtrack, storyline and gameplay did not disappoint. The combat system is a little awkward to get used to at first but once you figure it out you can get to grasps with it quite easily. If you loved Bastion, then you'll love this.

Transistor is an Action-RPG created by the developers of the critically acclaimed Bastion.  As such, it has a large pair of shoes to fill.  Now, if you're looking for a game to match Bastion, I'd urge you to reconsider.  Yes, Transistor is the "spiritual successor" to Bastion, but expecting it to be the same is a mistake.  It is a unique game where the talents of Supergiant Games really shine in a new and innovative way while keeping the quality for which we know them.  I've tried to keep spoilers to a minimum.
--STORY--
The story of Transitor is in keeping with the Supergiant tradition: a mysterious, post-apocalyptic mystery that unravels as you progress.  The protagonist, Red, is silent throughout the game, with the majority of the narration done by the "Transistor."  Despite this, the personality and motivations of Red are illuminated through the brilliant dialogue and storytelling.  The Transistor's narration is top-notch; he is not an omniscient observer, but rather a real character.  I found myself drawn into the story and yearning to know what truly happened.  The only complaint I would have is that the story feels a bit rushed at the end (although the game is quite short, so this may just be me).
--GAMEPLAY--
This is where Transistor truly shines.  The gameplay is extraordinary; it allows so much versatility for such a simple concept.  As you progress, the Transistor gains new abilities to be used in combat.  The combat system is a combination of tactical planning and real-time action.  You can either plan your moves out and execute them rapidly or act in response to the environment around you.  The enemies are varied and get more powerful as you play, preventing the game from feeling stale.  Each enemy has its own "personality" in a way, and they provide a sense of comic reality to the game.  In addition, you can make the game as hard or easy as you want through the use of "limiters" (think the shrine in Bastion).  I would suggest you use a couple, as the game feels a bit too easy without any.  The skillset is varied and allows for a nice myriad of options, especially due to the option of using each ability as either a passive, upgrade, or main ability.
--SOUNDTRACK--
The Transistor soundtrack is fantastic, almost another character in the game itself.  It truly adds to the atmosphere, especially Red's almost ominous humming throughout the game.  There's not much to say here, just know that the soundtrack is nothing short of a masterpiece.
In the end, I wholeheartedly recommend Transistor to anyone, whether or not they've played Bastion.  It is a bit short (I finished it in 7 hours with almost all the limiters), but it packs so much content in those hours that you won't feel robbed at all.  And, of course, there is a new game plus mode that will satisfy your craving for more Transistor should you have one.

Transistor is one of the best indie games to have come out in recent times. Everything about this game is very well executed, from its astounding visuals and gorgeous soundtrack to its perfect difficulty curve and intruiging, intelligent story. The game is an action RPG that plays like the V.A.T.S. system in fallout 3, where you plan your attack beforehand and then proceed to execute your moves in a satisfying superfast motion. After you execute your attack, you leave yourself vulnerable to enemy attacks, so getting yourself into a safe position after the attack is all part of the strategy. One of the coolest features of Transistor is the ability to format your moves (called "functions()") into attacks, attack buffs or passive abilities. For example, one of your functions called Mask(), when set as an attack, makes the player (called Red) turn invisible. When set as an attack buff, it adds extra backstab damage into your attack. When set as a passive ability, the player gains brief invisiblity after killing an enemy. How you set up your functions into these three categories is entirely up to you almost from the get-go, allowing you to play the game how you want to, with no penalties for trying out different combinations. (In fact the game encourages you to try this out in the "sandbox" arena which presents you with fun mini challenges with pre-set functions.) The game also borrows the Idol system from its predecessor Bastion, where you can gain more experience at the cost of buffed up enemies and hindering your abilities, allowing you to make the game as hard or easy as you want.
Going into more detail about the aesthetics of the game, it looks and sounds amazing. While I found Bastion's visual style a little basic, Transistor's world is much more detailed and vibrant. Animation is beautifully smooth. The game has a very "neon" look to it allowing the game to immediately set its future dystopian setting the moment you start. The narrator from Bastion returns, this time as the game's titular sword (is it a sword? I guess so). In all honesty, I wasn't a fan of Rucks in Bastion with his overly gravel monotones and overlong speeches breaking up the flow of the game, so I was delighted to find the Transistor spoke with much more brevity, and the gravelly voice is gone. The female vocalist from Bastion also makes a return for the vocal songs in the game, and they are absolutely wonderful. "The Spine" and "Paper Boats" have quickly become of my favourite video game tracks ever. In fact, the vocal songs are so good they completely overshadow the non-vocal tracks in the game, not to say they aren't good. The story retains the spirit of Bastion's "show don't tell" mantra, leaving the story and relationships between the characters to be largely discovered and interpreted by yourself by the in game lore. At the same time, the Transistor's monologues are never so vague that you have no idea what's happening.
Game length is satisfactory, it'll take about 6 hours to finish the game, but with achievements, NG+ and the sandbox challenges the game would take around 15-18 hours to finish 100% (just an estimation as I haven't got there yet). I'd say its worth its full price regardless.
Faults with the game? Very few. The only real problem I had was accidentally progressing to the next area when I wanted to explore more, the game is quite vague in telling you which way is the proper way to go, and the majority of the time its a point of no return.
tl;dr if you like good games you should probably check out this game, its good at being good. In my personal opinion, its one of the finest games ever made, so major props to you, Supergiant games.

This action packed game hides a surprising depth and tactical thinking. Solo or coop, it's a blast.
The trailers for Broforce shows it as a fast paced carnage, a run and gun and leave no survivor type of thing. But this is probably not how you're gonna play Broforce. You will soon understand that rushing blindly will probably kill you long before you reach the end of a level. There are tons of stuff that can kill you, and it's usually best to plan your path into the next serie of enemies and explosive barrels if you don't want to get blown to bits.
But that tactical approach is what makes the game fun. Rushing blindly can be fun, and sometimes does work, but if the game had been all about that, it wouldn't be as interesting, and it wouldn't hold your interest for long. The free promo game "The Expandabros" is actually proof of that, it's much more lenient, and you can run and gun through it all, but it soon becomes repetitive and boring.
The tactical approach is greatly completemented by the huge cast of "Bros" that you will unlock as you play the game. Each of them is a spoof of a well known character from Hollywood action movies.
Beside the chuckle you get when you reach the next bro reveal, this allows change the gameplay drastically. All bros have unique weapons and special powers, and you will switch to a new bro everytime you die or liberate one of the prisoners (they act as 1-Up, giving you a free live) spread around the levels.
Therefore, you're constantly switching how you need to approach the game. Some Bros have great range to pick out enemies from afar, others have great power but require to get close. They are probably not balanced, some are clearly better than others, but even an underpowered Bro can shine in the rights circumstances. And in any case, this constant switch of approach keeps the game fresh during the whole lengthy campaign.
Behind it's apparent mindlessness, Broforce is a very clever title, and that makes it a great game, rather than just a flash in a pan. Solo players will enjoy being very tactical to survive, while multiplayers will bring more mayhem but also more leniency in how you approach the game. Both modes work great and are a joy to play.

Pleasantly surprised. I missed out on the release debacle, so my experience is entirely with the final release state of the game. Overall, I enjoyed the game, even with a few minor-to-major qualms.
Pros:
-Usability massively increased over previous titles. The campaign UI is improved, features are very transparent and well-communicated, and controls make sense.
-Factions feel specialized and unique. Some factions field better horsemen, missiles, light infantry, etc. and I have to be aware of how to take them down.
-Battles feel very responsive and varied. One of my complaints with Shogun 2 was that the battles felt incredibly samey, but with the way each faction in R2 is specialized and the great variance in units means that I feel like I rarely fight the same battle more than 2 or 3 times.
-Campaign terrain very well laid-out. Like Shogun 2, the limiting terrain feels designed to facilitate strategic movement and placement of units on the campaign map.
-DLC campaigns are actually worthwile. They're very well laid-out with some of their own neat features that vary up the gameplay. I'm especially fond of the Caesar in Gaul DLC.
Cons:
-Visually, a mixed bag. The visuals lack the coherence and beauty of Shogun 2. Most maps and objects look like pre-rendered assets slapped together and passed on. In order to put in complex facial animations, most soldiers skeletons got jury-rigged so that they are bug-eyed with weird-looking faces, and their outfits look like just separate pieces of clothing glued to an action figure. It's noticable if you look hard in battles, but really detracting in places like the campaign map. On battle maps, visuals get kind of bad. Zoom out to medium distance, and soldiers just look like pixelly blobs, and ground foliage looks like something from the Quake 3 era (I'm running this Ultra with over 60 fps).
-I haven't fully decided yet, but I think I'm not a big fan of having a large amount of varied factions. It's historically very cool, but it feels bad for the gameplay in some parts. For example, in Rome 1, the conquest of Gaul took a long time and was very rewarding as you beat a large faction. You slowly pushed your way through an entire country that could field several large armies at once. In Rome 2, you tend to just beat one enemy army stack, then auto-resolve the remaining few provinces to get all of their land. There are exceptions like in the starting turns or fighting larger factions, but I found it less satisfying than the expeditions into large countries like in Rome 1
-The battles kind of look like farts. The mo-capped animations are really slow and take up a ton of space, so when you zoom in you'll see soldiers engaging in glacial duels that take up so much space that they push each other around like those inflatable punching clowns.

It's basically more Dark Souls 1 with a few differences.
Pros:
- MUCH improved graphics, gameplay and framerate, everything is a lot smoother
- The DLC is actually good and fairly lengthy (like DS1's was), in fact the DLC is probably better than the main game
- Online play has been improved, it's far easier to play with friends, and generally the online community is pretty active, meaning you don't have to wait around to summon/be summoned
However, it has issues.
Cons:
- I found the main game to be quite dull, pretty generic story and lacks the atmosphere and deep background lore DS1 had
- It's much easier than DS1. Some people might find this good but I liked the challenge
- PVP is basically broken, the arena matchmaking system is awful (you can get matched up with people of any level, so a level 50 could face off against a level 200 on NG+ with insane gear... It happens more often than you think), and the hitboxes are a joke. You can get hit by something you were miles away from on your screen, and vice versa, leading to a weird and unfulfilling experience most of the time
- Most of the bosses are pretty generic and easy (but there are a few exceptions)
Basically, if you never played DS1 you'll probably enjoy DS2. But if you did play DS1, I think you'll be disappointed. It's still a good game, but it just lacks what made DS1 so memorable. Honestly it's kind of hard to describe. Either way, you should check this game out.

With its awesome storyline and tight combat system, this western shoot-em-up game can be summed up it two words: PLAY IT!

Call of Juarez is an extremely linear shooter; although, it does hold  a solid amount of entertainment.  The game-play isn't anything new apart from the duels, but the story and voice acting are both top of the line.  The player gets to meet and kill many of the legendary outlaws of wild west, and the way the game-play follows the dialog of the main character can be both fresh and, unfortunately, annoying at times.
The shooting always comes down to the same thing: the player picks his or her semi automatic western influenced weapon of choice, then proceeds to blast heads off of cowboys, outlaws and different Indian tribes while following a set path until the duel at the end of the chapter is reached.  The game-play falls short after a short while due to how easy the game is.  The player is given a slow-mo ability, but the game is a push over even without it.  The fault comes from the lack of aggression in the AI.  The bad guys simply stay in the same spot or run back and forth from one of 2 cover points until the player kills them.  Only a select few enemies will actually advance on the player's position.  Granted, the duels that at the end of most chapters can be a lot of fun and a good challenge.  Each one feels a little different from the last, and getting the hang of the dueling controls can take some time to master.
The story is told by the main character as the player progresses, and the ending has a nice and unexpected twist.  Something that was not expected from Techland after giving such a bland and unexciting end to Dead Island.
The weapons all feel and sound great, and there was a lot of effort put into the detail; however, there is a lack of options given that the pistols all feel alike -- the same goes for the rifles and shotguns.  There were some nice touches, though.  For instance, when shooting a double barrel shotgun, each of the hammers have a separate animation and work independently from each other.
If you are looking for five or 6 chill hours of western shooting, this is a fun game.  If you are looking for a shooter that is going to keep you on your toes and thinking outside of the box, avoid this game at all costs.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger, the good, the bad, and the ugly.  First off I loved the approach the developers took to the game.  Now if you have read my other reviews you will know I'm not a huge fan of first person shooters.  I am however a gamer!!  So the game play is secondary to this larger-than-life storytelling.  So you take on the role of Silas Greaves legendary bounty hunter.  The best way I can think to describe the game it your character Silas is telling about his legendary life in a true old west fashion.  Its a first person shooter  told by yourself in a third person storytelling style.  You are Silas Greaves walking into a saloon taking advantage of your bounty hunter status and storytelling ability for some free booze.  Are they all big fish story's or true?  At a certain point I was thinking the gameplay got in the way of the story.  That is how good it is being told.  But the game play is basic nothing expectational or revolutionary as far as a video game goes.  The duels are probably the best part. AMAZING GAME!!! I feel bad for people who don't have computers because they cant play the two best games ever undertale and FACTORIO.  If u are a dumb dumb digalo or aren't interested in building stuff, this game isn't for you, but everyone else should get this game.

Already this game is more complete and polished than a lot of games that I have played. With that in mind there is still a lot to add and reaching the end game kinda gives you a 'plomp' feel. Also I've been playing the game off of steam a lot more than on steam so yeah, obligatory 'don't judge muh hours!' thing.
So one of the biggest let downs I have so far is the alien ai. It's just pretty much terrible and there's nothing to it. Not to mention that there isn't a lot of variety to it either. I'd like to see more to that.
Well now that I got my one complaint on the game out of the way, lets talk about what's good. The game is top down as you can see from gameplay or pictures. You start out like most of the 'survival' style games using a pick axe or literally hammering♥♥♥♥♥♥with your hands, and work your way up to automation. This has to be the first game where I felt it mixed the feeling of automation with progression in a smooth fashion. There's a few things here and there that are weird, like how you can't build a roof or actual building, but meh, who does that when they're trying to build efficiently and aliens can't fly (hint hint).
I find the game surprisingly intriguing as I've never really been into the automation aspect of things. I feel as though completing the same thing over and over again is as tedious and boring as it comes. With facotrio though I feel more like I'm working with a living breathing blueprint. You will often find yourself upgrading sections, building new sections and generally you might even feel a bit creative. Is it the best game in the world? Actually it might be among some of the best honestly. This game is damn good!
In terms of building and all that, you start off basic and eventually you will move onto new things, either manually walking from place to place or creating a rail system or some other form of automated management. Really I like that progression involve such a large scale change and the whole time you have aliens breathing down your neck.
The one time I played multiplayer I pretty much played the military defense managment guy. I built walls and gun turrets and♥♥♥♥♥♥and made a special system for manufacturing ammunition and rotating it throughout the guns in a cosntant cycle. it was a pretty great feeling especially when I got to see it in action. Sadly we outgrew my system and had to move, but making another defensive system would have been just as fun if we didn't stop.
Really I feel like this game stands on it's own even with only singleplayer, but the multiplayer aspect just amps it up so much. So few games go beyond 'local multiplayer' and it baffles me since online multiplayer is such a greater field. So many of us nowadays keep connected and enjoy the company of others over the internet more than we do from our couches and really who plays a computer game locally anyway? Not me. At least not since return fire 2! As always, make sure you check out a gameplay video before you make the decision to purchase the game. It helps you understand what you're getting into.

If your game crashes  a lot or has unusual low fps try one of the following:
- disable Screen Space Reflections (in graphics section)
- turn down Water Details to low (blame Nvidia Waterworks)
- "downclock" your GPU by a few Mhz and/or disable your used overclock setup
- set the game to run on single CPU core ("set affinity" in task manager)
- refund and miss an otherwise great game
Speaking of fixes, there's two mods you should have:
- "no intro" which removes the long superflous intro that you cannot get rid of otherwise
- "extended LOD and texture budgets" which basically reduces pop-ins of objects a lot
I hate it when games won't run 'out of the box' and you have to find a solution yourself, but it was totally worth it.

Fun little game for a few minutes of fun.   Don't expect too much, but it'll kill a few minutes.   Not much to do after you've built up your eggplant, cabbage, and lemon farm.

.Premise.
This is your garden (though I suppose farm is more accurate). You put down crops and the only thing you need to do to take care of them is sit and watch. That's it. You can harvest fruit, vegetables, and various things from your livestock, as well as shoo off wild animals, but that's all option.
You could "play" this game by doing nothing more than plopping down plants and animals when you've got the coin for it, because you have Helpers who do everything else for you. Albeit, slowly. It's very simplistic.
.Gameplay.
You can do everything I mentioned above with a click of your mouse. There's no need for your keyboard here.
-You level up as your Helpers (or you) gather from your garden and it's denizens. In the typical iOS game style, you can buy little powerups with in-game coin that extend the amount of time your Helpers work when you're logged out and the coin multiplier for your profits.
-You can also buy little, panting canines that bark at garden invaders and scare them off. These pests will disrupt your animals or steal your crops, but are otherwise harmless. The leveliling up allows you to buy new crops and livestock and, since the catalogue is rather limited, once you unlock everything (There's five options for small plants, bushes, trees, and four for animals) levels add stars to what you already own, therefore making them worth more.
-You can also expand your land, allowing for more Helpers, plants, and animals. Your little garden can get very cluttered, very quickly.
-You can't see your entire garden on-screen at once after you start expanding. You can click-drag to pan or use the arrow keys.
The UI is a little wonky when it comes to selecting plants: they are each on three different planes, one behind the other, and sometimes it's hard to choose something on the first plane. After you start expanding your garden and levelling up, there's a TON of stuff on-screen at all times, but I've never experienced any sort of frame rate issue.
.Atmosphere.
I'm a sucker for cute, cartoony graphics, so this is right up my alley.
The soundtrack is my one complaint. It's the same song looped over and over again. It was charming at first, but it begins to wear on you quite quickly.
.Longevity.
At about 5 hours in, I'm level 55. Not sure what the level cap is. That being said, there was a patch released today that added 8 more in-game achievements and that's a definite thumbs up for me. I'm glad the devs are still adding on to this game because I enjoy it a lot.
.Bottom line.
Absolutely adorable. It's a relaxing game that you can play for a few minutes or even hours. It's worth the 2.99 original price tag, but getting it on sale would be even sweeter.

If there was a middle of the road between yes and no I'd pick it. This game would be a 100% yes for free but as a pay for clicker game I gotta give it a no.  I myself will hold onto the game for a few more days before tossing it if the devs don't show that they have MANY more things coming for the game to help draw it out.
Pros: the music is lovely and if you tire of it there is a muti button for either sound or music, though sound helps you listen for bonuses and stuff going wrong.
Your clicking is always rewarded, when fruit is ready to be picked you can click on it to drop early and in turn start the next fruit sooner making you money faster, as well as clicking to fend off foes giving you a reason to keep clicking in this clicker unlike so many other clicker games.
Everything looks rather cute... other than your workers but still everything else looks cute in the game.
NO IN GAME FEES!  I know it's unheard of and I don't know why it's not there but yes for once a clicker that doesn't look like it's trying to make it's game impossible to beat without paying 50 bucks to win, looking at you AC!
The cons: Level ups don't matter very fast, what happens when you get a new level but you've unlocked everything?  Oh they double the worth of your oldest plant, meaning the first plant that got  you one gold now earns you two but seeing as you'll have plants making about five gold at that point, there is no reason to enjoy said level ups anymore as your most expensive plant will still be making more.
The guard dogs, I do enjoy that we have them but they are not dependable.  You can place them anywhere you like at first but at times they may walk off the map or never simply there to defend your farm even if you have ten of them because they all thought it would be best to head left vs right.  I'm all for them having to patrol but it would be better if there was a reasonable set amount of ground for them to cover.
Paying for a clicker game, Sounds stupid after the pro DLC bit I know but I myself just hate spending money on clicker games, maybe a buck or two, heck the 2.39 sale may yet have me keep it.  I just never feel it's right to pay for games like these.
#1 problem!  It's too short.  In this small amount of time you see logged, 1.3 hours at the time of posting, I've more than beaten the game.  Everything is unlocked I'm getting stars for my plants already and there is nothing to do other then check in every 11 hours or so now simply because of another con, you have to, in game, pay for how long you can be offline and still make money.(I could be misunderstanding that but it sounds like that's what it is.)
Final verdict: I said it at the start I'll say it again this is not a yes review it's not a no review it's a middle of the road one.  This game just was released so I'm VERY hopeful that the game will fix it's largest problem, in which I'll be changing it to a yes review but till then it's a no.  Come on guys it's a clicker game with plant life I know you can find more fruits to add in, prep a valentines thing where you have to click flying babies, or even blue babies like your workers, away much like the crows.  I understand it's a better more complex interface than AC but it's still a clicker game you can give us a reason to push us to septillion other then achievements.

I waited 3 years before finally coming back to try to play it again, and guess what? The game still continues to crash every 2-3 turns today.
Even when I actually managed to play a few turns and progress, the gameplay is somewhat disappointing. Shogun 2 (the previous Total War game) was superior in almost every way. Combat is lackluster, the UI is ugly and clunky, the AI often makes terrible decisions, navies are weak and pointless, etc...
In addition, when you reach about 50% completion in the grand campaign, the game decides you need an extra challenge. Even if you've managed to keep a good balance in politics, 3-5 full strength armies spawn directly on your capital with no warning.
All in all, this game is probably the worst entry in the entire Total War series, and I have yet to buy another one since. Save your money and avoid this game.

Reign of Kings, while in early alpha, shows a lot of promise to being a game that I could regularly play and want to play with friends. That being said, there are a ton of mechanics that should be implemented to make the game what it could fully be instead of the base outline it feels like right now, as well as a ton of things that need to be changed in order to make the game more playable and fair.
First of all, what I liked. The learning curve is not too bad. It gets harder as you progress, but there's a friendly community and a wiki page to help with later game crafting and building. Not only that, but the building in this game is so satisfying. The hours I've sunk in have resulted in some of the most badass looking fortresses and castles I could ever have imagined. And the feeling you get after hours of mining when you put on a suit of steel armor like the knights of old is one of the coolest moments in the game.
Now, on to what i hated. This game is frustrating. Like, Dark Souls level frustrating. The amount of materials you need to acquire to get basic building blocks is a bit ridiculous and really stalls out the building process. And the blocks that you can build quickly are so weak it takes any new character 10 minutes to break in and steal all your stuff. The character creator has little to no variability, with deformed, creepy looking characters being the majority of what you see and taking away from the gameplay experience. Combine that with the glitches that characters can do based on their height and weight, it makes the game unfair and forces you to have setbacks that shouldn't really be there. I've lost tons of bases due to midgets hopping on each others' backs and boosting over walls or going under rocks that normal sized people get stuck on.
The combat is sticky and buggy at best. I don't have a high end rig, but every battle I get into ends up with me lagging out and ending up dead within seconds despite having better gear and armor. The ranged mechanics are average at best, but with little to no hit detection on other players, you can't really use a bow on someone. Oh, and armor is useless in this game. All it does is slow you down. People with starter clubs can beat down people in steel suits of armor like its made of aluminum foil. You're better off avoiding anyone at all than risking a fight.
Lastly, the resources are so stupidly placed. You have to run around to find a dirt "node" to harvest dirt when you have been running on nothing but dirt for hours. Iron and Stone are always surrounded by either a lot of players or hostile wildlife, neither of which will let you get away with hard earned resources.
I've ranted for a bit, but like I said, the game shows promise. If the developers added in RPG elements, it could be a fantastic game that rewards the time you put into it. As of right now, however, its simply not a fun experience for invested Roleplay players or passive players. If/when these issues are addressed, I will be happy to play the game to my fullest extent. Until then, avoid it.

This game features beautiful visuals and a great soundtrack as well.  Overall it shares a lot of themes with the developers other game, Bastion.  Unlike Bastion, it is strictly linear.  Transistor also features very little exposition, so if you want to be slapped in the face with a story instead of piecing it together then this might not be the best game for you given its linear nature.
I enjoyed the combat in the game, but I did have one complaint with it.  You cannot examine your equipped skills outside of terminals found around the environment.  Normally this is not an issue, but it's annoying during the challenge rooms found in the game.  You're given a predetermined loudout of skills in these rooms.  If you get stuck with a skill you haven't unlocked you can't read what it does.
Aside from this minor gripe I really enjoyed the game and I recommend checking it out if you like action RPGs.

This game is really good. Especially if you love the Elder Scrolls universe.
My review is from a singleplayer viewpoint (with no friends in the game before I started playing). Also, totally personal, not an objective review.
As a veteran MMORPG player, we all know that after your first long MMORPG you keep returning to it after you quit 'for good' and eventually after a few years you chase the magic dragon; i.e. that fresh feeling.
for me it was EQ, for others WoW, Rift, whatever.
You'll never repeat that original feeling, but ESO Online was a very good experience, and will be awesome if you never played an mmorpg (for a long time) before.
For a few weeks, I got lost in the game.
Anyway, the game would've hooked me for years if I had never played an MMORPG before.
Good starting zones, very nice tempo of advancement, beautiful and vast world, good non-subscription value, challenging dungeons that are frankly, more fun and very well designed than I expected. But for an old fart like me, I feel too much adrenaline and stress after a few. Especially as a healer.
Too bad nobody roleplays or gives you the time to indulge yourself in the dungeon lore, cause it's pretty damn good.
As a singleplayer that's probably the only negative point I experienced. The game's tempo is so good, that you end up in a grind mode which is very satisfying at first. After a while you realize you want to slow down and experience more lore.
As a singleplayer who groups, this is hard to do.
However, you can stop grouping and start exploring the world and take all the time you need. Very nice.
After a few days you'll want the subscription just for the storage benefits. Paying for the auto-trade bag saves you tons of time. This doesn't mean you can't play without subscription, but not if you want to tradeskill and hoard ;)
conclusion: bit of a time sink / grindy, but worth the purchasing price and maybe even 3 months subscription.

is the fourth installment in a series of shooters dedicated to the Far West, developed by the excellent Polish team Techland and distributed by Ubisoft. Well, some may argue it's only the third real
game, since the previous one,
, did have a rather different and more modern-day background. As
did not get a particularly positive reaction, many thought the series had went off-track. But they were far from the truth: with
, Techland has for me made not only the best game in the series, but probable the best Far West-shooter ever. A bold statement, so let me explain in detail.
The concept of the game is original and well thought-off. You play as the bounty-hunter Silas Greaves, who tells his story in a Far West-saloon to a bunch of regular customers. As his story unfolds, it soon becomes clear Silas has a penchant to exagerrate some parts of it, which is why his  story is more and more questioned by his audience. This idea of "truth or false" is cleverly catched upon by the collectible items that are to be found throughout the game. These "nuggets of truth" give a fairly detailed amount of information on the history of the Far West, its main protagonists and some lesser-known historical facts.  The entire game provides prove of the love of Techland's crew for this setting: every bit of it, from the very easy to manage menu's right up to the credits, bathes in a unique Old West-style. There are countless references to the history of 19th-century America, and to the influence this period had on later arts such as literature and, ofcourse, movies.
As for the actual gameplay: it leans more towards an arcade shooter than towards a tactical or realistic game. There is a fair arsenal of weapony, each with some characteristics of their own, but most enemies go down easily and swiftly. What makes the shooting really fun, is the idea of the "combo": whenever you manage to shoot several enemies in a row, a multiplier comes into play, so that your experience-points go up that much faster. Getting one more kill in a row so becomes a goal of its own. Since experience-points are connected to a clever system of levelling-up and gaining interesting skills, getting longer kill-streaks soons becomes a true challenge. Added to these are two special effects: bullet-time, triggered by special shots like headshots or piercing shots, and the "sense of death", which allows you to dodge bullets at the last moment. Boss fights come in two types: normal ones against more powerful foes, but also as typical Old West-duels, in which a totally different method of playing is needed. These feel a bit trial-and-error at first, but after some practice, still can provide their share of the fun. And they provide great links to several Westerns, starring the great Hollywood-heroes of decades ago.
Graphically,
is very good-looking. The game uses a comics-style with cel-shaded graphics, loosely comparable to the
-series. Enemy-animations are fairly standard, and enemies don't come in that much varieties. However, these are minor criticisms, since the game comes at a very acceptable price, although it has the scope and content of a true AAA-title. After finishing the main story (which took me about 8 hours), there's a New Game Plus-mode, very useful to collect the XP needed in order to unlock all of the skills, and a True West-difficulty, in which most of the HUD is disabled.
Very entertaining is the Arcade-mode, in which ten of the games' maps can be replayed with as sole objectivity to get as much points as possible by making very long kill-streaks. Since the Steam-integration also comprises global leaderbords, tihs is great fun as I tried to get up the rankings a bit.
Gameplay: 26/30
Graphics: 17/20
Sound: 8/10
Technical stability: 9/10
Longelivety: 8/10 (thanks to the several difficulty-levels and the Arcade mode)
Steam Integration: 10/10 (really perfectly done, with a great bunch of achievements that let you discover several special aspects of the game - and do try to collect all of the "nuggets of truth"!)
Personal appreciation: 10/10 (I just LOVE this game)
Overall score: 88/100
