A fairly good western shooter with solid mechanics and artistic visuals while they are cell shaded it is done in a way that does not make it look over cartoony like many other games.  Graphics wise there’s not much to write home about, however it does not follow the gritty and overly brown color pallet, instead many of the levels are very colorful and vibrant.
The way the story telling is done is fairly good and somewhat unique; certain parts of the landscape can change as the main character’s story changes based on the input of the listeners.  The settings are varied and different though some town maps tend to repeat themselves a few times during the story mode.  The story is not open at all, it is liner and there is a “good or evil” choice at the end but that is the extent of the player choice.  Throughout the story mode you will be able to find “nuggets of truth”, these items are small history lessons which help to flesh out the truth in the stories that the main character tells.  While they do nothing to alter the story, they do give the player some interesting tidbits on what the events actually were like, or who these people were, granted this is all dependant on whether or not you enjoy history, if you’re the kind of person who doesn’t well then these will just be items for you 100% completion.
There are a limited variety of weapons however that limitation is not necessarily a bad thing they function and are upgradable via a 3 part skill tree, which is separated into 3 playstyles: Shotguns for close range, Pistols for medium and close, Rifles for long and medium.  While these skills are not as weapon or range centric as they may sound, some add some very interesting new options when dealing with enemies.  You are also not bound to a single tree, you can work on all 3 different weapons styles, and in order to bring more replayability to the game, you can continue your progress and max all three out which can be quite fun.
Aside from the boss fights, which tend to be western movie style duals, your main source of targets will be run of the mill cowboys and Indians.  The cowboy models will be repeated throughout the entire game with very little variation, however for a small budget game I do not blame them as to me it did not matter.  AI wise they are fine, nothing major, they will duck behind cover, but most of the time will simply shoot at you from cover or break cover to engage you.  You can die pretty quickly if you’re not careful however so don’t take their basic AI as easy.
I mentioned boss fights and Duals, well the duals as far as I’ve seen are fairly universally hated or at the very least disliked immensely.  While the idea may seem good, the application and the way it was implemented defiantly did not help the fun factor of it.  The controls are fairly skittish and wavy, on top of watching your opponent’s movements and tracking them, you need to watch your own hand position and your concentration, all while you either wait for them to draw first (honorable way) or draw first when you are ready.  It really could have been done better and since many of the boss fights are indeed duals it means you can not progress until you’ve beaten them.
For $15 bucks or less, I’d say it’s a good enough game to kill time or if you really like western themed games.

The games story is pretty stock basically being your standard western revenge tale about the main character seeking to avenge the murder of his brothers. However the game does its own take and makes it entertaining through its Borderlands style humor with the narrators adding tons of funny moments you will enjoy. The gameplay is fast and fluent. You actually feel the difference of each weapon, and it feels really realistic because enemies can die from one bullet even if it doesn't hit them in the head. The game has a level up system where you gain EXP from special kills and you can spend your points for upgrades on your prefered style and gain new weapons as well. Another way to get a huge boost of EXP is to find these special items called Nuggets Of Truth which tell you interesting facts about the west and common misconceptions people had associated with the time. Arcade sections are challenging but extremely rewarding in the end to see your hard work allow you to finally get the nearley impossible 3 Gold Star award. A few cons are that there will be certain moments where you have to dodge falling debris or wreckage heading straight towards you and can result in a few cheap deaths. Also duels are kinda annoying due to how the mouse controls are change, but this could probably be fixed by using a controller.

The plot of this game could have been taking straight out of an OC wild west fan fiction.  Your character meets basically every famous cowboy there was and even <incredibly minor spoilers for the end of the game> a young Eisenhower </spoilers>.
However, the game play is fun and the narrator is entertaining.  The style of what you are playing being a story allows them to do some humorous things with the game play (watch the trailers for an example or two).  It only takes about 4-5 hours to play through the story mode so there isn't enough time for the gunfights to get old.
The game also has an arcade mode.  Basically the most fun part of this is that you can filter it to see your friends scores and compete just against them.
Overall, perhaps not worth $15 bucks but is definitely fun enough to pick up during a sale.

So i probably should not compare Factorio to Tycoon p0rn or mention titles like Transport Tycoon Deluxe (or Open TTD) but i'm not afraid to say it, Factorio is better than TTD by an order of magnitude!!!
I have only spent about 30h ingame, automated blue science packs last night and playing on really easy settings but i already have solutions coming to me in dreams, i wake up, have my coffee before leaving for work and instead of reading the news i'm building the better-faster set-ups that came to me while i was asleep.
Graphics might not appeal to everybody but being used to tycoon games, this is very impressive, the single locomotive available is better looking than anything one can find in TTD.
With 227 robots flying on the screen, all of them pathfinding (they follow the character to deliver goods to your inventory) there is no lag on pretty low-end/average PC which is very impressive.
I can't praise this game enough, there is still a lot for me to research but what i have seen so far is well worth the money.
Before i got the game i was reading the reviews and "managing the logistics" being really important was coming up a lot. That is misleading, as long as you have the supplies - things will work. Optimising is a challenge as different things are produced at different speeds but even if ou produce required part once a day - the rest of the production chain will keep ticking over adjusting itself to the slowest supplier (bottle neck). For most part, with no experience playing Factorio, it's actually quite easy to have an overflow of pretty much anything (again, depending on map settings).
Not sure if this counts as a review, just my random thoughts about the game which i couldn't stop my self from putting up here. It wouldn't be fair to grade the game on well established merits like graphics or sound would be unfair as i can't compare the it against anything else other than the Tycoon series which are nowhere near what Factorio is.

Supergiant has done it again with Transistor.
From the makers of Bastion comes Transistor, a narrative journey through the desolated city of Cloudbank where the sky is blue "because we want it to be".  When a shadowy organization called the Camerata steals the voice of Red, a renowned singer and starlet, with a mysterious weapon that speaks to her, she is left to pick up the pieces and understand the most crucial question anyone would ever ask: Why.
On the surface, this game provides about 8 hours of entertainment with Supergiant's unique narrative process that worked so very well for Bastion.  This time, the narration comes from the massive sword that the main character carries with her.  Combat and narrative go hand in hand, one never taking a back seat to the other at any point during the game.  The musical soundtrack is breathtaking as well, with Red's haunting humming adding a haunting layer onto some already moving melodies.
A few of the encounters during the course of the game can be rather hair-loss inducing, but the sense of accomplishment is more than enough to balm those sore nerves.   Even a year and a half later, the story nor its ending leave anything to be desired.
This game is simply fantastic.

Transistor is a 2D isometric adventure game done by the same creators of bastion. Like bastion, the game looks beautiful, has a good soundtrack, and similiar to bastion, you're accompanied by a narrator/partner of sorts.  Unlike bastion, the combat is a bit different. Transistor is a game best described as unique. The game looks, plays, and sounds like nothing else out there, and, even more impressively, exexuctes nearly all of these innovative ideas to perfection. The best game of 2014 so far.
Pros:
- The combat. It's a hybrid of turn based strategy and arena action a la Bastion. The standard mode allows free movement and usage of up to 4 equppied abilities (mostly) without cooldown. Pressing space initiates Turn(), which allows you to expend a set number of action points to move and perform abilities at hundreds of times the speed of the standard mode. Turn()'s cooldown length varies based the percentage of action points you used, and all abilities are locked while these points regenerate. Its a brilliant system made more so by the enemy design that forces you to quickly and strategically switch between the two modes.
- The customization. Every ability is a function that can be equipped as an active ability, a passive ability, or overload an active ability with additional functionality. Additional memory and slots to equip functions unlock as the game progresses, allowing for a staggering number of highly unique loadouts. This system allows for nearly any playstyle imaginable to be viable. Using a method in one of its three roles unlock additional backstory material, strongly encouraging experimentation without ever forcing anything. Losing all health in a battle temporarily locks an ability each time it happens, further encouraging creative loadouts while waiting for the locked ability to restore.
- Tests and limiters. The game features 23 tests (and additional Access tests available only on a second playthrough) of your ability to use Turn(), to survive unwinnable situations, to clear enemies with only select functions available, and your speed in standard combat. The majority of these tests are very well designed and often very challenging. All are entirely optional and unlock tracks for the music player. Similarly, limiters are fully optional abilities unlocked at various points in the story that can be equipped to increase the challenge and XP gain of combat. They're a clever way to provide and reward customizable difficulty.
- The art and music. The screenshots and videos on the store page really don't do it justice. Transistor is one of the best looking and sounding games ever made.
- The story. Like Bastion, the critical parts of the story are delivered largely through narration. Unlike Bastion, the non-critical majority of the story is found in terminals, function descriptors, and view points that are all fully optional and found only through exploration. All of it is interesting, well written, and best left to experience on your own.
- New game+. Transistor calls NG+ "Recurse." This allows you to play through the game again with all of your abilities and limiters from before. Enemies also retain their abilities, however. Recurse also provides access to higher player levels and additional tests that are not unlockable in a single playthrough.
Cons
- Some of the dialogue is a bit weak.
Notes:
- The story is much better than it gets credit for. That said, it's much more abstract that what you usually see in games. There's a good chance you won't like it if you're looking for a story that gives every question a clear resolution. This applies especially to the ending.
- The game is about 5 hours long on first playthrough. Recurse can likely double that. I think it's good enough to justify a $2-$4 an hour price tag. If you don't, wait for a sale.
- Although by no means necessary, some basic knowledge of programming terms will likely make the game more slightly more interesting. It's entertaining to see how some terms were turned into combat abilities, and knowing what a few mean in reality will add a bit to the story. None of it is essential for understanding.

Can't in good conscience recommend this game. Not even minding the features of the game, it's incredibly laggy, prone to disconnects, huge delays between using an ability and it actually firing, and ZERO means of fighting bots absolutely plaguing every single map to the point of making it impossible to level unless you are a heavy duty DPS/AoE class.
As for the game itself, it's incredibly niche and way before its time. There is no forgiveness in class/skill/stat choices, with skill and stat resets being restricted to item mall features but even then, no way to reset your class. Several classes are supposedly getting an overhaul because they are that useless, except no notice of when that will happen and what will happen to players that have already leveled those classes, such as Pardoner and Oracle who have almost no attack skills; seriously, whose idea was this? Leveling is slow and grindy which means you can spend months getting to 200+ only to realize that your skill and stat choices have ruined your ability to keep progressing, so now you have to delete the character and restart. Months of progress, down the drain. There's so many classes, so many skills, it's unfathomable to offer that much choice ~without~ educating players at all (as there is no in-game information on classes, their future skills, tutorials, nothing except a sentence or two blurb when you actually choose your class) as to the future of those choices.
Finally, the game lacks any of the player-friendly features that have helped modern MMOs soar. There's no protection from kill-stealing, many classes can't solo on their own, credit for kills goes to the player/party with the most damage leaving higher-level players trolling lower level areas for easy exp/drops to sell that players of the correct level can't compete with, item drops upon death, EXTREME amounts of grinding for small amounts of progress, and so on. The worst part is the soloing, as the game removes the ability for some classes to solo while giving other classes more than necessary means to do so. What this means is, if you're the kind of person that likes partying in games, DON'T GET EXCITED: Just because some classes can't solo, it doesn't mean party play is enforced, or even encouraged. It's very strange to play a game that hinders solo ability yet doesn't give people a reason to party. It seems many classes are just there to look pretty, but in the end, just play a wizard.

Backstory: If you have watched the original 1979 Alien film (if you haven’t, what the f*ck is wrong with you? Go and watch it) you’ll know that Ellen Ripley put herself into cryo-sleep after defeating the alien and broadcasting an SOS message. She then goes missing for 60 years. In Alien Isolation, you play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen, 15 years after her mother’s disappearance, trying to get some information (or possibly closure) about her mother and what happened to her. Because of this, as soon as she hears that the Sevastopol space station has the flight recorder from her mother’s ship, the Nostromo, she boards the Wayland-Yutani ship, the Torrens, on route to the Savastopol. After boarding the Savastopol, she soon finds that the ship is home to something quite sinister. Your aim is to figure out a way to escape while staying alive.
Gameplay: The gameplay consists of sneaking around a space station in an attempt to complete multiple objectives. Some of these being an attempt to kill the alien, others being to get to a certain point in the station (for reasons I won’t divulge), resetting generators or hacking doors to get to your objective. Now, you may think this is mind-bogglingly boring, except, you are being stalked. Throughout this game, you are harassed by the alien who will not leave you alone and wants to take a big nom out of your head. As you move through environments, trying to complete your objectives, you will have to stay low, utilising your tools to keep you alive. Tools such as the noisemaker, Molotov, pipe bomb, and many others. You collect items throughout the game to craft these, but I never found myself running out of components.
“Well” you’re thinking to yourself “That’s not
bad. I can easily avoid that thing”. Well did I mention that hacking, restarting generators, rewiring areas of the ship, is all done in real time? That’s right, the alien can, and will, kill you while you’re completing these tasks. Oh, and not only that, but also save points. Yes, the alien can kill you just as you’re about to save. And with this game not having any checkpoints, when you die, you go back to your last save point. “For goodness sake” You’re probably thinking. “That’s a bit cheap” and I would agree. But the idea is to not let you think you’re safe even for a second. But it’s ok. The alien isn’t in every chapter. “Thank goodness, a bit of respite”. NOPE! Wherever the alien isn’t trying to kill you, a homo-sapien with a gun will try and plant one in your head. That, or a working joe will wait for his opportunity to break your neck, or cave your head in. Basically, you’re never safe while you’re playing this game.
Throughout the game, you get equipped with many pieces of equipment. Some of which are used simply to get through doors, such as the Ion Torch, Hack tool, and wrench. Others, such as the revolver, shotgun, and flamethrower, you are free to use at your own discretion. But be careful, the noise emitted by these weapons can, and will, attract unwanted attention. In the later part of the game, I did find that I was a bit too overpowered with the flamethrower being able to scare off the alien. Although it does get through ammo very quickly, I found it a cheap way to escape death if you’re noticed by the alien. One shotgun shell can kill a working joe which meant that I didn’t bother sneaking around them in the late game, I just walked up to them and one-shotted them and then walked around the area at a leisurely pace. I found facehuggers to be an annoyance late-game as they run straight for you and have to be killed or they jump on your face and it’s an inta-kill. I think it was the devs way of trying to balance out overpowering the player, but it’s done badly.
The AI: This is the point where the game shines. The game works on a system in which the alien knows your general whereabouts, but not your exact location. Meaning if you move from one area to another and lock the door behind you, you’re only delaying the inevitable. You’ll hear it in the vents and at any time, it’s only a few feet away. The human and Working Joe AI is passable. They mainly patrol back and forward and you just have to wait until their back is to you and then sneak past. They’re basically there to break up the alien encounters.
Story: Ever play Dead Space 1? It’s similar in the sense that you are given many tasks to complete, only to get a hearty slap across the face as you find it was all in vein. I understand the devs wanted you to feel like nothing can go right, but it does get a bit annoying as you work hard to complete your objective, only for it to all be for naught. Finally got to the door after avoiding the alien for the last 20 minutes? Being really careful and making sure you don’t get killed? Well tough, the generator will give out just before you get through the door and you have to backtrack for 10 minutes to restart it. That sort of thing. The story is ok with a very disappointing ending (which begs for a sequel) with you trying loads of different ways to escape the Savastopol.
Environments: Wow. I don’t think I’ve seen a game this pretty and well optimised in a long time. From dynamic lighting to smoke effects to the love and detail put into the ships, it’s fantastic. I have a friend who owns a 5th series GPU and he can play it maxed out with 60 FPS, optimisation 10/10. I have attached some screenshots linked at the end of this review but it doesn’t do it justice. It’s beautiful. Get it for yourself and experience it personally.
Characters: Largely forgettable. You talk to many different survivors on the station all while trying to regroup with your original 2 crew members which you were separated from at the start of the game (this being a side mission of sorts that takes a back seat as you realise you will only bump into these people again when the story demands it). The next part may spoil the story a little, so read at your own risk.
All other survivors you work with die at some point without exception and it becomes obvious no one but you will survive really early in the game. Again, a design choice to make you feel isolated (as the name of the game implies) but it does get slightly monotonous.
DLC: The Crew Expendable and Last Survivor are basically cash grabs cashing in on nostalgia. They each last about 20-30 minutes each and they cost £2.79 each, so unless you get the Collection edition, I wouldn’t bother unless you are a die-hard alien fan. Survivor mode is pretty good, but hackers have ruined the leaderboards so you'll be playing it just for fun, which is still good.
Conclusion: Overall I paid £8.70 odd for the Alien Collection edition while it was on sale and I think it’s fantastic. I wouldn’t pay full price (£30 for normal edition or £35 for the collection) put it on your wishlist and wait.

I enjoyed Wayward a lot over the last few days. It has a fun complexity in the vein of Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, Starbound, and Caves of Qud. For me, the learning experience of these games provides many weeks of entertainment. I suspect Wayward will be very successful, but it will take a bit more polish before it gets there.
Wayward drops you into the game with little backstory and a lack of a questline. Don't expect the rich backstory of a game like CoQ. The hook lies in the challenge of surviving in the world. The initial two days will be hard: I'd say you have a 20% chance of dying even if you are moderately good at it. Some seeds will simply be too tough - it is possible to spawn in on a map where you are tempted to start building a base in a great location, only to be ambushed by unexpected spawns. Learning the ropes and how to survive the first few days was amazingly fun for me. Then the fun comes from slowly expanding your base and learning new recipes to craft and lands to explore. That initial tension of the first day goes away pretty quickly once you establish a renewable food and water source.
It is a fun game and I would recommend folks getting it. As of 2017, there are some pretty annoying problems that require polish:
- Walking into a tree or wall will cause your avatar to accidentally harvest that resource. This happens frequently as the player tend to hold down a direction key to walk across a long distance. Caves of Qud handles this nicely with its option to walk in a certain direction and stop when you come up to an obstacle or sees a monster.
- Walking feels clumsy. I think a bit of this has to do with the fact that you need to explicitly rotate your character before moving in a different direction. In contrast, in graphically simpler games like CoQ and Nethack, going east-north-east-north is simply four key presses. An intelligent auto path-find algorithm will also go a long way in making moving around the map feel more natural.
- Crafting may use a number of substitutable ingredients. For example, a string can be crafted from two of any: bark strips, roots, hay, or anything else with a "cordage" tag. The player does not explicitly select each ingredient when crafting an item. This has pros and cons. On the upside, it makes the crafting process very speedy at times. The downside is that it is unintuitive which items will be used when you click the button to "craft a string". It's easy to unintentionally use an ingredient that you didn't want to use.

TL:DR -
This game is extremely good. The updates are pretty slow so that part sucks, but otherwise it's pretty playable as is. There's a decent exchange between the community and the developer, he's super active on the game's subreddit. In terms of community outreach I'd say the guy has been doing a phenomenonal job.
Having said that, some things can get a bit repetitive. One of my biggest gripes is how you can't craft things in batches and instead have to do it one by one. This may not seem like a huge issue initially, but when you're crafting 120 strings where each crafting action takes ~250-500ms then this adds up rather quickly (another good example is if you want to craft wooden arrows in bulk. You need a bunch of sticks first, and one of the best ways to get a bunch is to chop a few trees for logs and to dismantle them into bark and sticks, not mentioning gathering the feathers that are also required. Excluding the time required to gather the required feathers, it takes about 5 minutes to craft 120 arrows. 120 arrows may seem like a lot and it is if you're fighting stuff on land, but if you're fighting stuff that lives in the sea then each arrow is lost on a successful hit. It's very easy to go through a lot of arrows in the process. I do like this mechanic of losing your arrows since it mostly makes sense, though I think you should be able to salvage a few if you carve up the monster's carcass. It's just a hassle to make more and more arrows, especially if you want the higher-tiered ones like iron/stone arrows). You need to use your mouse as well to craft stuff, so my mouse has taken a bit of a beating because of this.
Getting resources can also be annoying since most of the precious ores/minerals that you need are underground versus being available on the surface. You have to go through this process of saving up food/drinkable water if your metabolism is fast (low limits for hunger/thirst), stockpiling on torches so that you can see, occasionally killing the monster that gets in your path (if possible. Aberrant ghosts are still a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to deal with), and then mining away at the rocks. You get a bunch of useless stuff in the process (stones, rocks, sharpened rocks) that only serve to make you encumbered (I mean there are actual uses for them, they just get in the way when you're mining for ores). So while you're mining you also have to drop a bunch of crap off to the side. When the max item limit per tile is 12 and each rock doodad yields ~6-10 stone/rock items, those piles stack up fast. It especially sucks if you're mining away in a long, narrow path since there's no room to dump your stuff so you have to go back to where there's empty space, dump your stuff, then walk back to the mining spot. If you're only a few tiles away from your mining spot then it's whatever, but there have been times where I'm 20+ tiles away in a zig-zag fashion. The walking quickly adds up. Some of this can sort of be mitigated by clearing out small areas and using them as checkpoints with chests installed so you can transfer your stones/rocks, but there's an inherent weight cap to these chests so it's overall not that useful of a strategy since stones/rocks weigh a lot (there is a mod that dramatically increases the chest's weight cap but you shouldn't rely on mods to fix game issues). This can be easily mitigated if you can set up an item filter where you can purposefully drop stones/rocks and only keep the precious ores/minerals that you want.
Which leads me to my next gripe: you can't choose which particular item you want to pick up from a stack of items. There is an option where you immediately drop all items that you gather, but because you can't pick and choose you either have to pick the entire stack up (wasting time to drop all of the stuff you don't want) or you have to gather the most recent item dropped into the stack one by one and hope you can get all the stuff you need without accidentally getting the wrong things. When a monster (or monsters) is chasing you and you want to get a quick item before you dip, there is a very real possibility that you can't because of the risk of becoming unencumbered when picking the entire stack up.
There are a few issues that I won't get into, mainly because they require you to become more familiar with the game mechanics (and this is supposed to be a review targeted for people deciding whether they should buy it!). Honestly all of this boils down to the fact that some of the game mechanics are still very rough. With some tweaks to the current game mechanics and completely getting rid of a few others, the gaming experience offered by this game would significantly improve.
By no means am I therefore stating this game sucks...the number of hours I've sunk into this game should be enough evidence that I very much enjoy it. Out of all the games I've played related to this survival genre (Dwarf Fortress, Towns, UnReal, Caves of Qud, Don't Starve, and a few others) this is definitely my favorite one. I've got to give props that it's fairly simple to pick this game up and learn how to play it. They even have a tutorial available that quickly introduces you to the game mechanics, which personally puts it ahead of Dwarf Fortress already. The controls are pretty intuitive and there are a bunch of shortcuts you can use to perform certain actions very quickly. The balancing is mostly all right (kind of BS that monsters seem to do max hp % dmg rather than flat dmg, doesn't make a lot of sense to me) so it doesn't feel like the monsters can steamroll you and vice-versa. There is mod support and you are given access to the developer console, so you are given more freedom to customize your playing experience. I need to reiterate that the developer is friendly and listens to your complaints if you voice them, giving players the sense that he genuinely cares about your playing experience. If you're really stuck on something and need help then there's an active subreddit that can give you a helping hand.
Overall this game is great, its current price is an absolute steal (hours played/$). Watch a few YouTube vids if you're on the fence of whether you should play it. Given 2-3 more years (because the development is pretty slow compared to a few other popular games like Caves of Qud) I'm pretty sure the game will have more refined playing mechanics in addition to lots of new content. There's also a free version you can try on their site, though it's about 1-2 years behind the current version I think.

I love everything Dark Souls.  Some argue that Dark Souls 2 delivers a lessened experience. After going back and forth playing both games for 200-300 hours, I must say I am very happy with the improvements.  The controls never fail me.  I only feel like animations pull me into  hits I legitamitely dodged in bad latency pvp (ds1 every grapple cheated, with worms pulling you back 10 feet) Most importantly to me every moment in Dark Souls 2 feels like I could overcome any obstacle with better timing. Dark Souls 1 had boss combos and abilities that are actually undodgeable.  A classic example is one of the giant enemies in DS2 starting a swing and hitting a player directly behind them, but that also existed in DS1, with even more ridiculous non animated movements. So now its less random chance and more skill.  Both games have issues with phantom range, or weapons hurting you without actually colliding with your model.  DS1 has more problems with enemy attacks having high phantom range, and DS2 has more issues in pvp with player weapon phantom ranges.   From Software makes excellent titles I own, but has rage inducing customer service interaction.  2 of their games in this genre are console only, and a lot of the screenshots and interview information given about this game has been totally false.  While I dont care too much about graphics not being as promised, or that there is a new version that has better graphics so soon after release, I am bothered a lot by them saying that it would be a full game without dlc, and then releasing dlc followed by a new standalone version with all dlc and improved multiplayer so soon, without this being an upgrade I could buy into without dropping another full game $$$$ on it.
TLDR
Dark Sould 2 is a great game that improves on many aspects of Dark souls 1.
Over the years as a fan of dark souls and Armored Core I have learned one thing.  Wait one year after release to buy and play any From Software title.

'Papers, Please' is a seemingly monotonous concept on its surface, but the game quickly takes the player on a journey through the life of a Border Checkpoint Official working for family and the citizens of outlying countries fighting to survive between high tensions of this European Cold War dystopian era.
Those who are hesitant to pickup a game that seems to be a simulation desk job about processing paperwork are already missing one of themes of 'Papers, Please'. The games challenges the player to not view the both the in game world and real world as if it is black and white. But at the same time 'Papers, Please' punishes you if you act with morals but shames you for acting against what is right vs. wrong thus adding to the tension of this intense adventure.
Each day you will meet new people, from high class citizens who wish to escape the 'pathetic lesser countries'. To middle class and below who are trying to run from something or someone, and they must now ask you to decide the next step of their life. Either you ignore the discrepancies and take a citation and pay cut for letting someone in without a Passport, or you send them back to where they came from and possibly sentence them to a life of sex slavery or worse. But what if they are lying? What if its a ploy to sneak into the country? What if this is one of those terrorists who is about to disrupt the border and not only dock your pay for making a mistake, but cut your work day short with a bombing-thus causing an even shorter salary pushing you down this slippery slope to another life changing decision; cut out rent in this salary's budget and face the rent raising, or cut out medicine for your sick child and hope the sickness does not progress. You cut out food last budget to help pay for heat this budget, your child should be OK... Right?
The fate of these countries and its citizens, and also the fate of your family is yours in 'Papers, Please'. With multiple endings, the player has many ways to journey through this story of, right vs wrong, conspiracy and revolution. All with one simple answer, 'Approved' or Denied'?

Supergiant has done it again with Transistor.
From the makers of Bastion comes Transistor, a narrative journey through the desolated city of Cloudbank where the sky is blue "because we want it to be".  When a shadowy organization called the Camerata steals the voice of Red, a renowned singer and starlet, with a mysterious weapon that speaks to her, she is left to pick up the pieces and understand the most crucial question anyone would ever ask: Why.
On the surface, this game provides about 8 hours of entertainment with Supergiant's unique narrative process that worked so very well for Bastion.  This time, the narration comes from the massive sword that the main character carries with her.  Combat and narrative go hand in hand, one never taking a back seat to the other at any point during the game.  The musical soundtrack is breathtaking as well, with Red's haunting humming adding a haunting layer onto some already moving melodies.
A few of the encounters during the course of the game can be rather hair-loss inducing, but the sense of accomplishment is more than enough to balm those sore nerves.   Even a year and a half later, the story nor its ending leave anything to be desired.
This game is simply fantastic.

TL:DR Add to wishlist
The game is very, very rough.  There's a bit of a gameplay loop currently but somehow the "live until you do something dumb and die" feel of it isn't that appealing.  As of now the game needs a lot of polish to get close to where existing games in the survival rogue like are.  If you haven't played Don't Starve, you'd be better off with that first.
The UI is a bit unintuitive mess, for instance each item has essentially its own set of hotkeys so that if you're moving items from one inventory to another en mass you could accidentally light your storage chests on fire.  The inventory and crafting system is tedious, there are more than a few items that only exist to be broken down and must be done in the context menu rather than a recipe.  Balance wise, the gardening update will need some tweaking as once you cover the island in apple trees there's little reason to eat anything else.
Combat is just... RNGeesus or at least my experience so far it has been.  I like the reputation idea for difficulty, that as you develop and disturb the island that the difficultly scales. There is a bit of a rock-papers-scissors system in play with weaknesses. But without some kind of summary stats about damage and hit percentage you'll either flee, flee and fire a few arrows, or hope that you'll kill the spider before you die of exhaustion or poison. I suppose they're encouraging a system that you choose when to fight but as of now everything moves at the same speed as you, so you may just end up running endlessly hoping you regain stamina to fight.
I want to like it, there are some interesting approaches to the genre, but its just not ready yet.  I'd wager you'd get early access burnout playing it too early.

Do not let the stigma of pretentious "in depth" survival games pull you away from this hidden gem. While Wayward is a survival game with a lot of depth, the game handles it amazingly well. Most games in this genre have difficulty finding the balance between managing resources and progressing. Wayward finds the sweet spot by having it be turn based rather than real time. Youre always trying to ensure you have a backup plan for all your needs, be it trying to create a suitable coop for tamed chickens, a garden of various status changing plants, or the early game rush of trying to build a water still in a suitable area before you run out of fresh water. The turn based system also lets you take a break whenever you need to, as with other games youre constantly using your hands for busywork for the sake of not dying.
4/5 great game, excellent developer. Easy to pick up and still challenging for older players

This one is a gem. It might be very difficult at first (you will die A LOT in the beginning), but the more you play it the more rewarding the experience gets. Wayward is a very complex game, you have to consider a lot of things, but this gives you a plethora of different strategies to tackle situations. There is not one way to get clean water, there are quite a few, just to give an example (distill it from sea water, purify fresh water, just drink dirty fresh water and then treat any symptoms...).
In any case, if you are not afraid of putting some hours into learning a game before it starts to take off this one might be fun for you. Bonus points if you like roguelikes, cause remember, you will die a lot and start all over. If that bothers you stay clear of this.

Bought this game after Splattercat did a Let's Play on it. Fun little game, the crafting system is very intuitive and someting I don't see often. They recently added dismantling so a log from a tree breaks down into bark, leaves, sticks, and wood poles, and each of those break down into oher items. As you get better crating skills the things you make have better durability and crafting will fail less and less. The world is pretty interesting to run around it, like an early online game on steroids, but with better polish.

It scratches my crafting game itch. You have a randomized inventory to start, and what you start with strongly effects your survival. Your actions have a fairly profound effect on your survivability, as your beneficence/malignacy affect the difficulty of the mobs which spawn near you; I believe this mechanic could have a better name, as most kinds of technological advancement are considered malignant. You can uncover crafting recipies by finding them, or by having the correct items in your inventory, and the procedural generation makes the explorer in me happy.
A little slow to update, but dev is active in forums. Well worth the price, with lots to see and do.

Wayward is a really good game. It is challenging, too, in that you need to choose your actions carefully (at least in the beginning) to ensure your survial. Only in my sixth gameplay I managed to get past the point of pure survival and started building a house and craft better armor.
What I, in particular, enjoyed about the game:
1.
The turn-based character of the game, which makes it very relaxing. You don't get hungry/thirsty/tired while just sorting through your inventory or reading mouse-over texts.
2.
The system of benign and malign actions, which influences how accepting the island is of your presence. That is a quite new idea to me, at least I have seldom encountered it, yet, in such a game.
3.
The music, I personally think, is brilliant for this game. It was floating in my head for days, too.
4.
The tutorial was well done, it does not take you too much by your hand and was not overpowering the gameplay experience. I like it that the player is expected to do a bit of their own exploration of it.
The negative:
1.
The crafting table: It is not sorted by categories, which could help. Also, as of yet is has a very limited number of items to craft. It could need a boost in the future, especially considering the late-game phase, in which players are looking for items to decorate their base, stuff to put in their houses, etc.
2.
Graphics: The floor tiles and wall tiles do not fit well together. Maybe the focus is more on survival than building houses, but it is where the game is leading (at least me).
3.
There should be a way to do away with excess items (like seeds). Some cannot be put in the fireplace without causing a wild fire, either. So after a time I got chest after chest of seeds and branches and leaves...
Alas, I had much fun playing, though at some point I had crafted about everything there is. For an early-access-game, it is a round and playable experience that was worth the money.

In all seriousness, I feel pretty mixed about this game, but not so mixed that I could say it's 'bad'. I actually got a refund for this game after play for 1.9 hours, but decided I would give it another go! It's another of those 'building something takes a realistic amount of work' games like project zomboid, Haven and Hearth, or Unreal World. I supposed it's a 'twist' in that its 'main mechanic' seems to be how the difficulty spikes based on actions you do. Actions like building and crafting takes it away, and actions like planting and taming increases it. Having this number below 0 makes hard enemies spawn.
On my most successful run, I had it at -64,000.
All it seems to do is just spawn harder enemies. The 'world' doesn't react to you any differently, and I found that most enemies would peel pretty early on if you start running, and don't seem to have any kind of ranged attacks. What gets 'hard' if you're geared out, is that enemies spawn that are, as the game claims "abnormally strong", and these enemies take my usual 9 damage down to 1 or 0, whilst they do tens of mine at a time.
It's one of those games, right? Like Banished, where only the first couple days are hard and once you understand how the game acts against you, you go from having a your best 2 day life to having a 30 day life. Getting that long life is fun, starting to make a large base is enjoyable, except when the game says "WOAH-OH you're killin' the trees man, you better stop that; here's a fire elemental to burn down your wooden base and all of the surrounding landscape including the trees you were cutting down BECAUSE ♥♥♥♥ YOU." Mm... Okay Wayward.
I know there's a casual mode, but it seriously feels like that's not the point. I feel like I could probably cheese the difficulty counter too, as taming animals increases it a lot. One of the easiest things to do, is grab a whole inventory full of leaves and slam them in some dumb goats face, over and over again, for years, and I imagine that would give you a pretty massive morality boost without changing your playstyle too drastically. I haven't messed around with the system to be honest; when an 'abnormally strong' elemental spawned in my base and a kraken just south of it, I decided to turn the game off and play something else.
It was a lot of fun thinking of how to craft everything though, without relying on a wiki for help gives it that brand new feel of adventure.
I do recommend this because, while it lasts, it's a nice casual buildy crafter. Item unlocks and some skills carry over lives as far as I can tell, so it seems to hold some long term playability, not to mention incoming multiplayer (take that Stardew Valley). However, I won't be buying this for any of my friends, nor telling them to get it. I enjoyed my time by myself before it became an "Mm, okay Wayward" sort of situation.
6/10, decent crafter. Its main draw is how the difficulty works, and that's totally fine. But if you're going to spawn extremely strong enemies in my only base that I can't kill and won't move, then I could probably just go play Haven and Hearth.

After about 24hrs and finishing the game, i can safely say:
This is an absolutely fantastic game. As a huge fan of the movies (the original from 1979 being my favourite film of all time) this game was essentially a dream come true. PERFECT atmosphere and tension that is so appropriate for an alien game. This is the game the alien franchise deserves. The AI is very intelligent, as it should be. We know how smart and dangerous Xenomorphs are so the AI was very important to get right and they nailed it. You have to be smart and careful and not be reckless running around carelessly. The game makes you think. Unlike most modern AAA horror games, it actually makes you think and doesnt just rely on cheap jump scares. The game is terryfying. Found myself sweating like hell after some really creepy but awesomely designed levels which i wont spoil. You get weapons, including the iconic flamethrower later on, to fend off the alien temporarily, which changed the tone of the game and kept it fresh.
There are also these cheap versions of Weyland Yutani androids called working joes who were a real challenge aswell.
I have only one gripe with this game, being i felt the last few hours dragged on a bit and were a bit frustrating.
Aside from that, its a brilliant game. If youre an Alien fan, go buy it, or hell if youre a horror fan in general go buy it, Hell even if you dont like horror, maybe give it a shot. A truly wonderful game and one of the best survival horrors ever created, and probably the best alien game created. Dont listen to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reviews from IGN and gamespot, who were pretty much the only ones who didnt like it, probably because they arent used to being challenged by games nowadays.
This game is an outsanding tribute to the original Sci-Fi Thiller. It is a must be to a fan of the franchise, or something that wants to attempt survival with some retro-space technology. 9.5/10.

I have only played the game for 7 hours by now, so my opinion might still change.
Turnbased empire building
The amount of micromanaging is more then I care to do. But that is just my personal preference. You manage technologies, citybuilding and your leaders. And all of these have lot's of parameters. For cities you have to worry about public order, food, growth and wealth which seems easy enough. But if you begin to take the factors into account that play into those it gets quite mind-staggering. Cultural influences, trading, technologies and not to mention your leaders all have a say in those matters. Said leaders have only 3 basic stats at first glance. But if you look closer you find lot's of additional traits and even more stats that you will want to consider carefully when making choices about what to do with what leader and whom to promote. If your into that kind of game it will be like heaven but I prefer games that are quite a bit lighter on the mirco management front.
Real time battles
The main reason I play Total War games is to crush my enemies, see them driven before me and hear the lamentations of their woman. Rome does deliver on that (well, minus the lamentations). You have real-time battles with lot's of troop types. These types all have their purpose. Have ranged troops rain death upon your foes, let your spear-units tie up the enemies main force while your cavalry outflanks him and attacks his rear. But even there things have become more complicated. Now high level leaders have abilities you can activate... which is in my opinion more fitting for a MOBA then a grand war-strategy game. On the plus side you have troop types you've rarely seem in other total war games. Heck, my main reason for buying this game was my urge to scythe trough my enemies with my egyptian war-chariots and I was not disappointed in that regard ;)
Bugs
Reading many comments about it, I'm quite happy that I waited that long to finally buy it since it appears that by now it is actually playable. I cringe to think about how bad it must have been at release. It still has bugs. In my 7 hours of gameplay I encountered 3 crashes. All of them occured during the AI turns and just restarting the game and loading the last auto-save did the trick for 2 of those crashes. The last one occured also during an AI turn, but it happend after I fought off a bigger force and emerged victorious. Reloading after the crash I found that I had to redo the battle. I was quite annoyed about that.
Verdict
Honestly I can't really say if it's good or not at this point. I like the battles but while I like the basic idea of the turn based empire building its level of complexity is a bit too much for me to really enjoy it. Many times if feels more like work then fun to me. The crashes can be annoying but they'll probably eventually fix them for good.
I'm giving it 7 out of 10 points which is barely a thumbs up. Consider carefully what kind of game you really want to play for what price before buying this.
Update: I'm changing my original rating to a thumbs down as crashes during AI turns are increasing and reloading doesn't seem to help anymore. There is what feels like a 200 step program on the CA support page that I will try eventually. Right now it feels more like "let's post a really complicated guide... no one will follow it so we can be freed of all blame" thingy.
The game itself would now get 8 out of 10 point from me. But sadly thats worthless if it crashes during every other AI turn.

2D Minecraft meets Don't Starve with a hint of Ultima IV. Mine, chop and plant your way to better crafting recipes and a stronger character, all while balancing the effects you have on the island you are deserted on.
For early access, this game is very stable with very few bugs  and also very addictive. You can even check out the free version online (alpha 1.9.4 I believe) which is worth doing if you are at all interested in this genera.
If you like the free version, I would totally recommend buying the game as there is considerably more depth to the paid version.
Note that a majority of the negative reviews I've read have to do with the the reviewer really not understanding how a roguelike works. You are supposed to die; that's part of learning the game. The Dev's have done a good job at easing the pain of death though as you get to keep any crafting recipe you learn, which works well.

I have to admit I was one of those 13 year olds playing this game. Well, back in 2009, when it came out. I'm 18 now however, and I have to admit, I love the game more now. It is a throwback to a time where I scrapped up $60 to grab it from the local video game retailer where I lived. To be honest, I didn't understand how to play the game when I was that young. I just shot wildly and would have tantrums playing it if I lost. I didn't end up having fun, and I'm sure I ruined the game for everyone in the matches I played. What I can say, is that I have grown to respect the game now, and that comes with age. It's not about the best kills or the best quickscope, its about playing the game to have fun, not pull a "Ohh, 1v1 me you♥♥♥♥♥ I'll no-scope you!". Games are meant for fun, not to be the biggest A-hole on the interenet. And it's no place for 13 year olds, the maturity to play the game may not be 18 for the content, but you need that maturity that comes with age to play these games.
I do highly recommend this game for the reasons as it is a highly fun and addictive shooter, That is meant for Fun.

Very fun action platformer, especially if you grew up watching 80's/90's action films as the characters are based off of them. They have many different characters to unlock, and you will (hopefully) recognize most. They all have unique weapons and specials, giving you many different playstyles. The environments are fully destructible so you can blow up everything you want. On lower difficulties and levels you can run through levels killing terrorists with ease, however on higher levels and hard difficulties you need to strategize a bit.  You start with one life, getting hit once by enemies kills you, and when you lose all you must restart that level. You gain lives by freeing bros from cages, and gaining or losing lives changes your character to a random bro, unless you've freed enough to unlock a new one, then you get that one. Freeing bros adds a bit more strategy, as you might have your favorite bro but only one life. You could keep going with your best bro, or take the extra life and risk getting a bad character. My only complaint is that the game was a bit short. It took me one day to beat, which I feel is too short. I know it has other modes  like custom levels and local/online multiplayer deathmatch, but I feel like it needs more campaign. This took me part of a day to beat, FTL took me almost 90 hrs, and was cheaper. Despite this I would still give it an 8/10, and because the devs have been adding more content, I'll give it a final score of 8.6. If you have friends who would enjoy this too, be sure to get it as there are a variety of local and online modes available, and It is much more fun and you'll get more content out with a few friends. Hope you have fun with this game!

No more Room in Hell is one of the most fun, challenging and co-operative post apocalyptic zombie experiences out there. Missions are variated, with variating difficulties. Some hard, some easier. Though most missions require a team of atleast 3-4 people, two experiences players who are co-operating in an excellent manner can do even the most complex missions. Guns have a secondrary role in this game, as the firearms are sometimes hard to comeby and you'll want to save that ammo for when you need it. The variation in the guns and melee weapons are excellent. Variating from pipes to sledgehammers, you're sure to never get bored on the armament front.
However, this game can be a little lackluster and slow at times. Pasting in the game is best described as limited since players really cant run or throw many attacks. This makes the game feel a little overly slow at times, which may bother some people. However, this is far from game breaking. Overall, the game has no directly game breaking issues, the biggest annoyance you will run into is other players. Since this game is very reliant on co-operation, ending up in a team that doesn't co-operate is truly gamebreaking and makes you a little sad.
This is defenetly one of those great co-operative games where the people you play with is everything, take it or leave it. Great oppertunities to make new friends if you can speak to other people in a nice manner!

Its is essentially left for dead in terms of how the game is played, a teamof about 4 (can be smaller or larger though) work their way through areas filled with zombies completing small puzzles to progress to the next game. Ammunition is far more scarce and zombies are more lethal now, and due to the lack of ammuntion in the game you will spend alot of time trying to pick of zombies with melee weapons. There are aslo some more advanced features. For example there are two ways to die, the first is by damage, so being hit by a zombie and bleeding out/ being killed from the damage, or if you get bit the screen goes increasingly grey and vieny as you turn into a zombie. There is no way i have found of stopping this from happening, you can take pills to prolong it, but once your bit eventaully you will turn, unless you mates head shot you or you shoot yourself. Also once you come back as a zombie (you dont play as the zombie you respawn) a zombie you will be running around the map for your mate to kill. Overall for a game that you dont pay any cash for and has no dlc/ microtrasactions (ok there is a dlc for music but thats), its great. It not your typicall hack and slash game or zombie shooter, its hard and teamwork is amust.

Four doctors go out duck hunting. The GP sees a duck, and asks the Physician if it was a duck.
The Physician unsure and asks for a second opinion, whether it was a common duck, a wood duck, a water fowl, a pheasant or a quail,
Then the Surgeon shoots five birds with six shells. BLAM, BLAM, BLAM, … BLAM, BLAM, BLAM, Handing the remains to the Pathologist, he orders “Here, see if you can find a duck.”
You are the hunter, you have your basic rifle, plenty of ammunition, deer call, binocs, and a handi-dandy pocket hunter.
Soon you learn that the HunterMate can help you to track animals and the red semicircular and dome shapes on the ground are actually animal tracks. So out you go from the camp… You want a mule deer, not the female but the big male, to hang his antlers on your wall. You hear a call, but (according to the HunterMate) it’s a whitetail deer. Forget that, so eventually you find a few female mule deer and you follow them down to the Bayfront of what (I imagine) is a wilderness of Washington State. There is a beautiful scenario, a male mule deer standing on the waterfront, but you are too far out cause your rifle is shaking around. He spooks and flees, so you track him for a while, then you lose his trail, damn.
So you go up into the hills, and you spot another two mule deer bucks. Which one is bigger you ask yourself. It is raining, but you don’t let that put you off. Then you lose both of them, oh dear. So you go back down to the cliffs and spot another few females and you follow them for a while before you lose interest and go home.
Next time in the camp, the weather is good, you find the range so you pop off a few rounds and hit the targets out to 100 meters. Full of confidence you head out again and repeat the above scenario. But every once-in-a-while…. You spot the mule deer buck and he hasn’t seen you yet so you move in quietly controlling your breath for the hunt. Then you get into position and he looks up at you - the Hunter, and you take the shot, he drops and you move in inspect your kill. Is he still there? Yep your bullet went through his lung, heart and spine from 43.6 m. Triumph! You think “Thank God the animal didn’t suffer”.
Sometimes you miss “The Shot” and the animal does suffer a lot, blood everywhere and when you find him tired and confused, and he looks up at you, his eyes pleading to end the suffering, well -perhaps some psychiatric counselling may help, you not the animal.
What I don’t understand, is why the ammunition is free. Everything else is pay to use: licences, weapons and supplies, clothes, etc.  You should have to pay for your ammo! Something like say 30 bucks for a thousand rounds for your favourite rifle, should last a while might even allow discounts on your other supplies. This is a great game about hunting and that really captures the spirit of hunting, and getting that one perfect shot.
The Multiplayer game is about camaraderie, working together in teams of hunters to improve your hunt. Or whatever you say it is - such as a hunting competition…
Good game. I have played over 26 hours and taken only 5 shots with three kills, plus I “accidently” shot a rabbit. Honest, Doc I was just checking the scope and the gun went off.
Is it worth paying an annual fee to hunt more animals with a better variety of weapons and equipment? I don’t know I have not done that yet but it is tempting.
Anyways I am off to go and get a first aid kit because I witnessed a feral hog maul a good mate to death, not pretty.

Emily is Away is a slightly interactive narrative experience detailing the relationship between two fellow high students: you'll do this by choosing different chat options while conversing with Emily and watching events unfold during the six years each chapter covers.
While short and pretty linear Emily is Away offers both a decent story and nostalgic throwback to the years of Windows 95 and AIM: it's an interesting project and can proviude some food for thought.
-graphics and sounds perfectly recreate the old Windows and AIM software
-overall decent narrative
-can create a fair amount of emotional pull
-while useless per se the fact you can choose an avatar and browse profiles is a nice touch
-while I understand it's part of the experience I found having to "fake type" each answer pretty annoying
-Emily can come across as a pretty unlikeable character
-while your choices definitely add different nuances to the story Emily is Away is still quite linear and you're basically shoehorned into the ending
-parts of the story feel quite cliched
-very short, it took me 30 mins to complete
As said above Emily is Away is a quite short and somewhat limited experience but I really enjoyed my time with it: this was due to how well it manages to capture certain aspects of human relationships, namely how people can sometimes drift away or fight despite deeply caring for each other.
It's this sense of slow estrangement, of words not said or said too late that makes Emily is Away worth at least a playthrough: I'm sure most people will surely be able to relate to what's depicted and felt here and will see the resemblance in their own past friendships or love relationships.
It's free so you only risk losing some bandwidth and HD space by trying it: I recommend it both as a trip down nostalgia lane (if you're old enough) and as a good piece to reflect upon.

I have only played the game for 7 hours by now, so my opinion might still change.
Turnbased empire building
The amount of micromanaging is more then I care to do. But that is just my personal preference. You manage technologies, citybuilding and your leaders. And all of these have lot's of parameters. For cities you have to worry about public order, food, growth and wealth which seems easy enough. But if you begin to take the factors into account that play into those it gets quite mind-staggering. Cultural influences, trading, technologies and not to mention your leaders all have a say in those matters. Said leaders have only 3 basic stats at first glance. But if you look closer you find lot's of additional traits and even more stats that you will want to consider carefully when making choices about what to do with what leader and whom to promote. If your into that kind of game it will be like heaven but I prefer games that are quite a bit lighter on the mirco management front.
Real time battles
The main reason I play Total War games is to crush my enemies, see them driven before me and hear the lamentations of their woman. Rome does deliver on that (well, minus the lamentations). You have real-time battles with lot's of troop types. These types all have their purpose. Have ranged troops rain death upon your foes, let your spear-units tie up the enemies main force while your cavalry outflanks him and attacks his rear. But even there things have become more complicated. Now high level leaders have abilities you can activate... which is in my opinion more fitting for a MOBA then a grand war-strategy game. On the plus side you have troop types you've rarely seem in other total war games. Heck, my main reason for buying this game was my urge to scythe trough my enemies with my egyptian war-chariots and I was not disappointed in that regard ;)
Bugs
Reading many comments about it, I'm quite happy that I waited that long to finally buy it since it appears that by now it is actually playable. I cringe to think about how bad it must have been at release. It still has bugs. In my 7 hours of gameplay I encountered 3 crashes. All of them occured during the AI turns and just restarting the game and loading the last auto-save did the trick for 2 of those crashes. The last one occured also during an AI turn, but it happend after I fought off a bigger force and emerged victorious. Reloading after the crash I found that I had to redo the battle. I was quite annoyed about that.
Verdict
Honestly I can't really say if it's good or not at this point. I like the battles but while I like the basic idea of the turn based empire building its level of complexity is a bit too much for me to really enjoy it. Many times if feels more like work then fun to me. The crashes can be annoying but they'll probably eventually fix them for good.
I'm giving it 7 out of 10 points which is barely a thumbs up. Consider carefully what kind of game you really want to play for what price before buying this.
Update: I'm changing my original rating to a thumbs down as crashes during AI turns are increasing and reloading doesn't seem to help anymore. There is what feels like a 200 step program on the CA support page that I will try eventually. Right now it feels more like "let's post a really complicated guide... no one will follow it so we can be freed of all blame" thingy.
The game itself would now get 8 out of 10 point from me. But sadly thats worthless if it crashes during every other AI turn.

Alien: Isolation is a first person survival game, with an emphasis on being stealthy and resourceful.
The Alien franchise to me is not one I personally have had much involvement with, but it is a franchise that has been treated criminally when it comes to the games associated with it.  I can safely say that this is THE Alien game that fans of the franchise should own.  It is incredibly intense and you can often find multiple ways through an area, let it be with a gadget that distracts, sneaking around quietly, or even by banging your tool on a metal surface to attact attention as you sneak away.  It was immensely satisfying to discover new ways to get things done.
There are a few types of enemies that you will run across, each with their own strengths and weaknesses.  Keep in mind that this is NOT an Aliens game where you want to run around guns blazing, generally that is the fastest way to a guaranteed death more often than not.  You will need to learn how to exploit weaknesses and not be wasteful with your ammuntion since it is very limited.  I absolutely recommend this game to anyone wanting a terror-inducing Aliens experience.  The ending is the only thing that disappoints me, but the experience makes up for it.

The overall RNG that is involved with many of the mechanics makes the game outright unfair and stupid. Have fun constantly starving or dying of dehydration because RNJesus decided that you weren't allowed to start a fire in a few tries today.
Combat is wayyyy too easy early game. You can take down pretty much anything you'd find during that phase of the game as long as you have a stone spear which is obtainable within 10-15 minutes of gameplay, tops. Losing health isn't even that much of a problem as you can easily heal it simply by resting in a bed, which is also easy to obtain through the early game. It seems the only real threats are EXTREMELY rare enemies or dehydration/starvation.

An extremely addicting little survival game with a highly detailed crafting system and a fantastic inventory system!
Hunger, thirst, energy, skills that level up while you do their respective things, like crafting, swimming, fletching and combat. (And lots more, I mean lots.. lots more)
You can set the game to casual so that you can pick up your items upon death, but that kind of ruins the game, so keep it at perma-death, trust me!

For being early access this game is amazing and way worth the low price for such a great quality game.
Survival games are at this point almost overused because of their lack of depth or realism but this game despite being 2D gives you much more than what is seen in other games. During my 60 hours of gameplay I have played many maps and runs and have still not lost the fun of exploring and discovering new recipes and items. The game adds mechanics that are seldomly used such as desalinization, multi functional tool usage, a sensable karma system, indepth recipes to craft items (like the struggle to make iron ingots, I will say no more due to spoilers) among other cool features.
I was chased around my house by a deranged goat who wanted to have his way with me while I slept. I was blockaded on all four exits by powerful creatures which all wanted to eat my flesh in exchange for the mountain I had tunneled into. I was stranded on a desert island where I had to carefully farm the couple cocunut trees in order to survive the dangers of thirst and hunger while also utilizing the much needed resource: WOOD!
Don't get me wrong, there is room for minor improvements and the game is open to a vast array of new features, expansions and items. Besides a few minor tweaks regarding menus sizes, item movement, floor stacking and an awkward imbalance in the karma feature this game is pretty solid and another awesome "just one more" game.

Personally it takes me a while before I'm willing to sink time into a game, unless it's something I've instantly clicked with then, guaranteed, I'll let it fade away into obscurity along with the rest of my bargain bin, steam crap.

I bought this game for £6 on sale and ME -O-MI, my opinion has taken a full 180 turn.
I might even go as far as to say that this is one of the most elder scrollsy elder scroll games ever.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The ability to travel across Tamriel as you please is very exciting as previously we've been bound to Cyrodil, Morrowind and Skyrim, personally (yet again) I've never felt like these games feel as alive as they should, somehow, ESO manages to make it work, baffling me as MMO's are usually stupid ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥nonsense♥♥♥♥♥♥grinding ♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ing world of warcraft.
It achieves something that every other MMO lacks in, the sense of adventure. Being able to step into the shoes of your character, travel as you please whilst the world scales to your level (Mostly) so you'll usually be able to handle anything thrown at you and giving you the option to avoid combat entirely and focus on other skills is a really handy feature.
An example of this is you could legitimately spend all of your time crafting items and furniture, sell it off or trade it and become Tamriels sexiest vendor.
As far as NPC'S in MMO's go, ESO has it nailed down. remember running around breaking into houses? pickpocketing unsuspecting strangers and going on chicken murder sprees?? Well ESO has all of this, stealth works well, random NPC's can be killed just as in previous games and guards will be sure to let you know that you've VIOLATED THE LAW! which can be paid off though any items you've ran around stealing (also making a valiant return) will be confiscated unless you visit an outlaw's refuge.

I would not reccomend this game based on the following reasons:
1. It's very buggy - some areas you can't access without it bugging out.
2. Lag - the game's FPS behaves strangely a lot of the time no matter how powerful your rig is. I've heard confliciting things about this issue from various people. For some it's fine but for others it's not. With regards to myself, I've experienced quite bad lag from time to time. E.g it'll go from 20 fps to 54 fps to 30 fps etc etc.
3. No trade feature - I was partying with my brother and there was no way for him to trade a weapon fit for me.
4. Incredibly linear - if you were expecting a comfy game with some nice exploration then I'd give this game a miss.
5. Music - pretty subjective but I expected the music to be better.
Something I did like about the game is the combat and the amount of classes though. If you're willing to put up with a few cons and you don't mind linear games then this might be for you. Otherwise I wouldn't bother getting too invested.
It's a quick download and a fun time waster if you're currently downloading a bigger game, or just need a quick game to hop into for ~10 mins.

I had high expectations for this, even tho i didnt want to buy early access i was pretty hyped. Now i am happy i didnt. Game has a lot of flaws, most major atm are server issues, euro server is not even that populated and it constantly lags, i am playing archer and i do double dps when it doesnt lag.
♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ auction system - you cant buy/sell anything for 72 hours when you start to play, when you finally can start selling tooltips on items you put on auction(average price and stuff) are completely wrong, you need to check every material(and after 72 hours i had about ~90 of them) manually. But that isnt everything, even if you manage to sell something you need to wait 48 hours to get your silver. This makes absolutely no sense to me.
Other major issue is forced party play. Being in a group gives you more xp then solo. In full group you can get 450% more xp per monster, considering half of the areas are dead/close to dead this makes no sense again. Why should solo gameplay be punished in a grinding game, i have no idea.
Next issue is dungeon queue. Considering you get even more bonus xp(600%) if you dont make premade group for dungeon, you need to queue for some to get good xp. Well, 99% of the time you just gonna stare at 'Searching for party' window for hours if you have nothing else to do. Also game has no info on dungeon locations, but that is tolerable considering queue mechanic itself. Queue should be long distance and not require you to wait at dungeon entrance, period. Oh and 1 more thing about dungeons, 90% of the time you get nothing, there are total 2(+1 when you get premium token) entrances COMBINED per day. Actually its not that bad since you cant even find group for 1 dungeon, lol.
Now about good stuff, art/locations/quests are actually pretty enjoyable, characters are really cute.
But considering party play will probably stay same and I am really not a fan of grinding normal monsters with other people, i have doubts i am gonna enjoy playing this game further.
