Bought this when it was still in early access, and continue to play it to this day.
Broforce isn't like any other 2D shooter/platformer I can think of. Your character (or Bro) is randomised each time you start a mission and/or respawn upon death. You are killed with a single hit, so avoiding enemy fire is crucial to your survival.Each Bro has their own attacks and special abilities, and most will have personalised melee attacks. A few will have a more specialised skill, such as Neo's ability to fly around using the melee button/key + a direction or the Terminator's ability to use his minigun kickback to fly across the map at great speed. You can play single player or up to 4 players local co-op or online.
The levels are varied and have a lots of challenges to overcome. Almost all terrain is destructible, meaning in most cases you can blast through terrain to safely clear a mission, though this is way less fun than chewing through enemy troops on the surface. The level of variety is not only visual but gameplay based, meaning one strategy won't cover every level you play through, and you'll need to adapt on the fly as levels increase in complexity, especially in the second half of the game.
While you can be killed with a single bullet, the same cannot be said for your enemies, many of whom will take sustained damage before dying. There's a small stealth element to the game which rewards you for playing smarter and avoiding enemy line of sight. Once you're spotted though you'll have less than a second to react - be quick with your trigger finger.
Enemies behave very somewhat unpredictably in Broforce despite them always being in the same place each time. While they only have a few states (idle, suspicious, attacking for instance) the way an enemy reacts can sometimes lead to interesting situations, and by that I mean they can sometimes kill themselves or their friends by accident. Personally there's nothing better than aggravating a terrorist and watching him shoot an explosive barrel, resulting in the death of everyone nearby. Sometimes you don't need to get involved at all; enemies can occasionally clear themselves out which always got a laugh out of me.
Oh, and did I mention you can ride pigs and melee them to fly in the air? Yeah, you can do that.
The drawbacks of this game are few but I've listed my gripes here to balance things out. In some cases it can be really unclear what to do in a boss fight and in some cases the boss fights seem impossible (I'm looking at you, Rail Fortress!) until you figure out what is expected of you.
Occasionally, the game has an issue where the sound degrades momentarily (announcer voice, or menu sounds for example), which has been present since the last patch. As I'm unsure the game will receive future patches I wanted to mention this - if that changes I'll remove this from my review.
When playing online, I've noticed it can be really easy to accidentally add another local player to your game, and then removing them is damn near impossible which can really sour the experience as this extra player will block you from progressing. Usually it'll occur if you're playing on a gamepad, and you touch the wrong key on your keyboard. Just keep an eye out for that if you are playing online.
The game is only mildly buggy, and the bugs that I've encountered tend not to spoil a run. In any case, one mission can take between 30 seconds and 5 minutes at most, so if you do get stuck or you kill a boss and die (which can result in a "mission failed" screen) you're not losing a ton of progress thankfully.
Overall for a simple game it has a ton of content, a lot of replayability and is one of the best couch co-op experiences I could suggest. Definitely pick it up if you see it on sale!
Tips:
- Holding the down key/button and throwing an explosive will throw it right in front of you. Great for Rambo and his grenades or Chuck Norris and his grenade launcher.
- The Predator can skin enemies and hang them from the ceiling which will induce a fear state in nearby enemies. This often results in enemies jumping to their deaths which is endlessly funny.
- You can be resurrected by the Universal Soldier, but if you are resurrected and are the only one left, you cannot complete a mission, as you're technically dead.

In my first fifteen minutes of the game, I have seen:
- My amazing first step to farming.
- Worker who pulls out the carrot, flings it on the floor and walks away.
- Major avian invasion.
- Chickens that makes a squirt sound as they leave their eggs everywhere without care.
- Rabbits hopping around waiting at the carrot fields waiting to harvest
carrots.
- Foxes that don't sneak up to steal their winnings.
- And every bit the cuteness those screenshots promised on store page.
Here, you have your farm, you cultivate crops and bushes and trees and you make willing slaves farm for you. Let animals poop everywhere, and fruits falling in every acre that workers can't always be bothered to walk a short distance over to pick it up for you. Then comes the amazing stack of eggs no one cares about that is as tall as your bushes have always instantly grown. But let's leave the voluntary slaves alone. They aren't paid after all.
It's really a casual clicking game. Not your usual clicker heroes and the similar, since it's not really about battling the hordes of monsters. If you want a clicker game with few bits of strategy, you're probably looking in the wrong place. For the price of this game, it comes with all in-game stuff unlockable and no micro-transactions. But this isn't a game that will keep bringing you back for months. It would probably be short, and quick to complete. I can't say that for sure, since I'm less than half an hour in. Plantera is definitely an option if you're looking for an easy achievement hunt, or for all the adorable graphics here, and perhaps just something relaxing to look at as you unwind your busy day with a casual clicker. It could be anyone's cup of tea, or never.
P.S. I couldn't resist the cuteness.

Immersive is definitely one thing that I would say about this wonderful game.  The permadeath, while something that I would normally grin and bear with, is almost enjoyable on its own, coupled with how you earn bonuses that give you a reason to try doing good in the first place.  The crafting system, an almost afterthought in some games, is wonderfully tuned to interact with and encourage the player to experiment with all that is on display. Overall the game is a breath of fresh air, and if the most popular 2.5 Wishlist items get successfully implemented, I think the game will be a success. Hopefully we will be hearing something soon!

TLDR:   BUY THE GAME YOU WON'T REGRET IT!!
First, let me start by saying, My game play style is usually casual.  I'm normally not a fan of rogue-like, perma-death games at all.  Games that even have the words rogue-like or perma-death, I wouldn't usually even give a chance.....BUT.....A friend that is, and always will be a rogue at heart in every game, that has played Wayward long before it even came to Steam, repeatedly tried to get me to play saying,  "just try it, I think you will like this one" managed to get me hooked on this game.
Well, that was April of 2016, and since that date I've so far logged 560 hours of play time, which would be even more if work didn't consume my spare time daily. :)

EVERYONE.. really needs to take a look at this game, even if you've passed over it before, I'd say, look again, just give it a try!  The Developers, are always working on Wayward, updates occur quite frequently, fixes are always being put into play for things that aren't they find aren't going the way they thought would originally work. Drathy, one of the Devs, streams the game on Twitch, usually twice a week. In my opinion, he's a very friendly guy, streaming while he's actively working on the fixes and updates, asking questions of his viewers that have been playing the game.  Drathy listens to comments and suggestions, has created a polls for player input, requests the input of things players would like to see in the game for possible future game updates. He has been actively working on Multiplayer with a few live stream nights where he opened up a multiplayer test game while streaming, for viewers to jump in for testing purposes.  Although multiplayer is not yet live at the time of this posting, it is actively being worked on and is coming, something I know many gamers, like myself want and look forward to.  I highly suggest looking into purchasing this game, I don't think anyone would ever regret owning this.  Also, I suggest looking up Drathy on Twitch, join his live stream of Wayward, hang out with a great group of regular viewers, make some new friends, or if lurking is your thing, then enjoy just listening and watching, I do that a lot too! ;)  You'll get a chance to see the game as he's playing and working on bugs/fixes/ maybe even a night of multiplayer testing. If you tried Wayward, maybe there was something you felt just off about it, I'd suggest you offer your input to Drathy, maybe it's also been the same thing someone else feels but hasn't yet said, or maybe it's already being worked on for a fix. I've watched live streams of other Dev's/Games and basically I was seriously bored, felt rather ignored, and I didn't stick around very long.  I have to say, Drathy's live stream and the group of viewers that are usually there hanging out, all make you feel welcome, input and comments aren't ignored. I've found him to be a very friendly, down to earth guy, who is genuinely interested in what Wayward players and potential players want and wish more games had.

Now more about my thoughts on Wayward. :)
Wayward is a rogue-like, perma-death game.  The game is heavy on crafting, (which drew me in immediately) gathering plants, seeds, resources, building a shelter, building storage spaces for all my resources, planting the seeds to create a farm for food and additional resources for crafting, getting the "farm" to expand to even more resources. Wayward is a "survival" crafting game that really does take a lot of patience and definate "perseverance". Once you get it though, and get your survival tactics down, I think everyone, either rogue or non rogue-style liking players will all find they really enjoy the game.  Game play challenge can increase and decrease at random, dependent on what you decide to do in your game, (You'll understand just what I mean by this when you play.) You will find you need new survival tactics dependent on the challenges you cause by your actions. This is the fun and definate excitement of Wayward!  Just when you think you got it, managed to survive for days and days and days.. all it will take is just one wrong action without planning ahead, and your done,game over.  Starting over though,is a new challenge, it's a new chance to try and beat what you didn't before, to do it different and survive. Rebuild, remake everything even better than the last game. The game will definately try to kill you, even if you have just logged in for the first time and haven't a clue where to begin, you're probably going to die. LOL
Wayward isn't a game to just jump in and begin punching trees and rocks bare handed for wood and stone, unless you like slow bleeding death  :)  Although, perma-death really is the thing liked most about rogue-like games, recently, an update included the option and palyers choice to choose casual play. You will still have a challenge after death though, you still need to recover your dropped items at the place of your demise while trying to avoid whatever may have knocked you down. :)
Whatever play style you prefer, the Dev's are really working hard to make it fantastic, fun and exactly what gamers want in a good game.
Best advice personally I would give is to DO THE TUTORIAL FIRST, and don't be discouraged if you end up dieing repeatedly. Try and retry again and when you are so frustrated you want grab anything within reach and hurl it at your screen.. close your eyes...take a deep breath and scream..     "CHALLENGE ACCEPTED WAYWARD!"
WAYWARD GIVES EVERY PLAYER A UNIQUE, RANDOMLY GENERATED WORLD IN WHICH TO LIVE AND DIE!

The crafting could be better, all it is is a little menu on the side, but the sorting feature is nice. The huds I think could be bigger, but then again I swear I'm blind ha.
This game does have a mix with Stardew Valley that meets Minecraft kind of feel to it. The turn base for me kind of lags a little here and there while I'm trying to get my character to move, but no biggie. I wouldn't say the controls are clunky, it is a typical WASD movement and right and left click. I do think a map needs to be added in, I can't say how many times I lost where I placed down my campfire, but it's not a huge ordeal. But besides those little blips and flaws of the game I like the adventure in it, and the potential that this game can have if the developers stick to it and keep on working on it.

If one manages trough the steep learning curve and the roguelike element of "having bad luck", this is a truly fantastic game under constant development. The Devs don't shy away from a challenge, by implementing multiplayer for example(as I am writing this, multiplayer is not yet released).
I must warn, there is little to no handholding in this game and some mechanics are not very intuitive. This does however make experimentation more fun, as there is more than one approach to many tasks.
The community and Devs are quite helpful and the development process is very open. There currently is no up to date Wiki, mostly due to the rapid and large updates in Wayward.
It is a fun game, survival can be as tough as you want it to be, the weight limit is somewhat cumbersome and the roguelike elements are fun and frustrating. And remember, “Losing = fun”.

Any feedback given to the devs is considered. This might lead to the “You can’t make everyone happy” problem, but for now Drathy seems to be in control. Upcoming features can be found at the trello and in the discord server of Wayward are often sneak peeks at implementations.

Personally it takes me a while before I'm willing to sink time into a game, unless it's something I've instantly clicked with then, guaranteed, I'll let it fade away into obscurity along with the rest of my bargain bin, steam crap.

I bought this game for £6 on sale and ME -O-MI, my opinion has taken a full 180 turn.
I might even go as far as to say that this is one of the most elder scrollsy elder scroll games ever.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The ability to travel across Tamriel as you please is very exciting as previously we've been bound to Cyrodil, Morrowind and Skyrim, personally (yet again) I've never felt like these games feel as alive as they should, somehow, ESO manages to make it work, baffling me as MMO's are usually stupid ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥nonsense♥♥♥♥♥♥grinding ♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ing world of warcraft.
It achieves something that every other MMO lacks in, the sense of adventure. Being able to step into the shoes of your character, travel as you please whilst the world scales to your level (Mostly) so you'll usually be able to handle anything thrown at you and giving you the option to avoid combat entirely and focus on other skills is a really handy feature.
An example of this is you could legitimately spend all of your time crafting items and furniture, sell it off or trade it and become Tamriels sexiest vendor.
As far as NPC'S in MMO's go, ESO has it nailed down. remember running around breaking into houses? pickpocketing unsuspecting strangers and going on chicken murder sprees?? Well ESO has all of this, stealth works well, random NPC's can be killed just as in previous games and guards will be sure to let you know that you've VIOLATED THE LAW! which can be paid off though any items you've ran around stealing (also making a valiant return) will be confiscated unless you visit an outlaw's refuge.

I really have no qualms as far as the world goes, its by far my favourite as far as Elder Scrolls goes and it really feels like its your adventure and not a forced story for

The one thing that grinds at me regarding combat is that bows don't work like bows, the draw is incredibly slow and doesn't seem to affect anything at all so you're much better off just spamming the left mouse for a series of quick blows, if you enjoy getting sucked into the world then this can definitely put you off as it did me for a while.

So... you may be asking why I am recommending this game. This game, while definitely not perfect, still manages to keep the feel that Just Cause 2 had with an immersive world and fun gameplay while improving on many mechanics such as driving/flying, grappling, shooting, etc. They also make the game so much more enjoyable by adding completely new ones like walking on planes and land vehicles and being able to hook 2 grappling hooks to an obect and pulling using an assigned key (shift in my case). I hear many people saying that the characters are uninteresting and the story is boring which I do not totally agree with as many of the characters are very well voiced and have a lot of personality! However, they forget that since the beginning, the Just Cause series was never about having a strong story... in fact the main premise and the strongest part of the game is destruction and causing as much of it as you possibly can. As far as the visuals go, the game is beautiful on the highest setting and even on "High" but it's optimization is lacking and I think the developers could have easily fixed it, however this is only really an issue when there are many explosions and NPC's in one area or in a select few of the larger towns. Sound is good but nothing MIND BLOWING like BF1 or Battlefront.
In short, this game probably could have used a few more weeks in the studio for optimizations sake but if you can get past that and a somewhat lackluster or rather generic storyline, then I guarantee you will enjoy the amazing destruction elements and non-stop action that this game offers as well as the beautiful land of Medici (not a real place sadly). If you liked Just Cause 2 a lot then please play this game!!!

Plantera is wonderful. It's simplistic. It's an idle-game; you don't need to babysit the screen. You can click, but the benefits to doing so after the first few minutes are fairly minor, and at no point does the game try to forcefully keep your attention, or make you feel guilty about being inefficient, or forgetting you've left it open in the background. It will still be there, waiting for you. The local critters will help themselves to your crops (though you can buy guard dogs to help defend against them), but there's no need to be greedy. There's plenty to go around.
There's no need for complex spreadsheets, to minmax your way to lording your superior progression over the casuals. You won't find any bloated complexity here; though your blue helpers are fairly blob-like. Checking in on your farm is a relaxing, satisfying experience, that brings a smile to your face.
Absolutely worth the price.

Alright so every popular review has a negative recommendation. I hope I can hope convince anyone reading why this is a legitimately good game. I have played for 17 hours at writing this review so I've obviously put in a good 2-3 days of binge playing the game.
Most people rage at this game, quit, uninstall and write a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ review. People have bad encounters with other people. It happens in every video game. I just checked my first every character I havent touched in a week - he is still logged out in my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ doorless home, on the stairs, with all of his stuff on a 22/40 people server. Not all people are bad.
Let's start with a good old fashion THIS IS AN EARLY ACCESS GAME. I am a hypocrite in saying I don't enjoy spending money on unfinished content but I have bought games like Starforge, The Forest and Verdun. Verdun I watched grow up and it turned out to be a great game, which means Early Access games can be really good... when they release. Anyways, the reason why I spammed Early Access was realyl for the reasoning of saying there will be bugs. This game is Alpha. This is not a clean cut AAA game like The Witcher 3 or GTA V (Which even have their fair share of bugs.)
Let's do a pretty Pro's and Con's list.
Pros:
- Not impossible but not easy survival challenge.
- Graphically, it looks decent. Animations are a lot better than most early access.
- The music is suprisingly good, besides the sad/spoopy music plays at random times.
- There are already 2 maps, Crownlands (orginial w/ the big king statue) and Stormwall which is 1.6x bigger.
- 5 tiers of equipment makes this not a quick 10min grind for a top tier gear (cough minecraft). I'd say to get every crafting station and full set a gear at least 2+ hours if you're also trying to build a home.
- ANIMALS! Hunting is pretty ♥♥♥♥in' great. Humans and animals leave a blood trail when injured so you can follow the trail to your prey. It's kinda awesome and a feature I really appreciate.
- A lot of cosemetic items and furniture. I've seen red demon masks and greek tragedy theater masks. Also there are a lot of chairs, beds, and lightnings to make.
- Kidnapping/Torture. Yes it sounds really sadistic but that is a fun feature of the game. Instead of being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who just kills people, you can simply kidnap them, bring them to your dungeon, lock em in a cage and be done with it until they starve. Or they can be sent to the gallows or guillotine. Your choice.
- King! Claim the throne or kill the king. You can set tax up to 20% so that every resource anyone gathers is taxed. King also has the best helmet and weapon in game. (Pls dont be like Joffrey).
Now here are the Cons and why they are Cons:
- Combat. Combat has obvious influence from Chivalry. It's better than Mount and Blade: Warband combat, or at least on par on a laggy day, but not close to Chivalry.
- Audio sounds.  Footsteps and horns are usually pretty accurate but I hear a deer running sometimes and it just is so off from their foot steps. Very minor, but the attention to this detail would make hunting cooler.
- Hackers. Alright this is everyone's HUGE issue. There are 2 types of servers; Official and Community. Official is pretty straight forward and are sponsored by CodeHatch. Then there are community which anyone can make if they look up how on the wiki. in 17.2 hours of playing, I personally have not ran into a single hacker. Maybe i'm lucky or they've fixed it since the popular reviews were made. These guys on the popular reviews also probably played on Communtiy servers that we can only assume less protected, and got hackers in full armor.
At the beginning of downloading the game, it installs an EAC, easy anti-cheat (or something like that). Honestly the devs are doing as much as they can for an EARLY ACCESS game to prevent hackers. Games like The Forest that have way better reviews for a way buggier game have better reviews because 90% of these negative reviews are whining about hackers. Hackers are way less prevalent on a survival game that's mainly single player (The Forest).
If you want to have like your own little Game of Thrones/Medival/Something experience and think this game will deliver- it will. Buy it while it is on sale because unlike ARK: Survival, this game actually went on sale during the Summer Sale for more than a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 17% off. (40% to be exact)

I'm so happy that I bought this game on a whim. I'm so happy that after hours of frustration over the inital difficulty level of Wayward, I continued out of pure determination. This game is SO MUCH MORE than the difficulty of your first few tries. For me, it was all about discovering ~balance~.
It took some time, but when I fully understood the impact of maintaining a good reputation - forraging and farming to start, crafting weapons and killing stuff later - the game got SO MUCH BETTER. I wish there was more stress placed on just how important reputation is from the beginning. It would have saved me a quite few hours of stress... but at the same time, I may not have appreciated this discovery as much? I avoided walkthroughs up until I was really established in my current run. As soon as I knew how to survive and sustain myself, I felt more comfortable seeing how others played the game.

This is a Rogue-like, and like ye olde Rogue, there is a lot of trial-and-error in this game. Mostly error. A great deal of error. I'll admit, there were plenty of times where I nearly rage-quit just trying to finish the tutorial, and a few times where I tried to burn the game world down in frustration.
But after toughing it out for a few hours, eventually forgoing the tutorial in favour of just screwing around, seeing for myself what works and what doesn't, I believe I've finally got this game figured out. And as a result, I'm really starting to enjoy it. I came into this game thinking it to be somewhere between Nethack and Survival Kids (gameplay closer to the latter, difficulty closer to the former), found what I expected, and also found a bit of Minecraft and Stardew Valley mixed in.
The devs pay attention to the community, and have shown up in some of my livestreams to see how I'm getting on and drop the occasional hint. They've even made small changes to the game based on seeing how people play.
This is a difficult game at first, and not a game for the impatient. But if you're willing to stick with it for the long haul, there's a lot to be discovered as your character gains skill levels and learns to craft new things. It seems nearly every time I adventure forth I find some new item and start looking into what I can make with it.
But I'd still like to know how that snake was carrying a sail.

First, I've really enjoyed my time in Wayward. Absoloutely worth it. However, a number of the other reviewer's criticisms are fair points.
- This game is challenging, and one wrong decision can kill you. Do not expect to survive for long your first half dozen playthroughs.
- In order to prevent Tough enemies from spawning before you're ready, it is wise to do a decent amount of literal farming. I enjoyed this, but some might not.
There's a bit going on behind the simple graphics (things like blunt vs slashing damage, food poisoning), but the interface, tooltips, and game messages do a lot to inform if you take the time to read them. Unlike most games that have a great wiki and tons of guides and Let's Plays, the online resources for Wayward are fairly sparse and often outdated. Wayward is about discovering it for yourself. Make mistakes, die, learn.
Conclusion: There is fun and satisfaction to be had in Wayward, crawling your way from "woke up on a desert island with nothing" to being the owner of a sprawling base with verdant fields of crops, making your own shiny armor, and standing atop a pile of exotic creature corpses.

A very typical straight forward on rails MMORPG. The game is pretty look at and has Elder Scrolls lore but that's where it ends for me. It's built on everything RPG gamers have known within the MMORPG world for the past 10 or so years.  You create a character that looks like everyone else, you kill stuff over and over, you speedily click through the extremely repetitive collect this or go there dialog. You will do this over and over with each new zone you enter. There is no inspiration in doing anything in this game. At times you will wonder why am I even bothering. I felt no reason to explore other than being fan of Elder Scrolls lore but even then that wasn't enough when the world feels small, bland, lifeless. If you do enjoy this game or MMORPG's similar I applaud you, truly. I believe majority, but not all of the gamers involved here become zombies, end goal? Max level best gear and grind grind grind! You will feel at times you have to waste away weeks of your life grinding to aquire these things within this style of game. To what end? You will wonder was the journey worth it because it was such a bland, yet meager on rails journey.
This game is nothing like Elder Scrolls series single offline variety, AKA Skyrim. However, I know they're different genres but you will play them strongly similar.  You will go through bulk of ESO alone, soloing quests. I managed to eek out 20 levels without grouping once. I couldn't stomach to continue the mindless, empty, lifeless journey of repetitiveness. I am not saying its a terrible game, but I am saying its not for me. I feel ESO can be written up as a WoW spinoff, I loved WoW when it was fresh and couple others that came out shortly after. However, I am extremely burnt out on these last gen MMORPG's. No developer seems to have the drive or talent to break out of the shadow of the most successful MMORPG of all time, very saddening. We have been force fed clone for long as I can remember and this one is barely any different.

I have just completed the main story and felt compelled to write a quick review for it. (no spoilers)
First up, the art direction and graphical design in this game is stunning. The atmosphere is beautiful and immersive. A stellar soundtrack magnifies the atmosphere to produce an overall, somewhat noire, cyberpunk theme for the game. The voice acting is top notch, serving only to enhance the in game experience and the storyline is enjoyable, intriguing, and well thought out.
The combat is innovative with an RPG-turn based strategy hybrid style which was a learning curve to begin with, but hugely rewarding to grasp. I found the game to be challenging in terms of difficulty, which I see as a good thing (though different people will have varying levels of skill). There are side training challenges, which you can sink hours into, as they get progressively harder. It also has a recursive mode after the game for enhanced replayability and challenge, though I am yet to explore this in any real depth.
So overall, I absolutely recommend this game. For a game coming from an indie developer (like seriously the credits are real short. they're over in a minute) this is simply sublime and competes with the big titles.

Transistor is a game about a girl and her sword against an all consuming enemy controlled by a shadow group with less than altruistic intentions. At first glance the combat system may seem simple with a Diablo like feel to it, that is until you begin to use the Turn() system making everything much more strategic giving you the ability to freeze time and carefully plan out your next move. While there are no talents or many lateral upgrades to choose from the game does have this intriguing upgrade system where you use one ability to augment another making it so you can tailor your ability set to best match your play style, or to better counter certain enemy types of which there are many. Logan Cunningham (Bastion) narrates the story from the point of view of the Transistor. What’s really nice is that they don’t try to hold your hand throughout the game, spoon feeding you the plot. No, instead the story unravels naturally letting you discover the plot for yourself which I really appreciated. All of this as well as a uniquely beautiful art style and an amazing soundtrack that is becoming a staple of these dev’s, Transistor makes for an excellent sophomore entry from developer Supergiant Games.

Thumbs up because:
- Pretty
- Quality voice actor (a true rarity!)
- Flexible combat skill management system
- Innovative non-death penalties for losing
Shame I don't enjoy playing it. Especially since Supergiant also made Bastion, the undisputed best creative work mankind has ever produced.
The plot? I don't get the plot, which is amazing considering how much talking that damn memory-stick-for-a-sword does. At the onset, characters are introduced in quantity and events transpire rapidly... I promptly acquired an unrecoverable amount of plot knowledge debt. Storywise, Transistor quickly spreads out in width, but not in depth... not until my anticipation had degenerated into indifference. I perpetually felt one step behind whatever was happening.
Transistor has a hybrid real-time/turn-based combat system (which makes up the bulk of the game) that isn't worth dwelling on. It's admirably done, and there's surely an audience for it, but I found it repetitive, predictable and boring.
The way that Red's skills are managed however... this is the good stuff. The real good stuff. Your combat abilities are called "functions". They sit in a great, big uncategorized pile. You can combine and use them however you see fit. Functions can be "installed" in 1 of 3 ways; as one of your 4 active abilities, as upgrades to those 4 abilities, or as passives. There are combinations that work very well, and combinations that work very poorly. Playing around with them is a treat. And you WILL play around with different function combinations whether you like it or not... because when your health runs out, rather than die, you lose the use of an active function. It stays disabled for long enough that you'll be compelled to replace it with something else in the meantime. It's a clever alternative to traditional gaming death that doesn't break flow, does invoke a penalty, AND promotes experimentation. Out of desperation, I was forced into using function combinations that I never would have otherwise... and oftentimes the effects were a pleasant surprise.
I believe that other people will find virtue or indifference where I find fault. Thumbs up and uninstalled.

Are there bugs? Yes. Are the enemies somewhat moronic? Often, yes. Did they ♥♥♥♥ Sheldon up and totally ruin the character as a whole? Hell yes they did! (Skip to the last paragragh for short version.)
So... you may be asking why I am recommending this game. This game, while definitely not perfect, still manages to keep the feel that Just Cause 2 had with an immersive world and fun gameplay while improving on many mechanics such as driving/flying, grappling, shooting, etc. They also make the game so much more enjoyable by adding completely new ones like walking on planes and land vehicles and being able to hook 2 grappling hooks to an obect and pulling using an assigned key (shift in my case). I hear many people saying that the characters are uninteresting and the story is boring which I do not totally agree with as many of the characters are very well voiced and have a lot of personality! However, they forget that since the beginning, the Just Cause series was never about having a strong story... in fact the main premise and the strongest part of the game is destruction and causing as much of it as you possibly can. As far as the visuals go, the game is beautiful on the highest setting and even on "High" but it's optimization is lacking and I think the developers could have easily fixed it, however this is only really an issue when there are many explosions and NPC's in one area or in a select few of the larger towns. Sound is good but nothing MIND BLOWING like BF1 or Battlefront.
In short, this game probably could have used a few more weeks in the studio for optimizations sake but if you can get past that and a somewhat lackluster or rather generic storyline, then I guarantee you will enjoy the amazing destruction elements and non-stop action that this game offers as well as the beautiful land of Medici (not a real place sadly). If you liked Just Cause 2 a lot then please play this game!!!

Okay, so this is going to look weird with what I'm about to say, but giving it a thumbs down. Here we go.
Pros:
-I really like the simplicity of this game. It's very straight-forward with it's approach to grinding.
-The gear you find at the Level 60000+ areas makes you feel like a god, as it should.
-The Shifter class feels broken, but as it's the last one you get, that makes sense. I like it overall.
-The game runs extremely smoothly, even when being forced to run at 50x normal speed. (I'm impatient.)
-The visuals are pretty nice, and it's interesting to see where all the little things they've added in the battles and what not from other games and other forms of media.
Cons:
-There's no real penalty to the game. I get it, it's mostly a idle game, but the RPG elements work against that, since in RPG's you get punished for failure. It's not a huge problem, just kind of bothers me. Maybe add another dungeon that has risk/reward?
-It does not take long for your gear to get VERY cluttered, and when you have to go through five characters multiple times each for each piece of gear, this quickly gets tedious. The outfits (wardrobe?) don't really help much, since you'll constantly be upgrading gear. That could be improved by having the outfit upgrade each piece in level as you get a higher level piece of gear of the same type. (E.G. Dragon Shield lvl 3 being replaced by lvl 7.)
-Spell balance is all over the place. Single target heal fully recovering HP regardless of level, but at higher lvls the AoE heal is pretty much worthless, except to get rid of debuffs. Certain other spells have this problem as well.
-A certain boss monster that you encounter every 500 levels during the first 10 worlds requires a certain way of defeating it... while in the very last area of the game, it does not. This feels very backwards.
-Once you hit the last area of the game, well, time to stop playing. I'm not saying this to be mean, but simply because there's no pay off. I've hit level 150,000+ expecting something, *anything* to be said about it, or at least just end credits. Nothing. I hope there's more content on the way, or the sequel addresses some of these problems.
That all being said, I thank the devs for making the game. It killed some time for me, and I don't regret that overall. Still, for somebody who likes grinding, the last detractor is what kills it for me. Peace. (edit is due to typo)

EDIT: mods fix this issue.
I did find the alien bugs to be way too over-powered in the early and mid stages of the game (mainly the stationary worm spitting defenses), but as soon as I got the tank, they became no match for me. I just plowed through their massive bases like it was no big deal, and retreated to the gun turrets to repair the tank a bit, then went back to plow through some more, rinse and repeat until they're all dead. My only concerns were simply to not get stuck. The AI in this game is very basic though, they travel in a straight line and in the exact same spot each and every single time, so you really don't need to defend your entire base, just the areas each enemy bases send their bugs to. They also attack on a predictable schedule.
There are obstacles in the game which blend in way too much, especially when zoomed out, to the point where running your vehicles into stuff at least once is to be expected. Once you run into them, and you happen to not destroy your vehicle in the process, it'll make a health bar on that obstacle, so at least you'll be able to see it next time. Or you can magically destroy it with your weapons because... reasons.
You're able to zoom in way too much to the point where the textures are extremely muddy and gross, I'd actually prefer if they limited that a bit cuz I really don't want to see muddy textures like that.
I also wish the minimap was a bit smaller as it takes up a lot of my 4:3 screen. It'd be really nice if I could play the game on the primary monitor and have the entire map displayed on my secondary monitor.
It would also be nice to be able to build bridges and stuff onto the lakes... especially hydro lines and pipes.
None of my complaints are major, but they are worth mentioning. Aside from that, the game is perfect.

This game is basically 'grey goo simulator', in a way. You start off on a planet. You have exactly one objective; Take your environment, and every last bit of mineral or liquid wealth in it, and use it to get more mineral wealth, occasionally setting a bit off to the side so you can reach endgame once you finally get tired of building more factories to build more factories to build more factories.
Now, I don't really like writing long winded reviews, but bear with me on this one; There are so very, very many facets to this game, that I can't really describe them all in one review. So let's go with the first really complicated thing you'll have to do.
Say you finally climb out of using your hands to punch rocks into usable chunks, and now have a cute little setup with a few furnaces and mining drills. Everything's happy and fun and you feel accomplished for a while. Then you realize, 'hey, shuffling all these raw resources to and fro is getting kinda tedious.' So you decide to start feeding what the drills make into the furnaces automatically. Easy enough, right? Few conveyor belts here and there, yay, automation. Then you realize a little later, 'hey, making all these complicated new things takes really, really long on my own. Maybe I'll start automating production of some of them...' And so, the vicious cycle of automation begins yet again; A few more conveyor belts than last time, with some optimization for speed of processing here and there, and hey, an hour later, it's finally done! You're finally making little bottles of stuff with no input from you! Then you realize, 'Hey, I think --' And yet again, the vicious cycle of automation rears it's head, and a few hours later, (if you're like me anyways) you end up with a big jumbled mess of conveyor belts taking who only knows what to who only knows where to make I don't even know anymore.
And you. Feel. Victorious. And also kinda hungry and thirsty and - holy moly it's been twelve hours maybe one more hour before i get up and go get dinner...
So yeah, I think I summed up the very basic gameplay pretty well for you. This game is fun. It's addictive. And it is most definitely worth every penny, go buy it now. And remember to feed and water yourself regularly inbetween automation binges.

Papers, Please is unlike any game that I've ever played. As some of the negatives review say, at times it can seem tedious and uninteresting. However, I feel like all those negative reviews are missing the very concepts that made me fall in love with this game.
On the surface, it seems like nothing more than a pretty tricky job simulator. On the surface.
It might just be me, but this game really caused me to think. Glory to Arstotzka. As you sit at your desk, faces come and go. A name in the game is nothing more than a credential that might be an error or a scam, if the citizen is trying to get in. You meet a man, inspect his passport. He's clean. He mentions that his wife is behind him, and asks that you be nice to her.
Another face steps up to the gate, and is missing some of the papers needed to pass. She begs you to let her through with her husband and tells you that if she's sent back, she'll be killed.
Do you let her through, getting a "strike" against your job, or do you send her back? Glory to Arstotzka.
This game is a job simulator, but it's also so much more. It's a game about a corrupt government and the importance of individuals. People are people, important, not pawns or items that should be tossed around and mistreated. It's a game about chosing to do the right thing, because after all, you're human. Everybody has a story. Faces, names... it's all important.
People matter.
Glory to Arstotzka.

I really want to say that I love this game, since I am really into top-down gathering/building games (similar to Harvest Moon and Stardew Valley), and I really like the simple, pixel graphics... but, this game is challenging. Really challenging. Infuriatingly so sometimes. I've owned the game for a whopping 24 hours now, and I've died at least 47,295,290 times. Give or take.
It's great that your skills carry over, but it's so frustrating to be farming materials for something big, only to die by the hands of a giant rat, and have to start over on a new map, where those materials are harder to find. I do like this game, and will definitely keep playing, but aside from the challenge of the game, there are a few, BIG things that are keeping me from totaly loving it:
1) The screen feels cluttered when the inventory/quests/etc. are pulled up, and even still after closing them.
2) The controls are a bit touchy, and it's easy to run face first into trees and rocks, or right over the item you're trying to gather.
3) The combat mechanic is a hot mess, and it's hard to tell if you're even hurting the enemy, then suddenly, you're dead.
4) The weird sound effects for when you do ANYTHING. Sure, you can turn the volume down/off, but then it's just... quiet.
Maybe I am passing judgment prematurely. It is the Beta after all! It's still fun. We'll see!

Despite my time spent playing this on Steam, I have likely hundreds of hours on the web version, which I played long before Steam had it. I started playing this back before it on Steam; it has an 8-bit pixel charm to the world and complemented with a wonderful music soundtrack. I definately recommend this if you have any interest in roguelikes, I definately recommend it if you enjoy survival crafting games with long-term subsistance, and I recommend it if you love 8-bit retro games in general. It really is great for playing in small doses, unlike many survival games, you will feel like you got something accomplished in 10 minutes, especially further into the game. It is equally well-suited to longer durations, though you will likely feel the sting of defeat a few times before getting the hang of survival. I won't spoil anything by giving details, because exploration is certainly a big part of Wayward.
Additionally, for those who have been burnt by early access - this is one of the exceptions, like Project Zomboid and Neo Scavenger.
Very Addictive

Although I would recommend this game there are some caveats to that so read the full review before you chock this one up as solely positive:
I really, REALLY want to love Wayward, but it's pretty flawed. I realize it's in early access and many of these things are likely to change over time and I certainly think it's worth the cost in it's present state but you need to know what you're getting into if you opt to buy the game.
You will spend A LOT of time managing your inventory. Much of this will include simply dropping items you don't need at the moment, and it gets really old doing so since each square can only hold a limited quantity of items. It's also not a very large quantity when you consider how much of each item you will end up with. A single tree, with all of the ingredients processed, can take several squares worth. You CAN just drop things all willy nilly, which is great until you need something specific.
This is particularly irritating when you're doing something like trying to build a shelter. You end up filling your inventory screen up in a haphazard fashion in order to get a few logs which you can use to construct one square's worth of floor or wall.
Pretty much everything you do in the game is like this. Building a stone shelter? Get prepared for three types of items, repeatedly processing items and sorting them while working around the small amount of weight you can hold.
It's inventory management hell. It reminds me of working in the back of a thrift store, where all we did was go through donations and sort items repeatedly.
Apart from the ridiculous inventory management, however, it's a solid game. I like the malignity mechanic, the depth of the crafting system, and the ridiculous, true-roguelike difficulty curve a lot. You can make awesome shelters, balance your actions in the world to avoid monster encounters for a long time, and do all sorts of fun things.
The only problem is that you'll spend half of your playtime managing your inventory... once you're used to the interface. You'll spend even more of it before that.
If you can handle that, it's a good game, possibly bordering on great with a lot of room to improve. If you can't... well, the game isn't something you'll enjoy in it's current state.

At first I liked everything about this game especially the awesome music, cute graphic design and also the simple mechanics. Everything was perfect for me and  I was really happy about this game. I was really excited what this game has to offer.
But I was relly sad to discover that  after 3 hours of idle/active gameplay I still had the same features that were there from the beginning, well to be fair there were actually some new things but only 3 and they weren't even exciting at all, I am talking about: Offline time upgrade, Dogs and Coin multiplier. So because I still had the same things to work with and nothing new to unlock after lvl 20 (that's when you have all the plants and trees unlocked and they just get upgraded as you level up) It started being just repeating the same thing over and over (Plant some plants --> Idle a bit --> Plant some plants etc.) without any goal. Plantera is a farm simulator in the "Clicker" genre that you can actively play or leave your workers to do the work for you.
It's obviously a farming game, the goal of the game is to expand your farm, buy more trees, buy more crops, buy some animals, some bushes and a few upgrades. Everytime you level up, you get access to new type of crops and everything. When you have unlocked everything, every levels after that gives bonuses to the first type of crops so they don't become useless.
The game has a very nice cartoonish artstyle and some pretty good background music. There's only one track in the game, but it doesn't get on my nerve like other idle games, it's relaxing. You can sit in front of your huge garden and just spend your time watching your workers loot everything for you and upgrade whenever you need to!
You must also defend your garden from birds and other animals too! Otherwise, they will steal your crops. You can also buy guard dogs to defend your precious plants! The game features 20 achievements and trading cards, which is great! The game will keep you occupied for a good 10 hours at least, but it does get repetitive. Taking into consideration the low price tag, if you like Idle games or Clicker games, I think this is a good purchase after all.
Overall, i'd say this game is worth it. It's simple, it's definately fun and really inexpansive! If you end up liking it, you should check out the other games from the same developer. He has tons of Clicker games on Steam and they're all fun to play!

Thumbs up because:
- Pretty
- Quality voice actor (a true rarity!)
- Flexible combat skill management system
- Innovative non-death penalties for losing
Shame I don't enjoy playing it. Especially since Supergiant also made Bastion, the undisputed best creative work mankind has ever produced.
The plot? I don't get the plot, which is amazing considering how much talking that damn memory-stick-for-a-sword does. At the onset, characters are introduced in quantity and events transpire rapidly... I promptly acquired an unrecoverable amount of plot knowledge debt. Storywise, Transistor quickly spreads out in width, but not in depth... not until my anticipation had degenerated into indifference. I perpetually felt one step behind whatever was happening.
Transistor has a hybrid real-time/turn-based combat system (which makes up the bulk of the game) that isn't worth dwelling on. It's admirably done, and there's surely an audience for it, but I found it repetitive, predictable and boring.
The way that Red's skills are managed however... this is the good stuff. The real good stuff. Your combat abilities are called "functions". They sit in a great, big uncategorized pile. You can combine and use them however you see fit. Functions can be "installed" in 1 of 3 ways; as one of your 4 active abilities, as upgrades to those 4 abilities, or as passives. There are combinations that work very well, and combinations that work very poorly. Playing around with them is a treat. And you WILL play around with different function combinations whether you like it or not... because when your health runs out, rather than die, you lose the use of an active function. It stays disabled for long enough that you'll be compelled to replace it with something else in the meantime. It's a clever alternative to traditional gaming death that doesn't break flow, does invoke a penalty, AND promotes experimentation. Out of desperation, I was forced into using function combinations that I never would have otherwise... and oftentimes the effects were a pleasant surprise.
I believe that other people will find virtue or indifference where I find fault. Thumbs up and uninstalled.

NMRiH is another coop zombie shooter, but what sets it apart from the others, is its higher degree of realism. Although zombies do not exist in the real world, your limitations as a human are very real and are accurately portrayed in this game. You have limited carrying space, your movement slows as you carry more weight, and you tire after throwing repeated melee attacks. You cannot take a million attacks before you die. You also do not have an unlimited stockpile of guns. This for sure makes the game more difficult, but it's great for gamers who enjoy a more realistic challenge. You also can become infected, which eventually leads to you turning into a zombie. You can use pills to prolong the infection from taking over and there is an item that can cure the infection, but it's rare to come across.
NMRiH is based on oldschool zombie movies. Most of the zombies in the game move slow, but occasionally there are zombies that run. The zombies have a significant amount of health, so it is important to aim for their heads to save ammo and stamina.
The game has both wave-based and objective-based maps. Both are fun and challenging in their own ways. The only downside of some maps, is they are very difficult to complete without a group. I completed many maps with one other teammate, but a few maps are overwhelming with just two of us. This is not a flaw with the game, though. After all, humans have a better chance of survival while in groups and this game was designed to be played with a group.
If you are a fan of the George Romero zombie films, then you will appreciate the plentiful references to his films in NMRiH.
There are maps based on the settings of movies such as Night of the Living Dead and Day of the Dead. There is even references to slasher films like Friday the 13th and Halloween. Even if you are not a fan of oldschool zombie movies, there is still plenty of fun to be had with NMRiH.
To top it all off, the entire game is free!

It was a few years until this reached steam, and I was playing it on and off, and still do. Way back when there was a small number of players and people submitting bugs, I was there submitting a few as well, and Drathy was keen to resolve them. I also included ideas for improvements, and recently did again. One important issue about movement was addressed in the latest update around mid August, 2017, which I know is a big aspect for some people because of the coding and foundation this game was built on.
I have likely put in around 40-50 hours of play time since first stumbling across it. It was hard to find; games like this are not common, and I did a lot of research back then to locate such a game.
While this is rogue-like, it’s so much more because of how intricate the details are within the gameplay. The learning curve is steep, but that’s a huge part of the fun, just like life. I recall the days when we had no wiki’s or online guides — we had to teach ourselves while finding the most efficient ways of doing things — this is a key aspect of the game, as it’s important to die so you can begin again, as beginning again is fun (again, just like life). There may come a time when you are tired of repeating the same things, over and over again, so then you change the rules and perhaps do things a bit differently — that option is there in the game.
Some people complain that the game is too hard… that’s the point of rogue-like games. If it was easy at first, it would be somewhat boring. It’s important to play, learn, grow and master the many elements, while enjoying the journey along the way.
If you are looking for a rogue-like survival RPG that cares about the detail, and is well supported by the developers, then this one is
.

Papers, Please is unlike any game that I've ever played. As some of the negatives review say, at times it can seem tedious and uninteresting. However, I feel like all those negative reviews are missing the very concepts that made me fall in love with this game.
On the surface, it seems like nothing more than a pretty tricky job simulator. On the surface.
It might just be me, but this game really caused me to think. Glory to Arstotzka. As you sit at your desk, faces come and go. A name in the game is nothing more than a credential that might be an error or a scam, if the citizen is trying to get in. You meet a man, inspect his passport. He's clean. He mentions that his wife is behind him, and asks that you be nice to her.
Another face steps up to the gate, and is missing some of the papers needed to pass. She begs you to let her through with her husband and tells you that if she's sent back, she'll be killed.
Do you let her through, getting a "strike" against your job, or do you send her back? Glory to Arstotzka.
This game is a job simulator, but it's also so much more. It's a game about a corrupt government and the importance of individuals. People are people, important, not pawns or items that should be tossed around and mistreated. It's a game about chosing to do the right thing, because after all, you're human. Everybody has a story. Faces, names... it's all important.
People matter.
Glory to Arstotzka.

Well, I recommend it from an historical standpoint, mostly. Being from Italy I felt a strong connection with places and events, so I gave it a go after playing Shogun 2, to which I could not possibly relate. And...I have to agree with most other opinions out there. Rome is very bland and random, as Total War gameplay is concerned, but if you come from the Mediterranean region this will be offset by the sole satisfaction of moving on familiar ground.
Why bland and shallow? At my first play, I conquered half the world like a steam roller, without being aware of doing anything subtle or strategic. I just won battle after battle on full auto drive, eventually defeating armies four times bigger than mine >_> That does not sound...normal. The game will offer no real challenge, and the little aggression you will suffer will be totally random and uncalled for. There is also a vague Warhammer feel to it, with units clearly pulled out of imagination and with fictional legendary stats.
If you want an epic impression of ancient Mediterranean, Rome 2 is great fun, but as Total War depth and challenge, it is no big deal.

Insane clickity-click framing game. As you can see from the screenshots it gets crazy. I was surprised how fast it happens though. One minute you're tapping butterflies and shooing away a rabbit - the next, you're swinging the camera wildly from left to right hoping that there's not a flock of rogue birds stealing your carrots. It's a very simple game, you collect money and plant fruit and vegetables. Your little farmers do the harvesting (you can too, by clicking on the ripe fruit/veggies) which nets you more money to buy higher grade plants which land you more cash. Will you buy an adorable (if extremely slow) guard dog? Speed up the harvesting rate? I'll leave that decision to you.

Save yourself from spam clicking your mouse to death and let your helpers do it for you. You'll eventually get more as you progress in the game. So, what are you waiting for? Build your garden today!
Let's talk about the art style of this game. I absolutely LOVE it! It's simple, yet cute. Vibrant colors but doesn't hurt your eyes. I adore the animals and critters too! The music is peaceful yet bouncy, which is an interesting mix btw :D
Now let's talk about gameplay. I played for approximately an hour and was able to expand 3 times and unlock at least 2 of each item category. The gameplay isn't overly time-consuming as far as I can tell from my experience with it. I did lose interest about 20 minutes into the game because the concept of the game just isn't my kind of thing. However, it's a cute little game which is suited more towards a younger audience. I have to say that the art style is what really got my interest into trying this game out!
I can't say that there's much replay value though. I don't think I'll be playing this game again but I know my younger cousins would love it!
-This game is mostly suitable for a younger audience; (I am 22 years old but this game was cute and amusing for a while!)
-Family-friendly
-Cute art! Seriously who doesn't like cute art and vibrant colors?
-TONS of items to unlock!
-ADORABLE critters that sneak up on you
-Super repetitive - "Grinding" = Time-consuming
-It does take quite a bit of coins to progress in the game (especially for buying more items; the price increases after each purchase for any item)
-I don't see it as having a high replay value mostly because the grinding of the game is time-consuming. BUT, you can definitely start over and play it through again
However, what I've mentioned above doesn't diminish the quality of the game. This might be by design of the developer and it's pretty reasonable
It's tough to say. If you enjoy farming/gardening games or games that require tons of grinding, then yes!
If you have a younger sibling, cousin, friend's siblings, friend's cousins, etc. etc. let them give it a go

A friend of mine had asked me to try this game numerous times. I finally decided to give it a shot. We played the entire campaign together. I like the graphics. The gameplay was fun... a lot of explosions and me getting lost in all the action that was happening all at once. The characters and level descriptions were amusing. The music suited the game. I laughed hysterically, and genuinely enjoyed a lot of the game. I
say this is a solid multiplayer experience, but...
Too many times while we played, the game bugged and we had to exit the campaign, go back to the main menu, go back to the campaign, and reinvite him to my game to pick up where we left off.
Sometimes, on my screen, his character would be standing there doing nothing, while I could hear him fighting stuff.
Other times, his character would be in the ground (not as if he'd dug down... the ground would still be there and he'd be in it), or floating off to the side somewhere.
Sometimes he'd be fighting stuff I couldn't see, or vice versa.
On a few occasions, the camera stopped following us and we couldn't navigate the level further.
At least once, his character died but still appeared as alive on my screen.
And finally (and this is the one that put the nail in the coffin for me) we got to the final boss. We struggled a bit
, and then it bugged. We waited around for a few minutes hoping it'd start working again, but basically the boss went up in the air and stopped doing anything at all. We could still move and attack and whatnot, but nothing would happen. We couldn't progress or finish the fight.
It's like almost finishing a violent, gory, pun-filled jigsaw puzzle, only to find out you're missing a piece or two. That was the final straw. Was totally off-putting and I had no desire to try again.
Some of those may have been latency issues, but it's worth noting that we were both in the same room, on the same network, using the same internet connection on two different gaming computers. I play other games online and never have had quite that many issues. My buddy swears that he's never had those issues in single player or local co-op, so maybe online multiplayer is just a bit rough right now. I feel like the multiplayer side of this game is a major selling point for some though, so it's definitely something that needs to be ironed out a bit.

This game immediately entered my top 5 of all time, as there is really no aspect of Transistor that isn't excellent. The combat is well served by both the real time and turn() strategy system, and is blended into the story in a way that both provides gripping exposition and invites experimentation with the well-designed mechanics themselves. The setting is richly created and the characters, voiced or not (see below), are interesting and multi-faceted and really do invite thought from the player. As expected from Supergiant, the art and voice over work is spectacular. The entire game welcomes inquiry from the player into the rich, character driven tale presented by the city of Cloudbank and its people, and never disappoints.
The soundtrack deserves singular mention. On its own, it is good music. However, in the game, it does more than any soundtrack for any other game I have ever encountered. It manages to fulfill the normal soundtrack responsibility of creating ambience, while simultaneously providing subtle exposition and even characterization for a voiceless protagonist. Characterization through music was a brilliant answer to the bold (and often perilous choice) of a silent protagonist, and it succeeded in every way. I don't want to spoil anything, but there is one instance in which one song heard previously is played again in a boss battle with notable lyrical changes that, combined with information obtainable through experimentation in combat and by listening carefully during the boss fight, reveals an incredible story absolutely critical to the understanding of the narrative. This is a mastery of interactive storytelling that is rare to behold.
This leads to my one and only gripe, which is that the separately sold soundtrack does not include the corrupted version that I just mentioned, despite its importance. Hopefully it will be released in the future.
Anyway, I heartily and fully recommend this incredible game.

The obvious strength in music and visuals makes it easy to treat Transistor as the gaming equivalent of a snack, but the more patience you invest into the game the greater the reward and the more engaging it becomes. It's beautiful in every way - sound, art, gameplay, plot, and the way they all mesh together to turn what could be a good game into a
game.
The music is tied closely to the plot and the art brings out the ethereal and ephemeral feeling of Cloudbank in an amazingly unique way, while reinforcing the overall atmosphere and excitement of the entire game. They underscore SuperGiant's (by now) trademark way of storytelling: letting the atmosphere speak for itself, with the narration more like a tour-guide than noisy friend.
The battle system is a fun hybrid of action and turn based - you can play as purely one or the other, but utilizing both makes for an interesting blend of twitch and chess-like strategy. With plenty of skills, a staggering amount of ways to combine them, and variable difficulty - you can choose which limitations to use and how to power up enemies to make the perfect personal challenge - battles never feel like a grind, and are always exciting. Since "function file" plot and character information is unlocked by using skills in different ways, it encourages you to constantly change up your playstyle, try everything, and keeps things interesting. Even going through the game multiple times feels fresh since both you and enemies retain your strength upon "recursion". The battles grow with you every time through.
However, to understand the game fully you need to play it through twice. If you love the game this is an easy plus, but requires investment. The depth of the plot doesn't really come out until right at the very end, and important details are in the ignorable function files. The ending might leave those expecting things to go a different way feeling unsatisfied, but I believe it fits the game perfectly, and suits the bittersweet inevitability hanging over the entire game.
Overall, highly recommended.

Awesome game. Well worth the money, espcially if there's some OCD in you. The game does feel complete for the most part. It's definitely stable and runs really well for me. There's just a few minor complaints I have with the game in it's current state.
My biggest complaint is just the late stages in the game where it requires way too much resources and time in order to get that rocket to launch. By way too much I mean it would have required me to spend 10+ more hours with my current factory (even longer if I tried to automate it better), just to reach 100% and then hit the launch button which is just a basic flight animation that doesn't benefit anything or really do anything. In the end, what's the point of all that effort in launching the rocket if there's no reason to?
I wish I could have better control over the inserters... being able to control which side of the belt they place items onto, and also be able to control their pickup and drop-off angle (like, instead of only 180 degree, allow it to do 90 degree pickup and drop-off). Maybe even be able to pick up or drop off from multiple directions. What's the point of smart inserters if they're not really smart?
EDIT: mods fix this issue.
I did find the alien bugs to be way too over-powered in the early and mid stages of the game (mainly the stationary worm spitting defenses), but as soon as I got the tank, they became no match for me. I just plowed through their massive bases like it was no big deal, and retreated to the gun turrets to repair the tank a bit, then went back to plow through some more, rinse and repeat until they're all dead. My only concerns were simply to not get stuck. The AI in this game is very basic though, they travel in a straight line and in the exact same spot each and every single time, so you really don't need to defend your entire base, just the areas each enemy bases send their bugs to. They also attack on a predictable schedule.
There are obstacles in the game which blend in way too much, especially when zoomed out, to the point where running your vehicles into stuff at least once is to be expected. Once you run into them, and you happen to not destroy your vehicle in the process, it'll make a health bar on that obstacle, so at least you'll be able to see it next time. Or you can magically destroy it with your weapons because... reasons.
You're able to zoom in way too much to the point where the textures are extremely muddy and gross, I'd actually prefer if they limited that a bit cuz I really don't want to see muddy textures like that.
I also wish the minimap was a bit smaller as it takes up a lot of my 4:3 screen. It'd be really nice if I could play the game on the primary monitor and have the entire map displayed on my secondary monitor.
It would also be nice to be able to build bridges and stuff onto the lakes... especially hydro lines and pipes.
None of my complaints are major, but they are worth mentioning. Aside from that, the game is perfect.

This review contains spoilers. Beware!
What can I say? It took me over a year to complete the game, but I kept coming back because the world building was so good. System Shock 2 and many Resident Evil / Biohazard games have taken me a long time to complete as well. I often become exhausted at the constant stress or anxiety of playing a game that actively wants to cause fear and makes you feel like you could die at any time.
Alien Isolation is without a doubt on the extreme side of that. The first thing you'll notice is that it takes the atmosphere from Alien and Aliens very seriously, liberally taking the SFX and visuals from both films.
It takes a while before you have any way of defending yourself; the few options you have against the Xenomorph are a flamethrower, Molotov coctails and pipe bombs. The only one of the three that is remotely effective in a quick encounter is the flamethrower. It'll be your constant companion after you find it, and will change the pace of the game dramatically.
The game is essentially as a combination of System Shock 2, Amnesia and Resident Evil. You shouldn't have much trouble finding supplies to build bombs to fend off aliens and androids, (the secondary threat) but you'll usually have to be sparing on the weapons, treating flamethrower fuel as gold. This is a good thing, as it forces you on hard to be stealthier.
Overall, I am satisfied with the game. It has good writing, voice acting, scripting, animations and graphics. It's a stunning game. The ending is abrubt but satisfying enough. Is it worth $40-60? Maybe not. It's definitely worth $10-20, and with all the extras you can justify $30. But don't pay over that as the replayability isnt quite there. Once you complete the game you'll probably feel exausted and not want to do it over again. This is actually a good thing.
Final rating: 90%

Honestly I can't recommend this game, all the issues that arise make it unplayable and frustrating.
The game itself is pretty fun, you got a lot of variety in classes and the combat is enjoyable, not your generic mmorpg type of gameplay, but that's pretty much where the positives stop.
It tries a bit hard to be Ragnarok, from visual design to certain mechanics, but it's obviously not. If you're going into the game looking for that, you'll be disappointed. There's a ton of monsters to kill, there's a big boss monster awaiting around every corner, but after a while I just start wondering whether those bosses were any different or meaningful to kill, none of them drop any interesting loot and overall the game is lacking in variety of loot. You have only a few tiers of items and often they don't even look different and you won't get any new usable items for a long time. You also find a ton of materials, but you got nothing to do with them, the crafting system is very shallow and boring.
There are performance issues, the game isn't optimized very well, but it's not a dealbreaker. My computer isn't amazing, like 5 years old at this point and the only times I get bad performance issues is in towns with a lot of people, which doesn't matter that much since most of the gameplay takes place in other areas, so while I see a lot of people complaining about this, I think this is a minor issue that can be overlooked.
Lag, however, can't be overlooked. If you ever played Lunia or Spiral knights and experienced lag in those games, you'll know what I'm talking about. This game is an action game that requires you to dodge attacks or attack and retreat, but the game is server based, meaning that every movement and attack you make on your screen doesn't matter, since it first has to register on the server and if there's even the slightest lag, things won't go your way. Even regular attacks become a chore to execute, as your character gets stuck after each attack until the server decides that you had executed the attack. Now you might say that lag is related to your internet rather than the servers, but that's not true, if you don't live anywhere near the servers(not the same continent), you're gonna have a bad time. Personally I get 150ms ping and that's already unplayable, at higher levels you need to react faster, but when enemies attack faster than your signal gets sent to the server and back, the game becomes unfair and frustrating. If the server is having issues, lags rise even higher and you start teleporting back constantly while going somewhere, enemies hurt you long after you ran past them and all kinds of things like that.
The jumping mechanic seems like an interesting feature for this kind of game, but it is useless and not done right. Most areas don't utilize it, most maps don't even let you fall down from places to lower ground and just force you to go around or don't let you jump over some low obstacles like fences as if there's no such thing as jumping in the game. Jumping is meant to be used as an evasion maneuver and it's meant to be a split second action, but since the game is server based, if you're experiencing lag you can't use that at all to your advantage.
Bots and spammers are also a big issue in the game, there's constant spamming and advertising of gold selling sites, the people that spam don't get banned for hours and keep spamming it in shouting chat which scrolls their message across the top of the screen all the time, which can't be turned off. Even after blocking a lot of those people, they constantly make new users and spam more and more of their crap. You also see a bunch of bots around the battlefields, reporting them doesn't seem to help much. I get that this issue is difficult to deal with for the GMs, but it's still incredibly annoying, I forgot that these things even exist considering I haven't seen them for a couple of years.
Overall, I really dislike that this game is so server reliant, I get that it helps prevent cheating and all that, but it's also preventing me from playing the game properly, just like it used to be with Lunia and Spiral Knights for me.

Wayward is a rogue-like survival type of game in which you will be brutally punished for not thinking ahead and not working fast to gather the necessary supplies to survive.
Much like that of Minecraft and Terraria, its vital to gather enough supplies and atleast attempt to find shelter before nightfall where you're more likely to be ambushed and killed.
What this game does, I believe it does well. It isn't perfect and is more difficult than your typical rogue-like, but perhaps that is due to it having more of a diminishing sense of accomplishment when you finally make a thought-out base just to die and to have your world deleted.
Graphics: 5/10 - They could really use to improvement. Obviously they are meant to be pixels, but some of the items are difficult to distinguish in your inventory. A higher resolution item picture would solve that.
Gameplay: 8/10 - I rather enjoy the game play. A few corrections here and there would easily make it perfect. Every action has a consequence, and the level of detail is almost akin to games like Dwarf Fortress; for example, if you need water but are unable to find any, digging in the same spot may result in water being found. Continue digging and you'll likely make an entrence to the dangerous underground area. I can only hope the makers continue to add more and more fine variety. More creatures, more items, more recipes, more buffs and debuffs, etc. I'd love to see a combat system like the one used in dwarf fortess, being able to target specific body parts, etc. That would be insane in a game like this.
Difficulty: 9/10 - This game will punish you and you will die. Over and over again. Think you can kill that rat? Think again, you just ran out of stamina, your bleeding, and now your over-exerting yourself, which causes more damage. Trying to build a defensible base? Nope! The wood and stone needed to do so effect your reputation. The lower your reputation, the harder the game gets. Pretty soon you'll have nigh impossible to kill monsters hunting you down.
Replayability: 8/10 - Atleast for now, this game has had me coming back for a few days now. I want to see just how far I can go, what new items I can craft and how much of an awesome base I can make. Perma-death makes it brutally tough to reach those goals, but its fun to try again.
Overall, I highly recommend for the current price. I've had plenty of hours of enjoyment thus far, and I anticipate many more. The game has such potential to even further improve. I can't wait to see where it goes.
