So I have won this game in a Giveaway by Drathy so I decided I should at least review the game, I'll say however this doesn't mean it gets a instant recommend because of that, this review is earned.
Alright so what is their to say about this game, well first it looks pretty nice for that sort of format, I like the fact you get better at doing stuff by doing stuff, it gives you a feeling of progression in your development beyond having your growing constructions. What can be said frankly beyond that? Its like Minecraft basically but in 2D, but top down instead of sideway like Terraria, and  turn-based... now the major thing different at this point would be that its harder, alot harder. Also Death = Start from Scratch, a pretty brutal system, so not only are you thrown into the sea to learn to swim, but they'll keep going at it if you die, and tossing you into new ones you haven't got a feel for its environment yet.
Now a few things negative, I felt the tutorial was a bit awkward, I felt it didn't convey what it wanted you to do always clearly, also some task are pretty brutal, one of them require killing something for meat, if you got a bad spawn and have too tough enemies nearby, that tutorial mission will kill you.
Also I saw in the screenshots how you had someone with like a village nearly at one point built... yea... that would take legitimately a MASSIVE amount of time to accomplish, building things eat up a ton of ressources quickly, I found just try to build a safe house to be pretty intensive in ressources gathering, considering you need to do that before Night 1, just like Minecraft... well its pretty rough... the fact that if you fail you have to restart at the beginning... yea its extra brutal.
Another thing, your 'Bad Karma' style stat is rising ridiculously fast, for doing things even fairly benign, I can get killing animals and stuff to give you 'Bad Karma' but building tools also do so, why would making tools give me 'Bad Karma'? Is their something I am missing with that system? Anyhow considering in next to no time I had acquired a couple thousands of 'Bad Karma', I was fairly shocked, having no idea at which point that will probably bite me in the behind, it was far too worrisome.
One thing which I'd like to see also at one point is a clearly female char, being a girl I like to play girls in games, if their was a storyline that sort of made that counterproductive, I could understand, but in such Survival games? I don't see why I can't have a girl char.
Anyhow at this point to the question, would I recommend it? I would say yes, but its not for everybody, casual gamers beware, this isn't for you, this game is made for fans of survival, roguelikes and challenging games, the last two are the part where I'd really make sure people like those before buying this game.

Dark Souls2 is one of the notorious souls game series developed by From Software.
It's series are known for their ridiculously designed maps, mobs and boss fights.
Although souls game fans often criticize the game for it's linearity and repeatative patterns, I personally value those factors as pros of this game.
First, developers tried to get rid of unreasonable level designs and map designs. Predecessor of this game concentrated too much on complexity of the map so it may not encourage majority of  light gamers to play that game. Buy it now. This game may not look like much, but it is the most unique expierience I ever had in a game. You are selected by a lottery to work in a border checkpoint in the glorious country of Arstotzka and you spend 10 minute "days" checking peoples documents and either accepting them or denying them. Each day the difficulty raises, whether it is having to watch out for criminals or stop terrorists who are attacking the checkpoint. At the end of the day you have a home screen. If you didn't process enough people, you may not have enough money to buy heat or food for your family.
This game shines with the people you process. In between the hundreds of people you process in your checkpoint there are little stories that are told. A basic one that you get very early on is that a husband has the required papers but his wife doesn't. The wife pleads to let her in and it is up to you. Do you go against your new rules and risk getting fined, or do you deny her and leave the family seperated (I denied her, Glory to Arstotzka!). Later in the game deeper stories uncover, including a plot to overthrow the government. Everything can change for these digital people because you decided one of two choices. It is amazing.
There are 20 different endings and an endless mode after you beat the story once. Overall this is one of the best indie games I played and I recommend it to everyone.
Glory to Arstotzka!

Have you ever come home from work, hours of paperwork, filing, playing games on government time? Wasn't it exhausting? Would you like to continue in a fictional world? Then all hail Arstotska! While the game is very punishing, it also isn't too hard to get into the swing of things. As far as 8-bit games go, this one is a winner.

A friend of mine had asked me to try this game numerous times. I finally decided to give it a shot. We played the entire campaign together. I like the graphics. The gameplay was fun... a lot of explosions and me getting lost in all the action that was happening all at once. The characters and level descriptions were amusing. The music suited the game. I laughed hysterically, and genuinely enjoyed a lot of the game. I
say this is a solid multiplayer experience, but...
Too many times while we played, the game bugged and we had to exit the campaign, go back to the main menu, go back to the campaign, and reinvite him to my game to pick up where we left off.
Sometimes, on my screen, his character would be standing there doing nothing, while I could hear him fighting stuff.
Other times, his character would be in the ground (not as if he'd dug down... the ground would still be there and he'd be in it), or floating off to the side somewhere.
Sometimes he'd be fighting stuff I couldn't see, or vice versa.
On a few occasions, the camera stopped following us and we couldn't navigate the level further.
At least once, his character died but still appeared as alive on my screen.
And finally (and this is the one that put the nail in the coffin for me) we got to the final boss. We struggled a bit
, and then it bugged. We waited around for a few minutes hoping it'd start working again, but basically the boss went up in the air and stopped doing anything at all. We could still move and attack and whatnot, but nothing would happen. We couldn't progress or finish the fight.
It's like almost finishing a violent, gory, pun-filled jigsaw puzzle, only to find out you're missing a piece or two. That was the final straw. Was totally off-putting and I had no desire to try again.
Some of those may have been latency issues, but it's worth noting that we were both in the same room, on the same network, using the same internet connection on two different gaming computers. I play other games online and never have had quite that many issues. My buddy swears that he's never had those issues in single player or local co-op, so maybe online multiplayer is just a bit rough right now. I feel like the multiplayer side of this game is a major selling point for some though, so it's definitely something that needs to be ironed out a bit.
As fun as it was. I can't recommend this game. It was frustratingly broken and that really overshadowed any fun I had playing it.

Plantera is a unique, refreshing, cute and addicting clicker game.
I'm not a huge fan of clicker games like Clicker Heroes and similair clicking games as they are brain killing for me.
This game is really... believe me... it is different, it's different in a truly positive way.
You have your own piece of land where you can place plants and vegetables based on your own taste, you like carrots? than you choose carrots as your base vegetable.
Be aware that carrots are the cheapest vegetable, so for the money-wolfs, you better choose a more advanced vegetable.
You can also plant trees, bushes and you can place animals, they will all make you earn coins which you can invest in new bushes or other plants but also game upgrades like a extended offline timer, which gives you more coins while you are offline for a longer time. ( default is 1hr ).
Offline timers in other clicking games are basically letting you still earn your currency while you're not ingame/offline.
This game starts at a default 1 hour of offline gain, but it is increaseable with ingame currency.
Start playing, earn some coins and you can increase the offline gain timer a bit.
I still recommend playing the game as it's very relaxing, especially on late nights after work.
This might be a downside for people want to idle this game only, i don't need offline gain since i like to play it myself.
As you have seen above, there are actually not things that i had to mention which were negative or bad.
This game made everything from gameplay to graphics top notch in the critically-acclaimed clicking games genre.
To be honest, their previous games haven't been so great, and this games is better than i ever expected it to be.
It's still a clicking game, but i recommend it for it's decent price tag ( 2,99 ) .
Happy Clicking, Happy Farming !

Review of Plantera :
The pros of it are-
1. Very simple clicker game. By simple I mean its as simpler as it can get.
2. People of all ages will enjoy just clicking their mouse all over the place and collecting foods from the   garden and keeping away birds, animals etc in their leisure.

The Cons of it-
1. The game is too simple and will get boring after a while.
2. Not much to offer as far as content is concerned. You are going to be clicking on some wild birds and animals and collecting food for all the time to come. These all takes place by just a matter of clicks. Unfortunately its pros is also its con. Nothing to be excited about and almost no sense of achievement.
3. Game has no story.
How it could be better-
1. Add more options or things to exprience.
2. Add zoom in and zoom out options as its really annoying that you can't keep an eye on the full garden at a time. Also the scrolling was annoying.
3. Add a rewarding feeling to the game and a story even if its just a point and click.
Overall the game could have been far better by adding more options and things to do. But overall for $2.99 you don't have a lot to expect. I hope they keep on developing the game and adding small features or new things to do. But I will recommend it to people as its just $2.99.

All in all I rate this game as recommended with reservations. I like Tree of Savior, kind of. Though it has issues, many issues.
1) It is a broken game. When you cannot get from point a to point b because of a bug, the game is broken. Which is exactly what is happening in this game. That there is a "workaround" does not count. Why does it not count? Because that information is not readily publicly available. It should be in all caps, large font somewhere on the home page of the game site. It may be in the forum somewhere who knows.
2) Which brings me to second issue. Trying to access the forums is... iffy at best. First you have to log in to the site at the home page with either Google+ or Facebook. Yep, no making a user account for that gaming site; G+ or FB. Then in order to access the forum you click on the "forum" link and once that loads... you have to log in again! LOL Yes it auto logs you out changing pages! Then you have to scroll down past two pages of nothing to actually reach the forum. Still have your hair? Now click on the forum section that you want, say for example:bug reports. Get 405 message! Click "try again", maybe it will load; maybe it won't. Eventually you get to the page you want and... you see the "bug reports" are broken down by effects, like "game play", "graphics", etc. Yep, 405 hit and miss agian! Here's where I gave up on using the forum. It seems like it's being run using flash or some such crap. Overly complicated, which is 3/4 of the problem.
3) Which brings me to my third issue. Trying to report the bug via the "ticket" system. To submit a report you first have to... verify your Steam account! Then why TF didn't they just have me log in to the site using my Steam account? GAAAAAAAAA! This is where I have up trying to submit a ticket. Why did I quit here? Because what little I was able to poke around the forums I noticed more than one complaint of tickets being umanswered for a week or more.
In spite of all that I still like the game. It's the first game in a very... long... time... that I haven't turned off the soundtrack to within 1 min. It is not your typical, 15 sec of mildly annoying music looped endlessly; one track per map. The songs are long enough that while they do loop, you don't really notice when they loop. And there is a battle theme too! For every map! Old School feel game play. I won't say I grew up playing games with a similar feel. I didn't. Mainly because I was already an adult when games with a similar feel and look first came out! XD I never played any of those games anyway though. Never owned a Nintendo, and never played any of the original MMO's. *shrugs* I was overseas, serving in the military. I didn't have the option of a phone line in my barracks room, so no dialup. I did however, play computer games where you controlled everything via arrow keys to move and letter keys to attack, cast spells, etc. So for me, no "learning curve" of getting used to the controls. There is an option for a gamepad controller and for mouse control as well. So if either of those are more your thing, no prob.
Now the bad news: it is a F2P game. As such it has gold sellers shouting all the time in global shout and in some area yell chats as well. If you've played any F2P game by any publisher, you know how bad it can be. It isn't as bad as I've seen in a few other games, but still more than a little annoying. Especially when blocking a particular player/bot is not intuitave. Add in selling crafted items/rare drops requires that you have the game currency that you can only get by spending IRL money and you get a game that isn't really "free player" freindly. If you're OK with spending IRL cash to get extras, you shouldn't really have any real issues. There are all kinds of vanity items and exp enhancers and the like to keep the paying customer happy. It is also a Korean grinder. The good news is it's really easy to party up and boost exp production via questing as a group. If you prefer to solo most stuff and party up for dugeons only, no prob; there's a party finder.
It has potential. It might yet be a great game in spite of it's various problems. If what I've listed as problems send up red flags for you, don't bother. You'll only end up frustrated and bald (from tearing out your hair). If you think there's potential and it sounds fun in spite of the issues, have a go at it!

Wayward reminds me a lot of Don't Starve in how it works; but it is turn-based. You slaughter animals, craft items, and warp your surroundings into what your character needs to survive and thrive! The game already feels like it is worth playing; despite not being content complete. One can only imagine what the game will allow you to do in addition to what it already allows you to do in it.
It notably has an interesting mechanic called malignity, where the more hostile actions you take against the world, the more hostile actions the world will take against you. This keeps you from just being able to go crazy, since all manner of hell will come bearing down to kill you - both figuratively and in the realistic sense that bears will spawn and come kill you.
Interestingly, the game has a sort of progression in it, where new characters that you start will be stronger when you reach milestones with a character in a current run. However, when you start, you may not really notice that progression - which makes the game feel very close to a Traditional Rogue-like experience where you start over from scratch.
It is always wise to wait for a game to come out of Early Access to get the game when it is more polished, feature complete, and has fewer bugs. Wayward however very much already feels polished, feature complete, and with little to no irritating bugs. If the developer wanted to they could release this game now as it is, and likely few could argue that it is an incomplete game. As such I give a full recommendation for buying this game.

Dark Souls II is, strangely enough, a very different beast to its predecessor.
Yes, the 'world' you remember returns... but it's changed, thematically and in presentation. Yes, the controls you remember are back, but they've been tweaked towards playing 'fast and loose'. Yes, you will be punished for making mistakes, but you're given very obvious and clear guidance and alot of support (if you look for it).
Returning to the Souls world after Dark Souls, DaS2 is a queer experience - That's really the best way I can describe it, queer. You return to the world you remember, a supposed thousands upon thousands of years after the events of the first game. Nearly everything of 'that old world' has been forgotten, and you are presumedly given the task of picking up where the last game left off: Leading the world into a new age.
Something's different though, there's much more co-op, you can dual wield and can be very flexible without committing to a certain play style, the enemies can be very obviously forced into the same pattern and feel like a 'plastic-ey' AI as opposed to the almost organic feeling reactions and patterns of DaS 1's enemies.
Overall, all I can really say is this: If you love DaS, but wish you could've played with other people more often, you're all set. But if you're looking for the same feeling the first game gave you all over again, you're in the wrong place.
I can't describe it, but Dark Souls 2 comes away closer to a tribute to the first game rather than a true successor as Dark Souls was to Demon's Souls. It's still enjoyable... It just won't give you the same feeling the old games did.
Take that as you will.

This review contains spoilers. Beware!
What can I say? It took me over a year to complete the game, but I kept coming back because the world building was so good. System Shock 2 and many Resident Evil / Biohazard games have taken me a long time to complete as well. I often become exhausted at the constant stress or anxiety of playing a game that actively wants to cause fear and makes you feel like you could die at any time.
Alien Isolation is without a doubt on the extreme side of that. The first thing you'll notice is that it takes the atmosphere from Alien and Aliens very seriously, liberally taking the SFX and visuals from both films.
It takes a while before you have any way of defending yourself; the few options you have against the Xenomorph are a flamethrower, Molotov coctails and pipe bombs. The only one of the three that is remotely effective in a quick encounter is the flamethrower. It'll be your constant companion after you find it, and will change the pace of the game dramatically.
The game is essentially as a combination of System Shock 2, Amnesia and Resident Evil. You shouldn't have much trouble finding supplies to build bombs to fend off aliens and androids, (the secondary threat) but you'll usually have to be sparing on the weapons, treating flamethrower fuel as gold. This is a good thing, as it forces you on hard to be stealthier.
Overall, I am satisfied with the game. It has good writing, voice acting, scripting, animations and graphics. It's a stunning game. The ending is abrubt but satisfying enough. Is it worth $40-60? Maybe not. It's definitely worth $10-20, and with all the extras you can justify $30. But don't pay over that as the replayability isnt quite there. Once you complete the game you'll probably feel exausted and not want to do it over again. This is actually a good thing.
Final rating: 90%

Plantera is a clicker-type game, where you can click to get resources quickly or just let the game idle collecting resources for you at a lower rate. Upgrade your stuff, multiply your resource, income, etc.
However, Plantera is not quite like the other clickers. Where in others all you do is watching numbers go up, in Plantera you build your own farm and ecosystem that you can watch grow and co-exist the more you play it, making for a really satisfying experience. The click mechanics are also diversified enough to be fun. You don't click randomly on the screen, but rather you use your clicks in specific places to collect or help your blue friends, or click on animals that are trying to steal your food to scare them away, making it a nice micromanaging experience. The cute artstyle and the music make it a very relaxing and soothing experience.
Since it's a paid title and has no microtransactions, it lacks the bloat that some F2P clickers have. It is then easier and shorter than those, but it's also a much more enjoyable experience. It is simple, and you can interact as much or as little all you want either way, but there's something neat about tidying up your farm nicely instead of just letting it idle.
Might be my favorite "clicker" yet, mainly because of how tangible your progress is and how you can watch your farm grow and grow and get more populated and just watch a whole ecosystem growing and the interactions with it. Very recommended for anyone that likes clicker games or that just want a soothing relaxing experience with a cute style..

Plantera is a clicker game minus the clicking. It has all the traits of a clicker but the advantages of clicking are very minor, it’s more of a sit it and forget it kind of game. This time around the goal is to make as much money as possible, this allows you to increase the size of your plot, get more and better fauna and flora and defend yourself from the pesky critters.
Plantera is definitely more on the simpler size, and that’s saying a lot for a clicker game. While I have over 13hours played for the game I’d say only about an hour or so of that is actual gameplay. The reason for this is that while you gain full money while the game is not running, you can only gain a maximum of 1 level while the game is closed. Levels are extremely important as they are the main tool for progression, they unlock more farmers and increased fauna and flora quality and variety ,so they’re pretty much mandatory.
So what you end up with is a very simple clicker game that is defined by its medium, farming. Personally I love seeing my little garden evolve into something that I cannot manage without the help of the workers, but others who are more interactive with their clicker games might find it a bit shallow. It’s pretty cheap so it’s not a big risk, though I’m sure if you’re a clicker fan you’ll know exactly what you’re looking for.

Supergiant Games has done it again.
Transistor is an amazing experience in line with the developers previous game, Bastion.
Story:
Absolutely fantastic. You feel attached to the main character immediatly and the constant chatter of the Transistor deepens the experience to a whole new level. It isn't narrate in the vein that Bastion was, but in the fact that Transistor talks to you and makes comments as you go along. My only complaint in this section is that the game was short (about 5 hours). You'll be begging for more.
Gameplay:
Solid action RPG with a nice twist. The Turn() system is akin to the VATS system from Fallout where you pause time and can move and attack without much repercussion. The downside of this is if you use all of the meter, you have a cooldown where you can't attack and are vulnerable. Combat can be a little tough, as a lot of the enemies can deal some serious damage later on, so you have to be smart about your attacks.  As you level up you get to choose new skills, upgrade exsisting skills, and choose limiters. Limiters are akin to the Gods of Bastion, in which you can toggle them to increase the difficulty of the game.
Music:
Engrossing and enthralling. It sets such a mood in the game. Some serious talent here from the composer. Way better soundtrack than Bastion, and I thought Bastion was incredible already.
Conclusion:
While it is short, it is totally worth the admission price. It is a wonderful experience and I am looking forward for more games from the developers.

Inspired by resource manager games like Dwarf Fortress and Minecraft, Factorio is an industry-building RTS that takes the means of production to the extreme. The player is stranded on a hostile alien planet after a botched space colonization attempt. Using furnaces, assembly machines, an army of machines, and more, he strikes out against the endless alien swarm in every direction. Yet, the biters and spitters are enraged by his factories' pollution, and attack from every direction.
In a nutshell:
Excellent RTS resource management game, developed by an independent studio based in the EU
Great community, though not very large
Multiplayer support still in the works, but this should be an excellent game with other people
Well optimized game, runs very well
Big updates in the works
Some downsides:
Tedious game play - essentially, this game puts into into an infinite management loop, forcing you to continually jump through hoops that force you to expand your production.
Poor mod, multiplayer support - at the time of writing, steam workshop and servers have not been integrated into the game's system. It's currently easiest as a single player game.
Rating: 94/100

Transistor is yet another masterpiece from SuperGiant Games. The story has players in control of Red, a widely beloved singer of the setting city, Cloudbank, where all voices are heard so to speak. When our Heroine finds herself trekking throughout the city without her voice after being attacked by a secret group that wishes to use her voice for their master plan for the city, Red must take use of the Transistor, a oddly sword that downloads the data of people in order to store them inside.
Within the first fewminutes of the game, we see this in action as the swords main entity is Red's boyfriend, a figure unknown by not just the player but the also the city itself. With him guiding her along the way the game really opens up some interesting dailogue between them that range from comedic relief and worry. the Characters are all fairly written and the background data on the people you download into the sword keep you playing to find out more on why they were killed and the truth behind the Transistor.
The Combat is great, and engaging; combining elements of strategy and action. You have a feature called turn which in essence allows the player to stop time, plan their next move, and then re-initiate time and watch your plan play out. THe best part about this feature is that it's mostly optional save for some bosses and puzzles. The most of the game can be played without ever activating Turn for the more hardy of players looking for a decent challenge. Not enough you say? well how about the added limiter that allow you so make the game harder in order to earn even more experience. Limiters are a great way to give that extra wager to your skills from making enemys immune to status effects to giving them more health and power to having them break your skills should you get hit with no health.
Darren Knob Has outdone himself again with Transistors Soundtrack. This and Bastion are two example of just how good Game OST's are getting, and I'd recommend picking it up like I did. I could sit here all day trying to sweeten up music for you, but my moto on music is the only way I could get someone to like music is to have them hear it for themselves, and that's just what you need to do. Check some of it out on Youtube, and if you enjoy the jazzy/blues tunes of the game then you simply must purchase the soundtrack.
All-in-all, Transistor is a great game for those that enjoy a great action game, with a few twist here and there, a interesting story, and great soundtrack. Overall i'd give the game a 8.5/10, and I'd reccomend it to anyone who does and doesn't hold interest in the title already. Trust me, it is a well worth buy.

Transistor is the second game from Supergiant Games, the creators of the critically acclaimed Bastion. It is an Action-RPG set in a futuristic sci-fi world full of dangers and mysteries.
Transistor features a gorgeous hand-drawn art-style, a brilliant soundtrack and great voice-over as well as a deeply satisfying combat system. You play as Red who has been rendered mute at the beginning of the game and found herself in the possession of a mysteries sword that talks to her during the course of the game. While you uncover the secrets behind the sword and the mysteries of Cloudwalk City, you battle tons of enemies in a mixture of real-time and turn-based combat. During a combat situation you can enter a turn-based mode which enables you to give Red specific commands which she will subsequently execute upon pushing the “activate” button. This will give you the upper hand in most situations as each individual enemy type requires its own strategy. However, after executing these commands, Red will remain vulnerable for a couple seconds and if she loses her health points during this period, she will lose one of her four abilities and continue the fight with less abilities and a higher difficulty until the next checkpoint. Therefore, you have to choose wisely how to tackle each encounter.
The game features an extensive upgrade system with active and passive abilities which you can combine at will in order to match you preferable play style. Furthermore, you can apply specific limiters at any time which will make the game on the one hand more difficult, but on the other hand will give you a greater experience reward.
There is not much negative to be said about the game, however, some might criticize the fact that there is no equipment in the game at all. Furthermore, the story can be a bit confusing at times and while each enemy requires a specific approach, there are not that many different enemy types. However, these are tiny issues which should not keep you from playing and enjoying this great game. Thumbs up! 9/10

Tree of Savior is a great F2P MMO and is my favorite Korean MMO to date.  It's got all that mob grinding we love in a Korean MMO, a fun, great looking art style, plus plenty of quests that you can get lost in for hours. Oh and quick FYI, the music in this game is pretty fantastic.
It's got some "americanized" ideas implemented, like EXP cards, that you earn throughout questing that give you boosts of exp throughout your whole leveling process, if you choose to do the quests along side your grinding.  Some of you hardcore grinders might like to grind mobs all the way to the top and this is possible with plenty of places to grind. I like to pickup quests and complete all the zones as I grind my way through because of the Collections and Adventure Journal features that earn you small perks along the way, if that's your thing. Side note... another thing I love is that the Collections are shared amongst all your characters server wide. So you are always working towards completing them no matter what character you are playing on.  The current max level in English version (aka iTOS) is 280.

There are currently 4 base classes being Archer, Cleric, Swordsman, and Wizard. From there you can build many different types of characters with around 80 total classes that have their own skills and abilities.  At the time of this writing, each character consists of 7 total ranks and at each rank you choose one of these many classes to add more abilities to your build as you progress. You will want to do a bit of planning on your build before you start getting too far into the game because once you pick a class you are unable to reverse that decision. There are Skill reset(class ability points) and Stat reset (STR, CON, INT, SPR, DEX) potions in the game but they are not available unless you use the microtransaction cash shop or received a Founder's pack before the official release. Also, they only reset your points allocated. Once again, you can NOT reset your classes once chosen. So research a bit and choose wisely! There are some great tools on Fan Base sites that can help guide you in the right directions. Whether you want to see what the current top cookie cutter builds are or make up your own awesome and unique build, its all possible.
The cash shop in Tree of Savior uses a currency called TP.  TP will get you things like Tokens, EXP Boost Tomes, Skill reset potions, warp scrolls to get you back to town, etc. Along with cosmetic vanity type items like hairstyles and clothing for your character.
A fun note, in TOS they require the use of an item "Megaphone" to be able to use the /yell chat channel. Megaphones are ONLY accessable on the cash shop for TP.  This seemed weird to me at first but its actually a decent idea to help reduce the gold selling spam bots and lets you decide if that /yell you want to spam is worth the 1TP. The megaphones are 1 TP which means you can easily buy 5 a day when you need to burn your free TP that you earn slowly overtime. Free TP maxes out at 5 and then stops earning so you need to spend it to reset it.  Personally Ive been using TP from my Founder packs and then the  free 5TP to buy a EXP tome per day. It allows me to purchase a Tome for 4 TP instead of the full price of 9 TP. It's not bad for 1HR of 30% xp boost.
You CAN NOT trade in game currency between players, that includes your own characters. Each of your characters has their own silver.  Though you still see people spamming for trades using other items as currency like Talt (an ore earned from loot boxes on world bosses and dungeons). Talt venders for 5k to venders so its a stable 5k silver coin.
Tokens are Tree of Savior's version of that usual F2P "Premium Status".  They give you 30 days of Token user Status which allows you to do things like using the Auction House with less restrictions, less trading restrictions, 30% xp boost, and gain an extra dungeon entry before your daily lockout among other things.  You can still play "F2P" without Token status, you will decide.  Personally I wouldn't play without it.
BTW, I've only been checking out the PvE aspect of the game so far because that's what I truly enjoy.  There is PvP with guild vs, guild and arenas are comming soon. Guilds can declare war on each other making it open pvp season between characters in those guilds.
So far, as of this writing on May 14th, 2016, I am very much enjoying this game. I've been playing for 15days and have invested about 160 hours.  There is so much to do especially if you are interested in playing around with different classes and experimenting with different builds.
If you enjoy the Korean MMO style grinding then you should definitely check out this game.

First, let me say that I am obsessed with rogue-like games but I seldom enjoy them. They are just. TOO. HARD. I would prefer a difficulty slider myself, with extra prestige achievements for those crazy enough to try the hardest of the hard. So trying to be objective, I would rate this game a 4 out of 10, compared to the other rogue-like games I have tortured myself with. I love survival, and inventory management and there is plenty of that in here.
But with this game, it seemed for every thing I built, I just lost too much energy, until I hit a point where I cannot build anything to keep up with the actual use of the item. To me this seems like a game-breaking balance issue. For example, if it takes me half an energy bar to produce an amount of food for 1 day, but it takes 2 days to fill the energy bar back up, then it is impossible to stay ahead of the curve, never mind having a stockpile. So do you see what my simplistic example is getting at? There has to be a slightly larger return than the investment, even if it is just tiny, or the game is not sustainable and it breaks and you die every single time guaranteed 100%, and never mind any of the content because you will never live long enough to build it, let alone even see it.
Or maybe I just really suck at these games that bad. It's possible.

Wayward is the most realistic survival experience you can get with it still being a game. Of course, there are demons and zombies, but also an intricatly intertwined crafting system that is also simple. Think of the top-down view and mechanical detail of rimworld, but alone and with more crafting and surviving.

Wayward is not your typical roguelike. While it certainly contains many elements of the genre, it sets itself apart with unique gameplay that focuses on survival and crafting in a foreign environment.
Stranded and alone, the player must explore their surroundings in order to gain their bearings. They must then collect numerous resources in order to establish a camp, eat, drink, and craft equipment. While combat is certainly a part of Wayward, as the protagonist battles the local wildlife, the true enemy is nature and one's own body.
This creates some very interesting moments. One example was on my second attempt through the game, wherein I had set up a camp of sorts and was well on my way to a solid playthrough. I murdered some of the wildlife that encroached upon my camp, wielding a spear I made with my own hands, but soon realized that I was low on resources. I set off to find a solid water source and materials, protecting myself from every beast that came upon me, only to die to some snakes that cornered me in a position that I probably should have never entered.
While that may sound like standard roguelike fare, the context of establishing a foothold and battling for resources against nature makes the game extremely intense at times. It is extremely fun when you succeed, and when you fail you typically understand why.
As far as criticisms go, I would say that the menus could certainly use some work. They are functional, yet I had trouble reading and navigating them at times. The inventory and crafting menus are also rather unintuitive and could use some work.
The game's art style is nice, however, it is very monotonous. This is bound to happen in a game that takes place on a (relatively) realistic deserted island, however, it would be nice to see something breaking up the constant streams of the same tiles.
Despite these criticisms, the game is excellent. As an Early Access game I have high hopes for it, and I expect that the developer (who is actively updating the game rather frequently) will address some criticisms as they already have. For $7.99 you are getting quite a bit of content and replayability in a package that will likely only improve as time goes on.

A great mixture of by the basics survival in a fantasy world without relying on apocalyptic tropes. Fans of games like UnReal World will find a lot to like here. Many frustrating and tedious features are being continuously adjusted and removed, and the developer is amongst the most active and community driven I've seen. Things are already in a very fun and playable state, and I don't expect it to go anywhere but up.

It's a sci-fi setting with beautifully presented locations. As you encounter almost no people during the story, due to Camerata's machinations, there are no dialog options. The game boils down to reading news, listening to Transistor - talking sword(ish) artifact, and encounters. Active pause means you can do some tactics and various skills at your disposal make for an interesting mix.
The first playthrough took me around 9hrs, with trials and looking at everything. All in all well worth the admission price. Highly recommended.

I honestly did not expect anything less from SuperGiant Games and they did not fail to please. Transistor is beautifully constructed, utterly gorgeous to look at, and the soundtrack lives up to the action too. The only sad thing about this game was that it didn't get the hype that it deserved :(

If you loved Bastion, and especially it's soundtrack, you will love Transistor. It's got another silent protaganist who's a bit easier on the eyes, and so is the landscape. Bastion was beautiful, but there wasn't much left in that world. Transistor takes place in a city and the landscape is accordingly more populated. And the music, oh the music. Master Korb has done another wonderful job, and you can even have Red hum along to the background music for a bit if you want.
The combat is considerably differernt from Bastion. You have many more moves available and you can play along the same lines, whale on the enemy  and take a few hits; you do heal after every battle more or less. The true difference though, is the ability to "program" an attack sequence via Run(). It has some cooldown, but you can do anything from string together a sequence of attacks to just get out of harms way; allowing for a considerable number of tactics.
If you missed out on the Summer Sale, it's still entirely worth getting, but if you are tight on funds it might go on sale again this holiday season if we are lucky. Hopefully I'll have someone needing a cool gift like this that I can surprise.

Excellent small survial / crafting game for cheap monis

Qualification: started playing browser version a few years ago. 12+ hrs in steam version
Disclaimer: received a free copy via a Twitch contest during Devs live stream.
Wayward is a Roguelike-lite featuring turn-based game play, procedural generated worlds and Permadeath. Loosely inspired by Ultima Online and Minecraft (according to the dev, and visibly).
It features a crafting mechanic, more like Skyrims blacksmith than Minecrafts crafting, in that as long as you have the materials you will have the recipe and can craft the item. Some recipes will appear if you craft a similar item, some can be found on monsters or in chests around the world.
There are over three hundred craft-able items and recipes are retained across playthroughs.
It also contains a Malignity mechanic which in effect acts as difficulty meter, the higher it is the tougher the monsters that will come after you.

It is raised through many actions (arguably too many) such as chopping trees, mining and crafting most objects, it's lowered through things like planting trees and crafting some items.
The mechanic seems to lean towards being far easier to raise than to lower, but I have not broken that down statistically.
What's cool though, is that it can be linked to role play. So I generally play as a hippy, at one with the land type thing. Only using what I need, and as such keeping my malignity low. My reward is that I get to live in relative harmony with the island I'm on, rarely being mobbed.
Alternatively you can play as a true climate change denier and plough through trees, seeing the island as another gift given to man by God.
The trade off being that the island, much like The Zone in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. starts sending it's anti bodies at you in attempt to cleanse itself of the foreign antigen that plagues it.
The U.I. can be daunting to a beginner but everything is movable and resize-able, There are even options for regular text (Tahoma font, I think), as opposed to pix-elated.
You use both hands and can duel wield weapons, tools, sword and shield etc. However the system is not explained well and it can be confusing as to what tool/weapon is being used.
Generally, you want a tool in your right hand as that is the hand used by default when you walk into a tree or a rock by mistake, and killing durability on your fragile weapons can be a real pain early on.
There are caves to explore and treasures to find. There are I think, 5 biomes or "environment types", about three dozen enemy types and a deep skill system. Some mechanics are lacking like heat/weather system. Campfires offer light, and a place to cook but there are no warmth bonuses or coldness debuffs like you might find in UnReal World.
The game supports mods and the developer welcomes them, so some mechanics I'm sure will be added through workshop.
If you're in to modding, then Wayward is written in Typescript, a strongly-typed superset of JavaScript. So edits are easy, and there is already a dev toolkit in the workshop.
There is an "end game", that will give you a nice splash screen with your "score" but the game doesn't "end", at that point.
In it's current state Wayward is a great game, not quite as deep as UnReal World but a lot more approachable, and subjectively, better looking.
Very accessible dev with a small but robust community.
Well worth the price of admission, well worth your time.

Disclaimer: Given that I've been considered as an "influencer", the developers were kind enough to send me a steam key.
Having said that, I am having a ridiculously fun time with Wayward. Granted, I have just over three hours (at the time of this review), but have had a blast playing/dying in this procedurally generated world. There's clearly a vast amount of depth and complexity to the game (from what I've experienced for myself and seen in several Let's Play videos).
The game can be tough at the onset, but if the player sticks to the fundementals and just tries to survive (as opposed to clearing a forest, or mining half a mountain), the progression you experience is very rewarding. The starter quest works very well in introducing the player to the mechanics of surviving as well as the crafting system, and a large part of the fun is in experimenting with what you can find/craft in the world.
The base price of the game is a steal and with the current sale price, it's an absolute no-brainer. Have fun folks, this is a real hidden gem! :)

Thanks to the People at Unlok I got to try out this lovely Pixel game.
Here is the Video I am basing the review on.
And with that out of the way this game is very well done, it has a insane amount of items places to explore and monster, and NONE of the monster will give up on wanting to kill you. They will chase you forever and if you run into more they also will join the chase! it's crafting system is easy to use and you start off with random assortment of items each time you... die. Which hurt me a lot because there was not enough I could find to finish the tutorial, but there is so much more to find on this game and I will do it! so without more wait here are my Pros and Cons.
Pros
- Fantastic environment, scarce, yet when you get the right tools everything starts to become clear
- Crafting does NOT leave you in the dark you get a whole page on what you can craft with the items you HAVE!
- Survival system is well made with everything you can think of involved, from water hunger stamina, and you can kill yourself quite easily if you don't pay attention.
- Battle system is NOT live if you move they move, it allows you to make choices and have plenty of time to do so.
- Great music and artwork in this game simple and clean.
- UI is easy to manage and can open and close everything at will
- Controls are simple and effective from mouse click commands to gathering with or without a tool!
- Item Rarities, with increased durability of items and such gave a desire to craft as much as possible!
- Randomly spawn as different genders
Cons
- Monsters... They are so aggressive there is no way to escape if you get caught in the beginning.
- Needed resources seem scarce at times, making it difficult to find build and achieve greatness.
- Tutorial Should provide the basics and items in order to achieve the learning process, as I ran around looking for things I got hurt hungry and died. If anything a tutorial MODE would be a good options for the basics, then they can start a REAL MODE after learning.
- Durability on items was horrible, after you craft a knife to defend yourself you get it broken shortly afterward. with the lack of resources I was doomed in my attempts.
This was not a complete list but it is what I recall off the top of my head.
Overall this game is GREAT and I will be playing more of it, and I hope to actually progress in it! I would love to see this balanced and developed more as currently I believe the survival rate is way too low unless you're very lucky!

First of, I absolutely LOVE Tree of Savior. It really had a ton of potential to be a great game. Unfortunately the company running it has caused problems and ruined their own game. The combat style is fun, but allows every player to afk farm certain mobs (due to static respawn points) by simply setting a book on their attack key. There is no forced logouts, which means (you guessed it) bots are RAMPANT. Half the palyers you meet will seemingly teleport around your screen and attack mobs before you can, or you are simply fighting them for spawns. This problem is awful from level 15-40. The bots seem to die off a bit after that, but I haven't made it to max level to see what that is like.
IMC has done NOTHING about their botting problem, nor about the pretty toxic playerbase whom are pretty rude at the best of times, I can only imagine their attitude is due to their profits. Someone is supplying these people with tokens, be it themselves or others, and they are getting paid. The economy is a joke, and the restrictions placed on trading an item or using their auction house are god awful.
I really enjoy their game, but until the botting problems and gold spammer problems are fixed a bit, I can't recommend this game to other people, which is such a shame.
If you made it this far, I'll share some of the things I love and hate.
-There is quite a lot to do
-The art and music are AMAZING. Totally my style.
-The combat is fun, but if you lag with a melee class you will be VERY annoyed in short order. (Most of my lag is due to my poor internet connection, not the servers but the punishment from the lag is totally lost melee attacks. Like, I attacked, I saw my character swing his weapon... and NOTHING happens. Unless you attack 2+ times, this will happen with a bad connection and you will almost always lose that first attack.)
-Real-money is the ONLY option for resetting your skills or stat points. This is good because it means your choices matter, but this is really bad because it means new players are required to research everything BEFORE starting the game, or simply picking a cookie-cutter build that walks you through each step.
-Sadly, you are locked into your class choices. If you pick the wrong class, or the class you picked turns out to not be so fun ONE time... Guess what? Better start over. Even if you are level 200 and simply made a bad call or thought something
worked a different way.
-There are very few resources for information. I know this is due to how new the game is but, ecause of the beta testing, a lot of information you find is old and has since been changed. Even trying to research a good class selection or which stats to pump at max level is next to impossible. Which is why I feel being locked into class choices is such a bad idea.

Possibly the most fun I've had with any entry into the Western genre,
has pretty much every iconic element of the Wild West that you could ask for in a game (except horse riding).  The only Westerns that might beat Gunslinger in my book come from the very same IP, in a series created by Polish developer
, the same group responsible for
.
In addition to iconic scenes, lore and activities, the player is treated to excellent story delivery through the bounty hunter Silas Greaves.  He's a big talker and actually narrates his own story to a small crowd over some whiskey in a saloon while the player essentially relives his memories by going through the motions.  The excellence in this episodic format comes from the playful characterization these developers inject into his tales, many of which end up being a bit "tall."  It provides some thoroughly entertaining moments.  Developers seem to be utilizing overt humor to more and more advantage since the advent of Borderlands' success.
The story itself is solid.  I found myself enjoying the villains while rooting for Silas, who is something of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ himself.  Visuals and audio are good by modern standards, the game runs beautifully on a decent machine and there were no bugs or issues that I could find.  The art direction seems less gritty and more colorful than in some of the CoJ predecessors.
The First Person Shooter formula is well done here and has a combo point system tacked on to encourage flashy moves rather than boring, mechanical efficiency in dispatching foes.  Those combo points earn experience for a mini-progression system that specializes your bounty hunter into a close range heavy hitter, long range sniper or fast-firing, guns blazing dual six-shooter.  Design for a few areas is commendable for facilitating some great shootouts.  The dueling mechanic is great in  campaign but challenging enough that I gave up on it in the actual dueling mode.  Other gameplay modes, which I briefly played and finished at the lower ratings, were fun but low in replayability value.
I took the time to read the history blurbs that can be discovered along the way.  Part of what makes the game feel like an authentic Western are these cards plus the pseudo-historical events and figures featured in Silas' recollections.  I have always been a big fan of speculative, historical fiction so this is just the kind of thing I want to see more of in games and other media.
If you're looking for a linear, straightforward, almost arcade-like first-person shooter that captures a genuine Wild West feel along with some Borderlands-esque color and humor, you will be pleased with Gunslinger.  I recommend it to any Western fan as well as FPS players in general.
TIP: Avoid the easy and standard difficulties from the very start; opt for hard or "True West" for a much better experience.
TIP: Duels require some serious focus!  Multitasking the two components is harder than it looks.
TIP: Perks from the Ranger skill tree for revealing secrets throughout the game are of limited use, however if you are good at generating combo points you'll have more than enough experience to fill one tree and start on the other two.
TIP: The Trapper's armor perk and the Desperado's dual wielding perk are useful to have early on, even if you are primarily Ranger.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a perfect example of a proper "Western" shooter that's also the story of one man's trip through hell, sort of "story of his life", albeit in a playable form. Add some gaming conventions such as fast reflex, dodging death, and "Concentration mode", and a bit of special skills that can be accumulated for a bit of RPG depending on how you play, and you have one heck of a game.
Technically the story takes place in a saloon in the early 1900's. It's end of the cowboys era, law is coming to the land, and this guy, who said he's Silas Greaves, famous bounty hunter, and possible braggart, is regaling the audience... a kid, a few other players, the saloon "belle", about the story of his life... How he got started on his life of revenge chasing down killers of his brothers, how he's present at almost every major shootout involving the most famous criminals of the Wild West, everybody from Billy the Kid to Butch Cassidy, and just about every who's somebody in the West. It has such makings of a tall tale, it's fun, yet when the story itself is PLAYABLE... It makes for one heck of a game.
You see, when Silas talks about his adventures, you the player are taking the place of Silas in the game, as you walk yourself through towns, forests, trails, canyons, swamps, and more, shooting at enemies along the way. You can only carry 2 guns... a long gun and a revolver, but you often have choices. For the long gun, you can choose Winchester rifle, short rifle (carbine), or shotgun. For the short gun, you can choose short shotgun (i.e. saw-off shotgun), or three types of revolvers, six-shooter, quickshooter, or ranger.  You can swap them out later when you find them.  When enemies get close you can melee, and if you find some dynamite you can throw them too.
As you gain skills you can choose one of three specializations... rifle, pistol, or shotgun. They make the game very different, as they give different bonuses. Pistol specialization, for example, unlocks dual wield (two pistols at once) and other skills, while rifle specialization gives you long-range stuff like further zoomin, carry more ammo, and so on. When you complete 6 / 12 skills in that specialization you get one or two special edition weapons that are better than the normal versions.
The game also has two special modes: the "reflex" mode is a special gift that Silas have that lets him see death coming... in the form of bullet that will kill him... and gives him a chance to dodge it (by ducking left or right). Obviously you have to dodge the right way... or this is not going to work. Obviously this ability needs a little time to recharge. Also, the "concentration mode" lets Silas basically enter the Matrix... where everything slows down, and enemies are highlighted giving him a chance to shoot down enemies (and even dodge bullets) otherwise not possible, and is recharged via kills (preferably heatshots).
As this is a western, you can't go without duels, and this game has them. Some of the end bosses must be dueled, while others can be killed without a duel. Duel is basically simultaneously keep your crosshair on the target while keeping your "hand" near the gun for perfect draw position, both of which affects how you will draw and how good is your aim when you do.  And let's just say there's even a Mexican standoff as the grand finale, where you need to duel both bosses together.
The graphics are quite nice, and runs fine on slightly older hardware with a bit of tweaking. Sound's very good, with good voice acting and very good Western-y music.
There are plenty of "secrets" left in the game for you to find, that reveals the REAL history behind the places and people mentioned in the game. There are also some extra challenges like "Arcade" and "Duels" if you don't want to slog through the story again. Or you can play "Story +" where you go through the game AGAIN, with the skills you have earned from the first playthrough (but obviously enemies have been scaled up a bit too).
There are multiple difficulty levels, all the way up to "true west". And achievements galore.
All in all, this is one of the best Western shooters for the PC.

Awesome game. Well worth the money, espcially if there's some OCD in you. The game does feel complete for the most part. It's definitely stable and runs really well for me. There's just a few minor complaints I have with the game in it's current state.
My biggest complaint is just the late stages in the game where it requires way too much resources and time in order to get that rocket to launch. By way too much I mean it would have required me to spend 10+ more hours with my current factory (even longer if I tried to automate it better), just to reach 100% and then hit the launch button which is just a basic flight animation that doesn't benefit anything or really do anything. In the end, what's the point of all that effort in launching the rocket if there's no reason to?
I wish I could have better control over the inserters... being able to control which side of the belt they place items onto, and also be able to control their pickup and drop-off angle (like, instead of only 180 degree, allow it to do 90 degree pickup and drop-off). Maybe even be able to pick up or drop off from multiple directions. What's the point of smart inserters if they're not really smart?
EDIT: mods fix this issue.
I did find the alien bugs to be way too over-powered in the early and mid stages of the game (mainly the stationary worm spitting defenses), but as soon as I got the tank, they became no match for me. I just plowed through their massive bases like it was no big deal, and retreated to the gun turrets to repair the tank a bit, then went back to plow through some more, rinse and repeat until they're all dead. My only concerns were simply to not get stuck. The AI in this game is very basic though, they travel in a straight line and in the exact same spot each and every single time, so you really don't need to defend your entire base, just the areas each enemy bases send their bugs to. They also attack on a predictable schedule.
There are obstacles in the game which blend in way too much, especially when zoomed out, to the point where running your vehicles into stuff at least once is to be expected. Once you run into them, and you happen to not destroy your vehicle in the process, it'll make a health bar on that obstacle, so at least you'll be able to see it next time. Or you can magically destroy it with your weapons because... reasons.
You're able to zoom in way too much to the point where the textures are extremely muddy and gross, I'd actually prefer if they limited that a bit cuz I really don't want to see muddy textures like that.
I also wish the minimap was a bit smaller as it takes up a lot of my 4:3 screen. It'd be really nice if I could play the game on the primary monitor and have the entire map displayed on my secondary monitor.
It would also be nice to be able to build bridges and stuff onto the lakes... especially hydro lines and pipes.
None of my complaints are major, but they are worth mentioning. Aside from that, the game is perfect.

This game is basically 'grey goo simulator', in a way. You start off on a planet. You have exactly one objective; Take your environment, and every last bit of mineral or liquid wealth in it, and use it to get more mineral wealth, occasionally setting a bit off to the side so you can reach endgame once you finally get tired of building more factories to build more factories to build more factories.
Now, I don't really like writing long winded reviews, but bear with me on this one; There are so very, very many facets to this game, that I can't really describe them all in one review. So let's go with the first really complicated thing you'll have to do.
Say you finally climb out of using your hands to punch rocks into usable chunks, and now have a cute little setup with a few furnaces and mining drills. Everything's happy and fun and you feel accomplished for a while. Then you realize, 'hey, shuffling all these raw resources to and fro is getting kinda tedious.' So you decide to start feeding what the drills make into the furnaces automatically. Easy enough, right? Few conveyor belts here and there, yay, automation. Then you realize a little later, 'hey, making all these complicated new things takes really, really long on my own. Maybe I'll start automating production of some of them...' And so, the vicious cycle of automation begins yet again; A few more conveyor belts than last time, with some optimization for speed of processing here and there, and hey, an hour later, it's finally done! You're finally making little bottles of stuff with no input from you! Then you realize, 'Hey, I think --' And yet again, the vicious cycle of automation rears it's head, and a few hours later, (if you're like me anyways) you end up with a big jumbled mess of conveyor belts taking who only knows what to who only knows where to make I don't even know anymore.
And you. Feel. Victorious. And also kinda hungry and thirsty and - holy moly it's been twelve hours maybe one more hour before i get up and go get dinner...
So yeah, I think I summed up the very basic gameplay pretty well for you. This game is fun. It's addictive. And it is most definitely worth every penny, go buy it now. And remember to feed and water yourself regularly inbetween automation binges.

If you are a fan of Bastion, I'd definitely pick up this game. First thing, I'd like to say that I was skeptical, to say the least, about the "turn" system implemented in this game. Upon playing Transistor I was pleasantly surprised. Don't let the idea of the turn fool you, this is a fast paced game and you will find yourself implementing "turn" with joy time and time again, I know I did. I think SuperGiant games is starting to become a studio I'll follow. While feeling INCREDIBLY similar to Bastion (you can definitely tell this was done by the same studio: the narrator is the same voice actor, the music is scored by the same person, the challenges share similar ideas to those implemented, and the main character stay [mostly] silent), the game establishes it's own differences, even if rather minor, in the art of the game. SuperGiant has a way of using overall theme in their games so far, and it shines here:
The narrator is as charismatic as ever, the visuals are abosutley stunning and keep the painterly feeling that was present in bastion, and the soundtrack is absolutely breathtaking.
If the theme of bastion was the Wild West, the theme of this is definitely Jazz Noir with a twist of dystopian future. The game doesn't exactly hold your hand either. The story isn't exactly minimalist, yet while you are being fed information on the city, enemies, or events, it never feels spoon fed.
I could go on and on about this game, but really I don't want to spoil to much. I say if you are reading these reviews, take the dive. You'll have tons of fun tinkering over your abilities and testing them out on the Process.

This game is amazing! As expected from Supergiant Games, the soundtrack and art direction are both stellar. There are two different choices for combat: real-time combat and turn based combat. In the turn based combat you can plan out your moves and execute them at the end of the planning turn. Your moves are called functions and can be implemented as an active, upgrade, or passive. The number of combinations surpasses even Bastion which leads to lots of flexibility to match all kinds of play styles. The story and cutscenes are also great.
The game is a little short, it took me about 6 hours to beat. The whole experience was worth it though. You can also recurse through the story after you beat the game and keep all of your old functions. To recurse through the story and get all of the acheivements it took me an additional 12 hours (I liked wasting time testing out function combinations).
If you liked Bastion, you will love Transistor. I can't recommend this game enough. Amazing.

Really fun game. I've played it lots both on console and PC. The campaign is the second-best campaign in CoD, CoD 4 being the first imo. You can also play the second game mode which you can play in co-op and get three stars in all missions and stuff, I did it on the Xbox and it's really fun to play with a friend.
Multiplayer is pretty good. It's not as dedication-rewarding as the newer games, prestiging resets everything litteraly so it's not very fun to prestige. The guns are really fun though. Lots of traditional weapons such as UZI and M4A1, good off-hands (shotguns are secondaries, overpowered but fun). All the guns are fun in their own way if you know how to use them. Attachments are as usual. Red dot sights, silencers, noobtubes (which are horribly overpowered in this game and has never been fixed, probably because IW doens't care about gaming experience), nothing new. You can unlock different versions of attachments by using that attachment which is pretty cool. Using the Red Dot Sight unlocks Holographic Sight, using underbarrel grenade launcher unlocks underbarrel shotgun, stuff like that. Emblems and titles are really cool and well-made imo. Killstreaks is nothing new. Care package, chopper support, airstrikes, controlling AC130s weapons and being a chopper gunner, stuff like that. They're cool and fun to get but not original.
Maps are really cool. A russian snow map, a woodland map with a really cool cabin on a hill, tight urban combat in an afghanistan-like map, love the maps in this game. They're the best maps in any CoD game imho. You can also buy a map pack that gives you the maps from CoD 4 (not sure if all of them) which is really cool
If you're a CoD fan then this game is nice to play sometimes when you want a good CoD game to not dedicate yourself to or take seriously. Of course, there will be hackers, as in all IW CoD games.

Transistor left me spechless. At the time it came out I didn't even had a chance to put my hands on Supergiant Games Bastion, so I had to play it first, so I could feel the style of its developer. And now that I played both I can say that the game feel was surely saved (if not enhanced). The graphics are just fascinating. Bastion also has great visuals, but the setting here is different and comparing these two is kind of stupid. Can say the same about the music. As a Kid, you had to put up a new home for yourself and the others, you were the only hope, the person that felt kind of sad and scared of the burden, but on the other hand brave and ready for the unexpected. And so is the music. Transistor puts you in a sci-fi city, and the situation Red is in is really tough - her voice is stolen, the man that is close to her heart is stabbed with a somewhat electronic sword, and there is a group of people that are chasing her. Most songs have that post-rock feel to them, which made me melancholic and sad, and relaxed at the same time. But there is one thing I'm sure about - the soundtrack to Transistor is something else.
Since it's hard to not to compare it to Bastion, I need to say one thing - it really is a great enchanting game, but Bastion is a bit better, imo. There are not much games that give you goosebumps, but both of the games did that to me. !!Bastion Spoilers!! The part where you're carrying Zulf back to the Bastion, accompanied by the Setting Sale, Coming Home song was much more impressive than the Transistor ending. Maybe the culmination part of Transistor should have the ending song being played during it, but anyway, that's just my opinion. Transistor is still a great game, and it's definitely 10/10. I recommend it to everyone who played Bastion, and to everyone who likes the game's plot to make you slightly sad, but satisfied.

Awesome stealth / survival horror game! If you are fan of the films, it's a must play, one of the best Alien games out there (still prefer Aliens vs Predator 2 though).
In this game, you are basically defenseless, you can't kill the alien, only scare it away for a few seconds. And it always comes back. Always. That's why this game is terrifying. Never a moment, when you feel safe, that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ can pop up any second, and you have to really mind your step, and hide, hide and hide. Run, and you are dead. So the tension is great, but sometimes it gets more frustrating, than challenging. You can craft items for survival, which is great, but in the later missions I had so many of them, that I didn't need any materials at all, so just left them there (I played on Hard).
The graphics is great, especially the lighting and the environment effects. The sound design is fantastic, it's the main reason why this game is so tenseful.
For the negative part, I have to mention the glitches (all kinds of, with the flashlight not working to graphical glitches), and the backtracking (if you want to collect all the collectibles): the maps are huge, and can be confusing, where you were, and either you have perfect memory, or you have to write it down that "oh, in map XY there was a locked door, gonna have to check it out 5 missions later". Relating to the backtracking: there are some missions, that REALLY needed more save points, because if you die (you will), you have to start from the last save point, which is 5 minutes of walk from there (I'm looking at you, Mission 16). Irritating.

With this, nothing can dristract you from enjoying the fear. Prepare to die. A lot.

Loved the second game on the Xbox 360, but it was missing fluidity and was a little clunky in my opinion. Those problems are solved in just cause 3. The game is very fluid and is easy to transition between hook/parachute/wing suit and the clunkyness is totally gone. As a fan of the second game, this one is looking to be far superior. I would only advise having a decent PC because it does use a lot of system resources (and looks great too!). I can run mine pretty well at low - medium settings, but similar to Arkham Knight, this game still looks awesome even on its lowest settings. Overall, I would recommend if you like Just Cause 2, explosions, destruction, great graphics, or amazing third person combat and movement. Not a bad deal on sale either - $12 for the game and $6 for the season pass (I wouldn't pay more than $8 for the seaon pass because the content to dollar ratio is very minimal). RIP my hard drive tho.

Now, I would recommend this game if I had the chance to play it. From the screenshots I saw during gameplay, it looked nice, the map is huge, and there is possibly lots of stuff to keep you busy.
Conclusion, don't buy if you have 8GBs of RAM. They are not nearly enough for what the game actually uses. Don't be fooled by the specifications tab at the bottom of the store page, please.
